en: K.A. Subramania Iyer,
*Vākyapadīya*, 1963.
Now begins the section on the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
(1) Since "the direction is the means of accomplishment" was mentioned immediately after [the discussion of] direction, he speaks in order to define that means of accomplishment:
They know that the capacity for the accomplishment of actions— whether those actions are inherent in its own substratum or likewise in another substratum— is the means (sādhana).

(2) Regarding the accomplishment of an action, the capacity of a substance is the *sādhana* (means of accomplishment); for the author of the Bhāṣya and others understand it thus: "that by which an action is accomplished is called *sādhana*. Accordingly, [the rule] states: "The agent (*kartṛ*) is the *sādhana*" (Pāṇini 1.4.54).

Thus it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "In this context, it is *śakti* (power) itself that is expressed by the word 'quality' (*guṇa*), because it is dependent upon its substratum and because it differentiates its own locus from others.
However, regarding the objection concerning the difference between the two *bhāva*s (actions/states) expressed by *kṛt*-suffixes and verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*):"
The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) states: "A substance (*dravya*) attains the status of a means (*sādhanabhāva*) toward the accomplishment of an action" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.4.67).
Since this [statement] explicitly excludes the status of a substance as a means in other contexts, [the status of being a means] is based on the mediation of a capacity (*śakti*).

It must be understood as follows: for a substance (*dravya*) is capable of being a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), whereas a power (*śakti*) cannot exist without a substratum. [As stated in Pāṇini's Sūtra:
"The *liṭ* [perfect tense] is used for what is past and not witnessed by the speaker" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.115).
In this case as well:
"If the collection of qualities (*guṇasamudāya*) is the means of proof (*sādhana*), then the means of proof is also accessible through inference.
But if the means of proof is something other than the qualities, then the possibility of both perceptibility and imperceptibility arises."

The commentary (*bhāṣya*) on [Pāṇini’s rule] *ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.27), which states "the [suffix] *gh* [is applied]," should also be interpreted in this very way: because capacity (*śakti*) is eternally imperceptible, it is improper to qualify it as being non-deviant (*avyabhicāra*), just as one qualifies an action (*kriyā*).
By the force of the qualification "being out of sight" (*parokṣatā*), a substance (*dravya*) permeated by capacity (*śakti*) is presented as the means (*sādhana*).
Likewise [in the rule] *upasargāc chandasi dhātvarthe* (Pāṇini 5.1.118).
Regarding this,
[it is stated]: "When this [suffix] occurs in the sense of an instrument (*sādhana*), it shall be joined with [the appropriate] gender and number" (Pāṇini 3.4.69).

Thus, the Bhāṣya statement "in a substance qualified by the power of accomplishment" (sādhanaśaktiviśiṣṭe dravye) is to be explained as follows: for if only "in a verbal root" (dhātau) were stated, since it is possible for [the term] to apply to the word-form itself, the comprehension of the action would already be established; therefore, by the inclusion of the word "meaning" (artha), it is understood that the meaning is produced by the verbal root, which serves the purpose of understanding the compound.

Substance is dependent [upon its modes]. For the word *artha* (object/entity) refers to the modification (*paryāya*) of the real thing (*vastu*). Since substance has an established nature by virtue of its own form, it cannot be produced by an action; rather, it is produced only through the forms of the factors of action (*kāraka*), such as the object (*karman*) and so forth. For it is action that brings about the factors of action.

Because the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding that [action] depends upon it, it is stated thus because the substance (*dravya*), by means of its nature as a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), is the instrument for the action. However, the interpretation of the *Bhāṣya* that "the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the purpose (*prayojana*) of this" is incorrect; for in this way, the action itself would be the power (*śakti*) in its state of being that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
If it were merely the purpose (*prayojana*), the substance (*dravya*) would not be conveyed. As for the statement:
"The substance is indeed the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and there can be no excellence (*prakarsa*) or deficiency (*apakarṣa*) of a substance" (Pāṇini, Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.3.55).

Thus, in the Bhāṣya on the explanation of the excellence (*prakarṣa*) of non-substances (*adravya*), the statement that a substance (*dravya*) is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) should be understood as being made without intending to express a distinction between the power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*). For instance, when an affix denoting excellence follows a verbal form (*tiṅanta*) that expresses the means of accomplishing an action, it refers to the power (*śakti*).

Since action—which is inferred from its effect as being momentary—is understood through its effect alone, and since the excellence [of action] is thus established by means of that very effect, one might raise the following objection: "If the suffix intended to express the excellence of action is included [in this way], and since power (śakti) has substance (dravya) as its substratum, why is there not also an excellence expressed by way of the substance which serves as the cause, just as there is by way of the effect? Anticipating this doubt regarding substance...
This was stated in order to express the absence of that [inherence]; thus, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is disregarded.

In that regard, action inheres in the agent and the object; therefore, their status as *kārakas* (factors of action) consists in the accomplishment of an action that inheres in their own substratum. However, for instruments and the other [kārakas], it is with respect to an action inhering in another substratum.
The state of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*). For action does not inherently reside (*samavaiti*) in instruments and the like.

The plural number in the word "of actions" (*kriyāṇām*) is used with reference to the distinction between individual instances. Alternatively, all [entities] possess the status of being a means with respect to their own inherent action, whether that action is a primary action or a subordinate action (*guṇakriyā*). For in the case of a subordinate action, they are indeed agents (*kartāraḥ*).

All [of these] are [required], because that which is incapable of producing an effect cannot logically function as a means (*sādhana*). For this very reason, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and "means" (*kāraka*), and so forth, is established. In this way, the use of the plural number in the phrase "of actions" (*kriyāṇām*) is well-justified. However, the primary action resides in the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*).
The [action] of the instruments and so forth resides in another substratum. (1)
But how is it understood that power (*śakti*) is the means of accomplishment and not the substance (*dravya*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Of the universe, which is a collection of mere powers and possesses manifold properties..."
Because [the object] exists at all times and in every way, something or other is intended to be expressed in some particular instance. (2)

(3) Entities such as jars are denoted by the word "universe" (*viśva*). They consist of a collection of powers (*śakti*) that accomplish various functions, such as the fetching of water. For this very reason, those powers are called "measures" (*mātrā*) or "parts" (*bhāga*); thus, jars and the like are merely a collection of powers. And these...

Powers (*śakti*) are of many kinds. Some arise solely from their own causes and perish even as their substratum perishes, such as the powers of illumination belonging to consciousness, lamps, and so forth. Others are produced by human effort and cease while their substratum remains, such as...

The powers such as strength (*bala*) and so forth; for these arise through the practice of physical exercise and the consumption of aphrodisiac substances (*vṛṣya*). Others, however, are maintained by human effort even while their substratum exists, such as the lethal power of poison or the sprout-producing power of a seed. Others...

They are transformed by that which possesses an excellence of power, just as a yogi effects a transformation of the form of all entities. Some are manifested through the passage of time, such as the capacity of merit, demerit, and so forth, to yield their fruit; in this way, many varieties are to be inferred.

Thus, if the collection of capacities (*śakti-samudāya*) possesses multiple natures, then when there is a diverse effect, the occurrence of specific means of accomplishment (*sādhana-bhāva*) is established according to the desire to express the distinction [of those capacities] as they correspond to their respective powers. However, if the substance (*dravya*) itself were the means of accomplishment, because it is of a single form, there would be no diversity of effects; this is the meaning. As it has been stated in the Bhāṣya:

"The collection of qualities (*guṇasamudāya*) is the means (*sādhana*)," according to Pāṇini 1.4.115. The term "collection" is used because the primary action cannot be accomplished by each individual power alone;
however, with respect to the subordinate actions (*guṇakriyā*), each power possesses the status of being a means. And of that...

The status of being an object (*karman*) and so forth arises from the diversity [of functions] in relation to the principal action (*pradhānakriyā*). Alternatively, even though each [power] is a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) individually, there is a mention of them as a collective; this is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*avyāpti*), since the differentiation of effects for a single entity is established through the differentiation of those powers when they function as the means of accomplishment. Thus, even for an entity that possesses multiple powers...

Even though [the substance] always remains in that same state, it is intended that a certain power manifests in a certain [substance]; thus, the status of being an object (*karman*), an instrument (*karaṇa*), and so forth— such as "see the jar," "bring water with the jar," or "place the water in the jar"— is established by necessity, and therefore there is no contingency of confusion among the factors of action (*kāraka*).
However, because a substance possesses a single nature, it is not logically possible for it to simultaneously function as the object, the instrument, and so forth;
this underlying reasoning should be understood here regarding the fact that it is the *śakti* (capacity) that serves as the means of accomplishment. || 2 ||

But surely, it is appropriate that those things which possess capacities should be intended [to be expressed] by necessity; however, where they are seen not to exist, how can there be an intention to express them? For example: "he imparts a capacity," "he accomplishes by means of a capacity," "he exerts himself toward a capacity," or "he departs from a capacity. For indeed, [there is no capacity] of a capacity...

The conjunction with another power [is impossible], because it would lead to an infinite regress. Likewise, it brings about the destruction of wealth; since it is described as being "joined with the absence of wealth," what power can there be in an entity that is non-existent? In the cases "he cooks in a pot" and "he cooks with a pot," the pot provides assistance through the functions of containing and supporting.

Anticipating the objection as to how [the distinction between] instrument and locus can exist [if they are not distinct from the object], he says: "The conventional usage of means (sādhana) is based on states of the intellect;
whether existing or non-existing, the distinction among the forms of objects is constructed by the intellect. (3)

(4) The linguistic usage of the factors of action (*kāraka*), such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, has as its basis those specific states of the cognition whose form is the intention to speak (*vivakṣārūpā buddhiḥ*), which are caused by words and are restricted to particular words.
For instance, when an object has been determined, a word is employed; and consequently, the application of the word occurs exactly according to that determination.

And even without depending on an external object, conceptualization (nirūpaṇa) independently constructs various specific objects. In that case, since power— which functions as a substance— is conceptually determined by the intellect through its own autonomy, it is contradictory for it to be associated with another power when it is denoted by a word.

For it is not the case that its connection with that [non-existence] occurs only while it is in the state of potentiality— which would lead to an infinite regress— but rather, even non-existence, when its form is determined by cognition,
becomes a substance (*dravyāyamāṇa*) in the state of being a substance and is thus denotable by a word. In this way, because its potsherds are exceedingly thin, the cooking-pot [is so called].

Since the agent's application [of the action] is not required for the act of cooking (*pāka*), it is intended to be expressed independently as the *kartṛ* (agent). However, when there is an intention to express that very [action] as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) without regard for the assistance provided by fuel (*indhana*), it is the *karaṇa* (instrument); but when there is an intention to express the actual substratum (*ādhāra*), it is the *adhikaraṇa* (locus). Thus, everything is logically consistent. For this very reason:
Expressions such as "the self kills itself by means of the self" and "the abiding of the self within its own self" are also well-established in their excellence. And this will be stated later:
"That which is one is divided by the intellect, and that which is divided attains oneness."

And so forth. Since linguistic convention is established through the determination of non-difference between the perceived object and its conceptual representation, the connection [of the word] must here be justified as being directed toward the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) regarding the external object, and not with respect to itself nor another; for it is only with respect to itself that [the word functions].

"Another [entity] does not abide," and so forth; for example, "the body of a stone-son. And thus, even when a word has been extracted from a sentence, if it is refined [grammatically], then even though another word has not been employed at the outset, it is indeed possible that the intended specific meaning is not determined due to the similarity of form.

The grammatical exposition [of words] extends as far as the word-base (pada), provided that a general relation is required; otherwise, how could the specific form of an object, determined by the intellect and dependent upon its connection with action and so forth, be defined?
For there exists no such thing as a "general object" whose nature is independent of its relata, as is accepted [by us].

The grammatical exposition has its limit at the word itself, because in the treatise [of Pāṇini], rules such as "suffixes [are applied] when there is a connection with a verbal root" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.1) have been rejected; and where there is a total lack of consistency [between the rule and the usage].

In cases such as "He cooks rice in a pot on wood," that [sentence] is not even a sentence at all; therefore, how could there be any occasion for the grammatical analysis of words extracted from a sentence? For this very reason, [the rule] is intended to prevent the disjunction found in expressions such as "My eyes are beautiful."

The scripture is indeed meaningful. For even a universal (sāmānya), being of the nature of a word-meaning, is praised only when it is capable of connection with other meanings; it is not [praised] when it is incoherent, such as "a hundred elephants are on the tip of a finger. And having established this regarding the Vedic language (chandas):

In passages such as "Those who carve the *caṣāla* for the horse-sacrifice post," the transposition [of word order] serves a purposeful function in order to dispel any suspicion of grammatical incorrectness (*asādhutva*).
This is because there exists a Vedic sentence with a fixed sequence of words; therefore, the extraction (*apoddhāra*) of individual words must be performed exactly in that manner.

Because it is logical. In common worldly usage, however, there is no such thing as an unstable sentence with a fixed sequence that is incoherent; therefore, there is no occasion for extraction (*apoddhāra*) from it. Consequently, even when words are extracted from the sentence for the purpose of grammatical instruction, the analysis based on words as its limit remains entirely faultless. And therein—

Since an object qualified by all its attributes is partless, when it is analytically extracted, the mere universal has a body that is purely a mental construction. However, at the very outset, when there is a requirement for specific details, the grammatical analysis is stated as being delimited by the sentence; this is not because of the infinity of sentences.

Direct grammatical exposition is appropriate; for it is only through the conceptual analysis of stems, suffixes, and so forth that the instruction of the *pada* itself becomes possible. Since such a *pada* cannot exist in isolation, when it occurs within a sentence and requires reference to a general correlate, it is delimited by the preceding *pada*.

However, when there is a requirement for a specific related element supplied by the sentence, the grammatical derivation is based on the sentence; this is the distinction between these two views. || 3 ||
In the Buddhist practice of proof, he states that which accords with the acceptance of the Commentator:
"When a speaker, having unified the Pañcālas with the Kurus by means of the intellect, divides them again, then disappearance (apāya) is perceived. (4)
Regarding the statement "the Pañcālas are more handsome than the Kurus," the sūtra *pañcamī vibhakta* (Pāṇini 2.3.42), which prescribes the ablative case,
has been rejected in the Bhāṣya because the departure (*apāya*) is merely conceptual (*bauddha*).

Since the status of the ablative (*apādāna*) is already established by the fact of "arising from" (*sambhavāt*), it is as follows: through the quality of shared beauty, one brings about a conceptual unity and a collective state between the Pañcālas and the Kurus; then, by virtue of their superior beauty, the Pañcālas are distinguished from the Kurus.
They are performed; thus, there is a separation preceded by a conjunction, which is *apāya*. As it is stated in the Bhāṣya:
"He who has attained equality with them uses [the word] in this way" (G.eṇa.od gh. 1.4.24).
By "them," [it means] with those Kurus, there is a similarity of the Pañcālas.

The meaning is: "he who first knew [them] by means of his excellence through the power of deliberation. By this, the Commentator states that the proximity of the lands of the Kurus and Pañcālas is due to their being established within a single cognition. Following that, however, there is the division of the finite from the infinite.

The word *pañcamī* (the fifth case) was not mentioned by the author of the Bhāṣya because it already possesses the technical designation of *apādāna*. Even for one who maintains that the sūtra must be commenced [separately], these [words] must be understood as forming a collective whole through the intellect alone, on account of their being the basis for selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) due to their shared quality; otherwise, [it would be impossible].

Since the distinction [of the members] is already obtained from the very context of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*), the mention of "divided" (*vibhakta*) brings about the understanding of an absolute division; thus, a real state of being a composite whole is not tenable.
In this way, it is understood from this that the status of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) is conceptual (*bauddha*). This is in the section on *kāraka*.

And because of the inclusion of the term *tama* (in Pāṇini’s rule), excellence (*prakarṣa*) is not intended to be expressed; thus, even when the departure is figurative (*gauṇa*), the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) applies here.
He states another corroborating passage from the Bhāṣya:
"And [the agent] regards Kaṃsa and others, whose forms are presented by words and which have become objects of cognition, as if they were perceptible, as being the means [of the action]. (5)
Regarding the rule *hetumati ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.26),
[the Vārttika] states: *ākhyānāt kṛtastadācaṣṭe...* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 3.1.26).
This and other such supplementary rules (*aupasaṃkhyāna*) have been rejected by the statement:
"Or rather, [the rule] need not be stated, because it is accomplished by the general principle; for [the cause] is indeed not distinguished" (Pāṇini 3.1.26, with the *Jātisamuddeśa* commentary).
For in the case of paintings, statues, and the like, there exists the form of a representation (*pratikṛti*).

Through the determination of the relationship between the instigator and the instigated, the forms "he causes Kaṃsa to be killed" and "he causes Bali to be bound" are established. Likewise, in the drama which is an imitation of what has been done, the actors' attainment of that form occurs through similarity in their imitation of Kaṃsa and Vāsudeva. In that regard:

The question was raised: "How [is it] in the case of the *granthikas*? (Pāṇini, Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.26). In that context, the *granthikas*—who are storytellers (*kathakāḥ*)—narrate the slaughter of Kaṃsa precisely by means of the verbal form (*vṛtta-rūpeṇa*). And since there is an absence of a representational form (*pratikṛti-rūpa*) therein, how...?
The objection is that there is a relationship of the instigator and the instigated (*prayojya-prayojakatva*). To this, the following resolution has been stated:
"For even they, by explaining the growths of those [entities] from their production until their destruction, manifest the existing things as objects of cognition" (Gautama Sūtra 3.1.26).

Thus, because Kaṃsa and others have long since passed away and are non-existent externally, [words] manifest them as existing—that is, they illuminate them as present—by means of being objects of the intellect.
For the referent of a word is indeed a form appearing in the intellect, not a real object. And so says the author of the *Kathā*:

Because the listener produces a cognition in the form of Kaṃsa and so forth, the usage "the wise one causes the intellect-Kaṃsa to be slain by the intellect-Vāsudeva" is justified through the superimposition of agency (*prayojakatva*). For it is thus:
from the specific forms produced by the power of the words uttered by the speaker...

The author of the Bhāṣya considers Kaṃsa and others—who have entered the range of the hearer’s intellect and possess an active form—to be instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth by virtue of being the means (*sādhana*) for the action; thus, it is established that the conventional usage of "means" is based on their state within the intellect. And this applies even to a figurative agent (*prayojaka*) within the section concerning grammatical factors (*kāraka*).

Because the designation "cause" (*hetu*) does not apply here due to the absence of protraction (*prākarṣa*), the *ṇic* affix used here in the Sūtra refers to its operation. "Pratyakṣam" is an avyayībhāva compound; it is an adverbial modifier of the act of reflecting (*manana*). The meaning is that one discerns [the object] with extreme clarity by means of cognition conditioned by the sense faculties. And this is as stated in the passage: "expounding the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*)."

This is an explanation of the intended meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*). For when an object possesses an excellence of power, a clear cognition arises by virtue of one's reverence toward it. And when the cognition is clear, the form appearing within it is determined to be of an external nature. (5)
Thus, since the practical application of means is established by means of the intellect, he concludes that even for a single entity, a plurality of powers is intelligible as a conceptual construct:
"And speakers, having superimposed the form of the activity of the intellect [upon the object]..."
A conceptual construction is made regarding the various capacities of objects.

(7) The activity (*pravṛtti*) of cognition is its operation characterized by discernment (*pariccheda*). Its form (*rūpa*) is its aspect (*ākāra*), which appears as the object. Having superimposed that [aspect] upon external objects, speakers postulate a multiplicity of powers (*śakti-nānātva*) in those [objects]. This is the meaning.

Because of the determination of non-difference between the perceived object and its mental construction, and because of the conceit that the diverse differentiation of powers belongs to the external world alone, they imagine a manifold causal efficiency therein.
This is due to their failure to understand that the appearance in the intellect is self-established, and thus they [impute] a diversity of action to it.
Furthermore, by conforming to the expectations of the speaker, it is understood that a thing possesses multiple capacities;

thus, the word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding external objects. Since there is no sublation of the connection between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka-saṃsarga*), and because there is correspondence, speakers recognize the validity of the sentence. [This is] for the Buddhists (*saugata*).

Because the distinctions of the reflection of conceptual construction are not apprehended, there is no engagement with external objects. However, the validity of words pertains only to the speaker’s intention (*vaktrābhiprāya*), since there is a suspicion of deviation regarding external things;
their status as residing solely in the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛttimātra*) applies to the external world. But for the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), however—

The difference in philosophical views is that [the cognition] has as its object a thing excluded [from others], and its validity lies precisely therein because of such determinative conceptualization (*adhyavasāya*). Furthermore, there is no confusion [of powers] because they are regulated by their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
And the powers that provide assistance are distinct for each limiting adjunct.

Because the object is a coagulated body, it is inexpressible as being either identical to or different from [its parts]; thus, there is no contingency of [the object] lacking dependence on adjuncts, assistance, or constituent parts. || 6 ||
And since the status of being a means of accomplishment exists based on the states of cognition, he says that this [other point] is also established:
"When the individual is the referent, for the action such as sound which is being produced..."
Likewise, its status as a means of accomplishment is established as being conceptually constructed by the form of the intellect.

(8) It has been stated that when an object is understood as belonging to a genus (*jāti*), one determines its future state through its non-difference from other members of that genus; then, by means of the application of suitable instruments, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅgatā*) to the accomplishment of the action is established by way of the genus, whereas its status as the object (*karman*) being brought into existence (*nirvartyamānatā*) is logically established by way of the individual (*vyakti*).

"Even in that case where an action (*karman*) is being produced (*nirvartyamāna*), the genus (*jāti*) is the means (*sādhana*). However, when the individual (*vyakti*) is what is conveyed by the word— as in "he produces sound" or "he effects conjunction"—
it is the sound or the like, which is being produced and is thus *nirvartya*, [that serves as the object].

Even in the case of future karma, because it resembles its present manifestation, although there is no communication of a universal (jāti), one disregards the distinction [between the two]; having delineated the form of the cognition, one employs the appropriate means; and because the mental [form] itself is determined as having an external nature, it is treated as if it were external.
The meaning is that while being produced by means of a form [is appropriate for other things], its status as a means of proof (sādhana) is logical only for a Buddhist.
By the phrase "of that which is being produced" (janyamānasya), there is an exclusion of the "modified" (vikārya) and the "attained" (prāpya).

For that which is to be transformed (*vikārya*) exists already in the form of its material cause (*prakṛti*). Regarding that which is to be attained (*prāpya*), he says that it is not superimposed by the intellect to any great extent, since it is [already] present by itself:
"Independence and dependence, as well as the nature of sequence, have been shown."
In phenomena that are devoid of activity, there is a conceptual construction based on imagination.

(9) Since the causal relationship has been refuted by means of the distinction between the positions of existence and non-existence, all entities are devoid of action and empty of effort. In that regard, "agency" (*kārakatva*)—
characterized by independence, dependence, and so forth— is the state of being an agent, instrument, and so on, within the context of action.

And succession, which is essentially the form of action, is a reality constructed by the conceptualizing intellect through the power of beginningless impressions from false habitual practice, according to how it appears; for although the universe is in reality devoid of before and after,
it manifests here as having before and after through [the Lord's] sovereignty and other powers.

The meaning is that this appearance of "mine" regarding objects is the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*). For in the system of non-duality (*advaita*), everything is sublated because it is unreal; therefore, verbal usage constructed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) must be accepted as established according to common experience, without being subjected to critical analysis.

"The establishment of the category of the means (*sādhana*) is like that of the categories of direction and so forth; it has been 'shown' by the commentators and others who follow the Advaita system"—this means that [the category of] the verb (*ākhyāta*) is [postulated] for the sake of establishing such usages as "the bank wishes to fall" (*kūlaṃ pipatiṣati*). || 8 ||
Thus, the proof has first been characterized by demonstrating that power is distinct from the substance.

He now speaks also by way of demonstrating that power is non-distinct: "For all those who maintain the doctrine of relation (*saṃsargavādins*), both powers and the possessors of power [are non-distinct]."
In those cases where words do not denote their own forms, the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) is determined [by the object].

(9) Those who, despite the difference between property (*dharma*) and the possessor of property (*dharmin*), claim they are as if non-different due to the force of inherence (*samavāya*) are the Vaiśeṣikas, the proponents of relation (*saṃsargavādinaḥ*). And they [assert] the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) and the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) of entities.

They maintain that power (*śakti*) is the capacity to produce its own effect; the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are the power, and the cause is the possessor of power (*śaktimat*). Likewise, for the auxiliaries as well, the cause is power, and their form as auxiliaries exists in relation to their own effect. Thus, all entities whatsoever consist of power and the possessor of power; there is no other [power] whatsoever that is beyond the reach of the senses.

Power exists as something distinct from the six categories of existence. Even so, the status of entities— that is, things— as being instrumental causes is not conveyed by words such as "ablative" (apādāna) and the like, but rather by case-endings alone.

And thus, the application of terms such as *apādāna* (ablative) and so forth occurs by virtue of mere fitness (*yogyatā*) for communication. In cases such as "he sees the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ paśyati*), that which is communicated by the accusative and other case-endings—namely, largeness and so forth, as restricted to a substratum—is the capacity (*śakti*) that constitutes the instrument (*sādhana*). However, largeness and so forth, when not delimited by a substratum [are not so].

That which is denoted by words such as "karma" (object) and so forth accomplishes nothing at all; it is apprehended solely through its case-ending (*vibhakti*), because that ending arises from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which denotes the substratum (*ādhāra*). Since the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) comes into contact [with the action] only when there is a co-inherence with the substratum, it exists in the state of being an auxiliary (*upakāra*).

Potency (*śaktitva*) exists in the state of being assisted, whereas the possession of potency (*śaktimatva*) is observed through valid means of cognition; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. For this very reason, since no further potency can be joined to the state of potency, there is also no infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Regarding non-existence (*abhāva*) in this philosophical system:
And because that which is spat out must be brought into being as something not yet an actual entity, its connection with power is not contradictory. || 9 ||
Regarding that, he provides an illustration to show what entity has what power and where:
"In the case of a jar being the object of seeing, largeness and so forth are the means;
in the case of color being the object of seeing, color-ness and so forth are the means. (10)

(11) In the expression "he sees the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ paśyati*), the substance "jar," which has become the object (*karman*) of the action of seeing, possesses as its inherent capacities (*śakti*) the qualities of magnitude (*mahattva*) and being composed of multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*); these constitute the means (*sādhana*) and the objective factor (*karmakāraka*).
Thus, indeed, says the Sūtra of Kaṇāda: [text follows].
"Perception [of a substance] occurs because it is large, possesses multiple constituent substances, and possesses color" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.6).

This is its meaning: that which has multiple substances as its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is "that which possesses multiple substances," such as a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth. That which is produced from such [a cause] is "that which possesses multiple substances."
The state of being that [is] reality (*tattva*). Therefore, perception occurs in a large substance due to that cause.

By means of that *bahuvrīhi* compound and the possessive suffix *matup*, two possessive meanings are expressed. Therein, by one [of them], the atom (*paramāṇu*) is excluded; for although it possesses color (*rūpa*), it is not manifold.

It is not perceived because of the absence of a constituent substance; however, the distinction from dyads and so forth is made by means of another possessive suffix. For this very reason, another sūtra was stated:
"There is no perception of an atom because it is not a composite substance."

Thus [it is said]. Here, the mention of "atoms" (paramāṇu) is intended as an illustration for that which is not being perceived. Furthermore, since the state of possessing multiple substances is the cause of perception when a large object is being perceived, it follows that the production of largeness in a triad (tryaṇuka) results from the multiplicity of its causes, their largeness, and their accumulation.
Because it is composed of three dyads (dvyaṇukas), even though it possesses multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*), it lacks that [visibility].

For this [quality] is enjoined as a predicate in reference to what is already perceived as large; thus, there is no consequence of invisibility for the invisible ocular ray (*nāyana-raśmi*). Indeed, largeness (*mahattva*) is not the cause of perception here either.

It is thus prescribed. For, according to the maxim that "the application of a single form has already been carried out," the commencement would have been made with the ablative case alone for the sake of distinction. Furthermore, because "largeness" (*mahattva*) is never absent from that which possesses multiple substances, the term "in a large [object]" (*mahati*) is not an indication of a logical reason (*hetu*), but rather merely a characterization of the object-domain (*viṣayopalakṣaṇa*). [The word] "from form" (*rūpāt*).
And this is the second reason for its invisibility: because a great mass of air, being formless and composed of many substances, is not perceived. As it is stated in the Sūtra:
"And because of the absence of the manifestation of color-form (*rūpa-saṃskāra*), there is no perception of air" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.7).

Thus, since it is the possession of multiple substances (*anekadravyatva*) and color (*rūpa*) that is the cause of visibility, and not even magnitude (*mahattva*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) has been demonstrated for these two alone. Furthermore, although magnitude is not a direct cause, because visibility has it as its object, it is useful through a mediated succession; therefore, "magnitude and so forth are the means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*).
Thus [there is] the plural number. Alternatively, the plural is used because the word "etc. includes the generalities and particularities such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth;
for in this context, the generalities and particularities are the primary basis for the presentation.
Because objects are characterized by those [attributes], their own nature is perceived through the exclusion of other forms.

However, when it is simply said "in the large," there is a deviation in the case of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth; therefore, by using the possessive suffix *-mat* in the phrase "because of having multiple substances" (*anekadravyavattvāt*), the cognition of a composite substance (*avayavidravya*) is manifested. This is expressed by the phrase "because of having multiple substances."

If it were stated again [as a *tatpuruṣa* compound], it would be understood merely as an accumulation of substances (*dravyapracaya*) due to the possibility of that [compound] being a *tatpuruṣa*. In the case of "he sees color" (*rūpaṃ paśyati*), the means (*sādhana*) for the action of seeing color consists of the universal "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) inherent in the color itself, and the inherence (*samavāya*) in a substance composed of multiple substances. And thus says the Sūtra:
"The perception of color [occurs] due to inherence in multiple substances and due to the specific nature of color" (Nyāya-sūtra 4.1.8).

That composite substance which has many constituent parts is "multiple-substance"; [perception occurs] because of inherence in that, that is, because of being inherent therein. The "specificity" of color is its manifestness (*udbhūtatva*). Therefore...

The form of the visual ray is not excluded because it is overwhelmed by the form of external luminous substances; however, others explain that "form" (*rūpa*) is qualified—that is, distinguished from other things such as taste—by means of its own nature, and thus "form-ness" (*rūpatva*) itself is taught as a specific universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*). Furthermore, this is because [the visual ray] lacks the state of being composed of multiple substances.

The invisibility of the atom and of the form residing therein [is established]; the mention in the plural number indicates that factors such as being in a suitable location are also, by implication, means of proof. || 10 ||

In the world, the tastes and other [qualities], being endowed with their own general and particular properties, have fixed perceptions; likewise, those powers are determined by their respective substrata.
(12) One tastes taste, smells odor, touches touch, and hears sound;

thus, the specific universals (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) such as tasteness (*rasatva*) and so forth, being inherent (*samaveta*), serve as the means for the functions of tasting and so forth belonging to the tongue and other sense organs. For it is by means of these respective [universals] that the restricted apprehensions occur in a restricted manner.

They are apprehended solely by the power of their own genus (*svajāti*), and not, like substances, through indefinite apprehension. For a substance is sometimes apprehended through its generality as "a substance," sometimes through a quality as "white," and sometimes through an action as "it moves. But as for taste-ness (*rasatva*) and the rest—
The very substrata of the powers (*śakti*) are their delimiters; thus, in the apprehension of the essential nature [of a power], that power itself is apprehended.

For just as in the perception of taste, its "tasteness" (*rasatva*) is also perceived because it is perceived as qualified by that [taste], so too there is an implication of the substratum (*āśritākṣepa*) upon the perception of tasteness. Similarly, upon the perception of tasteness, there is an implication of its own substrate (*svāśrayākṣepa*).
Likewise, when taste is perceived, its substrate—the substance—should also be understood as being perceived through that [taste].

And as before, inherence (*samavāya*) in a multi-substantial object is also apprehended, because taste and other qualities residing in atoms are not perceived. This should be stated similarly for the remaining [qualities] as well. In this way, they are mutually...
Entities are characterized as powers and possessors of power (*śakti-śaktimant*). Thus, there is no fixed or determinate power;

rather, among associated entities, they exist as powers and possessors of power relative to one another. Consequently, no power is fixed, because of the mutual relationship of the associated entities and because of other factors such as the suitability of the location.
Because the auxiliary causes possess that same nature. || 11 ||
In some cases, the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is the relationship between the sense faculty, the object, the mind, and the agent.
Whatever assists [the action] at whatever time, that is the means of accomplishment in that context. (12)

(13) "Cognition regarding form and so forth is produced from the contact of the self, the sense organ, the mind, and the object"; thus, contact alone is the instrument. However, in the case of pleasure and so forth, it arises from the contact of the self and the internal organ;
therefore, he says "in some cases. Or rather, what is the use of this enumeration? Whatever serves as an auxiliary in a given instance [is the means] there.

Regarding the term "means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*): as is appropriate, all entities consist of both power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*). For instance, it has been stated that number, dimensions, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, and action are visible by reason of their inherence in substances possessing color. This occurs when the parts [contribute] to the production of the whole.

Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is power (*śakti*). However, in the production of a quality, the inherence (*samavāya*) of the whole is the power. Thus, everything that assists another and is dependent conforms to the definition of power. || 12 ||

Furthermore, that state of being dependent on its own effect cannot be expressed by a word that denotes an object whose nature is established through means of proof and the like; rather, he says that its various case-endings and so forth are capable of conveying it accordingly: [The verse: "The state of dependence on its own effect is not expressible by a word that signifies an object whose nature is established by means of proof and the like; however, its respective case-endings and so forth are capable of making it known. [The commentary: And that state of being dependent on its own effect cannot be expressed by a word that denotes an object whose nature is established through means of proof (*sādhana*) and so forth; rather, its respective case-endings (*vibhakti*) and so forth are capable of conveying it. Thus he says: [the verse].
But when it is expressed by its own words, that property is not denoted;
rather, this assistance is understood solely through the case-endings and so forth. (13)

(14) That *dharma* is a state of being subordinate (*śeṣabhāva*) with respect to an action. Substances characterized by their assistance to an action are denoted primarily by such terms as "kāraka," "sādhana," and "apādāna," but not the state of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) defined as the assistance to an action.

From this, it is understood that [the substance] has arisen. For instance, here too, it brings forward the means (*sādhana*) by way of its substantial form (*dravyarūpatayā*). The property (*dharma*) characterized as the assistance to the action (*kriyopakāra*) is conveyed by the accusative case; thus, that which is conveyed by the accusative and other case-endings is that which has already received the assistance of the action.

The term *vastu* (entity) refers to the capacity (*śakti*) expressed by a case ending (*vibhakti*), or sometimes expressed by a secondary suffix (*taddhita*). For example, in *śatyaḥ* or *śatikaḥ* ("bought for a hundred"), the state of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamatva*) in the act of buying is expressed by the suffix. In expressions such as *yatra* ("where") and *tatra* ("there"), the state of being a locus (*ādhārabhāva*) is expressed by the suffix *-tra*.
[Examples include: "milk digests milk" (*payaḥ payo jarayati*) and "he looks at honey" (*madhu nirīkṣate*).

In the expression "he eats curd" (*dadhi samaśnāti*), the capacity [of the word] is understood from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself. However, in the case of "between you and me" (*antarā tvāṃ ca māṃ ca*), the indeclinable (*avyaya*) word *antarā* expresses the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); such is the meaning of the phrase "and so forth.
What, then, is this dharma characterized as assistance that serves as the means of accomplishment? He says:

"The state of being a cause (nimittabhāva) of entities, resorted to for the sake of assistance—whether it be bending (nati), attracting (āvarjana), or the like—is established and accepted as the means of accomplishment (sādhana). (14)

(15) In an action whose nature is yet to be accomplished (*sādhyasvabhāva*), the causal state (*hetubhāva*)—that is, the state of being a motive (*nimittabhāva*)—of entities whose nature is already established (*siddhasvabhāva*) is for the sake of providing assistance. *Nati* means bowing, that is, being oriented toward providing assistance;
"inclination" (*āvarjana*) means the surrendering of one's own self as a subordinate factor (*aṅgabhāvena*).

The term *kriyā* refers to the intent (*tātparya*) of producing an effect. The word *iti* indicates a manner. Even another [type of reason], which is designated by such words as "established" (*siddha*), meaning perceived as already accomplished, or determined by such a property (*dharma*), is called a means of proof (*sādhana*), and not merely by the mere possibility of its existence in the object.

Having thus established, by means of the Mīmāṃsaka and Vaiśeṣika systems, that power (*śakti*) is the means of accomplishment, he abandons the apprehension of [power] as being either distinct from or non-distinct from [the entity] within his own system:
"Is it distinct from them, or is it their very self? Thus [he asks].
Relying upon exclusion (vyatireka), it is conceived as a means of proof (sādhana). || 15 ||

(16) "'Saḥ' refers to the state of being a cause, which is synonymous with *śakti* (potency). Regarding the statement, 'The potencies of all entities fall within the scope of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on their effects,' let it be that for some [schools], these potencies are supersensible (*atīndriya*) and distinct from the objects themselves."

An entity assisted by the convergence of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) produces its effect by its very own nature; what is the use of postulating an unseen power (*adṛṣṭa-śakti*)? Thus, the self-nature (*ātman*) alone is the power of entities. The associated or auxiliary factors are not distinct entities [from the thing itself]. For an object [is constituted] through the succession of its own causes.

When a distinct entity arises that is capable of producing its respective effect upon contact with its respective auxiliary causes, what is the use of an unseen, separate power (*śakti*)? If one were to postulate such a power, one must state that the very nature of the entity itself is the cause for its restriction; therefore, it is better that this [nature] alone be accepted.
Therefore, let there be the doctrine of non-distinction here, or let the powers (*śakti*) exist as distinct;
we have no fixed preference regarding the doctrine of distinction or non-distinction. For we take scripture as our authority (*śabdapramāṇaka*);
whatever the scripture says is our authority. And the scripture [speaks] of the referents of words (*padārtha*).

In expressions such as "the jar’s status as the object (karman) in the act of seeing," it conveys the state of being a means (sādhana) as something distinct [from the substance]; thus, linguistic usage based on words relies upon this distinction (vyatireka). And so, when a substance has been denoted by a nominal stem (prātipadika), the capacity (śakti) that has already established its connection proceeds toward the specific power [of the action]. || 15 ||

Having stated the pervasion (vyāpti) that "whatever assists something at a particular time is the means (sādhana) for it at that time," he says the following in order to corroborate it with the view of the Bhāṣyakāra, who maintains that even action (kriyā) is a means:
Manifestation [of the goal] occurs when there is prayer; however, when there is resolve, it follows immediately.
Likewise, resolve leads to undertaking, which serves as the means for accomplishment. (16)
That very same activity which exists in the former is considered the means in the latter;
however, they know that consciousness is the specific means in the act of perception.

(17) Regarding the designation of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), since it has been stated that "the mention of the action (*kriyā*) must also be included" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.4.32), here someone perceives some object, and having seen it, [approaches] with a request.

One forms an intention (*vyavasāya*), from intention comes the undertaking (*prārambha*), and from the undertaking comes the attainment of the fruit; because [the fruit] is thus obtained through seeing and so forth, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* that "even action (*kriyā*) is a produced object (*kṛtrimaṃ karma*).
In that regard, although [action] has the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya-svabhāva*), it is nevertheless obtained through seeing and so forth.

It is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Action (*kriyā*) is also an artificial activity (*karma*). In that context, even though acts such as *sandarśana* (showing) possess the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), their status as a means (*sādhana*) is relative. *Sandarśana*—meaning seeing thoroughly or completely—is the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) directed toward the fruit; it [functions] in the sense of praying for that.

Regarding the desire for the means to the fruit, it serves as a means; that is, it becomes a means. For when there is a vision of the object, desire arises. Resolve (*vyavasāya*) is firm grasping, the determination that a specific action is the means to [the goal]. In that context, "immediate" refers to the prayerful longing (*prārthanā*).

The means (*sādhana*) is so called because it brings about certainty when there is a desire. And resolve (*vyavasāya*) is the means for initiating action—that is, mental activity—because by the power of resolve one begins to perform purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Furthermore, because it is that which is to be attained through such action, physical action becomes the object (*karman*); this is the summary.

When each preceding operation is required, that very action which is to be performed— having ceased from the preceding [operation] and existing at an earlier time— becomes the means (*sādhana*) for the subsequent, successively occurring goal (*sādhya*). This occurs upon the attainment of its own nature (*ātmalābha*).

Because it is employed as that which is already established (*siddhatvena*). This is the meaning: in the preceding act of perception (*sandarśana*), the very action such as requesting and so forth is considered the means (*sādhana*) for the subsequent one. Now, he asks: what is the means for the act of perception? He says:
"But consciousness [resides] in perception.
Here, the particle "tu" (but/however) serves to highlight a distinction. The Self, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), is that which experiences objects.
Its specific quality (*viśeṣa*) is its fitness for the desire for results. And although this is an action...

Although its nature as the *sādhya* (the goal to be accomplished) is not yet realized, it is nevertheless established in the state of completion; and although the capacity (*śakti*) is not inherent (*asamavāya*) there, it is logical for it to possess the status of a *sādhana* (means of accomplishment) because it is distinct from its substratum. Furthermore, since one action is not inherent in another action, it is that very [action] which [is the means].

The instrument (*karaṇa*) is that which brings about another action for the agent. This is the ultimate truth here: whatever is established in relation to something else becomes its means (*sādhana*), its producer (*niṣpādaka*), or its causal factor (*kāraka*).
For at that time, there is no other instrument for the agent in the accomplishment of the action; rather, it is a future part [of the action].

Action (*karman*) comes into being because it is being reached (*āpyamāna*) by an already existing portion of action (*kriyāṃśa*). For that which the agent desires to reach through his activity is the object (*karman*).

And here, since it is precisely this portion of action that is desired to be reached by another, already established portion of action—by means of an undertaking (*ārambha*), that is, a mental operation (*mānasavyāpāra*)—it is therefore a physical action (*bhautikī kriyā*).

By this, the status of the recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) is established for that which is intended by the agent as the object of the action, as in "he prepares for battle" (*yuddhāya saṃnahyate*) and "he exerts himself for the sake of the *śrāddha* rite" (*śrāddhāya nigṛhṇate*). Regarding verbs meaning "to go," there is a desire to express either distinction or non-distinction [between the action and its result] in cases such as "seeing" (*saṃdarśana*), whereas in cases like "cooking" (*pacati*), there is only a desire to express non-distinction; this is also the case in expressions such as "he exerts himself for the sake of the *śrāddha*."
And it will be stated that this is merely a desire to express a distinction. Thus, the statement "relying upon exclusion (vyatireka),

it is conceived as a means" illustrates how even an action possesses the relationship of the goal and the means by way of a relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary, based on exclusion, as described in the Bhāṣya.
This is established: that which is distinct from power (*śakti*) and is resorted to for the sake of assisting an action is called, in general, a means (*sādhana*). || 16,17 ||

In the Vārttika, the technical term *kāraka* must be applied by indicating its referent (*saṃjñin*) as *sādhana* (the means of accomplishment). Alternatively, the referent is obtained through the understanding that this is a term whose meaning follows its etymology (*anvartha-saṃjñā*). [Objection: "If it is argued that it is an anvartha-saṃjñā, then the word *kartṛ* (agent) would be inapplicable to anything other than an agent."

Thus it has been stated [in Pāṇini’s grammar, *od gh. 1.4.23*]. In that regard, in order to justify the application of the word "agent" (*kartṛ*)—meaning "the factor of action" (*kāraka*)—to instruments and other factors when they are not the agent, he says:
"The status of being an agent exists in every factor of action (*kāraka*) simply by virtue of its accomplishment."
When there is a requirement for a distinction in function, the status of being an instrument (karaṇa) and so forth is possible. || 18 ||

(18) Since actions are accomplished by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), all factors attain the status of being "factors of action" (*kāraka*) according to the distinction of their respective roles in the accomplishment of the action. However, when there is the intention [to specify] "who cooks" or "how he cooks," then [the factors] possess diverse operations directed toward the production of the primary action.

The factors of action (*kāraka*) receive their respective designations, such as "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and so forth, by virtue of their specific excellence of activity. For instance, the agent (*kartṛ*) is that whose function consists in the employment of other means of accomplishment;
and the object (*karman*) is that which is most desired by the agent through its own action, having been rendered fit for attainment through production, modification, or acquisition.
The instrument (*karaṇa*) is that whose operation is not intervened by the operations of other causal factors, as seen in the experience of fire and so forth.

The recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is that which, through its operations of instigating, consenting, or not objecting, connects itself with the object (*karman*). The point of departure (*apādāna*) is that which accomplishes the action by becoming the limit (*avadhi*) for the process of separation (*apāya*).
The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is that which serves as the substratum for an action mediated by the agent and the object. That which sends forth [the agent] independently is the cause (*hetu*).

Furthermore, because the particular is preceded by the general, the status of being a *kāraka* persists even during the intermediate operation; thus, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the instrument is a *kāraka*" is established.

Furthermore, that which is not an agent lacks a specific technical designation [as an *kartṛ*], as in the case of "the leaf of the tree falls. And when the operation of an agent is not required, as in "the pot cooks," "the fuel pieces cook," or "the sword cuts," these possess agency only with respect to the primary action itself. This also applies to the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and the point of departure (*apādāna*).

There is no intention to express independence (*svātantrya*) regarding its own operation, because it depends upon a second agent—namely, the receiver and the one who departs. For this very reason, [the Vārttika states]:
"But it is established that there is a distinction of action for each individual factor (*kāraka*). (Jainendra-vyākaraṇa on Sūtra 1.4.23).

Thus, it has been described that the operation of verbal roots such as *pac* (to cook) occurs only within the functions of the factors of action (*kārakas*) corresponding to their respective roles for the sake of the primary action. This very point is stated in the Bhāṣya:
"The action exists as a general entity; the *kāraka* is that which brings about its accomplishment."
(From Genuine Grammar, Chapter 1, Section 4, Sūtra 23) || 18 ||
Right here he provides an illustration: "Just as in the birth of a son, agency is attributed to both parents;
[the distinction] that 'this one is his' and 'she is from him' is made according to the speaker's intention. (19)

(19) When the distinction between the acts of procreation is not intended to be expressed—as in the statement "the parents produce a son"—it is well known that both possess the status of agent (*kartṛtva*) with respect to the act of birth. However, when the distinction is intended to be expressed as to how each produces—the father, depositing the seed, places the embryo in this mother; and she...

However, because the mother, by retaining this seed from the father, experiences the status of being the agent of the act of birth, she possesses the nature of the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*); whereas the father possesses the status of the agent (*kartṛtva*) and the status of the source (*apādānatva*).
Thus, the mode of activity differs: the mother is the agent, while the father is the source.
And because the particular is preceded by the universal, the term "birth" (jan) signifies the acquisition of self-nature through the universal;

it signifies the impelling toward the object of the particular, as well as the holding of the seed and the emission of the seed. Alternatively, while the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) remains undifferentiated, the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), namely the sense of the causative (*ṇic*), refers to the impelling and so forth, as in "he causes to be born."

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: although this is included within the side of the thesis (*sādhya-pakṣa*), it serves as an illustration (*nidarśana*) because it is well-known (*prasiddha*).

Thus, it has been established that the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) stands in apposition with [the agent] through the relationship of general and particular within the principal action itself. Now,
[we shall consider] independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to subordinate actions and dependence with respect to the principal action.
Even though [the action] has not departed, he says this in order to convey through another formulation the Bhāṣya statement: "The action exists as a commonality" (G.eṇa. od gh. 1.4.23).
The agents of qualities and actions have their powers suppressed by the primary agent;
yet, even while thus suppressed, they remain endowed with their own complete functions.
Known as instruments and so forth through their participation in various actions, they subsequently attain sovereignty and achieve the status of agents with respect to the primary action. (21)

(20) Because subordinate qualities and actions, which consist of intermediate operations such as burning and so forth, possess independence, they are all agents; however, with respect to the primary action, their power is subordinated by the independent agent who employs them, and thus their independence [is relative] according to that [subordination]. Therefore, accordingly—

Having been reduced to a state of subordination (*nyagbhāva*) and lack of autonomy (*asvātantrya*), even though they are thus subordinated, because their own autonomy does not depart from their respective functions, it is impossible for that which is ineffective to serve as a cause for the accomplishment of an action; therefore, [the factors] perform their own respective functions.
Even when they are employed by the agent as subordinate factors to the primary action,

they remain inseparable from all their own respective operations, such as burning and so forth; they are understood through the designations of instruments and the like, which pertain to specific aspects of that action, as if they were not abandoning their own essential nature.

The meaning is that even after the time of their specific application (*viniyoga*), having attained independence characterized by the performance of their own respective functions, they become autonomous with respect to the various sub-actions within themselves; thus, they assume the status of an agent (*kartṛtā*) and the status of a factor (*kārakatva*) specifically in relation to the primary action.
This explains how [the grammatical categories] such as "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and "factor" (*kāraka*) are logically established. For indeed, the instruments and so forth...
When there is an injunction by the agent, the [factors] remain subordinate while performing their own respective operations;
thus they become such because they are enjoined by the agent for the sake of the agent’s own agency in its operation.
While being so enjoined, they experience independence in their own operations, which constitutes their status as instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth.

There is no contradiction between independence (*svātantrya*) and dependence (*pāratantrya*), for the accomplishment of the primary action (*pradhānakriyā*) is what constitutes them; indeed, that which is independence with respect to one's own operation is itself dependence with respect to the primary action, and nothing else. And this occurs only after the agent’s application (*viniyoga*) has taken place; prior to that, however—

Independence (*svātantrya*) is said to consist merely in the capacity for being employed by the agent; and thus, there is no difference in the scope between [the definitions] "an instrument" (*karaṇa*) and "a causal factor" (*kāraka*), because independence in its own operation constitutes the state of being an instrument and so forth with respect to the primary action. This very point has been stated as follows:
"But it is established that for each individual factor there is a distinct action; thus, in the case of roots such as *pac*, the instrument and the locus possess the status of agent.
(Jainendra Vyākaraṇa on Pāṇini 1.4.23)
Thus,
having stated the subordinate actions (*guṇakriyā*) of the agent, the instrument, and the locus by means of the rule beginning with *adhiśrayaṇodakāsecanam...* (Pāṇini 1.4.23), [the author proceeds].

When it is further objected that "the status of [factors] such as the ablative (*apādāna*) is not established" (Pāṇini-vārttika 1.4.23), [it is replied]: "Not so; because those two [agent and object] are respectively independent and dependent, there is an alternative expression [for them], and the designation does not depend on [their actual physical state]."

Furthermore, it was established [in the Siddhānta] that this is a "designation" (*saṃjñā*). For instance, in the expression "the cloud flashes," since there is no intention to express a distinction from lightning, the status of the ablative (*apādāna*) indeed exists in its own function.

They say [this is] "independence" (*svātantrya*). However, when it is said, "He is coming from the village" (*grāmād āgacchati*), because another meaning is understood and the operation of the *apādāna* (ablative) is not determined, there is no such usage.
But there is indeed some [operation] of the village as the *apādāna* in the accomplishment of the action.

The operation (vyāpāra) is characterized by the attainment of the status of a limit (avadhibhāva). Otherwise, just as in the case of "he comes from near the village" (*grāmasya samīpād āgacchati*), there would also be a lack of agency for the village in the expression "he comes from the village" (*grāmād āgacchati*). Furthermore, [the status of the object] is not denied to the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) by the agent, due to both instigation and consent.

The operation [of the action] itself certainly exists as "thatness" (tattva). However, there is no usage such as "the Brāhmaṇa gives," because if the Brāhmaṇa were the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), the intended meaning would not be determined from this [expression]. For this very reason, the verbal root does not denote the operation of the ablative (*apādāna*) or the recipient (*saṃpradāna*); rather, [it denotes the operation of the agent].

It is precisely the activity of performing an action and so forth, as in such cases as "the rice is cooked by itself," "the sword cuts," or "the pot cooks. Thus, since a distinction of action is possible everywhere, the term "agent" (kartṛ) is applied even when [an object] functions as an instrument and so on due to its autonomy. If this is so—

Even if [the agent] possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, it would still receive the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) due to its independence (*svātantrya*). This is not the case; for while independence is already obtained from the governing context (*adhikāra*) of "factors of action" (*kāraka*), the repeated mention of "the independent is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*) is intended to convey an independence that is not obscured by dependence (*pāratantrya*); thus, it applies only to the primary sense of independence.

It remains as having the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*). Even so, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the designation "agent" would prevail, overriding the designations such as "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and so forth. This is not a fault;
for since the designations such as "instrument" have no other scope [for application], they override the designation "agent" in this instance.

The designation of a *kāraka* occurs by virtue of its continued application (*anuvṛtti*). Alternatively, since the technical term *kāraka* is based on independence (*svātantrya*), there is no relationship of sublation between the cause and the effect here; for in this case, dependence (*pāratantrya*) is itself the cause of independence.
Even when it possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, its independence (*svātantrya*), which has been inferred, certainly persists;

indeed, there is a coexistence (*samāveśa*) of this [independence] with the designations of *apādāna* and the rest, alongside the designation of *kāraka*. However, where the intention to express dependence is inseparable from the intention to express independence, there the instrument is subordinate to the others.

It is said that [the agent] "bādhante" (strikes). For example, as in the expression "he pierces with a bow. In that case, there is an intended expression of independence (*svātantrya*) which is inseparably connected to the bow's being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*). Furthermore, regarding the rule "the independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*), it is not determined that one is independent in all states; rather, it is when...
Thus, [the agenthood] is indeed independent; consequently, the designation of "agent" (kartṛ-saṃjñā) is established even in cases such as *sthālī pacati* ("the pot cooks").

Furthermore, by the force of the governing rule (*adhikāra*), it is not contradictory that the term "kāraka" (factor of action) applies even during the state of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, based on the inferred independence [of the instrument]. Thus, everything is well-established. In this way, previously, by relying on the non-difference of the action (*kriyā*), it was explained that agency (*kartṛtva*) consists merely in the accomplishment [of the result], and thus action, in its general form, has the nature of mere accomplishment. Now, however, by also relying on the difference between actions through the relation of subordinate and principal, the application of the word "agent" (*kartṛ-śabda*) to one who is not the [ultimate] agent has been justified.

And in that regard, the meaning of the Bhāṣya is that there exists a principal action which, being common to all, serves as the general property and is shared by all as the object to be accomplished (sādhya). || 20,21 ||
He provides an example for the fact that while they are independent in their own respective functions, they are dependent upon the primary agent in its function:
"Just as the status of being a warrior resides in the warriors who have been appointed by the king."
When they have been surrounded by those [allies], the king obtains victory or defeat. || 22 ||
Likewise, when all [factors] are appointed by an agent to perform a single purpose, their status as agents is not contradicted by their subsequent roles as instruments and so forth. (23)

(21) Just as when warriors are appointed and dispatched by a king, their lord, their status as warriors consists in their being stationed in battle arrays and so forth; and while they are fighting, once that conduct— such as the destruction of the enemy’s great divisions and regions— is accomplished, the king attains victory.

Or alternatively, one incurs defeat; this is what is said. Warriors are "warriors" insofar as they are the agents [of their action], because their activity previously resided therein. Yet again, due to the king's command, they are not independent; and yet again, when acting under his command, they are independent and indifferent [to other constraints].

The meaning is this: when the instruments and so forth are thus directed by the agent—just as servants act together for a common purpose such as cooking—the independence that arises in them subsequent to the direction is not contradicted by their status as instruments and so forth, which existed at the time of the direction. Thus it is.

If "agent" (*kāraka*) is a designation of a technical term (*saṃjñā*), then the bearer of that term (*saṃjñin*) must also be designated; otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence [of the term applying] to that which is not an agent, as in the case of "he comes from near the village. Thus, when it is urged that the bearer of the term—whether it be that which accomplishes or brings about [an action]—must be specified, [the following is said].
When [the objection] has been set aside by establishing a specific designatum through the understanding that the designation is based on its literal meaning,

and when the objection has been raised— that the designation "kāraka" is untenable for the *karaṇa* and other factors because it is not understood to carry over into subsequent sections due to the governing rule (*adhikāra*)— [the response is given] by considering the mere accomplishment [of the action].

The meaning of the section is that [the objection] has been refuted by resorting to agency for each instrument through the differentiation of actions, and by resorting to independence with respect to the subordinate action. || 22, 23 ||

Having established that when the status of being an *sādhaka* (the means of accomplishment) is predicated of that which brings about an action by relying on a designation based on its literal meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), the cause (*hetu*) is also a *karaṇa* (instrument) because it brings about the action— and thus [the use of] the third case is already established— what is the purpose of the rule "in the sense of a cause" (*hetau*)?
Anticipating this objection, [the author] demonstrates the non-difference between a cause and a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
He shows:
"When an operation does not depend [on another], it is accepted as a cause (*hetu*);
but when it depends on the state of being a limit (*avadhi*), the wise know it as a definition (*lakṣaṇa*). (24)

(22) That which, without depending upon an operation (*vyāpāra*), is resorted to as a cause by its mere fitness (*yogyatā*) for the accomplishment of the intended meaning, is the *hetu* (cause). And this is the domain of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) characterized by non-agentive case-endings—that is, the third case-ending, which supersedes the sixth case-ending of relation. For example: *adhyayanena*.

"He dwells" (*vasati*). Study is the cause (*hetu*); dwelling is that which possesses the cause (*hetumat*). When the genitive case of subordination (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply to the relationship between these two, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the cause. However, the Naiyāyikas state:
"The cause is that which is the basis for [the distinction between] a quality and a substance; and it is the domain of a case-ending that does not denote a kāraka. As for that...
The cause of an action expressed by a verbal root is indeed its *kāraka* (participant in the action), as in examples such as "he dwells because of ignorance" (*avidyayā vasati*),
according to the rule *anarthalakṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 1.4.84).

In this context, since the word *lakṣaṇa* is used to denote even the logical reason (*hetu*), one might suspect there is no distinction between these two; [the author] refutes this by stating "that which is dependent" (*āśrita*) and so forth. In the phrase "in the definition" (*lakṣaṇe*), the word *lakṣaṇa* is derived in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva-sādhana*). However, in the phrase "they know the definition" (*lakṣaṇaṃ viduḥ*), it is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*). [The term] "definition" (*lakṣaṇe*)...

Regarding the illumination of an object being characterized: that which "depends upon a state of being a limit"—wherein the dependence on a limit, meaning a boundary-form, is present—is known by the experts as a *lakṣaṇa*, i.e., an indicator, because it is by means of this that [the object] is characterized (*lakṣyate*). This applies where the state of being a limit is recognized, even in the case of a cause (*hetu*).
This is the definition of a *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic). For this very reason, the particle *tu* (but) serves to highlight a distinction. Others, however, say:
"The cause (*hetu*) is useful for the arising of the effect (*kārya*), whereas the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is for the arising of the condition (*pratyaya*).
That is incorrect, because even a cause is seen to have an operation (*vyāpāra*) in the arising of a condition, as is the case with knowledge (*vidyā*) and so forth.
The definition [of a secondary characteristic] is that which, by virtue of its operation upon a substratum such as clothing,
serves as a limit (*avadhi*) regardless of whether it possesses the capacity to produce the object being characterized or not.
For example, in the expression "the lightning flashes after the tree," the tree is the secondary characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding *vidyotana* (lightning): the meaning is that having reached a tree, it flashes. How then is the example "Śākalya’s *saṃhitā* followed by rain" (*śākalyasya saṃhitāmanu prāvarṣat*) given under the rule *anurlakṣaṇe*?
For in that case, the *saṃhitā* is not perceived as the delimiter of the raining merely by being a limit; rather, it is so perceived by way of being its cause.

Furthermore, the cause (*hetu*) is not the definition (*lakṣaṇa*); rather, because it possesses the common quality of being an indicator (*jñāpakatva*), the word "definition" is used here to refer to the cause itself—thus there is no contradiction. Now, one might object:
smoke is well-known to have a constant concomitance (*sāhacarya*) with fire, as its relationship has been determined through repeated observation.
Even a solitary instance might serve as an indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) by pointing toward a fire that is not currently visible but produced from some other cause;
