however, since the *saṃhitā* is perceived right from the very beginning, it does not have repeated perception—that is, a repetition of its perception—so how could it be an indicator? To this, it is replied:

Although it is true that in the world that by which something is repeatedly perceived is called its "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*), nevertheless, even a cause whose capacity for the arising of an effect is not [directly] perceived becomes a definition, provided it is of such a nature.
For when there is a determination of an effect, the cause also serves as its definition by virtue of being its instrumental reason (*hetu*).

Because it delimits its effect: for just as that which has grasped an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) through repeated observation makes another thing known, so too the cause, by producing [the effect] independently of anything else,
becomes the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) through its delimitation of the effect, owing to the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the effect.

Just as the rising of clouds is determined to be the cause of rain, it possesses the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of being a determiner even when rain is absent—since the world, upon seeing the rising of clouds, infers rain. Now, one might object: "Causality is determined by the force of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)."

When B exists whenever A exists, but does not exist even when another thing exists if A is absent, then A is the cause of B. Positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) arise from repeated observation, because positive and negative concomitance cannot be ascertained through a single observation. And although the collection [of causes] is indeed the cause...

Nevertheless, because rain occurs only once [in a given instance], its causality cannot be ascertained, since there is the possibility that the effect might occasionally arise even from some other object present at that time. And thus, like the rising of clouds, this [single observation] is not a valid definition [of causality]. To this we reply: even from a single observation...

The state of being a cause is understood [as follows]: for that which does not produce something else, that thing is never seen arising from it, just as a rice sprout is not produced from barley. Nor is another thing existing at that same time the producer, because it is not observed to produce it at other times. And so they have said:
When X exists, Y necessarily occurs; yet if one were to postulate another cause for that [Y], there would be an infinite regress of causes in all cases due to that [second] being the cause.

Thus it is said. Nor does its production from that occur by way of the "crow-and-palm-fruit" maxim (i.e., by mere chance), because that which does not possess the nature [to produce it] does not generate [it] even when [the conditions] are present once. Furthermore, the conjunction is observed through perception to be producing rain;
therefore, even from a single observation, the status of being a cause is ascertained here. Moreover, [this is known] also from scripture.

In this context, the causality of the *saṃhitā* with respect to the raining is certain; thus, it is stated that the cause itself is called a "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) here due to the commonality of being an indicator. As it is said in the Bhāṣya: "The cause is also subsumed under the definition" (Pāṇini 1.4.84).

Thus [it is said], because the definition (lakṣaṇa) is pervasive. For even a cause becomes a definition when it indicates the effect, just as the rising of clouds is the definition of rain. Nor is there any deviation (vyabhicāra), because a complete and unimpaired cause is productive, and because there is no deviation when one analyzes in that manner.

The principle is that validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in the capacity for attainment (*prāpaṇa-śakti*), not in the actual attainment itself. If, then, by the word "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) the state of being the cause for the delimitation of another category of object is described, how can it be said that [the definition] "depends upon the relation of a limit"? Even when a definition depends upon the relation of a limit...

The very nature of being a cause of delimitation (*pariccheda-hetutva*) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); otherwise, how could that which does not itself effect delimitation be a defining characteristic?

However, there is this distinction: while a tree is a cause of delimitation by virtue of being a spatial limit (*avadhi*), *saṃhitā* and the like possess the status of a defining characteristic through their common quality of being indicators (*jñāpaka*), even though they do not function as limits.

For a characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is indeed manifold. In some cases it exists by way of being a limit (*avadhi*), as when a tree is the basis for delimiting a flash of lightning. In some cases it exists through the delimitation of a cause (*kāraṇa*), as smoke [is the characteristic] of fire. In some cases...

Because it serves as a cause for determining an effect, just as the rising of clouds [is the cause] of rain; and thus, according to the manner stated, the *saṃhitā* is both a *lakṣaṇa* (indicator) and a *hetu* (cause). If this is so, then [the rule] "When an indicator (*lakṣaṇa*), a description of a state (*itthaṃbhūtākhyāna*)... (Pāṇini 1.4.90) [applies].
Since the designation *karmapravacanīya* is already established by the general definition [of *karmapravacanīya*] through such rules as these,
the re-enactment of the rule "anurlakṣaṇe" (Pāṇini 1.4.84) is purposeless. This has been stated.
Regarding the statement, "The mention of *anurlakṣaṇe* is redundant because it has already been established by the general rule" (*Pāṇini 1.4.84*), the reply is:
"But the mention is for the purpose of indicating a cause" (*Pāṇini 1.4.84*).

Thus it has been said. This word "artha" (object/purpose) is not a synonym for "that which is to be expressed," but rather it signifies "cessation" (nivṛtti). And by applying the term denoting the cause to the effect, the instrumental case of the word "hetu" (cause) is used [to form the compound].
Furthermore, since sublation (bādha) is nothing other than that which is to be sublated, the compound is analyzed as: "that whose object to be ceased is the cause itself."
Thus, it is stated that the re-enactment of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is for the purpose of subverting the notion of "cause" (*hetu*). But [one might object]:
"Since the technical designation is re-enacted, the cognition of the designated entity (*saṃjñin*) in the specific rules (*pradeśa*) would become more stable;
however, how could the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) be subverted? For it is precisely by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*) that it is the subverter. This is not so.
The technical term (*saṃjñā*), being prescribed more than once,
presents itself twice in various rules such as "the second case ending [is used] when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*. Among these, one presentation is for the sake of the second case ending.

As for the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) [introduced by the rule] *anurlakṣaṇe*, lest it be rendered meaningless, it establishes the second case itself by overriding the third case used in the sense of a cause (*hetutṛtīyā*). Now, one might object: "From the repetition of the application [of the suffix], the cognition of the name (*saṃjñipratyaya*) would become doubled; however, the injunction of the second case does not undergo such accumulation."

The designation is subordinate to the purpose of the ritual action; the ritual action, termed the "second," is the primary element. And there is no differentiation of the primary element due to a difference in its subordinate elements.
For what purpose, then, is the subordinate element mentioned twice? Let it be redundant;
however, the offering does not repeat itself merely because of this. Even though the primary element is for the sake of its own refinement...

A quality (guṇa) goes to its place of application just as a technical term (saṃjñā) or a paribhāṣā does; nevertheless, because a quality that has a requirement for further specification achieves its purpose through a single application of that quality, why would it go to the place of another quality?
Thus, there is only one [application], and a second would be redundant. That [second] would be sublated by the third due to its posteriority. But surely—

Because there would be the consequence of the loss of their own essential nature in the absence of a Pradhāna, a Guṇa whose purpose has not yet been fulfilled would manifest another Pradhāna. Just as ministers, seeking to maintain their own status and qualities in the absence of a king, establish another king; so too, in establishing him—
Their own form is established [as the cause], because without a king there would be no ministers and so forth.
This is not analogous, because between the king and the minister there exists a mutual relationship of beneficiary and benefactor;
for even the rule regarding the status of subordinate and primary is itself uncertain. To illustrate, the king...

He establishes the subjects within the boundaries prescribed by the treatises on dharma, and he himself follows them. Those subjects, in turn, discipline the king; thus, from the very distinction of the primary [the means], there arises the distinction of the qualities [the ends]. If this is so, then the injunction regarding the means itself becomes the injunction regarding the end. For example:

When it is said, "Be one who stands in the army," the state of standing in the army consists in the procuring of fodder and protection for the elephants; thus, by means of prescribing the state of standing in the army, that very task is enjoined. In the same way, by means of prescribing the technical designation (saṃjñā) of "karmapravacanīya," [that specific function is enjoined].

That action is thus prescribed as being precisely that which is designated by the second case (accusative). And so, the second case being prescribed once again serves the purpose of subverting the sublater, according to the principle of *nāprāpte* (where it has not [otherwise] obtained).

For the sixth case (genitive) would have obtained in the case of a relationship; this [prescription of the second case] is its sublater. Herein lies the force of the explicit statement (*vacana-sāmarthya*).

This is the basis [for the rule]. Otherwise, how could the prescription of a specific name itself serve the purpose of prescribing the second case ending? Furthermore, by adopting this view, another interpretation also becomes tenable; for the stated principle—that "a distinction in the primary follows from a distinction in the quality"—is set aside by this [specific] statement. And so says the Bhāṣya:
"Even in the case of an illustration, human effort serves as a means of cessation" (G.eṇa. od gh.

1.1.85). Alternatively, due to the difference in designation (*saṃjñābheda*), the word *anu* is differentiated as the designated object (*saṃjñin*). However, the injunction of the accusative case is not the primary element, such that a differentiation of the primary would rightly follow from a differentiation of the subordinate (*guṇabheda*).
Furthermore, because of the distinction in their designations (*saṃjñā*), that which has acquired superior strength through the second rule sets aside the third rule.

Moreover, under the view that the order of mention (*uddeśa*) is primary, a principal element (*pradhāna*) proceeding toward the location of its subordinate qualities (*guṇa*) does not become satisfied by a single quality alone;
for it requires everything contained within that context, as there is no distinction in its relationship [to them]. Therefore...

In this way, let one subordinate element (*guṇa*), its purpose unfulfilled, postulate another principal element (*pradhāna*), just as subjects [postulate] another king; nor is there any lack of analogy with the case of subjects, for even though they depend on the assistance provided by the king, they remain entirely subordinate elements,
since it is precisely for the sake of nourishing their status as his subordinates that [the postulation occurs].

This refers to a consideration of the benefit conferred by that [prior rule], and not for the sake of its own predominance. Even under the view that the operation occurs at the time of the effect (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the two designations in the rule concerning the effect present the two named objects as distinct entities. Therefore, due to the force of the statement characterized by the prescription of the designation once again, an excellence is attained.

It is indeed logical that a rule concerning the second case (dvitīyā-vidhi), having reached its own specific domain, should supersede even a subsequent rule concerning the third case (tṛtīyā-vidhi); and so he will state later:
"When the connection between cause and effect has been delimited by the word *anu*..."
"From its commencement, it is sublated; having reached the third [stage], it is characterized as a cause.

Thus, in the rule *anurlakṣaṇe*, the cause (*hetu*) itself is introduced as the object of indication (*lakṣama*) in order to express the pervasiveness of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), even though there exists an internal distinction between these two. For instance:

In the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.126), the term *hetu* is employed as distinct from *lak�ṣaṇa* with the intention of expressing the state of being a producer (*janakatva*). Thus, the general category of cause (*nimitta*) is divided into three types; by way of its essential nature, that which brings about an action [is one type].
The producer (kāraka) is, in general, a cause that brings about birth; the indicator (jñāpaka), on the other hand, is a characteristic (lakṣaṇa). || 24 ||

Although there is a similarity in their being producers (*janakatva*), he states the distinction between the cause (*hetu*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) due to the difference in their objects:

**The cause has substance and so forth as its object; the factor of action (*kāraka*) has a restricted function.** (23) A thing capable of accomplishing a substance, quality, or action is the cause of substances and so forth. For example:
A sprout [arises] from a seed, a lineage from wealth, sorrow from a daughter, fame from knowledge, skill from the practice of an art, and cooking from fire.
Although cooking and the like are capable of accomplishing their respective actions, they are indeed merely causes so long as they have not yet undertaken their specific operation.

Nevertheless, since fire and the other elements are intended here as being helpful through their mere proximity to those whose activity has ceased, they lack the status of instruments (*karaṇa*) and are therefore connected with the instrumental case of cause (*hetu*). The relationship of the family with prosperity is manifested by the act of attaining it together with wealth.

For the renown of a family is produced by wealth; and in that regard, wealth whose activity has ceased becomes the cause of the family by virtue of its mere suitability—this is expressed by connecting it with the instrumental case of cause (*hetu-tṛtīyā*), which supersedes the genitive of residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*).
Likewise, a daughter [is a cause] of her progenitor’s grief through the mediation of the act of birth, and learning as well.

In the case of "the cause of fame," the relationship of *śeṣa* (residual) is produced by the action of attainment (*prāpti*), since fame is attained precisely by one who is already famous. In other instances as well, this should be inferred accordingly. In the cases of "skill through the practice of an art" and "he dwells because of his study," the cause has as its object both a quality (*guṇa*) and an action (*kriyā*).

But a *kāraka* is that which is restricted to being a means for accomplishing an action (*kriyā*). For in that case, it is the action itself that is the restricted object; and the state of being engaged in an operation (*vyāpāra*) constitutes a difference in its essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*). He states that for some things, even when they are engaged in an operation and are objects of an action, their status as a "cause" (*hetu*) is taught by the technical treatises (*śāstra*).

**The agent is accepted as the cause in an action when it depends upon another agent.** (25) In the technical treatise (*śāstra*), the instigator (*prayojaka*)— the agent who is employed in the action through the mediation of the capacity of the agent being instigated (*prayojyakartṛ*), and who prompts that agent— is called the "cause" (*hetu*).

It is accepted as a cause because of [scriptural] statement; however, the meaning is that this is not a "cause" in its conventional sense, even though it is a specific type of causal factor (kāraka). || 25 ||
Now, although the status of being an object of action is the same for both the cause (*hetu*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*), he states the distinction between them:
"Just as a substitute is seen for that which is an instrument for the sake of an action, so too is it for the action itself;
however, since the action exists for the sake of the cause, it is not substituted. (26)

(24) The instrument (*karaṇa*) is that which provides the most excellent assistance for the accomplishment of an action, and thus it is subordinate; the action, however, being of the nature of that which is to be accomplished, is primary. Precisely because subordinate factors must conform to the primary, when no specific instrument is prescribed by scripture, the learned practice the use of a substitute. [The action] is the primary factor...

For since an action is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is capable of implying a suitable means of accomplishment (*sādhana*); thus, even when there is an implication of the means in general, the specific application of the means is heard [in the text] for the purpose of insertion (*āvāpa*). Therefore, even if that specific application is impossible, the general means implied by the primary action in its essential form— [The sentence continues: ...is indeed established as the object of the injunction. Thus, the injunction is established as having a general object. Furthermore, because the specific application is not mentioned, the general means is indeed established as the object of the injunction. Even when being nourished by another particular [instance] of that [general category], it is not capable of abandoning the meaning directly expressed by the Vedic text (*śrauta-artha*);

for the general [category] itself has been heard [in the scripture], and it is capable of encompassing all its particulars. Thus, the justification for the substitute (*pratinidhi*) has already been discussed at length previously. This remains true even in the event of a deficiency in the auxiliary elements (*aṅga-bhreṣa*).

Because the primary element must not be abandoned, and in order to preserve the essential nature of the act of offering, the cultured (śiṣṭas) adopt a similar substitute limb—known through the traditional lineage—with the very same notion that it is the principal;
this is the result of the primacy of the action. For this very reason, some maintain that the word "instrument" (karaṇa) is used here.

They explain that since the singular number is used for a genus (*jāti*) and denotes all grammatical factors (*kāraka*s), all the *kāraka*s are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*); thus, a substitute for a subordinate element is appropriate. However, in the case of "he dwells because of studying" (*adhyayanena vasati*), the act of dwelling (*vasatikriyā*), although expressed by the verb as the primary element, is nevertheless understood [as subordinate].

Due to the efficacy of the actual fact, [the residence] is dependent upon the cause known as study; for people say, "I am staying here for the purpose of study. And since the primary factor does not conform to its subordinate qualities, in the absence of study, nothing else can be substituted here for the purpose of residence.
This is correct. For if something else were taken as the object [of the action], the purposefulness of the action would be understood as being for that other thing;

in that case, that very thing would be the primary cause (*hetu*). Therefore, in the expression "he dwells for the sake of study" (*adhyayanena vasati*), this is not an instrumental case denoting instrument (*karaṇa-tṛtīyā*), but rather an instrumental case denoting cause (*hetu-tṛtīyā*) alone. Indeed, it is not by means of study...

Clothing is not produced by one who is engaged in an activity; rather, since study alone is the primary goal to be accomplished for the sake of clothing, study—being devoid of activity and serving as the intended object by its mere fitness—is the cause of the clothing. If study were engaged in an activity, [it would no longer be the cause] of the clothing.

When there is an intention to express conformity (*anukūlya*), as in the case of [the term] *bhikṣā* and so forth, there is the status of being an instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) because of performing what is conducive to that [action], as in "he causes [him] to study" (*adhyayane vāsayati*). Thus, regarding the sphere of the *kāraka*, the *kāraka* is subordinate while the action is primary; however, regarding the sphere of the cause (*hetu*), the reverse is the case.
By this distinction as well, the exclusion [of the definition] from the causal factor (kāraka) has been stated. || 26 ||

Now, in order to distinguish the scope of the fourth case (*caturthī*)— which concerns the sense of "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*)— from the scope of the third case (*tṛtīyā*), which concerns the cause (*hetu*), he says:
"The cause establishes the object through both reverse and direct order."
But that [status of being for the sake of another] follows from being a cause by way of conformity. (27)
(25) A cause in its state of diminishing produces its effect without delay, and is thus characterized by its inverse progression. For example:

A cause is that which, through contact with water, heat, and so forth, undergoes an accumulation of specific qualities, becoming progressively more increased, more increased, and most increased—thereby conforming to a succession of states characterized by such degrees of intensification. Conversely, a cause characterized by its conformity [to the effect] is that which, having its specific form augmented by contact with other factors, produces an effect that is itself highly intensified. For example, a seed, having acquired specific qualities through contact with water and heat, reaches a state of swelling that is capable of producing a sprout. Thus, the cause is of two kinds.

Its specific distinction, however, is *tādarthya* (being for the sake of that). It is a specific form of causehood characterized by being invariably restricted to favorability (*ānukūlya*) as the basis for the accomplishment of a purpose; it is a causehood or generative power accompanied by such favorability. The meaning is that *tādarthya* is the manifested form of the relationship between cause and effect. In this context, the dative case expresses that specific form of causehood characterized by favorability. The meaning is that *tādarthya* is the manifested form of the causal relationship. An example therein is: "gold for an earring" (*kuṇḍalāya hiraṇyam*).

In the expression "this is for that purpose," the word "this" (*idam*) refers to the benefactor (*upakāraka*), while the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the beneficiary (*upakārya*). Through the formation of a compound followed by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), the relationship is expressed in its manifested form. In that context, because the meaning of the final member—which is the causal form—is what is to be made known, it possesses primacy; thus, the relationship establishes its footing upon the quality denoted by the word "that."

For in that case, since it is said "it has arisen therein," when the causal factor's status as a benefactor (*upakāritva*) toward that purpose is understood, the dative case prescribed for the emergence of the cause-and-effect relationship applies only to the word denoting the effect. This is because the relationship residing in the cause is also exhausted through that [connection to the effect]. It is incorrect to state that the instrumental case does not occur after a word denoting the cause, on the grounds that the effect itself, having transformed into the motivator (*prayojaka*), is called "for that purpose" (*tadartha*).

Since the word *tādarthya* has the meaning of the latter member as its primary sense, it is logical that it expresses the state of being a cause; for this very reason, *tādarthya* is understood as being concomitant with causality. A specific cause is not the effect itself. However, in the case of the expression "that for the sake of which his going occurred has been accomplished by him," because the subordinate element—which was introduced by the pronoun *yat*—is referred to by the coreferential pronoun *tat*, it is appropriate that the referent of the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) be connected with the effect. Nevertheless, even so, the referent of the pronoun does not possess primacy here, because it is subordinate to the meaning of the latter member of the compound. (27)

Thus, although the agent (*kāraka*), the cause (*hetu*), the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and the purpose (*tādarthya*) are similar in being instrumental factors (*nimitta*), the categories of meaning (*padārtha*) have distinct natures and objects; therefore, there is no risk of confusion regarding their definitions. Having thus resolved this incidental matter, we shall now proceed with the investigation concerning the *kārakas* themselves.

To introduce [the topic], he says: "The innate power (sahajā śakti) exists everywhere as long as the substance persists; however, at the time of action, it assists by being manifested through its substratum. (28)
(26) Regarding impermanent entities, their arising as capable occurs solely from their own causes;

this is an innate capacity (*sahajā śaktiḥ*). For since entities cannot have any excellence added to them, it is impossible to impart a capacity to that which was previously incapable at the moment immediately following its production. However, in the case of eternal [entities]...

Power is inherent; however, powers that are inherent in a substratum cannot remain once that substratum has perished, as they would then be without support. Therefore, they exist as long as the substance exists. Nevertheless, when auxiliary causes are present, entities resort to the manifestation of their power, being thus disposed toward the production of their own effects.
Thus, they are called "means" (*sādhana*) precisely at the time of manifestation, because of their utility for the effect, and not at other times even though they exist then. For instance:
the power of the wall lies in its obstructing, while that of the axe and so forth lies in its splitting.
That dharma, however, though eternally existent, is determined at the time of action. || 29 ||

(27) A wall is an obstructor, and a weapon is a cutter; since these are known when the objects to be obstructed or cut are present, this is the manifestation of an existing capacity extended toward its object. Even that which pertains to the three periods of time is delimited by those of limited vision.

Indeed, due to the necessity of appropriation (*upādāna*), the capacity exists prior to the effect, and it exists again even after the cause-and-effect [process] has occurred. This is also corroborated by scripture (*āgama*).

Just as the nooses of the Daityas belonging to Varuṇa manifest their power when joined with their own limbs, so too do the powers of substances become manifest when they are in contact with those who desire victory.

(28) According to the traditional teaching (*āgama*), the nooses of Varuṇa, fashioned by the very actions of the Daityas, are always present within the palms of their own hands in the form of latent power (*śakti*). It is heard that these, however, become manifest at the time of conquering the enemy army. In this same way, [the powers] of substances are always...
It is also logical that the potencies, being present, manifest at the time of accomplishing their own effects.
That which was stated regarding the power [of weapons] such as missiles for tearing apart is now further elaborated:
when the edge [of a weapon], by means of its own sharpness, weight, hardness, and shape, is applied toward that which is to be cut, it is then perceived as possessing power. (31)

(29) Sharpness (*taikṣṇya*) is the excellence of thinness in parts that are densely compacted and gradually become finer toward the tip; it is the quality (*dharma*) that serves as the cause for cutting.
It occurs when there is a separation following the intermingling of parts belonging to different classes.

Gravity is the property that causes the falling of parts whose internal spaces have been eliminated due to accumulation; it is the property called density or hardness belonging to iron parts when they are heated and tempered,
from which a specific blow is produced.
A specific arrangement (*saṃniveśaviśeṣa*)—
the cause of differentiation within it— is its configuration (*saṃsthāna*), which is the basis for designations such as "the edge of a circle" and from which a variety of blows arises.
Therefore, it is understood that the sword-blade is capable when beginning the acts of cutting or splitting by means of these qualities;
however, when devoid of activity, it is not so perceived even though these qualities are present.
The same should be stated, as appropriate, for other entities as well, since the sword serves as an illustration.
He states that other alternative positions are also possible regarding this proof:
"Some maintain that the means of accomplishment arises from another cause prior to the action; some [hold it to be] innate; others maintain that the action itself exists first. (32)

(30) Once existence (*sattva*) is established, the expectation of its manifestation is reasonable. However, since existence itself regarding the capacities (*śakti*) is inferred from their effects, it is unestablished prior to the action. Therefore, due to a cause that must be awaited prior to the action, the capacities of substances arise as being conducive to that very action.
Even though [the cause] exists, something else must be depended upon as the occasion for its manifestation; therefore, that [occasioning factor] alone is the producer.

For indeed, since entities dependent on auxiliary causes possess the capacity to produce, they are inferred to have mutually distinct potencies that serve as the causes of their own effects; because they do not produce when alone, they are not potent at that time.
Thus, the birth of the capacity does not arise from its own substrate or its producer alone, but rather from another efficient cause (*nimitta*).
Furthermore, because it is recognized through re-cognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there is no difference in the entity itself despite the presence of both capacity and incapacity; so say some.
For this very reason, the restriction regarding the material cause (*upādāna*) is also established through the determination of fitness (*yogyatā*). Others, however, [hold as follows]:

Since power (*śakti*) is non-different from the entity itself, some maintain that the states of being capable and incapable are merely differences in the nature (*svabhāva*) of things. This is a restatement of the previously established position that "the innate capacity of substances is what is intended by the term 'power'. However, others [hold that] it is not for the same reason that an action [occurs].

Thinking that this means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is produced by that [action], and not by anything else, they consider it to be a distinct cause (*nimitta*) in relation to the action; likewise, they explain its "simultaneity" (*sahajatva*) as being precisely in relation to the action.
For indeed, entities bring about an action by bestowing their respective potencies upon one another.

Regarding "cooperators" (*sahakāriṇaḥ*): it is held that actions, which consist of functional operations, arise together with their causal powers (*sādhanaśakti*). Thus, since the powers arise from the very same sources from which the action arises, they are innate (*sahaja*). However, it is only when the powers have been produced that they bring about the action in the subsequent moment.

There is no contradiction regarding the relationship between the probandum and the probans, for the coexistence of the probandum and the probans is not established by valid means of cognition. || 32 ||

Others, however, consider that the action exists prior to the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). To the question of how this is tenable, he says: "Activity itself, initially independent of anything else, draws forth a single potency within a common substratum, like a flowing stream. (33)

(31) An eternal action (*kriyā*) is said to be independent of the operation of causes and not dependent on anything whatsoever; however, it is indeed inherent (*samaveta*) in its own substratum (*svāśraya*). For this very reason, within that substratum, it manifests the potencies of the means (*sādhanaśakti*), which accomplish their respective specific effects. Others [hold a different view].

They say that it is indeed independent. According to the tradition of certain ancient Mīmāṃsakas, the power of the means (*sādhana-śakti*), characterized by activity (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇā*) and consisting of a continuous flow of operation like the current of a river, drags along and carries away grass, leaves, creepers, and so forth. Or else, activity characterized by *rajas* is eternal.

The Sāṃkhya system maintains that [the cause], which persists through all states and is capable of producing its own effects, generates those effects. Since everything that is engaged in an operation is a producer of an effect, the operation must exist as a prior state; and by means of that [operation], the projection of power (*śakti*) is logically established. || 33 ||
He asks: "What is this eternal activity that is without support? [At this point, a portion of the text has been lost; the following is written as a reconstruction by Phullarāja:
Now, in order to describe the nature of the means (*sādhana*) according to another school of thought, he says:]
Some describe that entity characterized in this way as an unprecedented power of time, or as action, or simply as time itself, in some manner or other.

(32) Some say that *apūrva*—which is designated as the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) and termed merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*)—is an entity (*bhāva*) characterized by such a nature and defined by causal capacity. For it is through the power of the unseen that everything either comes to be or does not;
thus, the unseen alone should be understood as the cause of all effects. However, some proponents [of other views]...
They say that the power of time (*kālaśakti*) belonging to the Lord Brahmā is the means (*sādhana*).

For everything, when animated by the power of time, is capable of action. Or else, they say that action—of a passionate (*rājasa*) nature, whose essential character was described immediately above—is the means; but not that which occurs at a later time.
It is not possible to define what is called a "means" (*sādhana*). Previously, the means was explained as being rooted in action;
now, the distinction is that action itself is the means. For it is that very [action], as it proceeds by itself, which becomes the specific [means]; thus, it is indeed time [that acts].
Proponents of the doctrine of substance and time state that the proof [of their position] is characterized by such attributes as "eternal" and "one.
For it is due to time that all entities arise for the accomplishment of their effects; thus, time alone is the means [of accomplishment]. As he will say:
"If it were not to obstruct... (Jātakarmakalpa-kṣudrakasūtra, Dharmaskandha 5), thus [it is said]. || 34 ||
Now, in order to investigate the number of that potency (*śakti*)— characterized by capability— which was previously established as the means of accomplishment, he says:
"The six potencies of others are eternal and endowed with both difference and non-difference."
For the successful accomplishment of actions regarding objects, they are established like a genus. || 35 ||

(33) According to the opinion of others, it is established that six eternal powers—beginning with *karman*—which are characterized by distinct definitions, are fixed as residing in objects. Of what nature are they? They are endowed with both difference and non-difference;
for if they were described as being exclusively different from the objects, [the object] would...

If they were devoid of power, they would be formless; if, on the other hand, they are said to be non-different, then the emergence of diverse effects could not be established. Therefore, they are endowed with both difference and non-difference, being different in some respect and non-different in another.

Some maintain that powers (śaktayaḥ) reside in objects just like universals (jāti), just as the universals of existence (sattva), substantiality (dravyatva), cowness (gotva), and Śābaleya-ness (śābaleyatva) are always present in objects through a constant conjunction of both difference and non-difference. 35.
Although these [perfections] are infinite due to the distinctions of substance and so forth, their reality does not transcend being exactly sixfold; thus he says:
"And these, through the distinctions of substance, form, and so on, are as if immeasurable."
But when one abides in reality, these six powers are seen not to transcend it. || 36 ||

(34) Power (*śakti*) is differentiated by the difference in substance (*dravya*); for example, a sickle cuts in one way, whereas a sword does so in another. It is also differentiated by the difference in form (*ākāra*); for example, a sword [cuts] in one way, while a sword-vine (*khaṅgalatā*) does so in another. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is also [differentiated] by the difference in place and time; that very same [power] [is thus manifold].
The power of burning undergoes various manifestations as fire, yet its nature as the sixfold essence does not transcend its own essential form. || 36 ||
Now, he states that it is indeed a single power that, having attained a sixfold state through the distinction of its causes, constitutes the means of accomplishment:
"Due to the distinction of its causes, the single power is perceived as divided."
They say that this very agency is sixfold and is the basis for its activity. || 37 ||

(35) Because the very state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), existing in six ways through distinctions of purpose such as "that which is most desired" (*īpsitatama*) or through [distinctions of action] such as "flaming," is the basis— that is,
the causal condition— for the differentiation of the technical designations of *kārakas*, which arises from the differentiation of the capacities for its activity.
This must be understood: as it has been said— "The fuel will burn until the cooking is finished"— according to the logic that "cooking" is the instrument for the action of burning,
agency itself assumes the designation of "instrument" and so forth when there is an intention to express an intermediate operation.
Thus, it has been established whether power is one or many. Now, raising the doubt as to whether this [power] might be distinct or non-distinct [from its substratum], he says:
"Whether there is identity or distinction, that which is distinct is so designated."
The world has verbal testimony as its authority; it is followed by the treatise.

(36) It has been stated that this [reality] is inexpressible in terms of difference and non-difference, being merely endowed with both difference and non-difference. Now, if you subject this to a rigorous examination, what purpose would that serve for us? In every respect, the power and the possessor of power are absolutely one.
Reality is either non-distinction or indeed non-difference;
however, we, following the system of the Grammarians, assert that capacity (*sāmarthya*) is indeed distinct.
For the world has verbal testimony as its authority, and by this very treatise, that [authority] is followed.
Thus he says: "It is followed by the treatise (*śāstra*). For the meaning of a word is expanded in accordance with worldly convention (*lokapratīti*).

And the world follows precisely the non-distinction (*avyatireka*) of the power (*śakti*) that is the cause of the word's operation; for if there were distinction (*vyatireka*), [the word] would be constantly..."
It has been stated that this would entail the consequence of the completion of the action [at the very moment of its commencement]. || 38 ||
Now, if you do not attain cessation without an investigation into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is said in response to this:
"In the ultimate sense, however, there is no identity, because distinctness has a different characteristic."
Reality itself manifests in the form of both difference and unity. || 39 ||
(37) Due to its distinctness, there is no unity apart from difference, characterized as being different;

for reality itself manifests in the form of both difference and unity. Indeed, it manifests as difference during the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), whereas upon the dissolution of ignorance (*avidyā*), it manifests as unity.
It is to be understood. || 39 ||
To explain this very point, he says: That which is an indubitable distinctness does not differ from unity;
that which is an indubitable unity does not differ from distinctness. (40)

(38) That distinctness which is rendered free from doubt through the realization of the true nature of reality is not different from unity. And that unity which is free from doubt and devoid of delusion is not different from distinctness—that is, from manifoldness. || 40 ||
And so, when unity has reached its ultimate limit, then that alone shines everywhere;
thus he says: "The sky, the earth, the wind, the sun, the oceans, the rivers, and the directions."
The portions of the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇatattva) are situated externally. || 41 ||

(39) Or rather, let the investigation into plurality and unity regarding a few objects stand aside. As for these two great entities designated as the great elements— namely, heaven and the sky, and earth, which together constitute heaven-and-earth— and the wind that is third between them, as well as that which is characterized by the sun;
The divine splendor that is the foremost of all splendors; the waters, whether rivers or oceans, which are its modifications;

all these great elements (mahābhūtas) which constitute the life of the entire world; or the quarters (diśas), which serve as the basis for worldly transactions; and time (kāla), which will be described hereafter—all this is that [Brahman].

Regarding the phrase "of the reality known as the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇatattvasya*): these parts, which are reflections and appearances existing externally, belong precisely to that reality which is designated as the internal organ and which manifests internally by virtue of being the internal organ. But in the ultimate sense, what kind of internal-external distinction can there be? It is one alone.
The meaning of the verse is that the supreme Śabdabrahman, consisting of consciousness, exists in such and such a manner. || 41 ||
Having described its nature as the great elements and its nature as the directions, he speaks in order to establish its very same nature as time:
"That one [reality] alone exists in the form of temporal division."
For that part, being without prior or posterior, is perceived through the form of another. || 42 ||

(40) For that [time] is indeed without prior or posterior from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Alternatively, it is perceived through the sequence of "long," "quick," and so forth, by virtue of the power of time. Thus, the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is established according to the consensus of the world and the opinion of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) through the inherent capacity of things. Or else—

It is of the nature of a mental construction according to the Vijñānavāda perspective; or it is of the nature of a relation, being a distinct category (padārtha) according to the Saṃsarga-vāda; or it is characterized as the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), denoted by the word "pūrva" (prior), according to the Mīmāṃsaka view; or it is the power of time (kāla-śakti) associated with Brahman according to the Advaita philosophy; or it is action (kriyā).

It should be understood either as having the nature of *rājasa* activity according to the Sāṃkhya system, or as the form of time (*kāla*) characterized as an eternal, single substance, according to the view of those who maintain the existence of a substance called time (*dravyakālavādin*).
Furthermore, in the context of discussing the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), there is an investigation into the term "factors of action" (*kāraka*), and by way of that incidental discussion—

Having first examined the distinctions between cause (*hetu*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), agent (*kāraka*), instrument (*karaṇa*), and purpose (*tādarthya*), their essential natures have been briefly stated. Following that, there is a temporal alternative regarding power (*śakti*): does it exist simultaneously [with its substrate], prior to it, or at a later time? Furthermore, is that power distinct according to the differences of object (*karman*) and so forth, or is it indeed one and the same?

"It is conceptualized as such" refers to the conceptualization of number (*saṃkhyāvikalpa*). Furthermore, the inquiry into whether that [number] is distinct from or non-distinct from the category (*padārtha*) constitutes the reflection on distinction and non-distinction; and by way of that introduction, there is the determination of the nature of Brahman—this is the collective meaning of the section. || 42 ||
[The text provided consists of two vertical bars (||), which in this context serves as a section divider. || Section Break ||
Now, continuing with the very position of the Grammarians under discussion,
and establishing the existence of *śakti* (potency) by demonstrating its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), he says:
For even in the absence of non-difference, a difference is perceived; and even in the absence of positive concomitance (anvaya), [a distinction is seen].
Therefore, the meaning of the case-ending (vibhakti) is held to be something distinct from the meanings of "tree" and so forth. || 43 ||

(41) Even in the absence of distinction— that is, even when there is non-difference of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)— in instances such as *vṛkṣaḥ*, *vṛkṣam*, *vṛkṣeṇa*, *vṛkṣāya*, and so forth, there is a distinction (*vyatireka*) of the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), characterized as the grammatical factor (*sādhana*). Likewise, in that very same context, even when there is no connection of the meaning of the case-ending, there is a connection— that is, a following along (*anugama*)— of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

It is observed. Therefore, we conclude that there exists some distinct, undeniable object, characterized as a means (*sādhana*), which constitutes the referent of the suffix and is denoted by the word "capacity" (*śakti*); thus, the proof of the means is established. || 43 ||
Now, he states a verse for the purpose of concluding what has been explained and introducing what is yet to be explained: "The general agent (kāraka) has seven primary sources of division;
six are distinguished by the categories beginning with 'object' (karman), while the seventh is the remaining category. (44)
(42) "The general [category] is the agent" (*sāmānyaṃ kārakam*) is the conclusion of the explained meaning;
"its seven [types]" (*tasya sapta*) and so forth is the introduction to the meaning to be explained. In that context, "the first ones" (*ādyāḥ*) are those that are primary;
with respect to the general means of accomplishment (*sāmānyasādhana*), they are also of the nature of particulars (*bheda*), and they are the sources (*yonayaḥ*) of their own [derivatives].

"Of the divisions" means the sources of the divisions. Alternatively, the first seven are the sources—that is, the causes—of their own respective divisions. To the question "How so?", he says: "By the division known as the six actions," and so forth.
By means of the different designations such as "action" (karman) and the rest, the seven powers of the grammatical factors (*kāraka*) are now indicated.
The connection with the *Sādhanasamuddeśa* [chapter]. || 44 ||

The grammatical factor (*kāraka*) has been indicated as being divided into seven types according to the distinctions of *karman* and so forth. Now, following that sequence, he speaks in order to explain *karman* first, preceded by a demonstration of its numerical divisions:
"It is considered to be threefold: the produced (*nirvartya*), the modified (*vikārya*), and the reached (*prāpya*)."
Among those, the object most desired [as the goal of action] is the *karman*; the others are conceived in four ways. (45)
(43) Here, the specification of the particular *kārakas* is presented according to the sequence of case-endings (*vibhakti*).
In the *sūtras*, however, they are stated in the order of *apādāna* and so forth, following the rule regarding conflict (*vipratiṣedha-paribhāṣā*).
In that regard, the case-endings are *su*, *au*, *jas*, and so on. A *kāraka* may be either expressed (*abhihita*) or unexpressed (*anabhihita*).
In that context, the case-ending denoting the first-mentioned *kāraka* is prescribed for the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself.

Since all case-endings from the second onwards are "unexpressed" (*anabhihita*) *kāraka*-endings, they are introduced at the outset in accordance with the meanings of the second case and so forth, because they share a single commonality. And the meaning of the second case and the others consists of the object (*karman*) and so on.
As it has been stated:

"The second case ending is used for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.2), and so forth. Therefore, the explanation of the object itself is now reached at the beginning. In that regard, by means of the agent's action—
That which is most desired to be attained—that which is most intensely sought after—is precisely the definition of *karman* as set forth in the first sūtra.

This *karman* is to be understood as being divided into three types—namely, the produced (*nirvartya*), the modified (*vikārya*), and the reached (*prāpya*)—and it should be known that these various forms are indicated in many places throughout the treatise. Now then...
He says, "But another is imagined as fourfold," in order to distinguish that which is also taught in other sūtras. || 45 ||
He asks, "How so? and replies:
"That which is attained through indifference, that which is not desired by the agent, that which is not designated by other names, and that which has another as its predecessor. (46)

(44) That which is to be reached through indifference or neutrality, such as the base of a tree for one going to a village; likewise, that which is not desired by the agent, such as thieves or poison—
this [is the fourth type].
First, that which is indicated by the second sūtra, "And likewise [that which is] connected [to the action], though not desired" (Pāṇini 1.4.50), is of two kinds: namely,
when it is not desired in the very same manner that [the object] is most desired by the agent, being something other than the desired.
That which is to be avoided, such as poison and the like, and that other which is to be attained with indifference, such as the root of a tree and so forth,
as previously stated; likewise, even that which is not designated by other technical names such as *apādāna* (ablative) and the rest, yet is caused by an action— this [is what is meant].

It should be understood as that which is indicated by the third sūtra, "akathitaṃ ca" (Pāṇini 1.4.51). Likewise, regarding the phrase "yad yaccāpyanyapūrvakam": that for which another *kāraka* (grammatical factor) precedes. For example:
In the expressions "he is angry with Devadatta" (*devadattam abhikrudhyati*) and "he bears malice toward Devadatta" (*devadattam abhidruhyati*), the rule *Pāṇini* 1.4.38,

*krudhadruhor upasṛṣṭayoḥ karma*, applies; for when *kruddha-* and *druh-* are preceded by a prefix— that is, when they are connected with a preposition— the object is that person toward whom the anger is directed.
That agent, although designated as *saṃpradāna* by the preceding rule, receives the designation *karman* (object) alone.
Thus, in the example "he plays with dice" (*akṣān dīvyati*),
[the dice] are governed by the rule "And [the object] of *div*" (Pāṇini 1.4.43).

By this [rule], that which is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for reaching heaven, which by the preceding rule would have received the designation of instrument (*karaṇa*), now receives the designation of object (*karman*). || 46 ||
Now, he speaks in order to explain the threefold [classification] beginning with the *nirvartya*:
"Whether existing or non-existing, that whose changing material cause (*prakṛti*) is not relied upon is declared to have the nature of being *nirvartya* (that which is to be produced). (47)

(45) When a thing such as a jar being produced has a material cause (*prakṛti*)— whether existent, like clay and so forth, or non-existent, like sound for [the production of] conjunction and so forth— that cause is not resorted to as non-different [from the effect], nor is it intended to be expressed in such forms as "one makes clay into a jar"; rather, what is the case?

By such distinctions as "he makes a jar from clay," when there is an intention to express [the object] together with its material cause (*prakṛti*), those who know the object (*karman*) call that a "produced" (*nirvartya*) object. He speaks next to explain the "transformed" (*vikārya*) object:
When the material cause (*prakṛti*) itself is intended to be expressed [as the object], it is the "object of transformation" (*vikārya*).

(46) When the material cause of an action is intended to be expressed as undergoing modification (*pariṇāma*), as in: "he makes clay into a jar," "he makes grass into a mat," or "he turns charcoal into ash."
Thus, such [actions] are declared to be the "object as that which is modified" (*vikārya-karma*). Now,

under the guise of introducing another opinion, with the desire to explain the different varieties by means of stating alternative views, he speaks in order to define the "object as that which is produced" (*nirvartya*) and the "object as that which is modified" (*vikārya*):
By some others, however, it is demonstrated in the treatises that there are two types of objects: that which is produced (*nirvartya*) and that which is modified (*vikārya*). || 48 ||
To the question "How so?", he says:

That which, being non-existent, is brought into being, or that which, being existent, is manifested by birth—that object is established as twofold: the *nirvartya* (that which is produced) and the *vikārya* (that which is modified). (49)

(47) Whether, according to the followers of the Vaiśeṣika and other schools, that which is non-existent arises, or, according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine, that which is already existent arises—both of these are called "to be produced" (*nirvartya*) because they are manifested through the act of arising.
This is what is meant: for us, who maintain the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), it can be said that there exists an action that is "to be produced."

It is possible. Whether its material cause (*prakṛti*) exists or does not exist, there is no impairment whatsoever of its being a "product" (*nirvartya*) by virtue of being manifested through birth. Whatever is manifested through birth, whether existent or non-existent, is a product. That which is non-existent is born.

Thus, the fact that an action brings about what is not yet existent has merely been restated as previously explained, namely, that it is manifested through the birth of the non-existent. This, however, is the distinction here: for example, in the cases of "she gives birth to a son" or "he utters a word," [the object] is already present within the womb, even though it is intended to be expressed [as something newly produced].

The manifestation of sound occurs through its production and its application. For here, "birth" (janman) is intended as the manifestation of that which already exists, namely the sound intended [to be expressed]. By the mention of "birth," when there is an intention for activity (*pravṛtti*), [the manifestation follows].

He states that [the object] is something to be modified (*vikārya*). Furthermore, by the inclusion of the term "arising" (*janma*), he indicates that even for that which is manifested otherwise, there is an absence of the status of being an object as something to be produced (*nirvartya-karma*). Therefore, in cases such as "he studies the Veda" (*vedam adhīte*), since the Veda and so forth—which are being manifested through the act of study—lack the status of being an object as something to be produced, [they are classified as objects of manifestation].

"If it is argued that [the rule applies] when an object is being produced or modified (*nirvartya-vikriyamāṇa*), then there must be an addition [to the rule] for the study of the Vedas and similar acts. (Jainendra-vyākaraṇa on Pāṇini 3.2.1)
Thus it is said. And in this way, when there is a desire to express the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), this [term] must be derived as stated by Kātyāyana;

therefore, the view held by some that it is otherwise is incorrect. Consequently, this [distinction] exists according to the difference between the views of those who maintain that the effect pre-exists (*satkāryavādin*) and those who maintain that it does not (*asatkāryavādin*).

This must be explained. Previously, it was stated in accordance with worldly convention; here, however, the distinction is that it is also stated by relying on the views of the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika). || 49 ||

"And the object of transformation (*vikārya-karman*) is established as being of two kinds. Having previously stated the distinction between individual instances in order to describe the definition for each, he states the definition:
"Some [objects] arise from the destruction of their material cause (*prakṛti*), such as ashes from wood and the like."
[The soul is transformed] by the production of certain other qualities, like the transformation of gold and similar substances. || 50 ||

(48) From destruction without residue (*niranvaya-vināśa*), there is the annihilation of the primary material cause (*prakṛti*). For example, [the transformation] of wood and the like into ash and so forth;

one turns wood into ash. As before, the connection with action between the material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra*) should be applied. However, according to the previous definition, this object of action (*karman*) is that which is to be produced (*nirvartya*).

When the material cause (*prakṛti*) is not intended to be expressed, it is a "product" (*vikārya*). But here, even though the material cause is not intended to be expressed, because the effect—such as ashes—is understood to have arisen from wood and so forth by means of the destruction [of that wood] through its very specific form, it is a "product. However, in the previous case...

Primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is directly the object of transformation (*vikārya-karman*), and by non-difference from it, the transformation itself is also [the object]. Here, however, the distinction is that it is specifically the transformation that is directly [the object]. In the expression "he burns the wood," the primordial matter alone is expressed by the word; the transformation, namely the ash, is understood through implication. Likewise in "he cuts the stalks."

This should be understood from examples such as "he makes a hide" (*carma karoti*). However, there is another type of *vikārya* object characterized by the emergence of a different quality (*guṇa*), such as a new configuration (*saṃsthāna*) or other attributes, wherein a certain material cause (*prakṛti*), without abandoning its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), is called "modified" (*vikṛta*) due to having undergone a change in its arrangement. For example:

"Let there be golden earrings. According to the theory that the effect is non-existent [in the cause], although there is here the production of something previously non-existent, nevertheless, because of recognition and because in common worldly experience there is the determination of identity, it is said that only a different quality arises. And this...
When there is an intention to express the primary meaning (prakṛti), it is also included by the previous definition. || 50 ||

Now he states the definition of an object that is reached (*prāpyakarma*): "That is called 'reached' where the accomplishment of the specific qualities inherent in the action is not perceived either through direct observation or through inference. (51)

(49) In the case of a product (*nirvartya*) object, the very acquisition of its own being (*ātmalābha*), which is the distinction produced by action, is determined through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself. In the case of a modified (*vikārya*) object, such as ashes or an earring, the modification—the distinction produced by action—is determined by direct perception. In some instances...

Furthermore, the determination of a particularity arises from inference, such as the determination of [pleasure] in another person by means of signs like the expansion of the face; likewise, the particularity produced in trees by the application of actions such as the sprinkling of water is born at every moment.

Because of its subtlety, it is not perceived immediately after its arising; rather, it is determined in its final state through the observation of a more fully accumulated particularity. For such a fully accumulated particularity cannot arise suddenly and unexpectedly without depending upon a sequential process.

Inferred at every moment, it is of a subtle form; for that subtle form is difficult to discern, just as it is with the specific distinctions between the musical notes ṣaḍja and so forth, or between the high and low pitches.
Thus, where such a distinction produced by action is not perceived, [the existence of] its agent [is inferred].
The "attained" (prāpya) object is that which is most desired (īpsitatama) merely by virtue of being the objective domain of an action. For example:
"He sees the sun," "He approaches the city," "He studies the Veda," and so forth.
For in the case of the sun and others, no specific quality is produced [in them] by the actions of seeing and the like.

It is not determined [by the means of knowledge]. Rather, by the two means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), only the connection with an action (*kriyā-sambandha*) is indicated, and that alone is not the specific distinction (*viśeṣa*). For once the connection with an action has occurred, a difference existing in the thing itself is observed in the case of both the *nirvartya* (that which is to be produced) and the *vikārya* (that which is to be modified). In the case of the city, however, [the difference] is produced by the action of going.
Conjunction, although it is a specific quality residing in two things, remains unperceived in the case of Devadatta due to the city’s vast magnitude,
just as the contact between the Himalayas and a finger is imperceptible; likewise, a single part of the earth [remains unperceived] in relation to its own constituent parts.

The conceptualized [object], which consists of the specific substratum and its superstratum and is denoted by the word "city," is well-established; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. (51) Some maintain that there is no object to be attained at all, because in every case one determines a specific change produced by action. For instance:
A special attainment exists everywhere through seeing and other means;
for some, there is the accomplishment of its manifestation in cases such as the "poisonous gaze. (52)

(50) According to the view of some, modification (*vikāra*)—defined as the acquisition of a specific quality produced by actions such as seeing—is present everywhere; however, it is not perceived by everyone due to its subtlety. For those for whom that specific quality is within the range of perception, there is a certainty regarding its manifestation in that object.
Success! For an object gazed upon by snakes whose very glance is poison is perceived as if licked by tongues of blazing fire.

By analogy with that, some specific quality produced by seeing and so forth in other cases must also be inferred in the object. Indeed, the eye is composed of light (*taijasa*) and functions by reaching its object; therefore, it is joined [with the object].
An object is necessarily transformed by the mere sight [of it], just as by the gaze of one with "poisonous vision" (*dṛṣṭiviṣa*). However, there is this distinction:

in the case of poisonous vision, the intense heat from contact with the poison burns the object; in other cases, its presence is subtler. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), magnets and so forth are included. In their proximity...

Iron moves; for in such cases as "water becomes clear in the presence of the *kataka* fruit," there is indeed a modification produced by action (*kriyākṛta-vikāra*). However, this is not the opinion of the author of the treatise, because it is presented as the view of "some" (*keṣāṃcit*), indicating it is an alternative opinion. Even when a specific [change] is observed in some instances, [it does not follow that...].

It is logical that such a state exists everywhere, even where no specific difference is perceived. Furthermore, what is intended here as the "result of the action" (kriyā-phala) is a modification (vikāra). However, the object currently being observed is the cause of the action, not its result. Even in cases such as a "poisonous gaze," the modification occurs in the object due to contact with light (tejas), [and not in the subject].

By virtue of its inherent power (*kriyābala*). Thus, this is the very nature of things such as a magnet; it is not some modification produced by an action. Therefore, there certainly exists an object to be reached (*prāpya-karma*) that does not depend on assistance provided by an action. || 52 ||

If there is no connection with modification (*vikāra*) in the case of an object that must be reached (*prāpyakarma*), how can it serve as a subordinate factor (*aṅgabhāva*) for the accomplishment of the action, in order to fulfill its status as a means (*sādhana*)? It is said:
"The reaching of the appearance (*ābhāsopagama*), manifestation (*vyakti*), and the endurance (*soḍhatva*) [of the object] constitute the nature of the object."
The specific qualities are established for the accomplishment of the action of that which is being attained. || 53 ||

(51) Since an object enters the range of vision by being situated in a suitable location, its arrival at a suitable location— that is, its coming into appearance— is an auxiliary factor for its perception according to its own nature.
This is so even for that which is already situated in a suitable location.

Manifestation (vyakti) is a subordinate factor (aṅga), being caused by the presence or absence of obstacles to illumination such as mist, or by lamps and the like. An entity such as a piśāca, which possesses an invisible nature, exists in a location where the object is capable of being illuminated, provided there is no obscuring cover.

Endurance, the capacity to be perceived, and the nature of being an object of sight—through these excellences, the object to be attained (*prāpya-karman*) functions as a means (*sādhana*) in the act of seeing. Furthermore, these causes of the action of seeing are not produced by that [action]. This is also the case in examples such as "he goes to the village," where endurance and the other qualities apply as appropriate.

Villages and the like are to be expressed [as objects]. For villages and so forth, when they appear as the objects of one's striving (*samīhā*), accomplish actions such as going by being concomitant with those actions. Similarly, the Veda and so forth, while being studied, are concomitant with the act of studying. Even in the case of "he remembers his mother," the mother is one who has previously rendered assistance.
Even for one of cruel heart, when [the mother] enters the path of memory, it brings about mindfulness.

However, when there is no regard for the status of being the most desired object (*īpsitatama*), and one intends to express the general nature of a relationship, the genitive of the residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) is used, as in "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*). || 53 ||

Thus, action has been characterized according to its divisions. However, this must now be addressed: it was previously stated that all specific means (*sādhana*) are the agents (*kartṛ*) of the qualities and actions [of the object].
How, then, is the status of being an object (*karmatā*) possible? He thus provides the introductory transition for the investigation into the object and the agent.
Having first experienced independence in the case of things to be produced (*nirvartya*) and so forth,
it subsequently becomes the object (*karman*) when it enters into the operation of other agents.

(52) With respect to the acts of producing (*nirvṛti*), transforming (*vikriyā*), manifesting (*ābhāsa*), and counteracting (*apahatikriyā*), there are respectively the objects of action (*karman*) characterized as that which is produced, that which is transformed, and that which is attained. This is based on the independence (*svātantrya*) of the agent (*kartṛ*), which constitutes agency;
and in relation to that [independent agent], there are many other agents whose sphere of activity consists of the objects of action such as the produced and so forth.

In the operation characterized by instigation (*praiṣa*), such as the act of producing (*nirvartanā*) and so forth, the object (*karman*) arises because it is that which is being reached by that [agent].
For instance, [the agent] "produces," "transforms," "assumes appearance," or "manifests";
thus, due to the differentiation of objects within the agent's own operation, when the operation of the primary agent is intended to be expressed, [these distinctions arise].
It brings about, it modifies, and it causes [the object] to attain the state of being an object such as an appearance;
thus, under the command of the agent, like servants in the presence of a master, they become subordinate and undergo the status of being the object (karman).
If that is so, then the agent becomes the object; having become the object, how does it become the agent such that the status of being both object and agent is possible? To this he says:
"Even when separated from its [the object's] activity, it remains established in its own activity."
In some cases, he obtains rules prescribed by karma based on the authority of the scriptures.

(53) In cases such as "the granary splits" (*bhidyate kusūlaḥ*), when the instigation of an agent is absent because the granary and so forth experience splitting by themselves due to their fragile nature; and likewise in cases such as "the field is being reaped" (*lūyate kedāraḥ*), because of its extreme dryness there is no dependence on the effort of an agent; [and] "the rice is cooking" (*pacyate odanaḥ*).

In cases such as *svayam eva* ("by himself"), because the agent does not need to be relied upon due to the excellence of ease (*saukaryātiśaya*), the grammatical rule prescribes the status of being "like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*) with effort, so that the operations prescribed for the object may apply to the agenthood (*kartṛtva*) which rests on independence (*svātantrya*) regarding its own activity; thus, [the operations] prescribed for the object [apply].

Even though he is the agent, he obtains the prescribed injunctions and the duties [of the object]. For, by casting the operation of the object and the agent into his own operation, he possesses agency in his own activity; thus, the duties of the object would not otherwise occur—this is the purpose of the commencement of the treatise. "In some cases," it is said.
The meaning is: the domain of verbal roots whose states reside in the object and whose actions reside in the object. || 55 ||
But surely, once the instigation of the agent has ceased, let there be no status as an object (*karmatva*) dependent upon it here;

however, how can there be agency (*kartṛtva*), by virtue of which the designation "agent-as-object" (*karmakartṛ*) is applied? For instance, since an object is observed to have an operation toward its own action when a primary agent exists, in the absence of that [primary agent], it would follow that it possesses only the status of an object.
Anticipating the question, "Whence does agency [arise]?", he says:
"The action, when its instigation has ceased, remains within its own constituent activity; as its status as an object ceases, it abides in its own state of agency. (56)

(54) Effort that conforms to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the agent’s instigation (*preṣaṇa*), which is his own operation characterized by the employment of other factors of action (*kāraka*). When this [instigation] is not expressed with respect to the agent— as in "the rice cooks by itself" (*odanaḥ svayameva pacyate*)— it ceases [to apply], because the operation residing in the agent [is not being denoted].

Since it is expressed by the suffix (*pratyaya*) and not expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*), its being "understood" (*pratīyamānatva*) is stated to be untenable due to its contradiction with the *Bhāṣya*, which says, "the root *pac* has two meanings. Those [meanings] are other roots.

And because this will be stated [later], the author intends that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) consists of the agent’s activity (*kartṛvyāpāra*), distinguished according to its objects. When that [activity] has ceased— having become a subordinate part of the action with respect to the principal action— the object remains as the agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of its own activity.
However, its designation as "object" (karman) is based on its past state;

for even when the agent's operation is intended, it remains established in its own action alone, since it accomplishes the principal action through that [intermediary] means, and because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) expressed in the statement "the *kāraka* is the object."

Nevertheless, it should be understood that here [the agent] exists primarily by virtue of its capacity (*sāmarthya*). For this very reason, when its status as an object (*karmatva*) ceases in relation to the operation of the agent, it remains in its own agency (*kartṛtva*) regarding its own action within its entire sphere; thus, previously, in relation to the operation of the agent—

Having been an object (*karman*), it becomes a "subject-as-object" (*karmakartṛ*) when, due to the intent to express an excellence of ease (*saukaryātiśaya*), there is no desire to express [the agent's action] as such, and thus it attains the status of an agent. This is the meaning: the state of being a subject-as-object does not arise merely from the non-expression of the agent's operation; rather, it occurs when [the object] itself performs its own operation.

Even when there is a desire to express autonomy (*svātantrya*), the operations pertaining to the object (*karmakārya*), such as the suffix *yaṅ* and others, would not apply [to the agent] by virtue of the rule: "That which has an action equal to that of the object is treated like the object" (*Pāṇini 3.1.87*).
Thus they are established by the treatise (*śāstra*). This was stated by the author of the *Vārttika*:
"The status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) belongs to the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*), because independence (*svātantrya*) is intended [to be expressed]" (Pāṇini 3.1.87).
In that regard, even when dependence on another arises in the case of [verbs] such as *bhid* ("to split"), the granary (*kusūla*) and so forth remain independent of others.
This has been established in the Bhāṣya: "Indeed, a granary that has been recently constructed in a windless place where there is no rain may break apart by itself."

"In a place devoid of wind" (*nivāte*) excludes the agent's activity of not encountering the impact of air currents. "Without rain" (*nirabhivarṣe*) excludes contact with droplets of water. "Recently made" (*acirakṛte*)... [text fragment]
This excludes any excellence that might be imparted through long-term storage over time. For these causes of falling might otherwise be imagined to apply to a granary;
thus they are excluded. And so, because its structure is not firmly established, it falls apart by itself; this establishes its agency. Even in the case where the hand of the wielder [is involved]...

Devadatta is seen running about, [and it is said] "the field is being reaped by itself. Here too, the field—its moisture dispelled by contact with the rays of the fierce sun and its stalks completely withered—is falling apart; through its identity with what is contained within it (*tātsthyāt*), it takes on the form of rice and thus becomes easy to reap.

Furthermore, since actions are accomplished by a collection of causal factors (*sāmagrī*), it is logically consistent to employ expressions such as "Devadatta cuts," "the sword cuts," or "the pot cooks" by superimposing independence (*svātantrya*) upon each factor in order to highlight its specific efficacy. And in that context, [the status of] the agent belongs to the object itself.

The status of being treated like the object of an action (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply to anything else; for instance, one says, "the rope is being cut" (*cchidyate rajjuḥ*) or "the rice is cooking itself" (*pacyate odanaḥ svayameva*).
This very point has been stated in the Bhāṣya:
"In that case as well, there is no agent other than that which is called 'ease' (*sukaratā*)."
Regarding [the rule] *g-eṇa-od gh. 3.1.87*:

when the field (*kedāra*) is intended as the locus of an action characterized by an excellence of ease, Devadatta, though capable of being designated as the agent (*kartṛ*) of the cutting, does not receive that designation; rather, it is the field [that is so designated].

This is the meaning. However, in the case of the softening of rice (*odana-viklitti*), the agent's operation (*kartṛ-vyāpāra*) is not necessarily required, just as it is not in the case of cutting. For indeed, the grains of rice soften even without the exertion of an agent;
rather, here the primary operation of the agent is understood to consist precisely in the employment of the instruments and other factors of action (*karaṇādi-kāraka*). || 56 ||
