[The text provided consists solely of vertical bars and does not contain content to translate.]

But is it not the case that a single root, such as *pac* (to cook), sometimes expresses an object that is subordinate to the agent’s activity— as in "Devadatta cooks rice," "he splits the granary," or "he cuts the field"—
and at other times expresses an object whose subordination to the agent’s activity is not perceived?

Anticipating the objection that— since in cases such as "the rice is cooked by itself" (*pacyate odanaḥ svayameva*), the meaning is expressed as self-established (*svapratiṣṭha*), and since a distinction between verbal roots is difficult to discern when there is no difference in their form— the *bhāvanā* might as well be denoted solely by the agent-affixes (*kartṛ-pratyaya*), he says:
The wise understand those other elements to be like the case of the perfected bird;
even though there is a difference, they are conceived as one because their form is identical. (57)

(55) Verbs such as *pac* ("to cook") and others, which have the object and the agent as their referents, should be understood as distinct verbal roots from those roots like *pac* that express the mere action of softening (*viklitti*) and so forth, and which denote the operation of softening as subordinate to that [result]. This is because words differ according to the difference in meaning; for it is the primary [meaning]...

The meaning is that which is to be conveyed by words. According to the principle that "the subordinate follows the principal," the word differs with each distinct meaning. For example, since the root *pac* denotes the act of softening (*vikledana*), the root *sidh* denoting the act of completion (*viklitti*) is a different verbal root; yet, despite being different roots, they are treated as one.

The instruction in the *dhātupāṭha*—such as "ḍupacaṣ pāke" (the root *pac*, meaning 'to cook')—is based on the non-difference of form; for a thing whose form is not different is capable of being conceived as a single entity. However, where there is a difference in result despite a difference in instruction, there is a twofold or threefold instruction, as in the case of the roots beginning with *kṣi*, such as *kṣi* in the sense of 'perishing', due to the difference in *vikaraṇas*.

The root *bhū* belongs to the first class (*bhvādi*); *kṣi* in the sense of "dwelling" and "going" belongs to the sixth (*tudādi*) and fourth (*divādi*) classes; and *kṣīñ* in the sense of "injuring" belongs to the ninth (*krayādi*) class. || 57 ||
Now,
according to the principle that "some other investigators say that a single word has multiple meanings," he says:
Verbal roots such as *pac* (to cook) and others, being endowed with identical forms, function by their very nature to denote both a single constituent action and a collection of actions. (58)

(56) These elements (*dhātu*) are non-different because they are endowed with a common, undivided form or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), since a single uniform cognition that is not sublated serves as the indicator of their non-difference. If it is argued that multiplicity of referents is itself a sublation, we say no; for that [multiplicity] is established through a difference in functional capacity (*śakti*).

For even a single word is observed to possess the capacity to convey multiple meanings; for example, the word *grāma* denotes both a collection of houses enclosed by a fence and a community of people inhabiting such a place. Or, for instance, words such as *akṣa*. In that regard, with respect to its object and agent, the root *pac* denotes merely the act of softening.

In the expression "the rice cooks by itself" (*odanaḥ svayam eva pacyate*), because the agent Devadatta is not denoted by the suffix (*pratyaya*), his activity (*vyāpāra*) is not expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*).
For the primary meaning of the root *pac* is "softening" (*viklitti*), as this is possible in all cases; even when [an agent] is required.

For in the case of the agent's activity, as in "Devadatta cooks," because the act of moistening has the purpose of softening, the agent's activity is primary by virtue of its objective nature; and since both [the activity and the result] are expressed here, it functions as a collective whole. It is precisely in this context that the justification for having two referents is stated.

Regarding the object of the agent (karmakartṛ), however, because there is no agentive suffix (*kartṛpratyaya*), the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—which is the operation of that agent—is not denoted. For in this case, the object itself is the agent, and its operation is simply the softening (*viklitti*);
thus, it is that alone which is denoted. As in: "The rice grains soften" (*viklidyanti*) or "they are accomplished" (*siddhyanti*).

The operation of the agent is expressed precisely through the state of being split. Thus, in the expression "the granary splits by itself," the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the process of becoming divided into two. In the case of "Devadatta splits the granary," it should be understood that the process of becoming divided into two is subordinate to that [agent]. || 58 ||

Thus, because words possess diverse powers (*vicitra-śakti*), the distinction between their meanings has been established according to the difference in their objects. Now, in connection with the agent and the object, [the rule] "that which is the object of the causative when it is not the object of the non-causative" (*ṇeraṇau yatkarma*, Pāṇini 1.4.52) [is introduced].
In this regard,
since it has been stated that "it is established because [the object] is the agent" (Pāṇini 1.3.67), he investigates as follows:

In the case of the root *ruh* in its pure form, both the act of subordination (*nyagbhāvanā*) and the state of being subordinate (*nyagbhavana*) are understood; likewise, both are recognized even when the root is in its causative form (*ṇyanta*).
They call this the fifth state, which occurs when the root is used as both subject and object (karmakartṛ).
When the causative suffix (ṇic) is elided from a root that originally involved an external instigation, it is said to function in its primary sense.

(57) Here, there exists this usage, "The elephant mounts itself," which expresses the activity of the elephant and pertains to the object-as-agent (*karmakartṛ*). For that [usage], a methodological construction for its grammatical explanation (*anvākhyāna*) must be devised. In that regard, by means of what is set in motion through the following of the commonality of form...

The grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) proceeds by extracting the constituent parts (*avayava*), as in the case of a *gavaya* depicted in a drawing, and by resorting to those meanings [of the parts]. Thus, having placed one's foot upon as many stages of analytical meaning as serve as steps, this practical ultimate stage is reached.

The stages occurring in the interval, when being enumerated, are denoted by the word *avasthā* (states). In this context, the verbal root *ruh* is recognized in its initial part; its meaning elsewhere is well-known as consisting of two states, and that very same meaning is accepted here. This is what he says:
"Subjugation (*nyagbhāvanā*) and the act of subjugating (*nyagbhavana*) are understood in the case of the root *ruh* when it is pure.

This means "pure" or "absolute," that is, devoid of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). In the example "the elephant-keepers mount the elephant" (*ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ*), the meaning is "they cause [the elephant] to subjugate itself" (*nyagbhavantaṃ nyagbhāvayanti*). And in this case...

The intended purport lies solely in demonstrating the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*). The inclusion of suffixes such as *vikaraṇas* and *pratyayas*, however, is merely incidental (*nāntarīyaka*), because a word cannot be employed [in speech] otherwise.
Thus, by the expression "the elephant mounts himself," the very meaning of this verbal root is demonstrated. And so it is.

By means of a single word, that is, a verbal root (dhātu), accompanied by the suffixes that necessarily arise [with it], two states characterized by subordination and the state of being subordinate are conveyed. And here, following the portion of the verbal root...

The causative suffix (*ṇic*) is recognized as undergoing a modification produced by the substitution of its phonetic qualities (*guṇa*); if it were explained as residing in the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*) which terminates in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) exactly as it stands,
then there would follow the undesirable consequence of perceiving the activity of another instigator— which terminates in subordination— thereby resulting in a deficiency in the intended sense.

It may be so. Therefore, an intermediate state between [the two], which is obtainable through the restriction of the meaning of the root *ruh*, is assumed as the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) for the causative suffix (*ṇic*), consisting in the operation of the elephant. This is shown at the end of that [discussion] in order to resolve the aforementioned doubt.

By the statement beginning with "nivṛtapreṣaṇāt" (when the instigation has ceased), etc., the suffix *ṇic*, which is produced for the instigating activity residing in that [agent] and which brings about an increase in its prior state, achieves a meaning identical to that of the simple root *ruh*. Thus he says:
"Subordination (*nyagbhāvanā*) and the state of being subordinate (*nyagbhavana*) are understood even in the *ṇic*-formed [denominative] verb.

Thus, there are two examples: "The elephant mounts by itself" (*ārudyate hastī svayameva*) and "The mahouts cause the elephant to mount" (*ārohayanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ*). By the one [example], the operation of the prompted agent (*prayojya-vyāpāra*), which is the form of the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), is [indicated] by the *ṇic*.

It has been shown that this [agent] cannot be perceived otherwise; thus, when the status of being like an object (*karmavadbhāva*) would apply to the self-reflexive [agent], it is presented as an inseparable concomitant. By the second [suffix], the meaning of *ṇic*—the activity of the elephant-driver—is demonstrated, and that [activity] follows upon the activity of the one being impelled (*prayojya*).

The term *śakyadarśana* is derived from the root *dṛś* with the suffix *ruhir*. However, the inclusion of the suffixes and so forth is due to their necessary concomitance (*nāntarīyakatayā*), as in the previous case.
Thus, these are the four stages. Beyond that, a portion resembling the *ātmanepada* ending is observed, and there is the cognition of the mere operation of the elephant. And this—
Since it is impossible [to attain the goal] without the state of being an agent of action, that [state] which is obtained through the contraction of the previous states is resorted to. Thus he says:
"the fifth state."
And so forth. Thus, since the *ātmanepada* ending is established in the form *ārohayate* because of the status of the object as the agent (*karmakartṛtva*),
[the rule] *ṇeraṇau* applies here.

"If it is argued that [the agenthood of the object] is established because it is the agent of the action (*karmakartṛtva*), [we reply: this statement is for the purpose of excluding the *yak* and *ciṇ* suffixes," so said the author of the Vārttika. Regarding that, [it is stated]: "Or rather, it is not [necessary], because there is a prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.3.67).
By such statements, it is established as a settled conclusion that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs here precisely by virtue of the treatment as *karmavat* (like the object).
However, in the case of *gaṇo gaṇayati svayam eva*, the rule *aṇau* (Pāṇini 1.3.67) is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) for the purpose of excluding the middle voice.

Thus the Sūtra has been established by the author of the Vārttika. Furthermore, since the state of lying low (*nyagbhavana*) resides in the object—just like the action of softening (*viklitti*)—the root *ruh* possesses an action residing in the object; this is the subject matter of the "object-like behavior" (*karmavadbhāva*) according to the author of the Vākya.

And since it is observed that some roots, whether in their primitive form (*prakṛti*) or with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), have identical meanings, he provides an illustration for this: "The root *sidh* does not express the meaning of *pac* without the causative suffix (*ṇic*)."
That meaning of the causative form of the root *pac* is restricted to the context at hand.
(58) The verbal root [√sidh] in "siddhyaty odanaḥ" denotes mere softening.

In "pacaty odanam," however, the meaning of the root √pac, accompanied by the causative suffix (ṇic), expresses the sense of cooking characterized by moistening, with softening as a subordinate element;
thus, it means "he accomplishes the rice. The same applies to the causative form of √ruh.

"It occurs in the sense of 'somehow' (kathaṃcit)"—this is the intended meaning here. The two roots *ruh*, namely the simple root (*prakṛti*) and the causative (*ṇyanta*), have the same meaning as in the pair *pacati* and *sādhayati*; however, when the causative suffix is present, once the element of "commanding" (*praiṣa*) has ceased, the form *ārohayate hastī svayameva* ("the elephant makes itself mount") expresses something entirely different, namely "descending" (*nyagbhavana*).

The verbal root is thus explained through the conceptualization of a means (*upāya*); however, in this context, it does not possess the *ṇic* suffix in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), such that one might be challenged as to how it remains when the meaning has ceased.
For the explanation is directed toward worldly words, based upon the expressive word through the conceptualization of a means.
The instruction is given everywhere by means of the unreal division into base and suffix, following only worldly usage.
But even so, since an unreal extracted word-meaning (*apoddhāra-padārtha*) is impossible, how can there be such an instruction?
This is done solely in accordance with worldly usage.
[Objection: Even so, since the isolated word-meaning (*apoddhāra-padārtha*) is unreal, how can there be such a word? [Response:
In that case, there is no fault, because the excellence of the verbal operation (*karma-vyāpārātiśaya*), which is signified by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), does indeed exist.
Having thus established the agency of the action through the cessation of the command (*praiṣa*), he says the following in order to establish it even by means of superimposing the command:
"The operation of certain [agents], such as Devadatta and others, which exists in a transitive verb..."
It is intended [to apply] to mats and such things, even in the absence of Devadatta and others. || 62 ||

(59) In cases such as *kaṭaṃ karoti* ("he makes a mat"), when the meaning of the verbal root is transitive and concerns a primary agent such as Devadatta, there is an operation characterized by an injunction (*praiṣa*) belonging to the instigator who is the primary agent; when that [operation] is intended to express an excellence of ease for the object (*karman*), then—

In that case, even in the absence of an agent, the action is intended [to be expressed] as such; for just as Devadatta employs [the mat], so too there arises the intention [to express] that "the mat is easy for Devadatta. 62.
Having stated this in general terms, he now applies it to the present context: "When the instigation [of the agent] has ceased, the object becomes the instigator of its own agent;
when connected with another instigation, it is expressed by the *ṇic* suffix in the *laṅ* [tense]. (63)

(60) The operation of the agent is the instigation (*praiṣa*), which is superimposed upon the object; thus, when that instigation has ceased—that is, when the operation of the instigator is not intended to be expressed—and there is a desire to express independence, [the object] attains the status of being the instigator of its own instigator by virtue of an excellence of facility. In that case...

When there is another instigation (*preṣaṇa*)— that is, another operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*)— in the form of "the mat causes itself to be made" (*kārayate kaṭaḥ svayam eva*), occurring with respect to an agent such as Devadatta who is connected to the action of making the mat,
this is expressed by the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) following the causative (*ṇic*) in the domain of the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*); thus, it is denoted by the causative (*ṇij-abhidheya*).

The sense is that there is an instigation (*praiṣa*). And here, the instigation consists in the devising of a means (*upāya-parikalpanā*) by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), but it does not exist in reality; thus, there is no requirement for an object to be impelled (*prayojya*). Consequently, because the possibility of a "prompted object" (*prayojya-karman*) exists, and because there is no connection with another [actual] object that is present, the [suffix] being prescribed for the verbal root [applies].
One should not raise the objection as to how the *ātmanepada* ending occurs [in the case of the root *nī*] by the rule *ṇeraṇau*. For it is thus:

in order to demonstrate an excellence of facility (*saukaryātiśaya*), the actual instigation (*praiṣa*) of the object is superimposed; once that is perceived, there is no intention to express the status of being an agent (*prayokatva*).

However, by the force of the cognition of the object as the agent (*karmakartṛ*), a state of prior instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is understood; thus, the *ṇic* suffix pertaining to that [state] does not cease. In this manner, in connection with the topic of the object-as-agent (*karmakartṛ*), the rule *ṇeraṇau* has been examined.
Regarding the Vārttika on the rule *tyadādiṣu dṛśo'nālocane kañ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.60), which states:
"But there is no justification for the meaning of a *kṛt* suffix [in this case]."
Thus it has been urged. According to the rule *kartari kṛt* ("the *kṛt*-suffixes denote the agent"), the suffix-meaning must be the agent;

yet that [agent] is not applicable here. For words such as *tādṛśa* express an object characterized by similarity, and not the agent of the act of seeing—this is the meaning of the Vārttika. To this, it was replied:
"Moreover, this [suffix] is a *taddhita* in the sense of 'like' (*iva*).
This means that within the section beginning with *ive pratikṛtau*, this suffix should be stated as having the designation *taddhita*.
Thus, the meanings such as "like that" (*sa iva*) and "of such a kind" (*tādṛśa*) are established. In this way, by the author of the Vārttika...

This is the established conclusion. However, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), in order to resolve the objection that the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix is untenable, simply follows the traditional formulation by stating:
"It is established because of the status of being both object and agent (*karmakartṛtva*)."

Thus [it is said]. In that case, since the act of seeing (*dṛś*) is a state residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*), and because it expresses merely the activity of the agent—namely, the act of seeing—it lacks the element of instigation (*praiṣa*). Therefore, how could there be the possibility of it being a "reflexive object" (*karmakartṛtva*)? If one were to superimpose instigation, the causative suffix *ṇic* would have to be applied; however, the root is here without the causative suffix (*aṇyanta*).
In the Sūtra, it is presented as the act of seeing.
In this case,
the object whose causal operation has ceased remains within a portion of its own action;
when its status as an object ceases, it persists in its status as an agent.
According to this principle, some who seek to justify the status of an object as its own agent say:

"In cases such as *sadṛśa* ('similar'), where the object attains the state of being the agent, there is a state of being the objective domain (*viṣayatva*) with respect to both actions—the action of undergoing and the action of bringing about. (64)

(61) Regarding words such as *sadṛśa* ("similar") and *tādṛśa* ("such-like") which are to be derived [by suffix], the status of being both object and agent (*karmakartṛtva*) is attained; as for that which was stated regarding the object becoming the agent, since the two actions of "attaining" (*āpatti*) and "causing to attain" (*āpādana*) are to be expressed in relation to the state of being the object of the root *dṛś* ("to see"), the capacity for the status of being the object-agent is established by means of that basis.

For what is the meaning of "he sees"? It means that he brings about the object—such as a jar or the like—so that it attains the state of being an object of vision. In this context, the activity [of seeing] consists in the determination of the object; for that which has become the object (the karma), there is the bringing about of that [state of being an object].

The operation of the agent has the object as its purpose, not the agent alone. In that operation of the agent, the operation of the object—characterized by its coming into contact—is subordinated; thus, in its proximity, the object’s independence regarding its own operation becomes obscured. However, when [the object] is situated in a suitable location...

When the object situated in the middle of the field of vision becomes more clearly manifest, it then becomes "sudarśana" (well-seen), its own perception being self-evident; thus, by setting aside the employment of an agent, when there is a desire to express independence in its own operation, having been an object (*karman*), it attains the status of an agent (*kartṛ*). Thus it comes to be.
This concerns the object of the agent of the action.
He says that this is not tenable:
"If one were to bring some word from elsewhere and thus construct [the meaning] in this way..."
There would be the state of being an agent residing in the action for those [roots] denoting seeing and so forth. (65)

(62) Here, in the case of the root *dṛś* ("to see"), the verbal meaning (*vācya*) is merely the act of seeing residing in the agent, as in "he sees. For from this [mere seeing], the attainment of the status of being an object is not understood; rather, the meaning of the verbal root is simply the cognition of the object. Since the attainment of the status of being an object belongs to every meaning of a verbal root, it is precisely the specific act of seeing that is intended.
It is logical that the object of the verb *dṛś* (to see) must be expressed. And since that seeing is established upon an object,
by some such force [of the context], through the implication of an object, there occurs the supply of a word expressing the attainment of the state of being an object.
If one were to assume that the operation of the agent is subordinate to the communication of the operation residing in the object,

then even those [roots] denoting seeing, sitting, and so forth would necessarily be *karmasthabhāvaka* (having their state of being located in the object); consequently, there would be no verbal root at all that could be called *kartṛsthabhāvakriya* (having its state of being and action located in the agent).

Therefore, in order to demonstrate that this is incorrect, he says: "Since you conceive this by supplying some word from anywhere out of a desire for cleverness— namely, that 'that which undergoes [an action] causes it to undergo'— this being the case, [the fault applies] to those who express seeing and so forth."
The verbal roots such as *dṛś* (to see) would have the property of having the action residing in the object (*karmasthabhāvakatva*).

By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), this would also apply to verbs such as *ās* (to sit), which denote sitting and so forth. However, this is not tenable because roots such as *dṛś* have the property of having the action residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakatva*). In this regard, they would [otherwise] have the property of having the action residing in the object.
By stating this, it is meant that the status of these [roots] as having a state residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*), which was previously established, would thus be undermined. || 65 ||

Now, raising the doubt as to how it is to be understood whether an action resides in the agent (kartṛsthabhāvakatva) or whether it resides in the object (karmasthabhāvakatva), he speaks in order to explain this incidentally: "Where there is the perception of a specific difference, there the action is established."
But for others, the determination of action is revealed by words alone. || 66 ||

(63) It should be understood that action (*kriyā*) is established precisely where some distinction is observed between the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*). According to the intention of the author of the Sūtras, action is that which is accomplished by means of instruments involving motion (*saparispanda*), whereas being (*bhāva*) is that which is accomplished by means of instruments devoid of motion (*aparispanda*); [this distinction] is made without regard for such differences.
The author of the *Ṭīkā* intends that even an action (*kriyā*) is designated as a state (*bhāva*). Accordingly, there are the rules:
"In the sense of a characteristic or a cause of an action" (Pāṇini 3.2.126) and "When one state is characterized by another state" (Pāṇini 2.3.37).
In such passages as these, non-difference alone between action and its absence resides in the mind of the author of the Sūtras.
However, others do not accept this; thus he says:
"In the view of others, the determination of action is manifested by words alone. This is what is meant:

Even in the case of those roots such as *paci* (to cook) which have agents established in the action, a specific distinction such as exertion (*pariśrama*) is observed even in the agent. Therefore, this is not a definitive rule that "wherever a specific distinction is observed, there is an action. Consequently, it is only by means of words that a distinction is manifested or conveyed.

In that very case, it is appropriate to say that the action is established; for those for whom the word is the means of valid cognition (*śabdapramāṇaka*), it is logical that the expression of the word is exactly as the word denotes its object, and not by looking toward the nature of the thing itself. And the word [expresses this] in such instances as "he sees the jar."

It causes the cognition of [the object] as indeed qualified by the object of the act of seeing (*dṛśi-kriyā*). However, in cases such as "he splits the wood" (*kāṣṭhaṃ bhinatti*), it denotes the object of the act of splitting (*bhidi-kriyā*) along with its specific qualification; therefore, by virtue of that [qualification], one must designate it as having its state of being (*bhāva*) residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakatva*) or having its state of being residing in the object (*karmasthabhāvakatva*). And thus, [in the case of *paśyati*], it is not the case that "it is seen by itself" (*svayam eva dṛśyate*).

It must be understood that [the action] indeed exists. As for their stating the definition that "an entity (bhāva) is that which is to be accomplished by means of an instrument devoid of motion," and then asserting that "the entity of the root *pac* resides in the object (*karmastha*)," that too appears to be inconsistent. For instance, in the case of cooking grains (*pīlupāka*), one says, "He cooks the pot."
Due to contact with fire, in the case of a jar, through the process of motion in its constituent parts (*avayava-kriyā*), there occurs the destruction of the conjunctions of those parts;

this leads to the destruction of each preceding effect-substance, and consequently, the destruction of each subsequent effect-substance. Thus, the process of cooking (*pāka-kriyā*) directed toward atoms accompanied by motion also takes place. Therefore, this [theory of transformation] remains entirely unsettled.

Thus, having first explained the object (*karman*) characterized by the first sūtra as being divided into three types— namely, the produced (*nirvartya*), the modified (*vikārya*), and the attained (*prāpya*)— and having, in connection with that,

discussed the objects of the produced and modified types according to different opinions, [the author now addresses] the causative formed by the removal of the causal suffix (*nivṛttapreṣaṇa-ṇyant*) and the causative formed by the superimposition of the causal suffix (*adhyāropitapreṣaṇa*).

Having demonstrated the agent of the action and stated the refutation preceded by the demonstration of the object to be reached (*prāpyaviṣaya*), and having established— within that very context and according to different opinions— the distinction between actions residing in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*) and actions residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*), [the author] now...
He begins to explain the grammatical operations (*karmāṇi*) as taught in other sūtras.

In that regard, the *Akathita-sūtra* states: "Time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), the distance to be traversed (*adhvagantavya*), and location (*deśa*) are designated as the object (*karman*) for [verbs] that otherwise lack an object. (Pāṇini 1.4.51).
Having thus stated that [the action] is not to be undertaken, he says the following in order to demonstrate this:
"When all [factors]—time, action, substance, and location—are joined with intransitive verbs through the inclusion of other implied actions, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) arises. (67)

(64) Since intransitive verbs cannot have an object, the question arises as to how they could be connected with one; thus, it follows that time (*kāla*) and other such factors must be declared to possess the status of an object (*karman*) when they are employed in conjunction with those [intransitive] roots. To this it is replied: there is no need to state a technical designation of "object" here, because when time and the like are used in connection with intransitive verbal roots—
The status of being an object (*karmatva*) indeed arises. To explain how this is so, he says:

"by means of other actions that are included within [the primary action]. Those [actions] in which another action is included with respect to the principal action are "those by which [other actions are included]. When there is a connection—that is, a relation—with them, and for this reason:
Since their status as objects (*karman*) is already established in relation to other actions, what is the purpose of this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*)?

Thus, in examples such as *māsam āste* ("he sits for a month"), *godoham āste* ("he sits until the milking of the cows"), *kośaṃ svapiti* ("he sleeps in a corner"), and *kurūn svapiti* ("he sleeps throughout the Kurus"), one understands that he "sits pervading" (*vyāpya*) the month and so forth.

In the action of sitting and so forth, which is a constituent part of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the verbal root (*dhātu*) is employed. Since time and other factors are clearly intended as objects (*karman*) because they are desired to be reached by the action of pervasion and the like, there is no need for a further effort [to define them]. If this is so, then in the present case, [verbs] such as *ās* (to sit) and others—

Verbs become transitive through [the influence of] time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), path (*adhvan*), and object (*karman*); consequently, from such verbs, the suffixes *la*, *kṛtya*, *kta*, and those having the sense of *khal* would apply only when time and the others function as objects, and not in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). In that case, in the example "Devadatta sits for a month" (*māsam āsyate devadattena*), the *l*-suffix would not occur in the sense of the abstract action. [For instance, one could not say] "it is to be sat for a month" (*māsam āsitavyam*).
[Otherwise], the suffixes *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khalartha* would not occur in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) in examples such as *māsam āsitam* and *svāsaṃ māsam*;
yet, because of the rule stating "and [these suffixes] after intransitive verbs in the sense of the abstract action," they are indeed desired even there.
Therefore, since time and other factors exist as objects (*karman*), how can there be intransitivity? If [the verb] is transitive, [how can it take a suffix] in the sense of the abstract action?

How is it that the *lakāra* [is used]? It is said: action (*karman*) is of two kinds—internal (*antaraṅga*) and external (*bahiraṅga*). Among these, the substance-object (*dravyakarman*) is internal, and with that alone is there first a connection. The external action is characterized by time and so forth, as will be stated.

By the verse beginning with "śaktipramāṇa... and so forth, it is established that in this context, the designation of a verb as transitive (sakarmaka) or intransitive (akarmaka) is properly determined by its internal factor (antaraṅga). Thus it has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "It is said [in the rule] 'of intransitives' (akarmakāṇām)," and so on.

And since [the suffixes] such as *la* must also be considered internal (*antaraṅga*), he states the very nature of internal and external [operations] by saying "the locus" (*ādhāra*). For example: *godohaṃ svapiti* ("He sleeps for the duration of the milking of the cows"). This means: for as long a time as it takes for the milking of the cows to be completed.
Furthermore, a vessel and the like delimit another action by its own temporal measure.

Space, too, serves as a cause for specific distinctions such as sleep, insofar as it is delimited by being reached from a certain point of reference; thus, time and the other factors are distinct. Of these—

The meaning is that when *kāla* (time) and the others are used in conjunction with all verbal roots—whether they are intransitive (*akarmaka*) or transitive (*sakarmaka*)—the status of being an object (*karman*) arises naturally; therefore, it is not necessary to add a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyeya*) for their designation as objects.

For instance, in this context, the designation of "object" is not merely for the purpose of prescribing the second case ending (*dvitīyā*), but rather for the sake of the meanings of the *l*-affixes (i.e., verbal terminations).
Furthermore, there is a Vārttika on this point regarding the rule "kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge" (Pāṇini 2.3.5).

Regarding the rule *atyantasaṃyoge karmavallādyartham* (Pāṇini 2.3.5): the meaning is that even the *la*-affixes, the *kṛtya* suffixes, and those with the sense of *khala* are intended to convey the result of the action (*saṃjñāphala*). This is because, in this context, another action characterized by pervasion (*vyāpti*) is also accepted by verbal roots such as *ās* ("to sit") and others.

By entering into the state of being the object of the action of pervasion (*vyāpti*), a month and so forth become the "attainable" (*prāpya*) object, which is indeed the most desired (*īpsitatama*). Thus, this is simply a "natural" (*prākṛta*) object, as stated in the Bhāṣya: "just as one says 'he makes a pot' or 'he makes a cart'. For example: *māsam āste* (he sits for a month), *godoham āste* (he sits during the milking of the cows).

In expressions such as "he sleeps for a *krośa*" or "he sleeps throughout the Kurus," the verbal roots denote the seat (*āsana*) and other factors that pervade [the space or time]; the meaning is: "he remains pervading for a month" or "he pervades by means of remaining for a month.
The same should be applied accordingly in other instances. For example: "lightning flashes from the cloud."

Just as the verbal root (*dhātu*) functions in the sense of "illumination" (*vidyotana*) when it has the factor of departure (*niḥsaraṇāṅga*), so too here its function lies in the sense of the factor of attainment (*prāptyaṅga*). This is indeed another action (*kriyāntara*) which includes pervasion (*vyāpti*) and has time (*kāla*) and other factors as its objects. However, in the case of "Devadatta, what does he do? He sits," [it is different].
In the absence of pervasion, the verbal root (dhātu) resides in the mere act of sitting. Regarding this, it has been said:
"Roots such as *pac* (to cook) function, by their very nature, endowed with identical forms, either in respect to a single part or to the collection of actions."

It should be understood here in the same way as in the cases "he cooks" (*pacati*) and "it cooks by itself" (*pacyate svayameva*). Thus, since this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) has been rejected, the mention of "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) is purposeless; for even in the case of transitive verbs, as in "he cooks the rice for a month" (*māsam odanaṃ pacati*), the status of "object" (*karmatā*) is established for the month and so forth, because they function as the locus of the action's pervasion (*vyāpti*).

The meaning here is that [the verb] "pervades" (*vyāpnoti*) by means of the cooking of rice for a month. And it is for this purpose that the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is explained here. Even though verbs such as *pacati* ("he cooks") take two objects when used with an object of time and so forth, it has been stated that the application of the *l*-suffixes and other affixes occurs with respect to the primary object, which is a substance (*dravya*).

Regarding the rule: "In the case of verbs with two objects (*dvikarmaka*), when the primary object (*pradhānakarman*) is to be expressed, they say [the *l*-affixes and so forth apply]," even though tools such as axes involve the action of pervading (*vyāpti*), in cases like "the mat sits" (*kaṭa āste*), there is no pervasion of the mat by the act of sitting; rather—

Since it is precisely the month and so forth—being employed for the delimitation of actions such as sitting—that is pervaded, it alone possesses the status of the object (*karman*), and not the mat or other substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) which is merely in contact; thus, everything is well-established. || 67 ||

(65) Just as a locus (*ādhāra*) sustains an action by mediating between the agent and the object, so too does [time] such as a month; thus it partakes of the shadow of a locus. For instance, there are such usages as "he offers oblations at sunrise" (*udite juhoti*) and "he eats at night" (*rātrau bhuṅkte*). Likewise, one says "he sleeps for a *krośa*" (*krośaṃ śete*) and "he sleeps throughout the Kurus" (*kurūn svapiti*).

The status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) for the path and the place is indeed manifest, because they support the agent; and in cases such as "he cooks rice for a month," the support of the substance-object is likewise manifest in the case of a substance-object.
However, when pervasion (*vyāpti*) is intended, the state of being a locus ceases, and thus [the object] becomes a mere object (*karman*); this is the meaning of the word "as if" (*iva*).

Alternatively, the meaning of the comparison is as follows: just as the locus (*ādhāra*) undergoes connection with the action through the mediation of the agent and the object, so too do time and the other factors through the mediation of the substantial object (*dravyakarman*). Furthermore, the connection with the action occurs first with the substantial object, and only by way of that [substantial object] does it occur with the temporal and other objects; thus, its stages (*kakṣyā*) or states are distinct.

This is because [the objecthood] of action is distinguished from the properties of substance, such as capacity, measure, and number. Therefore, the connection with time occurs in actions; hence, the connection with the object of action occurs prior [to the connection with the action].

Thus it has been said. For a hard substance that requires cooking takes a long time to be prepared, whereas the opposite—being of large dimension and great number—is accomplished in a short time; thus, distinctions such as time depend upon the nature of the substance and the action. Likewise: "He sleeps for the duration of a cow's milking," "for the distance of an arrow's flight," and so forth.

The same should be stated regarding the word *pacati* (he cooks). In the cases "He studies the *kośa*" (*kośam adhīte*), "He studies his own portion of the Veda" (*svādhyāyam*), and "He studies the Kurus and Pañcālas" (*kurūn pañcālān adhīte*), there is an increase or decrease in the growth or diminution of the study with respect to the duration of time or the extent of the territory.

Temporal and other such factors are remote with respect to the connection of action to the object, when compared to the substance-object; for this very reason, their status as objects arises at a subsequent time. For once the connection with all the means of accomplishment has been established, temporal factors and the like are required as causes for the delimitation of the action; thus, they occupy a different level [of grammatical importance].
By means of the subsequent rule, *akathitaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.51), these [objects] receive the designation of *karman* (object), not by virtue of being the most desired (*īpsitatama*),
because there is an absence of intensity in the desire. Furthermore, this is established by the inclusion of *duh* and other such verbs in the enumeration within the *akathita* sūtra.

It is stated in that very [sūtra]: "Time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), the distance to be traversed (*adhvagantavya*), and location (*deśa*) are designated as objects (*karman*) for [verbs] that otherwise lack an object" (Pāṇini 1.4.51). Furthermore, when both a subordinate element (*guṇa*) and a principal element (*pradhāna*) are present, it is the principal element alone that is connected with the grammatical operation;
thus, the rule for the suffixes *la* and so forth applies to the substance-object (*dravyakarman*). For example: *māsam odanaḥ pacyate*, *pakvaḥ*, *paktavyaḥ*.

Examples such as "he has studied an *anuvāka* for a *krośa*" (*supacaḥ krośam adhīto 'nuvākaḥ*) should be cited. However, when a distinct word is employed, the second case (*dvitīyā*) occurs even with respect to time and other such objects of action (*kāla-karman*).
For a single verbal suffix (*lādi*) is incapable of denoting two objects of action, one subordinate and one primary; therefore, [the suffix] applies to the primary object.
There is a cognition of the object (*kāryasaṃpratyaya*). A case-ending (*vibhakti*) arising from two nominal stems (*prātipadika*) of different forms conveys two objects as well.
And since time (*kāla*) and the other factors possess the status of an object (*karmatva*) that pertains to all verbal roots (*dhātu*) and belongs to a different level [from the primary object].

Therefore, when the verbal root is joined with those [words] which are not substances (adravya) and are thus intransitive (akarmaka), it serves as the basis for the *l* suffix to occur in the sense of the object (*karman*) as well as the state (*bhāva*). (69)

(66) Where there is a substance-object (*dravyakarman*), because the object of time and so forth (*kālakarman*, etc. is subordinate in relation to it, the suffixes *la* and so on do not occur there [for the time-object]. However, where no substance-object exists, the suffixes *la* and so on occur precisely for the object of time and the like. Furthermore, this is because the mention of *la* is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).

The suffixes *kṛt*, *kta*, and those having the sense of *khal* [denote the agent when the root is intransitive]: *māsa āsyate* (the month is sat through), *āsitavyaḥ* (to be sat), *āsitaḥ* (sat), *svāsaḥ* (easy to sit), and so forth.

Furthermore, the designation of roots as "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) is based on the absence of a substance-object (*dravyakarman*), because an object consisting of time and the like is possible in all cases; for a qualification is applicable only when there is both possibility and non-deviation. Thus.

Even when an action such as time (*kāla*) is present, the designation "intransitive" (*akarmaka*)— which is based on the absence of a direct object (*dravyakarman*)— is not excluded; thus, the *L* suffix is established for the sense of becoming (*bhāva*),
as in "the Lord remains for a month" (*māsam āsyate bhagavān*) and so forth, and "Devadatta has remained for a month" (*māsam āsito devadattaḥ*).

And because it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Furthermore, in the rule concerning "motion" (*gatyādi-sūtra*), the designation of the object (*karmasaṃjñā*) for the instigator (*prayojya*) is established on the basis of its being intransitive, as in examples such as *māsam āsayati devadattam*. For this very reason, in that [rule]...

"The inclusion of those with time as their object (*kālakarman*) when [the term] 'intransitive' (*akarmaka*) is mentioned" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.4.52); "But it is established by the statement that those whose object is time are treated like intransitives" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.4.52)—this meaning of the Vārttikas is established by logic. And so says the Bhāṣya.

Furthermore, there are no roots that become intransitive (*akarmaka*) by virtue of [the presence of] time, state, or distance. We shall understand it thus: those which are intransitive in some instances [are meant]. Alternatively, it refers to those intransitives [which would otherwise be transitive] by means of that same object (*karman*) through which they become both transitive and intransitive; for by this very object, not even one root remains intransitive. Or else:
"That action which both exists and does not exist belongs to those who perform no action; yet this action is not non-existent anywhere. (Genu-od Gh. 1.4.52).
What is the distinction between these three refutations? It is said:

In the rule *śabdakarmākarmakāṇām*, those verbs whose objects are not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitakarmaka*) are understood as "intransitive" (*akarmaka*). For instance, in expressions such as *āste* ("he sits") or *śete* ("he lies down"), when there is an intention to express the mere action, the status of being intransitive is possible even with respect to time and other such factors.
In exactly the same way, for verbs such as *pac* ("to cook") and others, once the connection with an object has been set aside through non-intention (*avivakṣā*), [the suffix] *aṇ* [is applied].

There would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the agent being designated as the object (*karman*) when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied. Therefore, that which has an absolute lack of connection with an object is "intransitive" (*akarmaka*). And if this [lack of connection] is taken to refer to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then, since that [meaning], being of the nature of an action (*kriyātmaka*), differs according to whether it is intended to be connected with an object or not by virtue of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣāvaśena*), there would be a distinction between transitivity and intransitivity even in the case of [verbs] such as those denoting time (*kāla*) and the like.

The word would thus have its purpose fulfilled. Therefore, since the action does not exist [independently], the verbal root (*dhātu*) is resorted to as the meaning of the other member of the compound; for it is that very root which is introduced as the qualifier in the rules *aṇau* and *ṇau* by virtue of its meanings such as "going" (*gati*), and because the verbal root possesses its properties through those meanings.
Since there is no distinction in the form [of the verb] whether an action is performed (*karmayoga*) or not (*ayoga*), it is not tenable that [the verb] lacks an object (*akarmakatva*);

for all verbal roots (*dhātu*) are never dissociated from objects such as time (*kāla*) and so forth. Thus, by the force of the qualification [in the rule], only specific verbal roots—those devoid of connection with a substance-object (*dravyakarman*)—[are intended].
They are relied upon. In the first resolution, the point is that [verbs] are "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) with respect to the substance (*dravya*) as the object.

In the second resolution, however, the distinction of "internality" (*antaraṅgatva*) is relied upon, based on the fact that the object which is the meaning of the constituent member (*varti-padārtha*) directly assists the action. In the third, however...

Because it is stated that [the action] "occurs" or "does not occur" in relation to the avoidance [of the object], a specific qualification of the relationship being negated is relied upon. The meaning is that for intransitive verbs, the relationship occurs with that very same substance-object (*dravyakarman*) by which a connection might occasionally arise, and not with an eternally connected object such as time (*kāla*).
Furthermore, because the designations "transitive" (*sakarmaka*) and "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) depend upon the presence or absence of an object (*dravyakarman*),

they say that by the rule "after *ud* and *car*, when [the verb] is transitive" (Pāṇini 1.3.53), the ātmanepada ending does not occur in the example "smoke rises for a month" (*māsam uccarati dhūmaḥ*). || 69 ||
Nor is it only the object such as time (*kāla*) that belongs to a different category; rather, every unmentioned object (*akathita-karman*) is understood to belong to a different category.
For, indeed, by virtue of the difference in the intended goal of the verbal root's meaning, that [object] is considered the most desired (*īpsitatama*). (70)

(67) "He milks the cow for milk," "He begs a cow from the Paurava," "He shuts the cow in the pen," "He asks the boy the way," "He gathers fruits from the tree"— all such instances are considered *akathita* (unspoken), as they have not been specifically designated by technical grammatical terms such as *apādāna* (ablative) and so forth. Even though the cow and other such entities are objects (*karman*) in terms of substance (*dravya*), they are called *akathita*.

In relation to the primary object (*pradhānakarman*) such as milk and the like, [the cow] is a subordinate means (*upāyabhūta*) and, because it is inseparable [from the action], belongs to a different category. For, in the case of the root-meaning such as milking, the very distinction or qualification consists in being the intended object (*uddeśa*); for that reason, [the cow] is devoid of the intensity of desire (*īpsāprakarpa*) found in the milk and so forth, since one indeed intends the milk and the like.

The meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) has proceeded; in that context, however, cows and the like, which serve as the means, are invariably concomitant. Alternatively, "designation" (uddeśa) by the meaning of the verbal root is the act of making something an object [of cognition], and its differentiation arises from preceding and succeeding time.
For previously, the primary substance such as milk was made an object by the meaning of the verbal root.

Subsequently, cows and the like become instrumental causes (*nimitta*); or rather, with respect to the meaning of the verbal root such as "milking," cows and the like function as distinct means. Therefore, they belong to a different level [of grammatical status]. The word "it is said" (*kila*) indicates a lack of approval regarding this view. Thus, the object (*karman*) is indeed non-different.

He will establish this later. Now, one might object: "Granted that time and the other factors occupy a different level [of grammatical status] because they depend upon the substance-object (*dravyakarman*);
but how can this be the case for cows and the like? For in their case, the situation is reversed;
namely, milk and such are the objects (*karman*) that depend upon the cow and so forth. And thus it has been said:
The rule for the suffixes *lā* and others applies when there is a subordinate object (*guṇakarman*); first, there is a connection with the subordinate object.
Since one desiring to obtain the primary object (*mukhyakarma*) strives first for the cow itself, therefore the root *duh* (to milk) in its pure form is connected first and foremost with the cow.

"But before [the suffix] *payas*, [the suffix] *gha* occurs after *gorduh*"; therefore, *la*-suffixes and so forth occur in that case (Pāṇini 3.2.69). This is true; however, there is a distinction of levels (*kakṣyābheda*) here based on what is primary and what is secondary. || 70 ||
For it is thus:

that which prompts the action is called the primary object (pradhānakarman); for the sake of its accomplishment, another [object] connected with the action is traditionally known as the secondary object (akathita). (71)

(68) That which, being the fruit aimed at, causes the means to be prepared for the initiation of action, and upon the attainment of which they cease their activity—that which is grasped by the intensity of the agent’s desire—is the "most desired" (*īpsitatama*) and is therefore primary; it is thus designated as the *karman* (object) and is stated first. And that—

The meaning is this: although milk and so forth are not desired for their own sake, they nonetheless invariably accompany the action; yet, because they are not the primary object, they are "unspecified objects" (*akathitakarma*) and, being subordinate, belong to a different category. For example, [the cow] in the expression "he milks the cow. Thus, even though they are not primary, they are [objects] because they serve as the means (*upāya*).

First, in the application of action (*kriyāyoga*), it [the cow] serves as the cause for the grammatical rule regarding the suffix *la* (the present tense marker). However, when the milk is not yet required, the cow alone is the primary factor; thus, even though the milk itself serves no immediate purpose, one proceeds to the milking for the sake of refining the cow, so that there may be no interruption of its milk supply.
Thus [it is said]:
"The [kāraka] other than the *apādāna* [is called *kartṛ*]" (Pāṇini 1.4.1). [For example:
"He milks the cow" (*gāṃ dogdhi*).

Thus, the example is established by way of conflict (vipratiṣedha). Otherwise, if [the action] were merely called "object" (karman), since there would be no possibility of the application of designations such as "ablative" (apādāna) and so forth, how could this serve as an example of conflict?

For that which is "unspoken" (*akathita*) is an object (*karman*) untouched by specific designations such as "ablative" (*apādāna*) and so forth. Thus, because they exist in a relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*), the "spoken" and "unspoken" objects belong to different levels; consequently, since there is a distinction between them, the technical designation "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) would not apply to cows and the like [if they were considered merely instrumental causes].
And by the rule "and that which is not [otherwise] specified," it is established that [the action] begins from this point. 71.
Now, regarding the statement:

"It is the settled conclusion that among the two-object verbs (*dvikarmaka*), the inclusion of *nī*, *vah*, *hṛ*, and likewise those with the sense of motion (*gatyartha*), should be understood. (Garuḍa-purāṇa, Odghaṭana, 1.4.51).
He explains what was stated in the Bhāṣya:
"In the case of roots such as *nī* ('to lead'), the status of being an object (*karman*) is based on the non-mention [of another relation], just as it is with roots like *duh* ('to milk').
However, when the verb expresses 'lack of acquisition' (*anupayoga*), the status of being an object is desired for the person (*śeṣa*) by rule. (72)
(69) He leads the goat to the village; he carries firewood to the city; he carries the load to the market.

By the mention of "verbs meaning motion" (*gatyartha*) in the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārtha...* and so forth, those [verbs] which possess two objects (*dvikarmaka*) are indicated. And by the phrase "and likewise" (*tathaiva ca*), which has the sense of including what was not explicitly mentioned, verbs such as *jayati* ("he conquers") and others are included.

[Examples are: "He seizes a hundred [cows]," "He conquers a hundred Śatānīkas," and "He fines the Gargas a hundred. Here, the object such as goats and so forth, which is associated with the excellence of desire (*īpsā-prakarṣa*), is designated as the primary object (*pradhāna-karman*), just like milk. However, objects such as the village, because they function as a limit (*avadhi*), are subordinate objects (*guṇa-karman*), just like the cow and so forth.

Because it is invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyakatva*), it should indeed be regarded as an "unspoken object" (*akathitakarma*); however, by the restrictive rule (*niyama*) consisting of the enumeration [of specific cases], the designation "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) is excluded in the case of "non-instruction" (*anupayoga*) regarding verbal roots such as *ākhyā*. For instance, in examples such as *naṭasya śṛṇoti* ("he listens to the actor"), since the actor and others constitute the "source" (*apādāna*) when there is instruction, they are not so designated when there is no instruction.

Because it is not encompassed by the specific [kāraka] designations, it would be an "unspoken object" (*akathita-karman*); however, due to the restrictive rule regarding the definitions of the enumerated [kārakas], this remainder is the domain of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). || 72 ||

Thus, the status of an object (*karman*) has been explained by way of its being either primary (*pradhāna*) or otherwise. Some, however, maintain that this [primary] object alone is the true object; for instance, they argue that roots such as *duh* (to milk), which have an implied causative sense (*antarbhūta-ṇij-artha*), function like causative forms (*ṇijanta*).
The status of being an object [of the action] is established by what precedes; likewise, the rule applies to the causative (*ṇijanta*) form. || 73 ||

(70) In the case of verbs such as *duh* ("to milk"), *yāc* ("to beg"), and others, whose expressed meaning includes the causal agent's operation (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*)— characterized as an instigation (*praiṣa*)— the designation of "object" (*karman*) for the cow and so forth in sentences such as *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* ("he milks milk from the cow") is established by the rule *kartur īpsitatamam* ("that which is most desired by the agent") alone.

For example, in the case of *ṇij*-affixation, as in "Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to go to the village," the person being prompted (*prayojya*) is the object because they are reached through the activity of the prompter (*prayojaka*). Thus, the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇām aṇikartā sa ṇau* (Pāṇini 1.4.52) is a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) stating that when roots such as *gam* (to go) and others are followed by a *ṇic* affix, only the prompted agent is the object, and not others.

The rule *pacyādīnām* does not apply here in the domain of roots that lack a causative suffix (*aṇyanta*). For instance, the meaning of the root *duh* (to milk) is as follows: "the cow flows [milk]," and "Devadatta causes her, who is flowing, to flow. In this context, because it is being reached through the act of flowing (*kṣaraṇa*), the milk is the object (*karman*); because it is being reached through the act of causing to flow (*kṣāraṇa*), the cow is the object.

Although, in terms of the actual object (*artha*), milk is the primary element while the cow is merely the means (*upāya*), nevertheless, because the meaning of the word consists in the act of milking (*kṣāraṇa*) where milk is subordinate, the cow alone is the primary object (*karman*). Therefore, the *l*-affixes and so forth occur only with respect to it: "the cow is being milked" (*duhyate gauḥ*), "the cow is to be milked" (*dogdhavyā gauḥ*).

"Dugdhā," "sudohā"— by the rule "duhādīnām apradhāne," the state of being non-primary (apradhānya) is expressed through this form, even though milking is not possible without the intention of separation (apāya). Nevertheless...

Regarding the rule *apādānam uttarāṇi* (Pāṇini 1.4.1), the designation *karman* (object) alone applies here because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. For if the designation *karman* were stated here by means of the *akathita* sūtra (Pāṇini 1.4.51), then, due to its status as an *apādāna*, it would not be so designated because it has already been mentioned [by a preceding rule].

However, since the designation of *karman* (object) would apply by the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*) alone when both [designations] are possible, it was stated [by Patañjali] that "the subsequent rules override the *apādāna*," as in the example "he milks the cow" (*gāṃ dogdhi*). Thus, the description here as an intention to express the *apādāna* is incorrect. Likewise in the case of "he begs a cow from the descendant of Puru" (*pauravaṃ gāṃ yācate*).

The meaning is "he causes to give. In the sentence "The Paurava gives a cow," the beggar employs him by generating faith; thus, the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) of the root *yāc* (to beg) includes the command (*praiṣa*) as its expressed meaning. In this case, the cow is the object of the begging, whereas it is the object of the command. However, when the meaning is "he establishes," then...

The village (*vraja*) possesses the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). However, when there is the possibility of both designations applying simultaneously, the designation of "object" (*karman*) is stated because it is subsequent [in the order of rules].
In the example "he enters the house" (*gehaṃ praviśati*), where the house is the locus, the meaning is a location subordinate to the act of entering;
that is, he remains having pervaded the house by means of the act of entering. This is due to the relationship between the cause and the effect (*nimita-nimittibhāva*).

[The terms] "entry" (*praveśa*) and "place" (*sthāna*) are perceived [as distinct]. In that regard, since both [the status of] object (*karman*) with respect to entry and locus (*adhikaraṇa*) with respect to place would apply, the object is cited as the example because it is the subsequent [rule]. [Examples include:
"He asks the boy the way" (*māṇavakaṃ panthānaṃ pṛcchati*), "The boy tells the way," and "Him... (*taṃ*).
"Employing" (prayuṅkte) means "causing to declare" (ākhyāpayati). Or, the boy desires to declare (ācikhyāsati);

[the teacher] employs him, meaning he desires to cause him to declare (ācikyāpayiṣati). Likewise, the meaning is understood as follows: the Paurava desires to give a cow (ditsati); the beggar employs him. Thus is the meaning of the root *bhikṣ* as well.
It should be understood as follows: "He gathers fruits from the tree" means that the tree releases the fruits;

the sense is that he causes it to release them. Even when there is an intention to express the *apādāna* (ablative), by the rule "the subsequent [kārakas] take precedence over the *apādāna*," the designation *karman* (object) applies here. "He speaks the Dharma to the boy" means that he causes him to comprehend it. In that case—
The object (*karman*) of the act of practicing is *dharma*, whereas the object of the command (*praiṣa*) is the student (*māṇavaka*), as in the expression "he instructs the student in *dharma*.

This means that the student learns *dharma*; [the teacher] causes him to learn it. However, since the student is intended as the recipient of the action (*karmaṇābhipreyamāṇa*), he receives the designation of recipient (*saṃpradāna*) in this context.

It must be stated that here the designation *saṃpradāna* is superseded by the designation *karman*, which pertains to the object of the primary operation. Alternatively, when there is an action that is most desired by the agent, that which is intended [by the agent] through that action possesses the status of *saṃpradāna*; as in the example, "He gives a cow to the teacher. For the cow—

She is dear to the giver; for that very reason, she is given to one who possesses merit. However, merit is not the intended object for the agent, since it was already established prior [to the act]. Rather, it is intended that the boy (māṇavaka) be favored by him.
Therefore, the most desired object here belongs to the prompted (prayojya), not to the prompter (prayojaka); thus, the designation "recipient" (saṃpradāna) does not apply.

Others hold that this is the [proper] object (*viṣaya*). Likewise, in the case of *nayati* ("leads") and others as well, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is established by the preceding rule alone. For example, in *ajāṃ nayati grāmam*, the meaning is "he causes the goat to reach the village. Since the goat is connected with the primary action of causing to reach (*prāpaṇa*), the goat is the primary object (*pradhāna-karman*).

"It is established by logical principle that for roots with two objects, the *l*-affixes and others are prescribed when the primary object (*pradhānakarman*) is to be expressed" (Pāṇini 1.4.51 vārttika).
Thus, we have: *ajā nīyate grāmam* (the goat is led to the village), *netavyā* (to be led), and *nītā* (led), as well as *sunayā* (well-led).

In this way, other instances should also be cited as appropriate. Furthermore, even though the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is included here, the designation of the "object" (*karman*) for the prompted agent (*prayojya*)—as established by the rule regarding roots such as *gam* (to go)—is not revoked;
for that restriction depends on its own class [of roots], since it excludes [the object status] only in other cases where the root ends in the causative suffix. And in this case:
Since the meaning of the causative suffix (ṇi) is already inherent in the verbal root itself as the sense of "commanding" (praiṣa), the suffix ṇic does not occur.

But surely, since milk and the like possess primacy in their actual form, it is logical that they alone should have the status of being "most desired" (*īpsitatama*); however, it is not appropriate for cows and the like to have the status of being "most desired" merely in relation to an action that is perceived as subordinate.

Because, in the proximity of the act of giving (*pradāna*), a quality (*guṇa*) cannot be the object of an excellence of desire (*īpsāprakarṣa*). Nor [is it so] because of the rule in the section on grammatical factors (*kāraka*):
"The most effective means of accomplishment is the instrument" (*asādhakatamaṃ karaṇam*, Pāṇini 1.4.42).
Thus, it can be argued there that the superlative suffix (*tamap*) does not intend to express excellence because of its inclusion;

for the direct expression of excellence is intended by the explicit mention of the suffix *tamap* in the term "most desired" (*īpsitatamam*). However, the gender [of the suffix] has its purpose fulfilled elsewhere.

This is so that the designation of locus (*adhikaraṇa-saṃjñā*) may apply in cases such as "the cowherd station on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*). For direct statement (*śruti*) indeed overrides indicative mark (*liṅga*), since those learned in the principles [of Mīmāṃsā] have stated: "Among direct statement, indicative mark, syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*), each preceding one is stronger than each succeeding one, because of the remoteness of its meaning. How then [is this so]?

Anticipating the objection that "cows" and the like would receive the designation of *karman* by the preceding rule, he says: "Just as there is no recourse to excellence within the category of the instrument (*karaṇa*), so too there would be no such preeminence within the category of the object (*karman*). (74)

(71) Just as, when something has acquired a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) in relation to other causal factors (*kāraka*) and thus receives the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa*), no further superiority is required in relation to other instruments of the same class—by virtue of which [superiority] the function of every [instrument] would have to operate; for example: "He goes by horse, on the road, with a lamp," or "on foot."

"He goes; he strikes with his foot by force. Otherwise, it would belong only to the horse or such [objects] that are most excellent. Likewise, it applies to the object (*karman*) as well. Since the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the others are also employed in the action, their status as the "most desired" (*īpsitatama*) is established.
Even for all action that exists in the relationship of cause and effect (*nimita-nimittibhāva*), it is designated as "direct object" (*karma-saṃjñā*) by the same principle as before;
thus, there is no such thing as an "unspoken object" (*akathita-karman*). This is presented according to the opinion of certain [grammarians]. || 74 ||
He says that this is not tenable:
"Since a distinction is resorted to when it is accepted that action is desired to be attained, therefore there is an absolute difference from the previous [category of] action. (75)

(72) Here, since the status of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) pertains to all factors of action (*kāraka*), it is logical that the instrument (*karaṇa*), having acquired its status as a means through comparison with other factors of action, should not disregard the excellence inherent within its own category. However, the object (*karman*) possesses the state of being the highest degree of what is desired (*īpsāprakarṣabhāva*) in relation to other factors of action.
This is for the purpose of establishing the definition. For other *kārakas* are not "desired" (*īpsita*).

That which is to be attained by the agent through the action is what is "desired. Other *kārakas*, however, such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, are to be attained for the sake of the action, but not by the action itself.
Therefore, because excellence (*atiśaya*) is dependent upon something of a similar kind, the state of being "most desired to be attained" (*īpsitatama*)—

that is, the state of being intended as the object to be attained— is based on this very intention to attain. Since excellence is admitted by virtue of the inclusion of the suffix *-tama*, it is therefore dependent upon another object that is desired to be attained.

Thus, this excellence must be accepted as residing within its own domain; and so, milk and the like are "more desired" (*prakṛṣṭam īpsitam*) in relation to the cow and other things that are merely desired, and they fall under the scope of the preceding rule. However, for the cow and the like, since the designation "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) is not established by the preceding rule, it is [established] by the rule *akathitam*.
The position that "success" (siddhi) [is the object] is indeed the logical one. Consequently, those two actions belong to different levels.
For if the excellence of the action were not relied upon with respect to its own level, the suffix *tamap* would be meaningless.
Thus, if the designation "object" (*karman*) were applied to everything merely desired, [the rule would be redundant].

Regarding the rule *vāraṇārthānām īpsitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.27), examples such as "he keeps the cow away from the barley" (*yavebhyo gāṃ vārayati*), "he keeps the blind man away from the well" (*kūpād andhaṃ vārayati*), and "he keeps the boy away from the fire" (*agner māṇavakaṃ vārayati*) would not be possible; for in those cases, the barley and so forth would also incur the designation of *karman*.

Consequently, lest this Sūtra become devoid of a scope, the author of the Siddhānta established— within its own domain— that there is a distinction between the object (*karman*) and the point of departure (*apādāna*), based on a specific excellence inherent to the object; as it is stated in the Vārttika:

"The purposelessness of the object in the case of verbs meaning 'to ward off' [is established] because of the statement: 'the object is that which is most desired by the agent'" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.27, with reference to the Jaiminīya commentary).
This is also the Bhāṣya. As for what was stated previously regarding that which is connected with the desired [object]...

The inclusion of the term *īpsitatama* (that which is most desired to be reached) is for the sake of establishing [the correct application of the rule]; for it was stated by the rule *vāraṇārthānām* that the designation of object (*karmasaṃjñā*) would not otherwise be established for things like the blind person who is connected with something like a well—which is merely desired—by means of the rule *akathitaṃ ca*. Therefore, [the term] *īpsitatama* is used.

The meaning is that it is accomplished. As for that which is merely not desired [by the agent] and is thus "unspoken" (akathita) by the technical designations such as *apādāna* and so forth, the *Bhāṣya* states that the designation *karman* applies to such things as a cow by virtue of the rule concerning the "unspoken" (*akathitasūtra*).
However, that which is indeed desired will be covered by the rule concerning the "unspoken. || 75 ||

Furthermore, regarding what was stated— that the status of the object (*karman*) for roots such as *duh* (to milk) is established by the preceding rule just as it is for the causative (*ṇijanta*)— he says in that regard: "And just as in the case of the causative, the agent (*kartṛ*), being active, is employed [by another]."
In the same way, at the beginning of [the action of] leading and so forth, the agent is employed even though he is devoid of activity. (76)

In cases such as *gamayati grāmaṃ devadattam* ("he causes Devadatta to go to the village"), where the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is present, two distinct actions expressed by the base and the suffix are perceived; therefore, it is appropriate that both [Devadatta and the village] possess the status of object (*karman*) in relation to those two actions. However, in cases such as *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* ("he milks the cow for milk"), since there is only one action expressed by the base, how [is this explained]?

There is a connection with two actions. Nor can its validity be established by the inclusion of the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), because the meaning of *ṇic* is not applicable here. For the meaning of *ṇic* is "command" (*praiṣa*), and that is appropriate for an agent who has already initiated an action and possesses an operation. Thus, it applies to one who instigates that independent [agent].

The cause (*hetu*) is that which possesses such an operation (*vyāpāra*) expressed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*). For this very reason, the designation "cause" (*hetu-saṃjñā*) does not apply to an independent agent (*svatantra-kartṛ*) who instigates instruments (*karaṇa*) and the like whose actions are inactive. Thus, because cows and the like are devoid of action, milk and the like do not attain the status of an object (*karman*) through their operation either.

However, because both the cow and the milk are obtained through the very operation of milking (*doha*), which is Devadatta’s activity, the milk and so forth possess the status of *karman* by virtue of this excellence [of being the primary object]; whereas the cow and so forth are designated as *akathita* (unspoken) by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 1.4.51]. || 76 ||

Now, one might object: "Just as there is the usage 'he causes him who is going to go' (*gacchantam saṃprayunkte gamayati*), so too [in the case of *kṣārayati*] the meaning is 'he causes her who is flowing to flow,' which is to say, 'he milks' (*dogdhi*). Anticipating this objection, he says:
"But that sentence expressing a distinction which occurs with the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*) and that which occurs in the base forms of the roots *nī* and *duh*..."
Because it is a different word, there is no contact whatsoever between it and the element. 77.

(74) Regarding the statement beginning with "he employs [the goat] as it goes" (*gacchantam prayuṅkte*) in order to demonstrate the distinction between the meanings of the root and the suffix in causative forms such as *gamayati* ("he causes to go"), there are also such sentences as: "He employs the goat as it reaches the village," and "He employs the cow as it flows [milk]."

In usages such as *nayati* (he leads) and *dogdhi* (he milks), [the verb] is indeed a distinct word with a distinct meaning. For this is not, in the ultimate sense, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) here; rather, this is merely a statement of the general sense by way of proximity.
It is just as in cases like *rājapuruṣa*, where one says *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king’s man). Thus, one employs [the verb] toward someone who is going.

In such sentences as "he causes [him] to go" (*gamayati*), one understands an indication of the instigator (*prayojaka-kartṛ*); however, in the causative form (*ṇyanta*) such as "he causes [him] to go," only the action of the instigator is perceived, while the person being instigated (*prayojya*) is expressed by its own word, namely "Devadatta. And where this sentence expressing the distinction occurs far from the causative form—

The remoteness of *nayati* and similar verbs is even greater; for here there is no sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) derived from the verbal root itself. Therefore, that sentence or its sentence-meaning has no connection with roots such as *duh*. Consequently, since the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) is not included here, [the rule] does not apply even on the basis of two actions.
The justification based on a distinction between types of action is incorrect. Thus, this single, distinct action has two objects;
and consequently, every "unspoken" (*akathita*) object is perceived as belonging to a different category.
Indeed, that which is most desired [by the agent] is so designated through the distinction of the object of the verbal root's meaning.

Thus, this position has been established. Furthermore, even though the "unspoken object" (*akathitakarma*) is not primary, because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*), the rule for *la*-suffixes was stated first due to its prior connection with the action.

However, in the case of roots such as *nī* ("to lead"), since the primary status belongs to the beginning of the vowel (*aja-*, i.e., the agent), the *la*-suffixes occur there alone. But in the case of causative forms (*ṇyanta*), however—

Because the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) is primary and is that which is being reached (*prāpyamāṇa*), the agent alone is the primary object; therefore, the *l*-affixes and so forth occur only there. Consequently, it is said:
"In the case of verbs with two objects, they say that the *l*-affixes and so forth express the direct object (*pradānakarman*)."

In the case of roots such as *duh* (to milk) and others when used with a causative suffix (*ṇyanta*), the non-primary object is designated as the agent (*kartṛ*). Furthermore, in the case of a causative, the primary agent is also designated as the object (*karman*).
Thus, this has been cited as established by logic. || 77 ||
Now he reveals the established conclusion (siddhānta):
"Just as a single ablative case is shown with distinctions in the treatise, so too a single object (karman) is presented with distinctions. (78)
(75) By the rule *dhruvam apāye* (Pāṇini 1.4.24) alone, the designation *apādāna* is established in all cases, as demonstrated even in the Bhāṣya;

for even in the case of [verbs] meaning "fear" (*bhī*) or "protection" (*trā*), there exists a conceptual (*bauddha*) separation (*apāya*). Indeed, [the specific rules such as *bhītrārthānām*] are intended for the instruction of those who are not yet learned.
