The separate mention [of these] is by means of the rule beginning with *bhītrārthānām* (Pāṇini 1.4.25). And so he will state:

"The rule that applies when there is a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) from among those ending in the sixth case, and the rule that applies to those whose meaning is 'fear' (*bhī*) or 'protection' (*trā*), [are not applied here]."
Having observed the misfortune resulting from the practice of the ignorant, he [acted].

Thus, even *karman* (the object) is only one [in its essential nature], because the state of being reached by the agent's action exists everywhere. However, the subsequent elaboration of sūtras is for the sake of favoring those of dull intellect; such is the meaning of the verse (*kārikā*). And although the acquisition of cows and the like is for the sake of milk and so forth, nevertheless, it certainly exists.

Its status as an object is also due to its being connected with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). For example, in the expression "he cooks rice into porridge" (*taṇḍulānodanaṃ pacati*), the meaning of the root *pac* is indeed the act of moistening characterized by the softening of the rice grains.
In that case, by way of the quality called softening, the rice grains are also the object of the moistening.
The term *sākṣātkaraṇa* (direct accomplishment) means that while moistening the rice grains, [the action] brings about the cooking (*odana*). And thus,
just as there is a distinction of objects here based on the difference between actions expressed by a single verbal root where one is subordinate and the other is primary, so too,

when the meaning consists of the act of milking (*kṣāraṇa*) subordinated to the act of flowing (*kṣaraṇa*), there is a distinction of objects for the verb *duh* (to milk), namely the cow and the milk.
Since they experience the state of being an object (*karman*) at the very same time, it is likewise logical that the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is included [within the base].

Even in the case of a causative form (*ṇyanta*), because the meaning of the suffix—qualified by the meaning of the base—is predominant, the independent [agent] remains devoid of action (*niṣkriya*). For the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is not applied here in such a way that...

If the principle were followed that "the application [of a suffix] belongs to that which possesses activity, and that is the domain of the causative (*ṇic*)," then the meaning of the causative would be expressed by the verbal root itself. For example, the meaning of the causative in *sādhayati* ("he accomplishes") would be expressible by the root *pac* ("to cook"); however, the sentence expressing the distinction [between the two states] would not be very far removed [from the actual usage].

The meanings are distinct with respect to their absolute particularity (*atyantaviśeṣa*), but they are indeed one and the same meaning with respect to their generality (*sāmānya*), just like the expressions "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*) and "tree-sentence" (*vṛkṣavākya*). And thus, this sentence-meaning is indeed perceived in this usage.
Furthermore, it is not logical that cows and the like are devoid of action (*niṣkriyatva*), given the existence of the inherence of action (*kriyāsamavāyabhāva*).

Because there is an absence of agency (*kārakatva*). Even if [the action] were being commenced, the designation of "object" (*karman*) would not apply in the case of the *akathita* (unspoken) relation.

If it is argued that there is a lack of activity prior to the actual performance [of the action], this is equally true for the causative (*ṇyanta*) as well. And just as in that case, the agent is one whose action is merely potential, the occurrence of the instigator's operation is thereby established.

Thus, there is no fault here; furthermore, because the inclusion of the suffix *tamap* has been rejected, there is no reliance on an excellence of desire (*īpsā-prakarṣa*). As for the example given for the inclusion of *tamap*, namely "I would eat with curd" (*dadhnā bhuñjīya*), in that case, both the curd and the rice are objects of desire (*īpsita*) by virtue of being of equal status.

The inclusion of the term *tamap* (the superlative suffix) is of no consequence; for if curd (*dadhi*) functions as a purificatory agent (*saṃskāraka*), then it is the rice (*odana*) prepared with it that possesses the status of being the most desired (*īpsitatama*), and thus this cannot serve as an example [of the accusative of the object]. And so says the Bhāṣya.
"For even for him, only the boiled rice is desired; he has no regard for the condiments" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.49).
Furthermore, that which was [stated] for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction between the domains of the object (*karman*) and the ablative (*apādāna*):

It has been stated that the mention of *tamap* [in the rule] is for this purpose; however, there is no fault here because of the following interpretation: since verbs meaning "to ward off" (*vāraṇārtha*) signify the warding off of those things which are to be warded off, that which is desired among those things fit to be warded off is the *apādāna*. For instance, cows and the like are the objects to be warded off, that is, to be prohibited.

For them, barley and the like, which are desired, are indeed the *apādāna*. Thus, everything that is desired is simply the *karman* (object). And in this way, the examples beginning with *duh* (to milk) are for illustrative purposes; this is not an exhaustive enumeration. In cases such as "he listens to the actor" (*naṭasya śṛṇoti*), the actor and so forth are merely the cause (*nimitta*) for the act of listening, but not [the object].

Because it is intended to be expressed as that which is most desired by the agent, it lacks the designation of *karman* (object). Furthermore, in the act of hearing, the actor (*naṭa*) possesses activity; however, because of the inclusion of the term "utility" (*upayoga*), his status as an *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) is excluded.
Since no other grammatical designation has been prescribed for him, he is a *śeṣa* (remainder), which is the domain of the genitive case.
However, this is not the domain of the instrumental case used in the sense of cause (*hetu*);
for when an operation (*vyāpāra*) is not dependent [on another], the cause is accepted as the *nimitta*.
A cause has substance (*dravya*) and so forth as its object, whereas a *kāraka* possesses a restricted action (*niyata-kriya*).
Because of this statement. || 78 ||

Now, one might object: "Since it has been stated that there is a distinction among objects (karman) such as the 'to-be-produced' (nirvartya) and so forth, how can it be that there is only one kind of object?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The object, which resides in the means of accomplishment (sādhana), is either the 'to-be-produced' (nirvartya), the 'to-be-modified' (vikārya), or the 'to-be-attained' (prāpya)."
Since it is actions alone that are to be accomplished, [the agent] is designated as having an established form. || 79 ||

(76) Here, that which is the locus of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the substratum of power (*śakti*), and which possesses a perfected form (*niṣpanna-rūpa*), is expressed by nominal words (*nāman-pada*). However, by verbal words (*ākhyāta-pada*), the object whose nature is to be accomplished (*sādhya-svabhāva*) and whose essence is action (*kriyā-ātman*) is denoted. Thus, the definition of action (*kriyā*) and substance (*dravya*) as having the natures of the unaccomplished (*sādhya*) and the accomplished (*siddha*) respectively is established by way of those forms as presented by words.
It is said: as the Bhāṣya states— "For it is action alone that is brought into being, whereas substance is established by its own nature" (Pāṇini 1.3.1).

Thus, in such cases as "he makes a mat," "he cooks rice into porridge," and "he sees the sun," the object (*karman*)—as the substratum of the capacity [for action]—is conveyed by the nominal words as something undifferentiated in its established state; therefore, there is no internal difference in its own nature. And because, in reality, all things exist for the sake of action.

The designation [of the action] is by means of the action itself (*kriyādharma*). For actions, characterized by completion, transformation, or attainment, manifest an assistance toward their object according to their own capacity, thereby becoming the cause for distinct designations. And having established it thus, in its verbal form—

Since the action is already accomplished, its means of accomplishment is also logically established. However, when one does not rely on the distinctions of designations imposed by specific types of activity, everything is simply "desired" (īpsita) as the objective cause for the action; thus, all is designated by the general term "object" (*karman*).
Thus it is established that "it is told. || 79 ||

[The state of] being free from pride. Here, one might wonder how there can be the status of being "most desired" (īpsitatva) in such cases as "he eats poison" (*viṣaṃ bhakṣayati*) or "he looks at thieves" (*corān paśyati*);
anticipating this objection, [the author] says:
"In the case of things that are harmful, the agent's desire arises due to greed."
In the case of poison and the like, it proceeds in the same way due to fear and other such causes. || 80 ||
(77) Just as a desire arises for one who cannot endure dietary restrictions— desiring whatever food would be beneficial for a patient suffering from an imbalance of the elements such as wind—
and likewise for one who is oppressed by fear of a ruler or others, or afflicted by the pain of a chronic disease (*kṣetriya-vyādhi*).

For one who considers that "it is better to eat poison," the poison becomes something desired through the act of eating; likewise, that which is joined with it [the action] is also [regarded as] undesired. (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.50)
This action, moreover, is already established by what precedes. Thus the author of the Bhāṣya says:
"When this person is afflicted by suffering, having reflected upon other sufferings, he [considers] the consumption of poison..."

"One considers this alone to be superior. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.4.50). Regarding the phrase "due to greed" (*laulyāt*): the meaning is that desire for something is not always constituted by acting with foresight (*prekṣāpūrvakāritā*), but rather it can also occur through other means.

In this context, the state of being "desired" (*īpsitatva*) consists precisely in the attainment of the status of being the object of the action of eating; this is understood from the very inclusion of the term "tathāyukta" (connected in that manner). Even regarding the commencement of the Sūtra, poison that has been administered by another and whose poisonous nature is not yet recognized is indeed "desired" while it is being eaten. Likewise, by the action of seeing, thieves and the like are also "desired."
If something other than what is desired—such as the root of a tree—is neither desired nor undesired, even that, though previously not intended, becomes "desired" at the very moment of approaching it;
otherwise, it would not even attain the status of being the object of the action of approaching. And this is why the term *tamap* (the superlative suffix) is employed.

It is established that even approaching the foot of a tree on the way while going to a village for the purpose of dispelling fatigue is included under the term "rejected" (*pratyākhyāta*). Thus, by the previous rule alone, the designation of "object" (*karman*) applies to whatever is desired to be attained. Even when preceded by another technical designation, that which is desired remains indeed an "object."

This is established by the general definition. In cases such as *grāmamadhiśete* ("he lies down in the village") and *nagaramupatiṣṭhati* ("he stands near the city"), because the verbal roots become transitive through their connection with prefixes (*upasarga*), the designation "object" (*karman*) applies by virtue of its higher priority; thus, it is stated that [the village] is the object, as in *gehaṃ praviśati* ("he enters the house").

In the absence of a prefix (*anupasargatve*), the designation of locus (*adhikaraṇa-saṃjñā*) applies. In the case of "he plays with dice" (*akṣān dīvyati*), when the verb *divyati* expresses the act of throwing as subordinate to the desire for victory, the dice possess the status of the most desired object (*īpsitatva*). However, when it signifies mere play, as in "he plays with dice" (*akṣair dīvyati*), the dice possess the status of instrument (*karaṇatā*). Thus, both [grammatical statuses] are established.
The sūtra for the purpose of inclusion is:
"And [the object] of *div* [is also called *karman*]" (Pāṇini 1.4.43).
This has been stated in the Vārttika.
"And there is the inclusion [of the term] for those things that are causes of movement and play.

In the absence of this sūtra intended to effect a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*), there would be scope for the designation *karman* (object) in the case of "he plays with the mind" (*manasā dīvyati*). Thus, in the word *manasādeva*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied because it is an object (*karman*). However, as for the designation *karaṇa* (instrument)...

In the case of *devanokṣaḥ*, where the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), the third case ending alone would occur, overriding the second case by virtue of its higher priority [in the order of rules],
according to *manasastṛtīyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.4).

Thus, when the elision (*luk*) occurs, the scope for the designation *karaṇa* (instrument) remains only in the example *manasā devaḥ*; however, if the rule were formulated with the particle *ca*, the coexistence of both designations would otherwise be impossible, and thus the second designation (*karman*) is also established. In this way...

Even for the roots *kudh* and *druh*, when they are not preceded by a prefix, the recipient (*sampradāna*) status applies; however, when they are preceded by a prefix, the status of the object (*karman*) applies because it is a subsequent rule.
This very type of object has already been explained by us previously, and is now merely being recalled. || 80 ||

This has been explained. Now this is being considered: here, when two actions are conjoined, the suffixes *la* and so forth are stated to occur with respect to the primary action by relying on its predominance (*prādhānya*). However, since the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) arises even from two nominal stems (*prātipadika*), there exists therein a pair of actions consisting of a subordinate and a primary one.
Anticipating the objection— “Even when there is a single objective case (karma-śakti), why does a second case ending not arise to denote the other power once one has been expressed?”— he says:
“Where two actions of a substance are primary and secondary, [and are] distinct...”
Power (śakti) rests upon the qualities (guṇa); therein, it conforms to the primary cause (pradhāna). || 81 ||

(78) Here, there is a syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) among meanings conveyed within a single sentence. In that case, because two primary elements are equal in status, a mutual relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is not possible; nor is it possible between two subordinate elements.

"And because qualities exist for the sake of another, there would be no connection [between them] due to their equality" (JS 3.1.12.22). He states that when the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is established through the relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*), coherence (*samanvaya*) is possible: ...he says: [the following].
"Where there is [a relation] between the primary and the other," thus [it is said]. || 81 ||
In that case, because the qualities (guṇas) conform to the primary [action], when the karmic capacity regarding the object of the non-primary action is expressed,
the substance is manifested as if it were already expressed even with respect to the object of the quality-action; this is conformity to the primary.
He speaks in order to explain what was stated in general:

"When the power whose primary object is the principal [meaning] is expressed by the suffix, then, in the case of a subordinate element, that [power] shines forth even though it is not explicitly stated. (82)

(79) When the objective power (*karma-śakti*) concerning the primary action is expressed by a suffix such as *la* produced from a verbal root denoting that primary action, then the objective power concerning the subordinate action (*guṇa-kriyā*), although not explicitly stated, shines forth in the same manner; thus has this rule of extension (*anuvṛtti*) been explained.

Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "In the case of the two *pac* roots, when the object (*karman*) is not explicitly stated in the form ending in *ktvā* which expresses a state (*bhāva*), that very property [of the object] is manifested even when another power (*śakti*) is expressed in the act of eating. (83)

(80) "Having cooked, rice is eaten" (*paktvaudano bhujyate*) is the example. Here, according to the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra, the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), by virtue of the continued application of the rule for the suffix *tumun*.
For the Vārttikakāra [states]:
He recited [the rule] as "ā ca tumunaḥ samānādhikaraṇe" (Pāṇini 3.4.26), and according to the scope of its application,
"śakadhṛṣajñāglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhāstāraksam" (Pāṇini 3.4.65).

The meaning of the *vārttika* is that, following suffixes such as *tumun* which are prescribed by sūtras beginning with "ityādi," suffixes such as *ṇamul* should be stated to have the same denotation (*samānābhidheya*) as the verb used in the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*). By this rule,
[the form] "svādvaṃkāraṃ yavāgūr deavadatena bhujyate" is derived using *ṇamul*.
Because the word *yavāgū* (gruel) denotes the object (*karman*), the accusative case does not occur after it; however, the instrumental case does occur after the word *devadatta*.

Otherwise, since the action would have already been accomplished (*kṛtatvāt*), when the suffix *ṇamul* arises in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), the instrumental case would not occur after the word *devadatta*. By this very same logic, [in the example] "having drunk the curd... (*pakva tvā danaḥ*).

Even in the case of "bhujyate," the suffix *ktvā* arises with reference to the very same object (*karman*) denoted by the root used in the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), namely "bhujyate"; thus, according to the opinion of the author of the Vārttika, there is no non-denotation of any *śakti* whatsoever. However, the author of the Bhāṣya...

He refutes the Vārttika which claims that, by this same logic, the accusative case would not occur in the expression *paktvaudanaṃ gamyate grāmaḥ* ("Having cooked rice, one goes to the village"). He maintains that the introduction of the suffixes *ṇamul* and others is prescribed for the abstract action (*bhāva*), because the mention of the sense of *tumun* (the infinitive suffix) continues [in the rule], and the sense of *tumun* is indeed the abstract action. Since [the agent] is already established as the agent due to the suffix being a *kṛt*, [the suffix is used here for the action].

Because of the rule stating that [affixes] beginning with *ktvā* have the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*), there is a displacement of the agent. Since no other meaning for *tumun* has been specified, suffixes whose meaning is not specifically indicated occur in their own sense; thus, the "state" (*bhāva*) which is the meaning of its own base is established. The same applies to forms ending in *ktvā*, such as *apaktvā*.

Thus, in this [word *odana*], which expresses a state of being (*bhāvavācin*), the objective capacity (*karmaśakti*) of the rice with respect to the action of cooking (*pacikriyā*) remains unexpressed. When the objective capacity with respect to the action of eating (*bhujikriyā*) is expressed by the suffix *-la*, its property (*taddharma*) likewise manifests— that is, the property characterized by being made known (*pratyāyitatva-lakṣaṇa*), which belongs to that very primary [object] (*pradhāna*), is revealed.

The second [case-ending] does not occur after the word *odana* (rice). In the sentence "Having cooked rice, he eats," the third case (*kartṛ-tṛtīyā*) expressing the agent does not occur after Devadatta due to this very principle, because [the agenthood] depends solely upon the act of cooking (*pacikriyā*). However, in the sentence "He goes to the village having cooked rice," the motion inherent in the rice is understood through the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*) of the root *gam*.

The second case ending occurs because the potency of the action (*karma-śakti*) has not been expressed. Even though the case ending in *bhujyate* arises with respect to a number inherent in the same referent as the means (*sādhana*), nevertheless, because the number associated with the condition of the object (*karman*) of the act of cooking (*pac*) is not expressed, the second case would indeed occur.

This principle is proclaimed: for even in the case of the meanings of case-endings such as singularity and so forth, the objects [of the action] (karma) and others must necessarily be expected as subordinate factors (aṅga). || 83 ||

He states another example: "And because of the contact with the root *gam* (to go), when the suffix *lo* is prescribed for the root *iṣ* (to desire) in the sense of 'village,' there the enjoyment of the action of going is effected by the root *uṣ* (to dwell) alone. (84)

(81) "The village is desired to be gone to" (*iṣyate grāmo gantum*) is the example. Here, the verb *iṣ* has two objects, whereas for the verb *gam*, there is only the village; thus, when the object-status (*karmasaṃjñā*) pertaining to the village is not expressed in relation to the domain of *iṣ*, the [object-status] pertaining to the village likewise manifests [in relation to *gam*]. In that case, there is a desire for the sake of going. And so:

When a verb denoting an action is used as an adjunct to another action intended for its sake, the suffix *tumun* is employed; however, one might suspect that in this case the action of "going," which has become the result, is the primary element rather than the desire (*īpsita*). To dispel this doubt, here is another example: in the phrase *paktvā bhujyate* ("having cooked, it is eaten"), primacy belongs to the meaning expressed by the verbal form (*ākhyāta-pada*) because it is that which is to be accomplished (*nirvartyatva*).
Primacy also exists for the sake of the object [of the action], because cooking has the purpose of eating.

Regarding the phrase "from contact with a cow," the connection of the root *iṣ* (to desire) with another substance always occurs only by way of another action; thus, here too, there is a desire for the village by way of seeing and so forth.
The meaning is: "by means of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyopātta*). *Nirbhoga* means "chewing" (*carvaṇa*), that is to say, "narration" (*ākhyāna*).

Regarding the phrase "by the suffix itself" (*iṣiṇaiva*): it refers to the suffix *iṣ*, namely the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) prescribed for the passive voice (*karman*). For, by virtue of its grammatical capacity (*tantra*), the suffix denotes both powers simultaneously.
This has been determined in the *Vākyapadīya*. || 84 ||
He states an argument for this according to another view as well:
"In the expression 'having cooked, it is eaten,' for some [grammarians] the verb 'to cook' does not require [an expressed object];
that [object], namely rice (*odana*), is understood through inference. (85)

According to some, in this sentence the act of cooking (*pacikriyā*) does not require the rice (*odana*). This is because there is no syntactic connection between the rice, which is in the nominative case, and the word *paktvā* (having cooked). The rice has a connection only with the word *bhujyate* (is eaten); thus, there is only one objective potency (*karmaśakti*), and that has already been expressed (*abhihitā*).
What follows from this? [The objection is: "When the power of the primary [action] is expressed, the power of the subordinate action appears as if it were already expressed.

If that were so, then in the case of *pacati odanam* ("he cooks rice"), there would be no connection between the two, and the meaning would be "having cooked something else, rice is eaten. And thus...
Fearing that the intended status of the cooking of the rice as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) to the act of eating might not be understood, he says:

"That [status] is understood through inference. The word "that" (*saḥ*) refers back to the rice which has been mentally realized; the word "this" (*asau*) is a demonstrative reference imitating direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Although rice (*odana*) is not directly capable of being connected with the act of cooking (*paci*), it is understood as something to be expected by the act of cooking through its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*). If one asks what this functional capacity is, we reply:
it is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*). For a directly perceived connection is simpler than the postulation of a connection that has not been heard.

And since this [relationship] occurs only when there is a relation of subordinate and principal (guṇapradhānabhāva) and not otherwise, the very logic previously stated must be resorted to here; thus, the previously mentioned view alone is logical. For this very reason, it was indeed presented as another opinion out of dissatisfaction [with the first]. [As in the example: "The act of eating (bhuji) requires cooking (pāka)."

The expectancy must be fulfilled by that which is in close proximity. Since cooking precedes eating in time, the relationship of subordinate and principal is established, and thus the unity of the sentence is achieved. || 85 ||

This principle does not apply solely to the agent known as *karman* (the object), but extends to other *kārakas* as well; thus, he provides another example for the sake of establishing a universal rule (*vyāpti*).
In that case, the object (*karman*) is expressed by the verb ending in the suffix *yat* (as in *abhiniviśate*).
Even when the sense of location (adhikaraṇatva) is present in a word ending in the suffix *ktvā*, they do not accept the use of the seventh case (*saptamī*) there.

In the case of the statement, "Having eaten, he settles in the city" (*bhuktvā nagaram abhiniviśyate*), by the rule *abhiniviśaśca*, the city—which is the locus (*ādhāra*) of the verb *abhiniviś*—receives the designation of object (*karman*).

Thus, in the finite form *abhiniviśyate*, the capacity for the object (*karma-śakti*) is already expressed (*abhihita*) with respect to the primary element, the object. [This applies] to the gerund *bhuktvā*.

In the domain of forms ending in *ktvā*, the locative capacity (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*) also, due to its subordinate status (*guṇatva*), does not bring about its own effect, namely the seventh case-ending (*saptamī-vibhakti*). For if the seventh case were used here, the objective capacity (*karma-śakti*) pertaining to the principal action would not be perceived; thus, the subordinate element would cause an obstruction to the principal. This is not the case.

This is the correct principle: because subordinate elements (guṇas) follow the principal element (pradhāna), they remain indifferent toward their own function when it contradicts the principal element. Furthermore, the status of being the principal belongs everywhere to the meaning of the finite verb (tiṅanta), which is the resting place of verbal usage and constitutes the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha). By this very principle...

In the expression "having entered the city, he eats," the status of the city as the object of the verb *abhiniviś* (to enter) is set aside by its status as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the act of eating.

This has been explained. Here, how is there the status of being an object (*karmatva*) in the case of "he eats molasses" (*guḍaṃ bhakṣayati*)? For molasses, being already accomplished, does not require any further specific quality pertaining to the act of eating, nor is it something desired [as an end]. Rather, it is employed merely for the purpose of indicating the specific substratum of the act of eating.
This substance is for the sake of the action, but the action is not for the sake of refining the substance;

the powdering of the teeth and so forth is not the fruit of the act of eating, but rather [the means] of eating, which is characterized by the consumption of food in the form of swallowing. Satisfaction is characterized by satiety.
Regarding the fruit, there is no specific distinction such as origination (*utpatti*) or the like produced by an action. As it is stated in the *Vārttika*:

"If the desired object were designated as the *karman*, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of designating as *karman* that which has already been accomplished (*nirvṛta*) and yet functions as a causal factor (*kāraka*)."
"Because it is that which is most desired by the agent" (Pāṇini 1.4.49).
By the phrase "of that which has been accomplished," he rejects the status of the object as something yet to be produced (*nirvartya*). And this is merely an illustration.

Because there is an absence of modification (*vikāra*) and so forth, there is no status as a separate ritual action (*karmāntaratā*). The meaning is "of that which is free from expectancy" (*nirākāṅkṣasya*).

By the term "in the state of being a factor" (*kārakatve*), he indicates the state of being a cause for the accomplishment of the action; for molasses is taken up for the purpose of accomplishing the act of eating. Therefore, in the expression "molasses for the sake of eating," it is the action itself [that is primary].
Because it is attained through acts such as seeing [the deity], the desired object (*īpsita*) is the *karma*, not the substance.

For what is desired by the eater is merely the act of eating the molasses, and not any other specific quality produced in it by rejecting the eating. Regarding this, a resolution is stated in the Vārtika:
"Because both [the agent and the object] are desired," as stated in Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.49.

In that regard, in order to explain how molasses and the like possess the status of being "desired" (*īpsitatva*), he says: "That action which has its locus completed, yet is not accumulated through further attainment, becomes 'desired' by falling within the scope of objects such as food. (87)

(84) "Nirvṛta" means accomplished; for this very reason, it is "nirākāṅk�ṣa," meaning free from further expectation. It is the substratum (*āśraya*)—the substance such as molasses and so forth—of which the action is the power of the action (*karmaśakti*); thus, there is an exclusion of the status of being an object that is produced (*nirvartya-karmatā*). Furthermore, because it does not expect any transformation (*vikāra*), its status as an object that is modified (*vikāryatā*) is also set aside. [It is] "unaccumulated" (*apracita*) due to its non-attainment (*aprāpteḥ*).

Thus, because of the connection with the act of eating, even that distinction between increase and decrease [of the substance] is not applicable; therefore, the status of being an object reached by action (*prāpyakarmatā*) is also rejected in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). For the meaning of the *vārttika* on the prima facie view is expressed by the first half of the verse.
It is included. By the second half [of the verse], the explanation of the *Uttaravārttika* is provided.

The meaning is that this object (*karman*)—such as molasses (*guḍa*) and so forth—which is desired and to be attained, is differentiated and qualified by its becoming the state of being the objective domain of actions such as eating (*bhakṣi*) and enjoying (*bhuji*). For it is thus: not...
In this context, the action of eating and so forth alone is the desired object (*īpsita*). For in this way, one becomes successful even by eating a clod of earth.

Nor is molasses desired as the locus of another action, but rather as the locus of the act of eating; thus, both together, in the relationship of locus and located, constitute the desired object. Of that which...

For indeed, while the eating of molasses is desired by him, the molasses itself is also desired; moreover, in this case, the distinction produced by the action consists precisely in the connection with the act of eating, since no other distinction is required for its status as an object reached (*prāpyakarman*). Otherwise, what difference would there be between the *nirvartya* (produced) and *vikārya* (transformed) objects?

There would be a distinction. Here, the fruit of the act of eating is the excellence of pleasure (*prīti*). And that [pleasure] is possible only when there is a connection with the molasses; this indeed is the distinction. For a *saṃskāra* (refinement) is the capacity for the production of a fruit corresponding to the action performed. But [it may be argued]: "In the case of [the fruit being] characterized by satisfaction (*tṛpti*)..."
If it is said that "sugar is an auxiliary to the pleasure," how can this [sugar] possess the status of an object (*karman*) characterized as a primary factor? It is replied:
when sugar serves as an auxiliary to satisfaction, there is this specific procedure (*itikartavyatā-viśeṣa*):
its primacy with respect to that [satisfaction] consists in its being made the objective of the act of eating; otherwise, satisfaction would not occur.

It is possible to accomplish. Therefore, this is its primary function in being a constituent part of satisfaction (*tṛpti*). Just as a teacher, when served, becomes a factor for the arising of Dharma, and that [status] does not occur without his becoming the object of the act of attending upon him.

The statement "one should serve the teacher" establishes the primacy [of the action]. Thus, in this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), while the desire for the substance is set aside, the desire for the mere action is shown. Therefore, in the resolution (*parihāra*) consistent with that, the desire for the substance is also demonstrated. If, then—

The status of being an object (*karmatā*) is established merely by attaining the state of being the domain of an action; if that were so, then everything would be transitive (*sakarmaka*) even with respect to the mere action itself. Consequently, the designations of "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) found in the grammatical treatises would be contradicted.
Yet they are not contradicted; for it is not necessarily the case that [the term applies] to the mere action.

Arising from external objects: for some action rests solely in the agent and does not depend upon an external state of being, such as "he sits" (āste), "he lies down" (śete), and so forth. According to the statement that the root *pac* has two meanings, even in the case of all verbal roots, it is the meaning of the root itself—the operation characterized by *bhāvanā*—that is intended here.
Because it culminates in a mental realization (*bhāvanā*), that very object is what is to be realized (*bhāvya*). As in the expressions "he makes a seat" or "he makes a bed.

Therefore, in this case, the realization is fixed upon an external entity; thus, by virtue of that external object which is to be realized, the verb possesses an object (*sakarmaka*). And in that context, the question "what? is asked: "he cooks."

"What is the rice? and so forth. Since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is never absent in any instance, even though it is that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*), it is not possible to establish the distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs on its basis alone. This distinction depends rather on external objects (*bāhyakarma*), such as time and the like, which do vary; therefore, with respect to the pure *bhāvanā*—

The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the [internal] object (*karman*), whereas the external object is that which is qualified by the meaning of the verbal root. For this very reason, the experts in logic (*nyāyavidaḥ*) maintain that when the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is directed toward an external object, the meaning of the verbal root serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Therefore, the sentence-meaning of "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*) is "he brings about rice through cooking" (*pākena odanaṃ bhāvayati*). Even though here...

In the case of *darśana* (seeing), *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) is indeed the meaning of the verbal root; nevertheless, as it culminates in a result and consists of the agent's activity, it is capable of being treated as distinct from the mere collection of its constituent actions, which are more extensive. This principle should be applied everywhere. || 87 ||
Furthermore, he states that in some cases, even when external action exists in reality, there is still the designation of "intransitive" (akarmaka):
"Because [the root] occurs with a different meaning, and because [that different meaning] is included within the meaning of the verbal root itself."
An action is considered intransitive because its object is not intended to be expressed, despite being well-known. (88)

(85) When a verbal root functions with respect to a meaning other than its well-known meaning, then in that case its action is understood as being expressed without the inclusion of a common object (*karmasāmānyāvayarahita*). For example, the root *vahati* is well known to denote the act of bringing something to another location and is transitive, as in "he carries a load" (*bhāraṃ vahati*). That...

When, in the expression "the river flows" (*nadī vahati*), [the verb] denotes the action of flowing (*syandana-kriyā*), then—since that flowing, which consists of the trickling of water, is identical with the very nature of the river—there is no possibility of an inquiry as to "what [it flows toward]," and thus it is intransitive.
This productive urge (*bhāvanā*) depends solely on the meaning of the verbal root, such that [the sentence] means: "it flows" = "it performs the act of flowing. Furthermore, when...

When the object is included within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) during the performance of its action, then it is also intransitive (*akarmaka*). For example, in the case of "he lives" (*jīvati*), since the meaning of the root here is "he maintains the vital breaths" (*prāṇān dhārayati*), the object characterized as the vital breaths is included [within the root's meaning]. Likewise, "he dies" (*mriyate*) means "he abandons the vital breaths" (*prāṇān jahāti*). Similarly, "he exists" (*asti*)...

Regarding the expression "he sustains himself" (*ātmānaṃ bibharti*): even where there is the cognition of a specific action through its invariable concomitance, there too the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is that of an action devoid of an agent (*akarmikā kriyā*). For example, in the case of "it rains" (*varṣati*).
For here, just as the deity is cognized as the agent despite the invariable concomitance with the act of raining, so too [is it in other cases].

Since it is well known that action also has the characteristic of water, the past participle suffix *kta* is cited in the sense of the agent when there is no [external] object, as in "the god rained. However, when the object is not well known, this action is indeed transitive, as in "it rains blood" or "the autumn rains"; thus, "dust was rained down."

Thus, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Alternatively, even where a connection with an object exists, if it is not intended to be expressed because the purpose is merely to convey the action itself, then the status of being intransitive (*akarmaka*) is possible there as well. For example: "It is not cooked here," "It is not eaten here."

Because the intended meaning is the prohibition of the action, the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) occurs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). In the examples "the initiated one does not give," "he does not cook," and "he does not offer oblations," there is no intention to express the object (*karman*). Why is it that [the object] is not expected here?
Because the intended meaning is the prohibition of the action. || 88 ||
Thus, there are four ways in which the designation "intransitive" (akarmaka) occurs in the treatise. He states that other types are also possible:
"These four distinctions which have been shown in general..."
Furthermore, they are divided in many ways according to the distinctions of their signs and so forth. || 89 ||

(86) These four varieties, which have been explained as the basis for the intransitivity of even transitive roots, arise in many ways through the distinction of causes (*nimitta*) and so forth. "Cause" refers to an auxiliary such as a prefix (*upasarga*), and by the word "and so forth," place, time, and others are included. For example, the root *car-* [is used as follows]:

It occurs by virtue of the application [of the root] in another sense: "the vapor rises," "the smoke rises. Due to the presence of the prefix *ud*, this verbal root is intransitive when it signifies upward movement.
Because of the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), its intransitivity is manifested in certain instances through the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), as in "it rises up" (*utpatate*).
Regarding "vitapate": the meaning is "it shines. Regarding "yāvadbhaktamupatiṣṭhate":
the meaning is "he waits until the time for eating.
[This is governed by] Pāṇini 1.3.26: "And after an intransitive verb..."

Thus, this is the middle voice (ātmanepada): "He makes use of ghee" (*sarpiṣo jānīte*), "He makes use of honey" (*madhuno jānīte*). Because he proceeds by means of that [ghee or honey], the verbal root here refers to an activity preceded by knowledge.
With the continuation of the rule "apahnave jñaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.44),
[the sūtra] "akarmakācca" (Pāṇini 1.3.45) [is stated].
Thus, by the power of the sentence, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) sometimes manifests the state of being intransitive (*akarmakatva*).

For example, in the expression "the river flows" (*nadī vahati*), there is intransitivity because of the capacity of the specific agent characterized as a river, when the word expresses the act of flowing. Likewise, in "the wind blows" (*vāyur vahati*). Similarly...

Regarding the relationship between the object and the agent, because the object is perceived as the agent, the verbal root (*dhātu*) is considered intransitive when it expresses only a portion [of its full meaning],

as in "the rice cooks by itself" (*pacyate odanaḥ svayameva*). And this being the case, the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) that has as its basis the designation of a root as intransitive applies to this context.
"According to the rule *muco 'karmakasya guṇo vā* (Pāṇini 7.4.57),
as in the example *mokṣyate vatsaḥ svayam eva* ('the calf will release itself'),
the application of a verbal root to a different meaning varies according to the distinction between causes such as its being intransitive (*akarmaka*) and so forth."
Even when [the action] is subsumed within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), there is still a distinction based on differences such as the cause (*nimitta*) and so forth. For example:

in cases such as *jīvati* ("he lives"), although the object is included within the action because its distinctions are obscured by the cause characterized as the inherent capacity of the action's own nature, it receives the designation "intransitive" (*akarmaka*).
In some cases, there is an inclusion even of that which has a distinct form being determined through the rules of grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna-vyavasthā*).

For example, in the case of *putrīyati*, the object (*karman*) consisting of a son is included. From an ultimate standpoint (*paramārthataḥ*), the object characterized as a "son" has entered into the body of the action (*kriyā-śarīra*); it does not exist as a separate entity apart from having entered into the body of the action.
In the process of grammatical derivation, that which serves as the cause for the description is resorted to; and as he will state:
"In the case of *putrīyati*, there is no actual son [present];
rather, such a specific desire exists, which, even without following an actual son, remains fixed upon the son."

Thus [it is said]. In the case of the denominative suffix *kyac* used in the sense of conduct (*ācāra*), the object of the standard of comparison (*upamāna-karman*) is included within the base, while the status of being transitive (*sakarmakatva*) arises through the object of that which is compared (*upameya-karman*). For example: *putrīyati chātram* ("he treats the pupil as a son"). In the case of *muṇḍayati māṇavakam* ("he shaves the boy"), however, the general object (*sāmānya-karman*) is included within the base, while the status of being transitive arises through the specific object (*viśeṣa-karman*). In this same manner...

In examples such as *miśrayati tilān* ("he mixes sesame seeds"), [the object is external]. However, in cases such as *bāṣpāyate*, *ūṣmāyate*, and *romanthāyate*, there is an internalization (*antarbhāva*) of the specific object itself, whose form has been determined. For the root *pac* ("to cook"), the object is the earthen vessel, and for *bhid* ("to split"), it is that which possesses parts; these are well-known [external] objects, but they are not internalized. Of that [object]:
Because it is expressed even by its own word—as in "he cooks what is to be cooked" (*pacati pākyam*) or "he splits what is to be split" (*bhinatti bhedyaṃ*).

If [the action) were included [within the meaning of the verb root], there would be no designation by its own word; for one does not say "he lives his life-breaths" (*jīvati prāṇān*). However, one does say "it rains water" (*jalaṃ varṣati*). And because the object is included [within the meaning of the verb root]...
In the expression "he pays homage to the gods" (*namasyati devān*), the dative case does not occur when used in conjunction with the word *namaḥ*. Accordingly, the Vārttika states:
"In the case of *namas* followed by the *kyac* suffix, the occurrence of the accusative case is untenable. (Pāṇini 3.1.19).

Having raised this objection, it was resolved by the rule *aprakṛtyantarād dhi siddham* (Jainendra-vyākaraṇa 3.1.19). With this very intention, the word *namasyati* is shown to have its root-final (*dhātvanta*) as its final element.

The meaning is that the word *namaḥ* cannot possibly have the sense of "worship" (*pūjā*) here; rather, it is derived in this manner by means of analyzing its constituent parts. However, the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*), considering that such a derivation is possible because he accepts *namas-* as the base form during the process of grammatical explanation (*anvākhyāna*), raises the objection once again.
"But surely, in the word *namasyati*, there is the word *namaḥ*; since it is used in conjunction with that, the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) would result.
(G.eṇa. od ja. aḍodhe)
Thus [it is said]. And he refutes this: "The word *namaḥ* is grasped when it is meaningful, and in the word *namasyati*, the word *namaḥ* is not meaningful."
"(g.eṇa. od ja.
aḍodhe)"—this is a rule concerning the formation of *sub*-derivatives (*subdhātu*). Here, the meaning of the subordinate element (*upasarjana*) has become secondary to the meaning of the suffix.
Thus, in the expression "namo devebhyaḥ" (salutation to the gods), [the rule applies] due to its connection with the word "namaḥ," which functions as the primary element.

The meaning of the Bhāṣya is that because there is scope [for another interpretation] here, the fourth case ending does not occur. Furthermore, even where there is a well-known absence of an object (*akarmakatva*), a secondary distinction arises depending on place and time; for example, when "let it be cooked" (*apacyatām*) is said in the forenoon in the Deccan, it has *yavāgū* (gruel) as its object.

The cooking [of rice] is understood; however, in the afternoon, it is the means for preparing *odana* (boiled rice). In a region where meat predominates, cooking is well known as the means for preparing meat. Due to the inherent capacity of the nature of the action itself, a specific object is established in certain cases; from the word "it rains," water is understood.

An action is also established through the capacity of the agent; for instance, when it is said, "The wicked man acts," an action characterized by injury is understood, whereas from "The good man acts," assistance is understood. These [actions] are infinite due to differences in social circles and differences in locations.

Established usage must be followed; how much could be cited? In some cases, even the non-intentionality [of the action] is observed regarding the object (*karman*) because the sentence is intended solely to convey a mere similarity.
For example, in the expression "Kaṭha repeats after Kalāpa," there is a similarity between Kaṭha and Kalāpa in their speaking.

The object (*karman*) as that which is to be accomplished is not intended to be expressed. Likewise, when expressing a specific capacity for action, in response to the question "What is Devadatta doing?", the connection with an object—such as "he cooks" or "he speaks"—is not intended to be expressed. This is also the case when expressing the uninterrupted continuity of an action.
The object is intended to be expressed as "he cooks" or "he gives," and the various types of usage should be followed according to their respective application; this is the accepted view. || 89 ||
Thus ends the section on the object (karman) in the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja.

Here, in the rule-formula for the *svādi* suffixes, the grammatical relations (*kārakas*)— which are the meanings of those case-suffixes— are investigated according to the sequence in which the case-suffixes are arranged. Among these:
Having examined the object (*karman*) in the sense of the second case, the instrument (*karaṇa*), which is the meaning of the third case, is examined first.

The agent (*kartṛ*), however, will be examined later because it is subordinate due to its commonality as the referent of even the sixth case. In that regard, since the collection of factors (*sāmagrī*) is the means for the successful accomplishment of an action, [it is the instrument].
Anticipating the objection— "What excellence does an instrument possess such that it may be the most effective means (*sādhakatama*)?"— he states its definition:
"That whose operation is immediately followed by the complete accomplishment of an action..."
When instrumentality is intended to be expressed therein, then it is remembered as such.

(87) Among all the means that provide assistance through conjunction (*sannipatyopakārin*), that one whose operation is observed to be immediately followed by the action, and which has attained a superior excellence (*atiśaya*),
is the most effective instrument (*karaṇa*). For example, in the act of cutting, it is the sickle [which is the instrument] because it enters [into the wood].

By accomplishing the division of parts in that which is to be cut, [the instrument] attains a state of preeminent utility compared to other factors such as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth. In the same way,
one should cite examples such as "the eye being directed toward seeing" and so on, regarding the conventional usage of the term "means" (*sādhana*).

And he says that [the object] is intended [as such] because it rests upon a state of cognition (*buddhyavasthā*). For in grammar, only an object that has ascended into the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) is a factor (*aṅga*), not one that exists as an external reality; this is the meaning. And thus, in cases such as "he cuts with strength" (*balena lunāti*) or "he sees with light" (*ālokena paśyati*), one disregards the sickle and so forth, as well as the strength and so forth [as the actual instruments].

The *karaṇa* (instrument) is that which is intended as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*). In this regard, although other factors such as the substratum (*ādhāra*) exist in reality, they are regarded otherwise by the intellect, as in the expression "he cooks in a pot" (*sthālyā pacyate*).
However, the very nature of the *karaṇa* itself depends upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).

Even though it has been stated that "the conventional usage of means (*sādhana*) is based on the states of cognition," the phrase "is intended to be expressed" (*vivakṣyate*) is a redundancy. || 90 ||

He says this very thing: "In reality, that [agent] is indefinable, for no entity is fixed [as a single agent], since we observe the intention [behind expressions] such as 'it is cooked by the pot'. (91)
(88) It is impossible to define this very object as an instrument (*karaṇa*) by way of its fixed genus, because no object exists as a fixed instrument in a determinate state.
For even a cooking pot, though its status as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is well known, [is not fixed as such].

Because its constituent parts (kapāla) are exceedingly thin, it accomplishes the effect of cooking more rapidly; thus, it indeed experiences the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) according to the speaker's intention. For instance, the use of the instrumental case to denote the instrument—as in the expression "it is cooked in a pot" (*sthālyā pacyate*)—is well-known in common usage. Indeed, compared to wet fuel, a pot possesses a superior arrangement [of parts].
He draws near to the accomplishment of his task. || 91 ||
And since the instrument (*karaṇa*) is that which provides the most excellent assistance in the accomplishment of an action, the agents exert their effort toward it;
thus he says:
"But regarding the instruments, they repeatedly undertake the burden of refinement."
And [he taught] the specific applications for the sake of accomplishing the primary purpose. || 92 ||

(89) For the sake of accomplishing the primary object characterized by action, those seeking the fruit undertake the refinement—such as sharpening—and the repeated application of the instrument itself, which provides the most excellent assistance; for activity toward the end is undertaken by means of the method. In that regard, there is the placing of the fuel [upon the fire].

Refinement (*saṃskāra*) is the repeated restoration [of an object]. Application (*viniyoga*) is the employment [of that object]. Sharpening an axe is refinement; its use for lifting up and striking down is application. Eye-salve and the like are refinement for the eye; directing [the gaze] is application. This applies to other cases as well.
It should be stated according to the appropriate application. || 92 ||
How is excellence of assistance (*upakāraprakarṣa*) understood here in the expression “he goes by horse, on the road, with a lamp,” when many factors are intended to occur at the same time? He says:
there is no excellence among the instruments (*karaṇa*) within their own respective spheres.
But the state of possessing an excellence based on something else is the defining characteristic of that [cognition] from the perspective of another. || 93 ||
In this context, excellence (*prakarṣa*) relative to its own class (*sajātīya*), which exists in the state of being an instrument (*karaṇabhāva*) within its own category,

is not what is expressed by the suffix *-tamap*; rather, it is excellence relative to other factors (*kāraka*) that is expressed by the suffix *-tamap* as a concomitant of the general means (*sādhanasāmānya*), thereby signifying the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*).

For the suffix *tamap* produced from the word *sādhaka*, which denotes the general category of a causal factor (*kāraka*), expresses excellence precisely with respect to that [general category]. The phrase "from another" means from another means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Thus, because no excellence is admitted that is independent of the genus of the instrument (*karaṇa-jāti*), this applies to all [means] such as horses and so forth.

There is no contradiction in things being instruments when they have attained excellence in relation to other means of accomplishment. For instance, a horse is an excellent auxiliary for an agent in reaching another location; likewise, a path is excellent when it is good and free from disturbances such as thieves; and a lamp is excellent in dispelling the mass of darkness by its light.
By thus rebuking [other means], it establishes its superiority over other methods of proof. || 93 ||

One might object: "Since the operation of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) occurs only after the agent has assigned them their tasks, it is logical that the agent alone is the achiever (*sādhaka*) with respect to that [accomplishment]. Anticipating this, he says: "Even though they possess independence, the prompters [of the means] assist only from a distance."
For by means of the instrument, the activity of all [factors] is mediated. || 94 ||

(91) If it is stated that "the instrument (*karaṇa*) is that whose operation immediately precedes the accomplishment of the action," then it would follow that the agent (*kartṛ*) is also an instrument. For the accomplishment of the action does not occur immediately after the operation of the agent alone;
rather, the operation of the agent consists in the employment of the means (*sādhana*). It is only when the means have been employed that [the action is accomplished].

When beings are engaged in activity, the action is accomplished. In that process, the agent’s own activity is as remote from the accomplishment of the action as the locus (adhikaraṇa) and other factors, because there is no employment of another agent for its completion. This remains so even though the other means of accomplishment (sādhana) are subject to dependence [on the agent].

The agents (prayoktāraḥ) and performers (kartāraḥ), by means of the intervention of the operations of other instruments employed, accomplish the action only from a distance; however, the accomplishment of the action occurs immediately after the operation of the instrument (karaṇa).

Alternatively, he states that the consideration of excellence [in relation] to the agent is simply not possible: "Or rather, when an action is accomplished, there is either excellence or subordination in the agent. For once accomplishment has occurred, the general property of being the means (*sādhakatva*) is what is intensified. (95)

(92) Here, in the context of the accomplishment of an action (*kriyāsiddhi*), the excellence (*atiśaya*) of the instrument (*karaṇa*) over other means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is intended to be expressed. And when the factors of action (*kāraka*) have been set in motion and have assumed their respective functions, then the accomplishment of the action becomes the object [of that excellence]. However, when the agent (*kartṛ*) is required for the assignment of roles, [the excellence resides] in the agent.

They become subordinate; since the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), when their own operations have not yet been manifested, do not even attain the designation "means" which is based on independence and is common to all, how could there be any excellence of the agent (*kartṛ*) in relation to them? Thus he says:
"For when there is accomplishment (*siddhi*), the general capacity to be a means (*sādhakatva*) attains excellence.

That which is the general capacity to be a means attains pre-eminence when there is accomplishment—that is, when there is completion. And that completion occurs at a time subsequent to its employment by an agent.

When there is an entry into its own operation, and thus, in that state, excellence being considered, it remains with the instrument (*karaṇa*) alone— which is of equal rank with the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth—
and not with the agent (*kartṛ*). For the latter is the master (*svāmī*) prior to the commencement [of the action].
That which is independent does not compete with things that lead to death; for excellence depends upon its own kind (*sajātīya*).
But the agent (*kartṛ*) is indeed of a different kind, because other factors of action (*kāraka*) consist of both independent and dependent forms.
And this being the case, when the agent is present, the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), though dependent on others, possesses an excellence of being an instrument (*sādhakatva*).

It is logical that [a means] depends on other causal factors because their objects are distinct; therefore, one should not object by asking how a means could possess excellence if it were not independent. || 95 ||

If, then, there is a difference in form between the agent and the instrument, how is it that the instrument also possesses agency, as in the case of "the sword cuts"? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But when sharpness and so forth are the agents, they know the sword and such to be the instrument."
If sharpness and the other qualities were independent, the self would exist in a dual nature. || 96 ||

(93) Here, when the sword is intended to be expressed as independent— disregarding the application of the agent due to its extremely sharp edge with respect to the act of cutting— it does not function merely as an instrument (*karaṇa*), but rather [it is the agent] of that very action which occurs immediately thereafter.

The status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) belongs to sharpness, heaviness, hardness, shape, and so forth. Even for these, when there is a desire to express their agency (*kartṛtva*), their status as instruments arises from the differentiation of forms brought about by that very intention to express. For instance, one says:
"Sharpness cuts by means of its own capacity."
Although sharpness is a single entity, its form appears differentiated due to the distinctions imposed by words;
thus, it assumes the two roles of agent (*kartṛ*) and instrument (*karaṇa*).
It is established in two ways: as the agent when conceived as being independent, and as the instrument when conceived as the most effective means of accomplishment (*sādhakatama*) for the action.

Because of the invariable concomitance with the instrument, this injunction is intended to exclude other instruments; its purpose lies in cultivating that excellence [of the agent] such that sharpness alone is the most effective means for cutting, and nothing else. Thus, the agent and the instrument are indeed distinct. || 96 ||

If this is so, and there is no simultaneous application (*aprāpti*) of the two designations (*saṃjñā*) in a single instance, why has the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) been introduced by the rule "the subsequent [rule prevails] over the preceding... (*parāṇi...*)? To this, he says:

Even though there is a difference in the individual selves, the single object remains situated in that same way; therefore, because agency depends upon that [object], even given the difference [between individuals], agency is not sublated. (97)

(94) Even though there is a difference in form due to being designated as the agent (*kartṛ*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), that single object remains established in its basis and does not deviate from its own nature; this is the meaning. The justification for this is "because it has that as its substratum" (*tadāśrayatvāt*). That is, because it has conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) as its substratum. For the difference is merely conceptual (*kālpānika*).

The meaning is that it destroys actual oneness (*vastavikaikatva*). Alternatively, some explain [the phrase] *tadāśrayatvāt* as "because of being the substratum for a single object," referring to the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of "agent" (*kartṛ*) and "instrument" (*karaṇa*).

Even though there is a difference in their capacities (*śakti*), because the substance (*dravya*) which is their substratum is one, that [substance] is the subject of the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between the two designations.

It is established that a designation (*saṃjñā*) applies only to a substance (*dravya*) qualified by a capacity (*śakti*). Thus, when the unity existing in an object is intended to be expressed, then, in a conflict between two designations for the same object, the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) prevails due to its higher priority and subordinates the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa-saṃjñā*); this is illustrated by the example: *asiśchinatti* ("the sword cuts").

Thus [it is said]. For here, since there is a single object of reference, both designations would apply simultaneously—namely, the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) and the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa*)—because the desire to express independence (*svātantryavivakṣā*) is inseparable from the lack of desire to express the state of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatvāvivakṣā*). However, because it is subsequent [in the rules], the designation of "agent" prevails. Indeed, independence is superimposed upon that which is the most effective means, as for example:
The bow is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) only when there exists the act of piercing with it;
thus, it is established that the instrument is that which provides the most excellent assistance toward the action. || 96 ||
He also dispels this doubt: that assistance is rendered by you through an object that exists, and not through one that does not exist; and just as instrumentality is understood through proximity.
In the same way, it is understood that even in the absence [of the agent], the accomplishment of the action occurs. || 98 ||

(95) Just as objects such as a cutting tool are recognized as instruments when they are present and attain a superior capacity for assisting the action, in the very same way, wealth— even though it is not present at the time of liberation and so forth due to its absence— is well known as an instrument precisely because it accomplishes liberation. || 98 ||
Right here, he states the author of the Sūtra’s own view as corroborating evidence:
"They declare that the status of being an instrument (karaṇatva) belongs to 'a little' (stoka) and so forth, either because of the production of that [result] or because of its non-production. (99)
(96) Regarding the rule *karaṇe ca stokālpa...* (Pāṇini 2.3.33), the examples given are *stokānmuktaḥ* and *stokena muktaḥ*. Here,
although words such as *stoka* denote substances (*satvavacana*), they function with the intention of expressing a mere quality (*dharmamātra*).

By virtue of its application, it is a term for non-existence. And that, being a mere phenomenon (*dharmamātra*) characterized by a small measure, whether existent or non-existent, is said to be the instrument (*karaṇa*) that exceptionally assists in the act of liberation. Because a small portion of the object to be given has been accomplished and nothing else is possible due to one's state of possessionlessness (*niṣkiṃcanatva*), therefore—

He is "released" (mukta); or rather, he is released because a small portion of the object to be given remains or has been exhausted. But if much were to be given, he would not be released; thus, it is by means of that which is "small" (stoka) and "not present" (abhūta) that he is released. In this way, in the expression "not twenty minus one" (ekānna-viṃśati), the absence of one constitutes the negation of twenty.
The instrument. || 99 ||

Thus, since the linguistic usage of a "means" (sādhana) is dependent upon the speaker's intention, whatever is intended as the most effective instrument (sādhakatama) is that which constitutes the instrument (karaṇa). And so,
[the object] is distinguished by the difference and non-difference of its properties from that which possesses them.
Just as [a single entity] is differentiated by the specific distinctions of action, limit, and exclusion. || 100 ||

(97) He states that by the word "dharma" only that which is supported [is meant], and by "tadvatā" (by that which possesses it), the support [is meant]. For instance, there is the usage "Devadatta cooks with wood," where the fire residing in the fuel is expressed through a desire to convey its non-difference from it. And thus, this act of cooking has Devadatta as its agent and the fuel as its instrument.

But when heat (*tejas*) is intended to be expressed as distinct from the fuel (*indhana*), then there is the action of cooking where the fuel is the agent and heat is the instrument, expressed as "the fuel will cook by means of heat.
Furthermore, when heat is distinguished from fire due to a specific causal factor, it is treated as the action itself.

The meaning is that just as an action is differentiated— that is, specified— by a particular delimitation (avaccheda) or particular distinction (bheda) of a limit such as a village, as in "he comes from the village" (*grāmād āgacchati*) or "he comes from the vicinity of the village" (*grāmasya samīpād āgacchati*),
so too should it be understood here. For [the action occurs] in a forested area (*sāraṇyaka*), in a place with boundary marks (*sasīmakā*), or in a leveled clearing (*sasthaṇḍilaka*).
When the word "village" (grāma) denotes [the village] as a non-distinct whole, the usage is "He comes from the village" (*grāmād āgacchati*).

But when the word "village" denotes [the village] as enclosed by a fence, the point of reference (*avadhi*) is distinct in the usage "He comes from the village," and due to that distinction, the action is qualified. Thus...

Furthermore, even due to the difference in instruments according to the speaker's intention (*vaivakṣika-karaṇabheda*), that very same primary instrument is expressed by the verbal suffix *lyuṭ* or the suffix *ghañ*, like the third case ending, in accordance with the speaker's wish; for example: *pacanaṃ medhaḥ* (the fire is the cooking), *pacanaṃ tejaḥ* (the heat is the cooking), *pacanī sthālī* (the pot is the cooking), *pacanam auṣṇyam* (the heat is the cooking), and so forth—examples should be cited accordingly.
That which is born of application is desired. || 100 ||
Thus ends the section on the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the *Sādhanasamuddeśa* of the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa*, composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja.
(98) Having examined the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārthe*), the agent (*kartṛ*) who possesses that same meaning is now examined;
its definition [is as follows].

"The agent (*kartṛ*) is independent" (Pāṇini 1.4.54). "Independent" means that its own self (*ātman*) is its *tantra*, its primary factor. For while the agent alone is the primary factor (*tantra*) for the instruments and other factors, because they are employed by him for the accomplishment of the action; the agent, however, is not to be employed by another.

It is called "independent" (svatantra). In this regard, one might raise the objection: "Since even instruments and other factors possess independence with respect to their own respective functions, what is the special distinction of the agent?

Anticipating this, he establishes [the agent's uniqueness] as follows: "Because [the agent] acquires its power from no other source beforehand, and because [it causes others] to enter a state of subordination."
Because the activity of those who have engaged [in it] proceeds dependent upon that, and because of the cessation [of that activity]. || 101 ||
Because no substitute is observed in the case of isolation, and because [the result] is seen even when there is assistance from afar, the independence of the agent is asserted. || 102 ||

Prior to the engagement of the instruments and so forth, [the agent] acquires capacity from another cause such as desire for the result, and not from the instruments alone. For it is the agent, desiring the fruit, who procures the instruments and the rest; thus, he is already possessed of power and independent even beforehand.

However, the instruments and so forth possess independence in their own respective operations solely through being employed by the agent, and not from any other source. For this very reason, they are brought into a state of subordination and dependence upon the agent; their activities are contingent upon him. The agent, however, being himself possessed of activity, exerts effort for the sake of the result.

The instruments and other factors that have been set in motion are brought to cessation by the agent; however, upon the attainment of the fruit, the agent ceases of its own accord. While a substitute for the instruments and other factors has been declared in the event of their unavailability when enjoined, there is no such substitute for the agent. For another person who might perform the action would not be a true substitute.
It is not so stated; for even that [agent] who is a seeker, capable, and not excluded possesses the qualification [for action].

Furthermore, in the case of isolation (*praviveka*), when other causal factors (*kāraka*) are absent, the agent is observed, as for example in "it exists" (*asti*), "it comes into being" (*bhavati*), "it is found" (*vidyate*), and so forth. Even though locative objects (*adhikaraṇa*) and the like are possible here, nevertheless—
Those [factors] are not invariably concomitant when they are not perceived through the operation of words;

therefore, since there is no action without an agent, the agent is distinguished even from those who act in concert. By this collection of reasons, the agent is established as superior to the instrument in the accomplishment of the action.

The meaning is this: even when [the agent] is a remote benefactor (*viprakṛṣṭopakāraka*), it is said that independence (*svātantrya*) is based on predominance (*prādhānya*); therefore, only that [predominant factor] receives the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*), and not the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, even though they are independent with respect to their own respective operations.
By this, the following Bhāṣya is explained:
"That which, when all the means [of action] are present, becomes the agent and the instigator" (Pāṇini 1.4.23).
And this Bhāṣya has been stated in brief, having internalized its inseparable implication.

This has been explained here by making explicit the meaning that was implicitly contained [within the root]. For instance, by the phrase "because its activity is dependent upon that," the status of being a direct instigator (*pravartakatva*) is explained;
and subordination (*nyagbhāvanā*) and so forth, which are implied by the force of the context (*sāmarthya*), have also been indicated. To explain further:
Because activity is dependent upon the agent, the subordination of the instruments and other factors is implied therein by the meaning [of the injunction].
And since that instigation is for the sake of the result, its attainment implies both excessive engagement and, conversely, desistance.
Furthermore, the instigator necessarily acquires power from something other than the one to be instigated; this too [is implied].

This has been explained. Furthermore, since there would be no initiator at all in the case of impossibility, the absence of a substitute has been clarified as being established by implication (*sāmarthya*). It has also been explained that the observation [of the result] in isolation—because one who is directly capable does not depend on anything else—is obtained through implication; thus, what was stated in summary has been expounded.
Having analyzed the commentary, it has been explained. || 101, 102 ||
Anticipating the objection that, since such a collection of properties does not exist in insentient things, they cannot possess agency, he says:
"The restriction [of grammatical gender] applies to the word through the emergence of these properties, but not to the actual object."
When there is an intention to express the agent as a property, the agent is understood from the word. || 103 ||

(99) A rule characterized as an independent agent— one defined by properties such as being an initiator, which are manifested through these aforementioned [qualities] like the acquisition of power from another source— must necessarily be resorted to in the domain of words; that is, it must be accepted by means of verbal expression.

That for whom these properties (dharmas) are made known should be understood as the agent; however, one should not seek the existence of these properties by treating them as having real entities (vastu) as their objects, such that [the properties] would apply even to insentient things, as in the cases: "The fire burns," "The fuel cooks," "The pot cooks," and so forth, or "The bank falls," "The river flows."

And in such cases as these, there would be no agency (*kartṛtva*). For when these properties are intended to be characterized as the agent, and are conveyed by the word according to that intention, then the agent is understood from the word as having a well-established definition; thus, like the instrument (*karaṇa*), the agent too is merely relative to the speaker's intention (*vaivakṣika*).

Thus it has been established. And by doing so, agency does not even become a metaphorical attribution in the case of insentient things, because the application [of the term] occurs everywhere without fail, making primary usage possible.
For in grammar, the meaning of a word is the conventional meaning (*śabdārtha*), not the actual ontological reality (*vastvartha*). Consequently, in another system of grammar...
The two definitions— "one who desires [the fruit]" and "likewise one who is engaged"— which were formulated with reference to sentient and insentient objects respectively, are not [correct].
This is what is meant by "skillfulness. || 103 ||
And when independence belongs to the intention to speak and so forth, then this [following] point is also established; thus he says:
"When a distinction is imagined for a single [entity] through its various mental states, the status of object, the status of instrument, and the status of agent arise. (104)

(100) In the expression "one kills oneself by oneself," we observe the application of three grammatical factors (*kāraka*s) to a single self, which depends on the differentiation of its forms brought about by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). This [application] does not hold up in a real, ontological usage of the *kāraka*s; for it is not possible for a single entity to [possess multiple roles] simultaneously.

A state of diverse and distinct forms can be apprehended; however, for the formless self (*ātman*), death produced by the operation of weapons and the like is impossible. Yet, the intention (*vivakṣā*) underlying the use of words is not obstructed in this case. For instance, there is a plurality of appearances in the various states of the intellect (*buddhi*).

Accordingly, the conceptualization of difference arises from the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). One who possesses the activity of raising and lowering the sword and so forth in accordance with the treatises and other sources is the "agent" (*kartṛ*) who "kills. Here, the self itself, having entered into the state of being an object, is likewise the "object" (*karman*). This is said when one intends to express an extreme degree of ease.
