If one were to exclude the operation of instruments such as weapons and so forth, the self would possess the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*) only in relation to the performance of an action; for elsewhere, the distinction between the agent and the instrument is observed. Therefore, in order to exclude that [distinction], it is stated here that the agent alone is likewise [the instrument] without distinction.
For this very reason, in the *Vārttika*, the application of the rule *karmavat* (treating the object like the subject) has been rejected on the basis of this principle.
"But it is established [as an action] because it is a natural action" (Pāṇini 3.1.87).
"Because an object is observed for an agent who is not performing an action when there is contact with the self" (Pāṇini 3.1.87).
Thus [it is stated].
"He kills himself; he is killed by himself. || 104 ||
He states that even something else is established regarding verbal agency:
"The non-existence prior to arising is based on a state of cognition;
being indistinguishable from any other existent, it becomes the agent of birth. (105)

(101) Regarding the statement "the sprout is born," does the agency of birth belong to that which exists or to that which does not exist? In this regard, [it has been argued] by such statements as: "If that which exists is born, from what [is it born]? Or if that which does not exist is born, how [can it be born]?
In that case, since agency is merely a matter of linguistic convention (*vaivakṣika*), it cannot even be used in a figurative sense (*upacāra*).

Someone says: "It is as follows. For, based upon those specific states of the cognition—which consists of the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) and is caused by words—that are restricted to particular words, the status of being the agent of production is established here, equivalent to the status of being the agent of another action."

For the word "sprout" (aṅkura) is employed when an object has been brought into proximity by the speaker’s intention; and that word reveals an entity that is already existent. Therefore, one might think: "How can this [sprout] have existence, given that its birth is determined by its association with the word 'is born'?"

The meaning of the sentence is established as follows: for a being whose existence is certain and whose capacity has been grasped through the accomplishment of its activity, there is birth in an external form. Consequently, that form by which it is a *satva* (being) is not the same as that by which it is an agent (*kartṛ*), nor is it the same as that by which it is a *satva*; thus, this arrangement is not ontological (*vāstavī*), but rather...

The meaning is "one would understand through words. Since the very meaning of the word is the object, and because the usage is unerring, it is primary in all cases; there is no secondary (metaphorical) sense whatsoever. || 105 ||
Regarding the practice of the actual state of things (*vastuvṛttacaryā*), he says that even in the case of a sprout, there is the following application:
"Just as the cause abides in the form of the effect, having then acquired the designation 'effect,' it arises as an effect. (106)

(102) It has been previously established, by relying on the states of the intellect (*buddhi*), that agency and birth are not tenable through the distinctions of the positions regarding existence and non-existence from the perspective of the effect. Now, it is demonstrated from the perspective of the cause.
For this very reason, the word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative position. In that regard, [the discussion begins] from the cause.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been stated that the effect arises as something entirely distinct [from the cause]. However, in the view of transformation (*pariṇāma*), this is said regarding the position of non-difference: since the cause and effect exist in the form of the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*), they are non-different, as in "milk becomes curd" or "the seed gives rise to the sprout."
In common usage, reality consists merely in the acceptance of specific states by a single persisting entity; thus,
in the process of bringing about particular modifications directed toward an effect,
the cause itself— being of the nature of existence— is designated by the superimposition of the expressive term belonging to those subsequent specific states.

The meaning is that it is logical to employ the expression "the sprout is born" (*ajāyate 'ṅkuraḥ*), because the agent undergoes birth characterized by the accomplishment of its subsequent state. || 106 ||
And this is logical— that the cause itself persists in the form of the effect— and in order to establish this according to his own tenet, he says:
"Just as the coiling of a snake, and the coming together of those who were dispersed."
In the same way, some proclaim that the nature of birth belongs only to existing things. || 107 ||

(103) Having previously established the impossibility of the relation between cause and effect through the distinction between the positions of existence and non-existence, [the author] has now concluded according to the doctrine of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) with the words, "But this process is most wonderful" (*ja.kṣkṣkṣ.sa.81*), and so forth. And therein, the meaning of birth is precisely this much:

When investigated, it is found to be nothing but a particular arrangement in such and such a manner. For example, the coiling of a snake is not a different thing from the snake itself; likewise, a fist or the like is merely a specific state consisting of a collection of separate parts such as fingers. Thus, the relationship between cause and effect has as its essence nothing more than a particular state of being.
Thus, because the substratum is non-different [from its states] and because it persists through the states, the status of being the agent of origination is established for the existent entity.
Now, even within the doctrine that cause and effect are distinct, he speaks in order to demonstrate that the status of being the agent of production exists in a real sense:
"That effect which proceeds from causes, having a distinct origin..."
Its own genus also becomes established through the form of the individual instance. || 108 ||

The source (*yoni*) is distinct and separate from this; for that non-existent (*asat*) object of transformation which is being produced, although it does not exist in a manifest form prior to its arising from its causes, it nevertheless exists by way of its generic nature (*jātyātmanā*). Therefore, having determined it as belonging to that class, [it is said to arise].

Because it is through the application of the means of production (*sādhana-viniyoga*) that the universal (*jāti*) alone is the motivator for the perfection of its own manifestor, it is conventionally said that "the universal itself is born in the form of the individual.
Thus, agency exists in the form of the universal, while being produced (*janyatva*) exists in the form of the individual; this is [the view of] the *atyantika* [school].
The meaning is that because there is no absence of distinction between the universal and the individual, their grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is established.
Now, in order to conclude his own established doctrine that "the meaning of a word is the object," he says:
"The application of a word occurs only toward existent things (bhāva), whether it be of cognition or of speech.
Even the [statement] 'it does not exist' does not apply to what is non-existent; therefore, it is not distinct from the existent. (109)

(105) Since the operation of both cognition and words occurs through the apprehension of a form (*ākāra*), it is impossible for them to be without an objective basis (*nirālambanatā*). Therefore, the form that is being perceived is always the object denoted by the word "existence" (*bhāva-śabda*) and the locus for the application of those two [terms]. For instance, there is no one whatsoever for whom the [cognition] "it does not exist" has non-existence as its objective basis.
Since both [cognition and verbal expression] arise by relying on a form imagined by another or conceived by oneself,
there is no distinction between these two— cognition and verbal expression— due to their reliance on a similar form;
for in conventional usage, the entire range of entities and non-entities is identical in its grasping of its own form.

The same applies here. However, the discussion of external objects is not a necessary part [of the argument], because practical discourse is fully accomplished by this much alone; thus, the formulation "when the apprehension of the form of existence occurs, the sprout arises" is easily established—this is the meaning. || 109 ||
He says that apart from the existence of cognition and words as objects, there is no external reality whatsoever for things in worldly transaction:
"Cognition and words function with respect to entities just as they exist."
For them, no conventional usage exists by means of any other reality. || 110 ||

(106) Since linguistic usage consists solely of designations and cognitions, the true nature of an entity must be sought in accordance with its cognition and its designation; one should not rely on some other essential nature of an entity that is neither perceived nor designated.

The meaning is that it must be countered. And thus, since a cognition devoid of the apprehension of an object is impossible, the agent is defined by means of that reality which is established [by that cognition];
and once defined, he is designated. Just as in the cognition "it does not exist," even though the object is non-existent externally...
An object that is being negated at a restricted place and time appears in a form perceived at another place and time,
and is thus designated by the grammatical suffix denoting the agent (*kartṛ-pratyaya*); likewise, even an object that is yet to come is so designated when it is oriented toward its effect.

The meaning of the section is this: it arises by the power of a capable cause that becomes manifest in the intellect through the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of an experience of that same kind; thus, it is designated as the "agent" (*kartṛ*) of birth. || 110 ||
Now, having fixed in his mind the principle stated in the *Saṃbandhasamuddeśa*, he demonstrates the impossibility of birth and destruction according to the doctrine of non-duality (*advaitanaya*):
"Just as there is no real division of space, and just as there is no real movement of a shadow..."
In the same way, birth and destruction are likewise postulated by some, even though there is no difference [between them]. || 111 ||

(107) It has been stated that even though space (*ākāśa*) is eternal and partless, a conceptualization of its differentiation is produced through the superimposition of spatial divisions based on the differentiation of objects with which it is in conjunction. Furthermore, although shadow, which consists of the absence of light, is devoid of motion, it appears to move by following the movement of the obstructing substance.
The superimposition [of activity] upon that which is inactive is thus untenable; for since non-existence has already been refuted,
and since the operation of a cause at the time of origination has been negated, it has also been demonstrated that such operation is impossible even at the time of destruction.
Furthermore, because the refutation of causeless destruction has been established, and because birth and destruction are impossible for the eternal reality— which is undivided and non-dual—

conventional discourse proceeds by way of the imagined forms of existence and non-existence, through the power of ignorance and the influence of birth and destruction which consist merely in appearance; this is explained in the *Saṃbandhasamuddeśa* itself.

This has been determined in detail. And thus, the meaning that [the world] arises like the conventional usage of existence and non-existence is established as being charming only so long as it is not investigated; such is the sense. || 111 ||

In order to establish that destruction is a conceptual construction, he says: "Just as the non-existence of space is described as being without a real form, so too the non-existence of form is based upon the unreal space. (112)
(108) Since the all-pervading space exists everywhere as a real entity, it is not absent anywhere.

Nevertheless, the non-existence of space—which is actually non-existent—is conceptually constructed by virtue of its being obstructed by the forms of objects such as jars that occupy limited locations.
For wherever jars and the like exist, there is the conventional usage: "space is non-existent. Thus...

Even in the case of corporeal objects such as jars and the like, their non-existence in certain places is determined by the observation of the intervening space; for it is impossible for an existing entity (*bhāva*) whose nature is real to undergo the destruction of its own essence, and if it were of a non-existent nature (*asat-svabhāva*), it would never exist at any time— according to this principle.
For it should be understood from the context that when the existence (*sattā*) of forms is concealed during the interval, people perceive only the ether devoid of them and thus undergo birth;
in this way, the fact that both birth and destruction are merely conceptual constructs (*kalpita*) is established.
And because conventional usage proceeds according to mental determination (*adhyavasāya*), things are established as being indeed without birth or cessation.
For space is not non-existence in reality; and since there is no absence of existence among things, nothing whatsoever ever undergoes birth, precisely because it always abides. (112)
Now, in order to justify the usage "he is born" even with respect to actual birth by means of another perspective, he says:
"Just as the self of action is designated by those activities which have that [birth] as their object."
This sequence of cause and effect exists because of the apprehension of non-difference. || 113 ||

(109) By the statement "the instrument [is designated] by way of being the effect" and so forth, the real non-difference between cause and effect was established. Now, however, it is stated by resorting to a figurative non-difference: for just as, in the case of the root *pac* ("to cook"), the softening [of the food] is the primary meaning.

By superimposing upon the primary action its constituent qualities and operations— such as placing [the pot] on the fire, pouring water, and so forth— which reside in the agent and others, and which exist for the sake of that [primary action], it is described as having the form of the principal action;
namely, the actions of placing on the fire, pouring water, pouring in the rice, and adding fuel belong to the primary agent.

In the case of "cooking" (*pākaḥ*) or "the pieces of wood cook" (*kāṣṭhāni pacanti*), where they burn until the state of being cooked (*viklitti*) is reached, the sequence of the cause is expressed as "the cooking" (*pāka*) and so forth; for this sequence or order of the cause exists precisely because it serves the purpose of the effect. Thus, in common usage, it is the cause itself that is designated by the word "sprout" (*aṅkura*) while acting as the agent.
The meaning is that it is appropriate to designate [it] as "being born" in the form of an effect. || 113 ||

Now, one might object: even if there is a superimposition of non-difference between cause and effect, agency with respect to birth belongs only to the effect and not to the cause, because the cause is already established. Anticipating this, [the author] states that in the context of the relationship between the material cause and its modification, agency belongs to both cause and effect alternatively.
He begins by establishing [the matter] through a distinction in application:

"In the doubt as to whether the agent of birth is the modification (vikāra) or the primordial nature (prakṛti), the views of the proponents differ according to the observation of indicative marks. (114)

(110) Here, in the context of the relationship between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is observed in such cases as "milk becomes curd" (*kṣīraṃ dadhi sampadyate*). Regarding this, there is a doubt; for since the relationship of primary and secondary status must necessarily exist because otherwise the syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) would be untenable, one must determine whether here the material cause is primary, or [the modification].
Is the modification (*vikāra*) the subordinate factor (*aṅga*), or is it the reverse? In that case, the primary cause (*pradhāna*) possesses agency with respect to production;
however, since the subordinate factor’s contact with production occurs through the medium of the primary cause, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
But when there is a designation by way of distinction, as in "the sprout is born from the seed," [the relationship is expressed differently].

Then, without any doubt, the agency belongs to the modification (*vikāra*), because the material cause (*prakṛti*) is designated as the agent by way of being the point of departure (*apādāna*), according to the rule: "The material cause is the [agent] of that which undergoes birth" (*janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*).

In this regard, the intention of those who hold that the modification is the agent is as follows: the acquisition of self-existence is what is called "birth," and it is the non-existent that acquires its self.
[The effect] is that which is to be obtained; and since it is thus a modification (*vikāra*), it is logical that the very same [effect] is the agent here.

However, those who hold that the primary cause (*prakṛti*) is the agent maintain that because a non-existent modification cannot possess the orientation toward the acquisition of its own self, agency is impossible in the birth characterized by that [acquisition].

For "birth" will be established as the tendency toward the attainment of selfhood; since the self is already obtained in the form of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), it remains in a state of orientation toward the attainment of selfhood characterized by subsequent stages. Therefore, it is appropriate that agency belongs to primordial nature alone. || 114 ||
In order to establish these two views through observations of indicative marks (*liṅga*) characterized by differences in usage and a division of subject matter, he says:
"When the sense of 'becoming' (*sampadyamāna*) is present, the dative case [used] therein is due to modification (*vikāra*)."
The statement concerning the earring is based upon the gold mass as its material cause.

(111) Regarding the Vārttika, "The fourth case ending should be prescribed when [the action] results in being prepared (*klṛpi sampadyamāne*)," this is its meaning: the fourth case ending is to be applied to the agent of the action of preparation. Furthermore, because traditional grammar (*smṛti*) is rooted in actual usage, when the fourth case is heard in connection with a word expressing a modification (*vikāra*), it belongs to the modification itself.

This indicates the agency of transformation (*sampatti-kartṛtva*). In the expression "the gruel becomes urine" (*mūtrāya sampadyate yavāgūḥ*), the meaning is that the gruel is produced as urine. Here, the connection of the material cause (*prakṛti*) with the action is mediated through its modification (*vikāra*), not directly. However, when a distinction is intended, [it is expressed as] "the agent of birth" (*janikartuḥ*).

In this case, the ablative case (*apādāna*) alone is the grammatical factor (*kāraka-vibhakti*), as in the expression "urine is produced from gruel" (*yavāgvā mūtraṃ jāyate*). However, when there is an intention to express non-difference (*abhedavivakṣā*), the dative case provides the scope. It is for this very reason that this determination was made when a doubt arose in that regard. Likewise, a lump of gold, when melted and recast...
Furthermore, in another formulation— "the two earrings become the color of khadira-wood embers"—

in this usage from the Bhāṣya, although the gold mass is the material cause (*prakṛti*), the singular number associated with it is not seen; rather, there is a dual number in "become" (*bhavataḥ*), which rests upon the duality of the two earrings as the modified effects (*vikāra*).
From this indicative mark as well—that the form of the agentive suffix is observed—it is determined that the modification possesses agency. || 115 ||
He states another mark (*liṅga*) that infers the agency of both the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*) by means of a difference in their respective objects:
"In a sentence, the agent is said to be that which is expressed by a root ending in a *saṃpadya* affix."
They become the junctions within the enclosure; such is the independence of the Brāhmaṇas. || 116 ||

(112) When there is a desire to express the transformation of something into that which it was not previously, the suffix * cvi* is prescribed after the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*, provided they function as the agent of the attainment (*sampadyakartṛ*). In the sentence constructed to demonstrate its meaning, the transformation is seen to function as the agent of the attainment. For example: "The Brahmins, who were not a *saṅgha*, become a *saṅgha*."
Because we observe the use of speech based on the unity inherent in the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha itself is the agent.

However, in the commentary (*vṛtti*) it is stated: "The Brahmins become united. Here, because the plural number is observed as residing in the Brahmins who constitute the base (*prakṛti*), the agency is determined to belong to the base.
Thus, in this way, the agency of both the material cause and its transformation, as established through the distinction of their application, is to be inferred.
Now, regarding the agency of *prakṛti*, he states the indicative mark (liṅga) mentioned by the author of the Bhāṣya:
"That which you do not become—therein, *prakṛti* does not have the substratum of 'you' (*yuṣmad*);
that which is derived from *prakṛti* is predicated of the *puruṣa*. (117)

The Bhāṣya cites: "(113) *atvaṃ tvaṃ sampadyate tvadbhavati*" (Pāṇini 5.4.50 with G. 1.4.108). Here, there is a modification (*vikāra*) of the meaning of *yuṣmad* ("you"), yet the second person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) based upon that [modification] is not observed; rather, it is "bhavati" [the third person].

Thus, from the observation of the first person (prathamapuruṣa) residing in the prakṛti which has the form of the meaning of "you" (yuṣmad-artha), it is concluded that agency belongs to the prakṛti alone. || 117 ||
Regarding how this [process] is logically established as being fixed according to the distinction of objects through the authority of its application,
he states the justification here:
"Without abandoning the prior state, while touching upon the subsequent property..."
The self of the object, as it were coalesced, is said to be "being born. || 118 ||

(114) Here, it is not said that non-existence arises in every respect; rather, since it does not abandon or relinquish its prior causal state, the possibility of agency exists here even for primordial matter (*prakṛti*). Nor is it entirely indifferent, but rather it touches upon a specific subsequent state.
The phrase "attaining" (*āsādayat*) implies the possibility of even a modification (*vikāra*) acting as the agent. Thus,
a single entity, delimited by the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of its prior and posterior states,
is oriented toward attaining a subsequent state in accordance with its prior state.
Thus, the sense of the verbal root and the sense of the suffix attain mutual consistency in the sense that "that which is being stretched forth, as it were, arises while being determined. And so,
both the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the material cause and its modification, as well as the agency (*kartṛtva*) of both, are established.
Anticipating the objection that, if this were so, both [the agent and the object] would be the agent in every case, he says:
In some instances, a certain property is perceived as being more intensely active; furthermore, the powers of entities, though distinct, may become conjoined. (119)

(115) Since both the material cause (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*) are non-different according to the principle already stated, they are equally capable of being conjoined with the notion of "origination" (*janisamanvaya*).

Nevertheless, it has been said that when an agentive suffix arises, in some cases the modification is endowed with activity (*savyāpāra*), while in other cases it is the material cause. Even so, this distinction is made through a division of subject matter (*viṣayavibhāgena*).
In the word "is born" (*jāyate*), the agency of both [the self and the body] has been established in the manner already described;

the meaning is that since the powers of entities, though distinct elsewhere, sometimes even attain a state of conjunction. Or rather, in every case, both possess agency, but for one [of them], it is...

"Directly" (*sākṣāt*) is said to mean "more intensely engaged in activity. For, since the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*) would otherwise be untenable, when one is the agent of production, the other must necessarily be understood as such as well. Indeed, that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is...

The primary [agent] is that which possesses an activity characterized by excellence; however, the other, being mentioned as a subordinate factor (guṇa), possesses an activity that is not preeminent. || 119 ||

And so, if there were a conjunction between the agent and the power, then one might ask why, in the case of the expression "tvadbhavati" (you become), the person (*puruṣa*) is not the substratum of the state of modification; anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The person's engagement with an object contrary [to its true nature] occurs in the state of error."
For in this case, the means of accomplishment (sādhana) is understood as being accompanied by an operation. || 120 ||

(116) In the case of "atvaṃ tvaṃ sampadyate" ("you become you") or "tvadbhavasi" ("you become from you"), when the second person is intended based on the referent of the word *yuṣmad* (the second person pronoun), the intended meaning is not perceived as being that the base (*prakṛti*) is the referent of *yuṣmad* and the modification (*vikṛti*) is the referent of *yuṣmad*. Rather, the referent of *yuṣmad* is the base, which is endowed with activity.

In the case of "arising from conditions," another modification of that [agent] is perceived. For in the expression "you become" (*saṃpadyase*), the agent—the referent of the second person pronoun—is perceived as possessing activity; thus, by virtue of its being the possessor of the fruit, another modification would necessarily follow for it. And so it is.

It should be understood that the referent of *yuṣmad* (the second person) undergoes a transformation into the state of being the referent of *na-yuṣmad* (the first person). Therefore, for the purpose of conveying that the base (*prakṛti*) of the word *yuṣmad* is that which is being transformed, the use of the first person alone is logical here. || 120 ||
He explains precisely what it means for [a cognition] to function with a contrary object:
"The conceptual construction there would be 'you are someone else';
just as when a king has fallen into the state of a servant, such would be the case. (121)

(117) Just as when it is said, "O King, you become a non-king," the fact that the meaning of the base *rājan* (king) is conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) through its connection with the meaning of *yuṣmad* (you), one understands that the king— who possesses activity— becomes the agent of the action of becoming (*sampatti*) by means of a state of servitude that is the opposite of his own [royal] nature; so it is here.

When it is said "tvadbhavasi" (you become), because the meaning of the second-person pronoun (*yuṣmad-artha*) is determined to be the agent in the establishment of the state, the intended meaning—characterized by the attainment of the status of being the second-person referent—would not be perceived; therefore, for the sake of that comprehension, the first person (*prathamapuruṣa*) is superior. Not [the second person].

For one who intends to express one thing, another cannot be expressed. However, in the case of "The gold lump becomes two earrings," even though the modification (*vikāra*) is the agent, there is no occurrence of a contradictory meaning, such as "the two earrings transform into the nature of the gold lump. [This is because the verb] *bhavataḥ*...

Because there is no necessary requirement for a change in the agent; indeed, it is only in the domain of the *cv*-suffix that a necessary entry into another state of change is said to occur for the agent. This is because the *cv*-suffix is prescribed when the original form (*prakṛti*) is intended to be expressed, and the original form is established in its own nature.

It is logical that the agent, undergoing a state of modification and being active, should be denoted by a word expressing modification (*vikāra-śabda*) for the purpose of attaining the cessation of a specific modification; for in the case of a word ending in *cv-* (the suffix of becoming),
when it occurs in a commentary (*vṛtti*) and is connected with an action, the rule prescribes the designation of "gati" (preverb), since a *gati* functions as an adverbial modifier of the action.
Since agency is impossible for that which is not a sentient being, it is appropriate that Primordial Matter (prakṛti) alone is the agent;

thus, [the suffix] *kyaṅ* occurs in relation to an action characterized by qualifiers such as "transformation," "form," "motion," or "designation," as in [the example] "he becomes you. However, in the sentence "the Brahmins become a multitude" (*saṅghībhavanti brāhmaṇāḥ*), [the situation is different].

Because both the material cause (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*) are explicitly mentioned by their own terms in the *cvya*-affix, there is a restriction regarding their agency based on the predominance or subordination as intended by the speaker. For instance, the inherent nature of the material cause is intended to be predominant when it is engaged in the act of transformation (*sampatti*). At other times, however—

The nature of modification is superimposed [upon the base]. For example, in the expression "the great moon" (*mahān candraḥ*), because the form of the base meaning "not great" functions as the agent, that very same entity is denoted by the word *mahat*, which expresses a modification; thus, due to its figurative nature, the substitution of *āt* for the sense of "great" does not occur.

It has been stated that [the rule] applies. However, in the case of the expression "mahadbhūtā brāhmaṇī," since it is intended that the modification (*vikāra*) itself, in the sense of "great" (*mahan*), is the agent as the subject of becoming (*bhavitṛ*), the substitution of the masculine form (*puvadbhāva*) certainly occurs by virtue of the characteristic of coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*); thus it has been explained. || 121 ||
The incidental discussion is concluded. This must now be addressed: independence (*svātantrya*) has been explained by the passage beginning with "prior to the acquisition of power from another.

However, that [independence] is not tenable for the instigator (*prayojaka-kartṛ*), for he [the instigator] exists within the operation of the prompter (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*), just like the instrument (*karaṇa*) and other factors.

Being subordinate (*nyagbhavan*), [the instigator] lacks independence (*svatantra*) even though he possesses independence with respect to his own operation. Consequently, the designation "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*), which is based on independence, would not apply to him; thus, in the sentence *pācayaty odanaṃ devadattena yajñadattaḥ*, the instrumental case expressing agency (*kartṛ-tṛtīyā*) would not occur for Devadatta, the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*).

It would be so; and thus the Vārttika states: "When the designation 'agent' applies to one who is independent, there must be an addition [to the rule] for that which possesses a cause [of action], because of its lack of independence" (Ja. on Pāṇini 1.4.54).
Thus: "cause" (*hetu*) means the instigator (*prayojaka*), and "that which possesses it" (*tadvat*) means the one to be instigated (*prayojya*).

Since the designation "cause" (*hetu-saṃjñā*) would apply to the act of urging (*adhyeṣaṇa*), where even for one who is being enjoined, that state of being an instigator is not contradicted, it is appropriate to take "in the sense of a cause" (*hetumati*) as a figurative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding this, there is a *parihāra-vārttika*:

"Or rather [it is] not so, because of independence" (*na vā svātantryāt*). Since the person being prompted possesses independence with respect to their own activity, the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) is established.

[Objection: But in that case, the same would apply to the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the other factors as well. [Response: This is not so; for they are assigned their respective designations, such as "instrument" and so forth, according to their own specific roles. However, no other designation has ever been stated for the one who is impelled (*prayojya*); thus, it retains only the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*). This being the case, since the activity of the impelled depends upon the impeller (*prayojaka*), how [is it that the impeller is not designated as the agent]?
Anticipating the objection regarding [the agent's] independence, he establishes it as follows:
"Because of the possibility [of success], one is established as the agent for the accomplishment of an action;
thus, in an action to be accomplished by oneself, one is the instigator of the means. (122)
Merely through its application, it relies on its own sovereignty to remain subordinate;
thus, it becomes indistinguishable from other independent [deities] who are free from doubt. (123)

(118) First of all, that which is to be employed while its activity has not yet commenced is employed only after its capacity for action has been inferred; otherwise, there would be no employment at all. For no sensible person ever directs one who is incapable of any action toward a task. Consequently, its power is ascertained.

Only an agent who possesses the capacity for action is employed independently; even one who is engaged in an action to be accomplished by himself, being active and setting in motion the entire collection of instrumental factors such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth,
is employed while his action is still in progress, lest there be a suspicion of desistance.
Thinking "he has ceased," that [agent] too, though an independent agent, is to be employed in his own activity;

and precisely because of his independence, he attains a state of subordination and dependence upon the instigator's command merely for the sake of being employed. For a command exists for the accomplishment of an action. And thus the action is accomplished if—

The agent to be employed attains independence characterized by the application of other means of accomplishment, and not otherwise; thus, independence is not contradicted by the act of employment. Furthermore, due to the difference in objects, there is dependence in the employment [of others], while there is independence in one's own operation. And this [independence] resides precisely in the means.

Independence (*svātantrya*) consists in one's own activity, while dependence (*pāratantrya*) exists in the act of being employed by another. Thus, one who is similar to others who are determined to be independent—by virtue of not being prompted by another and being self-reliant—is established as an independent agent (*prayojya*).
This has been stated in the *Vārttika*:
"Otherwise, one who does not act himself would still be 'causing to act.

[If it is argued: 'One who does not act is not [an agent],' then he must be independent (*svatantra*). [This is so] because it is impossible for a capable person who is indifferent or lazy to engage in activity."

The meaning is that only one who possesses recognized independence (*svātantrya*) is the "instigated" (*prayojya*). If this were so, then since an independent agent is the "instigator" (*prayojaka*), there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even instruments (*karaṇa*) and other factors—which are independent in their own operations—are designated as "agents" (*kartṛ*) when they are the instigators of [another] instigator. If you ask, "Let it be so; what is the fault? [the answer follows].

Regarding the phrase "even the cause" (*hetum api*), there is the contingency of the *ṇic* affix [to denote] that activity. If it is argued that this is not a fault because the [activity] has already been expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*), we say no; for the instigation (*praiṣa*) regarding the object would be included within the meaning of the verbal root, since the agent’s efficient force (*bhāvanā*) exists for the sake of the fruit, and the meaning of the verbal root is [accomplished] by that [force].

[This is] due to contact (*saṃsparśa*). However, in the case of a verbal root that does not denote an action (*akarmaka-dhātu*), the application of instruments and so forth, although existing in reality, is not determined; therefore, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) would arise in order to convey that [application].
From the word, only the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of an action possessing specific means is understood, but not [the specific status of] the instruments and so forth.

The agent [is defined by] the act of impelling. Furthermore, if the prompted agent were also designated as a *hetu* (cause), then the reference to the "independent" [agent] in the rule *tatprayojakaḥ* would be purposeless; for that [reference] is intended to exclude the prompter of instruments (*karaṇa*) and the like.
However, even in the case of such instruments and so forth, there exists a prompter who relies on their independence with respect to their own respective operations.
Reflection upon the notion of a "cause" (hetu-saṃjñā) is useless; moreover, the very notion of a "cause" is itself purposeless.

Let there simply be the rule "the suffix *ṇic* occurs after a word denoting an agent" (*kartṛ-mati ṇic*). And thus, [the rule] "after the roots *bhī* and *smi*, when the cause is expressed" (*bhīsmyor-hetumaye*) [is established].

Regarding the rules *'bhiyohetubhaye ṣuk'* (Pāṇini 7.3.40) and *'bibheterhetubhaye'* (Pāṇini 6.1.56), if the wording were *'kartṛbhaye'* instead of *'hetubhaye'*, an undesirable result would follow. Therefore, [the agent] must be independent (*svatantra*).
Regarding the term *prayojaka* (the instigator), one must strive to exclude the designation of "cause" (*hetu*) for the instigator of instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth.

To this it is replied: because the pronoun *tasya* in the phrase *tasya prayojakaḥ* refers back to that independent agent who is designated as the "experiencer" (*anubhava-kartṛ*), [it excludes] the instruments and others who have merely acquired the designation of "agent" [through their dependence on him].

The instigator (prayojaka) does not receive the designation of "agent" (hetu). For instance, although one is independent with respect to one's own operation, because instruments and the like are dependent upon the operation of the primary agent, they do not receive the designation of "agent.
Indeed, by the force of the scriptural mention of "independence" (svatantra), it is preeminent capacity that is intended.
However, since instruments (*karaṇa*) and the other factors cannot function as causal agents (*kāraka*) while merely imitating [the agent],

the independence (*svātantrya*) inferred from the impossibility of their functioning otherwise would at most be useful for the designation "instrument" (*kāraka-saṃjñā*), but not for the designation "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*).

Because they are overwhelmed by the application of the primary agent, there is an absence of superior independence; therefore, those who are agents are not themselves commanded. However, the one being employed, even while acting as an employer, does not at all relinquish his own superior self-dependence, which is characterized by the power to employ other instruments of action.
In every respect, it is logical that he alone is the agent. Therefore it has been said: "He is supported by the state of being an agent.
It is thus established that what is intended is [the soul] as an agent, whether past, future, or currently conceived by the intellect (buddhi). 122, 123.
It has been stated: "In mere application, [the agent] remains dependent on independence through subordination. To this he says: "Or rather, that too does not exist;
for all things proceed from causes for their own sake."
Even the compliance with another's intention is for the sake of accomplishing one's own purpose alone. (124)

(119) Since everyone acting out of a desire for their own self-interest does not thereby incur dependence on others in that activity, the fact that the activity of one person may merely be an auxiliary means for the accomplishment of another's purpose is the sole reason [for the employment] of servants and the like.
The state of being directed by another is described as following the intentions of the master and others.

For the activity of servants is indeed caused by a reward; however, even for those free from passion who act out of compassion, the accomplishment of the welfare of others is their own self-interest and the fruit of their action, since that is defined as what is desired.
This very point has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "All these beings strive for their own prosperity; no one here thinks, 'I must favor another. (Mahābhāṣya on Pāṇini 3.1.26).
Thus, in response to the objection— "When [words] are employed for the sake of their own excellence, what is the purpose of the object to be prompted?"— the following resolution has also been stated:
"They become attached to the intentions [of the speaker]" (Pāṇini 3.1.26).

Thus [it is said]. The intention of the instigator (*prayojaka*) is the accomplishment of the action. And that [action] is indeed accomplished by the one being instigated (*prayojya*), even though he proceeds by aiming for a result for his own sake. And having established it thus:
Regarding the rule *hetumati ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.26):

the intention of the instigator (*prayojaka*) consists in the accomplishment of the action. And even though the one being impelled (*prayojya*) acts while aiming for a result for his own sake, he nonetheless accomplishes [the action] for the instigator. Thus...
And having done so, the supplementary rules (*upasaṃkhyāna*) were rejected in the rule "ca kṛtvā 'hetumati ca" (Pāṇini 3.4.26).
"Or rather, it is not [so], because it is produced by a commonality; for it is not distinguished from the cause" (Patañjali on *Mahābhāṣya* 3.1.26).

This is because the rising of the sun at Māhiṣmatī was intended by the traveler as a natural occurrence, yet it came about by chance (*kākatālīya*), and thus [the expression] follows that underlying intention.
"Sūrya is to be employed," and so forth, should be applied accordingly. Thus says the author of the Vārttika:
"For activity occurs in both cases without dependence [on further proof]" (Ja. od Gh.
3.1.26). Even the activity that occurs toward one who is free from doubt when being employed does not belong to the person being employed.

"Having regard for its own meaning," that is to say, "for its own [verbal] self. However, in cases such as "he narrates the killing of Kaṃsa," one perceives Kaṃsa and the others "as if they were present before the eyes."

This has already been established by such [statements] as "ityādi. Even in the case of insentient objects, in instances such as "the lodging accommodates the mendicant," the status of being a prompter (*prayojakatva*) must be justified through the superimposition of intention based on the suitability for accommodation and so forth. And thus, by mere fitness, it is simply a cause (*nimitta*).
It has been stated that the "cause" (*hetu*) is the "instigator" (*prayojaka*), as in the rule regarding "on account of" (*nimittāt*). This is also stated in the *Vārttika*:
"The mention of a cause is merely a formal occasion (*nimitta-mātra*), as seen in the case of [the suffix] *bhikṣā* and others" (*Jaiminīya-vārttika* on Pāṇini 3.1.26).
Thus ends the investigation into the agent. || 124 ||
Thus ends the section on the Agent (*kartṛ*) in the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, the son of Bhūtirāja.
Following the investigation of the agent, [the author now discusses] the cause (*hetu*), since the agent himself, when acting as an instigator, is the cause.
One who deliberates,
or who performs the acts of commanding or entreating, and who performs actions conducive to those ends,
attains the designation of "hetu" (motive/cause) as prescribed by the grammatical treatise, just like the agent (kartṛ). || 125 ||

(120) *Vyāpāraṇā* preceded by a command is *preṣaṇa*; the meaning is that *niyoga* has as its object one who is inferior. On the other hand, when one causes a person of honor to engage in an activity, that is *adhyeṣaṇā*;
the meaning is that *prabodhana* has as its object one who is honorable. These [terms] are synonymous with those.

These are the activities conducive to the accomplishment of the action of the instigator (*prayojaka*). And this alone is the primary operation of the instigator, namely, the performance of that which is capable of bringing about the accomplishment of the action of the one being instigated (*prayojya*);
for it is all-pervasive, existing even in cases such as begging for alms. Of this very [operation]...
The distinction is based on the objects being inferior or superior, taking the form of "sending" (preṣaṇa) and "requesting" (adhyeṣaṇa).

Thus, according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (gobalīvardanyāya), what is intended here is conduct conducive to that [mendicancy] which is distinct from those two, having mendicancy as its object. These are mentioned separately because of the difference in their practical application.

Just as being "employed" (prayojyatva) was described as acting in accordance with another's intention, so too is "employing" (prayojakatva) the manifestation of one's own intention; thus, the performance of what is capable of accomplishing that [intention] is everywhere the function of the employer (prayojaka).
"The agent alone," it is said.

He explains the particle *ca* in the rule *tatprayojakaś ca hetuś ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.55) for the purpose of the co-occurrence of designations (*saṃjñāsamāveśa*). For if the particle *ca* were not present here, the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) would not apply, because of the governing rule that only one designation applies at a time (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*).

This is for the purpose of inclusion (*samāveśa*). As it is stated in the *Vārttika*: "The mention [of the root] *gam* includes both the roots *gati* and *div*, as well as those that take an agentive cause (*hetumat*). And: "In the case of what is prescribed in the *Śāstra*. The meaning is that its very mention should occur in the specific rule (*pradeśa*).
For a worldly cause (*laukika-hetu*) is a thing capable of accomplishing a result, having as its object substances and so forth.

However, this is its specific distinction: as an object of action, it is a causal factor (*kāraka*), a cause that is either instigated or instigating. Therefore, [the relationship of] commanding and so forth is based upon being a causal factor.
One's own operation (*svavyāpāra*) is indicated here; in that regard,
[the rules] "hetumati ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.26) and "bhiyo hetubhaye" (Pāṇini 7.3.40) apply.
In this context, there is the inclusion of an artificial cause (*hetu*). However, regarding the rule for the third case (*tṛtīyā-vidhi*),
since the instigator (*prayojaka*) is already established as an agent (*kartṛ*) by the rule "when [the sense is] cause" (*hetau*, Pāṇini 2.3.23), the third case is established for the worldly cause.
The mention of "cause" (*hetu*) [is made] because even in the rule for the fifth case,
the technical term [defined by] Pāṇini 2.3.24, *akartari* ("other than the agent"), is excluded.

In the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.126) as well, because the prompted agent (*prayojya*) possesses the status of a *kāraka*, and because its connection with an action is invariable, [the term *kriyā*]— by virtue of the capacity of the qualifier— refers to substance, quality, and action.

Because of the presence of both concomitance and deviation, only a worldly cause (*laukika*) is understood [by the term *hetu*]. This is likewise because of the governing context of verbal roots (*dhātu*).
For a verbal root does not function in the sense of a cause that is a grammatical means (*sādhana*). Thus [it is stated]:
"The suffix *liṅ* is used for the cause and the effect" (Pāṇini 3.3.156).

In this case as well, because the cause (*hetu*) serves as a qualifier of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), and because the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) does not constitute the root-meaning itself, the cause is purely worldly (*laukika*).
This is according to the rule: *kuño hetutācchīlyānulomyeṣu* (Pāṇini 3.2.20).

In this case as well, the cause is not the prompter (*prayojaka*). This is because the suffix *ṇic* is prescribed there, and because the term *kuñja* refers to the root *kṛ* itself, excluding the agentive suffix *ti*. Therefore, since the agent is obtained here by virtue of the action being performed (*kṛtva*), the worldly cause (*laukika-hetu*) serves as its qualification. And because there is no contradiction with that, the status of the agent is not negated.

And since the agent is denoted by verbal suffixes (*kṛt*) precisely in the form of capability (*yogyatā*), the cause (*hetu*) being presented as a mere occasion (*nimitta*) becomes a qualification; furthermore, the repetition of the word establishes a restriction, namely "only a cause. Therefore, knowledge and the like are non-deviant causes with respect to fame and so forth.

This has been established. Furthermore, in this context, these elements such as the logical reason (*hetu*) and so forth, though understood through the power of the cognition of a specific agent, are ultimately nothing but word-meanings (*padārtha*) by way of a traditional succession.
Otherwise, if they were perceived only in the state of the sentence (*vākya*), there would be no point in a grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*) that takes the individual word (*pada*) as its limit.

They would not attain the status of being a cause (*nimitta*). Here, in the sūtra beginning with *praiṣātisarga...* (Pāṇini 3.3.163), the *loṭ* [suffix] is conjoined by the particle *ca*; thus, in the sense of a command (*praiṣa*), it applies.
It is raised in the Bhāṣya that because both the causative suffix (ṇic) and the aorist (luṅ) are prescribed, there would be the contingency of optionality;
[the objection is: why does the causative suffix not occur in such instances as *pṛcchatu mā bhavān* and *anuyāṅktām mā bhavān*?
Regarding the rule *ghaṭādayo mitaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.159),

by using the self-reference "mā bhavān," [the author] demonstrates the injunction (*praiṣa*) residing in the instigator (*prayojaka*), thereby strengthening the application of the causative suffix *ṇic*. In this regard, a refutation has been stated in the Bhāṣya.

Regarding the rule "akartṛtvāt" (Pāṇini 3.1.26): for the suffix *ṇic* is prescribed here to denote an instigator (*prayojaka*) of an independent agent (*svatantra-kartṛ*) with respect to that agent's activity; [and such a suffix cannot apply] to one who has not already engaged in the act of questioning.

The meaning is that because there is an absence of agency, there is an absence of the designation "cause" for its instigator; therefore, the causative suffix *ṇic* does not apply to the instigation (*praiṣa*) of that activity. However, an impeller (*codaka*)—such as Time and so forth—is not an instigator of one who is incapable of questioning and the like, nor is he [an instigator] of one already engaged in action, because [in the latter case] the injunction (*niyoga*) would be purposeless.
He says that this is an instigation to act because the action is considered capable of being performed:
"Furthermore, O sir, an agent must exist for an action that is present, not for one belonging to the past or the future" (Pāṇini 3.1.26).

To this, the reply is: "In that case, a connection is established" (*G.eṇa od gh.* 3.1.26). The relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*) is one that is made possible by semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) with respect to past or future actions.

And in that context, since only the action of the instigator (*prayojaka*) is possible within the scope of the imperative suffix (*loṭ*), [the meaning is] "be the agent in the action," and not another operation of the instigator directed toward the activity of the one being instigated (*prayojya*). Immediately following this is the Bhāṣya.

"And as for [the question] 'how is the agent expressed by the agentive suffix? (Pāṇini 3.1.26), the answer to this is: "How can this verb *pṛcchati* ('he asks') function [to denote the agent] when it does not ask about this [agent]? (Pāṇini 3.1.26).
Thus it has been said: "In that context, a connection is established, [in the form]: 'One should perform this action. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.26)
Thus it was said. Immediately following, it was stated:
"In that case, the connection is also made by the agent [with the verb], as in: 'May you be the agent in this action'" (Pāṇini 3.1.26).

Thus, just as here the verbal root *pṛcch* (to ask) occurs even when one is not currently asking, by virtue of the intention toward the act of asking, so too the imperative suffix (*loṭ*), which denotes the agent, is employed because of its connection with that agent;
hence it was said, "the connection is indeed made with the agent. And so it is.
By the commentator (bhāṣyakāra) stating this, it is effectively said that because agency (*kartṛtva*) is not currently present here, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) does not apply.
For indeed, the agency being enjoined here is something new, not something already existing.
One is commanded, "Become an agent (*kartā*) in the action," and not "being already an agent. Therefore, [the suffix does not apply] to an agent...

The *praiṣa* (directive) of an existent agent belongs to the domain of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), which is inherent in the instigator; however, the *loṭ* suffix is prescribed for the agent and other grammatical participants.

The directive of that [agent] has the meaning of the verbal root as its adjunct and is indicated by it. Furthermore, that [directive] is not expressed by either the verbal root or the suffix, but rather, by implication, the speaker himself remains established as the instigator.

Thus, the injunctive force (*praiṣa*), which constitutes the property of that [causative suffix], remains present and is not cut off here by the restricted time [of the action] inherent in the verbal root and its suffix. And so, even when one is asking at the present moment, the usage *pṛcchatu* ("let him ask") is employed. However, since the injunctive force is the expressed meaning (*vācya*) of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), it is a property of the denotable object (*abhidheya*) because it is conveyed by the word itself.

The agent (*bhavan*) is delimited by the restriction of time through a suffix such as *laṭ* which denotes a fixed time; for [the agent] who is the instigator (*prayojaka*), related to that agent introduced by a *lakāra* expressing the agent derived from a causative (*ṇyantāt*) or by a suffix such as *tṛc*, is connected [to the action].

"It is understood" (*pratīyate*) is a property of the denotable object (*abhidheya-dharma*). For in the treatise, meaning (*artha*) is presented in two ways as a constituent part of grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*): one is a property of the speaker (*prayoktṛ-dharma*), such as repetition (*vīpsā*), negation (*bādha*), envy (*asūyā*), censure (*kutsana*), and so forth; the other is a property of the object to be communicated (*pratipādya-dharma*). Of these, this [is the latter].

The domain of the loṭ suffix—namely, an injunction (praiṣa) such as a command or an exhortation—is excluded [from being the denotation of the optative] because it is a property of the speaker, like a physical affliction or the like, and thus is not the thing to be expressed. || 125 ||
This very point is established with full intent:
"The imperative suffix (loṭ) is prescribed for the mere substance in the case of commands such as 'ask' and so forth;
however, when there is the employment of that which possesses an action, that is the domain of the causative suffix (ṇic). (126)

(121) For a mere substance whose activity has not yet commenced and which has not yet attained the status of an agent, when the sense of agency itself is to be expressed through a command (*praiṣa*), the suffix *loṭ* is prescribed. A suffix following a verbal root such as *pṛccha* or *anuyuñj* expresses the kāraka of the agent and so forth. However, in the case of one whose activity has already commenced, [the suffix is used] when there is a suspicion of cessation.
Intending that "the agent may not desist," the suffix *ṇic* is taught as denoting the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*) with respect to the independent agent alone;
for the position that the suffix-meaning is a qualifier [of the base-meaning] was established in the rule *hetumati ca*. Likewise...
And the Vārttika states: "'The term 'having a cause' (hetumatī) is used for the purpose of including the suffixes that denote the kārakas. (Ja on Pāṇini 3.1.26).
Thus, in this way, the scope of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the imperative (*loṭ*) is indeed distinct,
because a difference in the nature of the command (*praiṣa*) is determined here from the usage of words in common parlance;
for the command within the scope of the causative suffix is a property of the denotable object (*abhidheya-dharma*) and is expressed by the causative suffix itself.

This is because there is a distinction between those properties [of the speaker] and the object of the *loṭ* suffix, which is to be indicated (*dyotyārtha*) as a property of the agent. For this very reason, it should be connected with the two occurrences of the word "tu" (but). In examples such as "pṛcchatu mā bhavān" ("May you ask"), there exists no word that directly denotes the person who issues the command (*praiṣakartṛ*).

Since the agent is understood by implication as merely the one who utters [the word], the "impulsion" (praiṣa) here is not a property of the denoted meaning. Nor is it denotable in its own form by the *loṭ* suffix, because that is not what the *loṭ* denotes; rather, from the utterance of the word ending in *loṭ*, it is understood as a property of the prompter, just like "command" (*ājñā*) and so forth.

However, there is no word that explicitly expresses this as a *praiṣa* (an imperative command). If, then, there is such a clear distinction between these two types of *praiṣas*, why was it asked in the Bhāṣya: "Why does the causative suffix *ṇic* not occur here in the case of *pṛcchatu mā bhavān*? (Let your honor ask me)?
[This is] according to Pāṇini’s rule *gher ṅiti* (P.

7.3.111). This distinction is to be understood through worldly usage; since no such distinction is made in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) regarding the analytical description (*anvākhyāna*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) maintains that they are identical as mere commands (*praiṣa*). || 126 ||

This has been explained. Here, one might raise the objection that since everything involved in the activity of an instigator—such as commanding or requesting—is attained through the instigator's operation, the designation "object" (*karman*) would undesirably apply to the person being prompted. Anticipating this, he says: "Because of its independence with respect to the subordinate action (*guṇakriyā*), [the agent] attains the status of an object (*karmatā*) in the act of commanding (*preṣaṇa*)."
By virtue of the rule regarding the designation "karma," it is expressed by its own grammatical function (svadharma). || 127 ||

(122) Without abandoning its own independence, the prompted agent (*prayojya*) attains dependence upon the activity of the prompter (*prayojaka*). For it has been stated that its independence is not actually destroyed by the prompter; otherwise, one would have to say that "he causes [something] to be done" even when it is not being done. And thus:

Even in the case of commanding (*praiṣa*), the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) certainly applies because of independence with respect to one's own activity; however, the designation "object" (*karman*) would apply by virtue of being caused to act through the command,
as per the rule *gati-buddhi-...* (Pāṇini 1.4.52).

By such statements [the rule] is restricted: the *prayojya* (the one being prompted) is designated as the *karman* (object) only when it pertains to verbal roots whose sense involves motion (*gati*) and so forth, and not otherwise.

Thus, in examples such as *pācayaty odanaṃ devadattena*, the *prayojya* is expressed by its own inherent property, namely agency (*kartṛtva*). Now, one might object: even in the case of prompting (*praṣa*), independence (*svātantrya*) has not ceased.
Since the designation *kartṛ* (agent) would prevail due to its higher status, how can the restriction stated in [Pāṇini 1.4.52], "gati-buddhi... and so forth, be explained?
For if the designation *kartṛ* were to apply, the designation *karman* (object) would have to be introduced as a new rule; thus, it would serve as an original injunction (*vidhi*).
To this it is replied: here, with respect to the two powers residing in the domain of two actions—one subordinate and one principal—[the restriction applies].

It has already been established that it is the power of the *pradhāna* (the primary factor) alone that impels its own effect, and not the power of the *guṇa* (the subordinate factor). In this context, the operation of the one being prompted (*prayojyavyāpāra*), which is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), is secondary because it serves as a qualifier for the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*); however, the operation of the prompter (*prayojakavyāpāra*) is what is denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
The primary element [is the meaning of the suffix]. For in all cases, the meaning of the suffix is primary because it is delimited by the meaning of the base;

as it is said, "the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together. Therefore, since the activity of the instigator (prayojaka) is primary here, the karmic capacity (*karma-śakti*) itself performs its own function in relation to that.

It causes [the object] to reach [the state], but the agent-power does not have the activity of the prompted agent as its object. For example, although there is independence regarding the softening of the rice (*odana*), it does not receive the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*); rather, because it is that which is most desired to be reached through the act of softening—the activity of Devadatta—it receives only the designation of "object" (*karman*), as in the expression *pācayaty odanam* ("he causes the rice to be cooked").

Thus, since there is no possibility of both [designations] occurring here simultaneously, and therefore no contradiction, the designation *karman* (object) is already established for the domain of "going" (*gati*) and so forth through the application of the designation *kartṛ* (agent). Consequently, the formulation [of the rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*). In the domain of "cooking" (*pacati*) and so forth, by means of this restriction, the primary function [is restricted].
It is established that when [the capacity] is fully extended and unopposed, the independence of qualities and actions brings about its own effect and thus initiates the designation "agent. || 127 ||

It has been stated that the instigator (*prayojaka*) is the cause (*hetu*). However, one might raise the objection that since the fruit—which is the object (*karman*)—also possesses the quality of being an instigator with respect to the action, it too would follow that it is a cause. Anticipating this, the author demonstrates the distinction between the cause and the object.
Action is the impeller of the act, the cause for the agent, and the motivator;
and the performance of the act arises for the sake of the ritual through consecrations and acquisitions. (128)

(123) Because it accomplishes the three kinds of actions— namely, that which is to be brought about (*nirvartya*), that which is to be modified (*vikārya*), and that which is to be acquired (*prāpya*)— by means of cessation, transformation, and acquisition respectively, the fruit of the action (*kriyāphala*) employs the activity for the sake of the perfection of the agent-self (*karmātman*).
Furthermore, the cause, seeking the purpose of the action, [employs] the agent in the application of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

It impels [the agent], but not directly toward the action; for the agent’s activity is indeed for the sake of fulfilling that [action]. Since it is stated that "it is the instigator (prayojaka) of that agent," the meaning is that because the object of the cause (hetu) and the object of the action (karman) are distinct, the difference in the essential nature of their status as instigators (prayojakatva) is clear.

The word "ca" (and) indicates the reason. Since action (*kriyā*) exists for the sake of the object (*karman*) due to the assistance provided by its production and so forth, therefore the object is the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the action. For that which exists for the sake of something else is designated as its motivator, because it proceeds with that [object] as its aim. As for the other factors of action (*kāraka*), however...

Since they have action as their purpose, but action does not have them as its purpose, they are not the motivators of that [action]. For the commencement of action is not for the sake of the instrument and so forth; rather, those are merely the means.
Thus, this cause has been concluded by the preceding investigation. || 128 ||
Thus ends the section on the "Cause" (hetu) in the Sādhanasamuddeśa of the Prakīrṇaprakāśa composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja.
Having examined the grammatical means (*sādhana*) according to the sequence for prescribing case-endings, and having determined the agent (*kartṛ*) as the meaning of the third case,
he speaks in order to examine the recipient (*sampradāna*) as the meaning of the fourth case.

Because it is not rejected by the agent, that which is desired by the object as a factor for its relinquishment attains the status of a recipient (sampradāna), whether through instigation or through consent. (129)
(124) Because the term *sampradāna* (recipient) is etymologically significant (*anvartha*), it acquires the defining characteristic of being "a factor of relinquishment" (*tyāgāṅga*).

Relinquishment (*tyāga*) is the production of another's ownership through the cessation of one's own ownership of that which is being given. Since a factor (*aṅga*) therein may also be the cause (*nimitta*), such as the hand and so forth, he says: "that which is most desired by the object" (*karmaṇepsitam*). That which...
The meaning is that the action being abandoned by that which serves as the instrument is what was desired to be attained by the agent at the very outset.
And thus [it is said]:
"whom one intends through the object" (Pāṇini 1.4.32).

Thus ends the inclusion of the definition. Having raised the doubt as to how such a factor of relinquishment (*tyāgāṅga*) attains the status of a recipient (*sampradānatā*), which is a specific type of *kāraka*, [the author] points out the operation that grounds its status as a *kāraka* for the accomplishment of the action with the words "because of not rejecting" (*anirākaraṇāt*), etc.: "To the teacher, a cow... [The cow] is given by the giver who intends the teacher as the recipient, and the teacher, being one who does not reject [the gift], becomes the recipient (*sampradāna*). This is because the status of a recipient is established by the very fact of not rejecting [the gift]. For instance, when a person gives a cow to a teacher, the teacher is called the recipient because he does not reject it. However, this is not so in cases such as "He gives a cow to the thief," where the thief rejects it; therefore, in that case, the thief does not become a recipient. Thus, the status of a recipient is established solely by the absence of rejection. Furthermore, the status of a recipient is not something distinct from the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*) or other *kārakas*; rather, it is a specific form of the status of an agent. This is because the status of an agent is defined as "one who brings about the accomplishment of the action" (*kriyāsiddhau nirvartakaḥ*). Since the teacher also brings about the accomplishment of the action of giving by not rejecting it, he is indeed an agent. Therefore, the status of a recipient is nothing other than a specific form of the status of an agent. Consequently, the status of a recipient is not a separate category of *kāraka*. This is because the status of a recipient is merely a particular state of the agent, just as the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is a particular state of the agent. For example, when one says, "He cuts with an axe," the axe is called an instrument because it is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the accomplishment of the action of cutting. But since the axe is also an agent—being the most effective means for the accomplishment of the action—it is simply a specific form of the status of an agent. Similarly, the status of a recipient is also a specific form of the status of an agent. Therefore, the status of a recipient is not a separate category of *kāraka*. In such cases as "he gives," the object being relinquished—such as a cow—is connected with the recipient, such as a teacher, precisely because of the intention to give toward him. And that teacher, being thus connected, does not reject the gift; nor does he offer a rejection to the giver by saying, "Do not give it."

The author explains: For if one were to reject [the gift], the act of renunciation itself would not be accomplished, because that act extends until the attainment of ownership by another. Furthermore, [the sacrificer] consents to what is being given;
likewise, he does not reject the offering, such as the *bali* and so forth, when it is being presented to the deity and others—this too is an auxiliary element (*kriyāṅga*) of the ritual action.

Furthermore, in the case of a gift preceded by a request, the instigation—the urging toward the act of giving through entreaty—is also the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the recipient (*sampradāna*). Thus, because it is conducive to the relinquishment (*tyāga*), the recipient is indeed a causal factor (*kāraka*) that constitutes a limb of the relinquishment. Now, one might object: since the gift has that [recipient] as its purpose...
Since the dative case is already employed in the sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*), what is the purpose of the technical designation "recipient" (*sampradāna*)? This is not correct.

For it is the recipient who exists for the sake of the act of giving, whereas the act of giving does not exist for the sake of the recipient; this is because all *kārakas* exist for the sake of the action.
However, that which is being given for the sake of the recipient is the "object" (*karman*), as established by the meaning of the sentence.

Since the act of giving (*dāna-kriyā*) does not have that [the washerman or the thief] as its purpose, the dative case is not applicable when there is no such purposiveness; therefore, it is logical that the designation "recipient" (*sampradāna*) applies to that which is for the sake of the gift. However, in expressions such as "he gives the garment to the washerman" (*rajakasya vastraṃ dadāti*) or "he gives his back to the one who strikes him" (*ghnataḥ pṛṣṭhaṃ dadāti*), the meaning of "giving" is absent, for giving is essentially an act of relinquishment (*tyāga*). And by that...

Since the relinquishing of ownership—which consists in the severance of the sense of "mine"—is necessarily implied by the very intention to benefit another, the transfer of the object to the status of another's property is also accepted. And since that [intention] is absent here [in the case of the *prāyaścitta*], this use of the verb *dadāti* (to give) is figurative. However, regarding gifts made to a deity...

The donor certainly possesses the intention that [the gift] shall belong to him. Likewise, in cases such as "one gives food to one who has no appetite," the lack of utility is not a matter of verbal meaning. Furthermore, even in the case of "one should not give alms to a Śūdra," there is indeed utility for another, since the continuum of consciousness does not pass away. Thus...

And in the expression "he receives from the preceptor," the preceptor is the one who causes the cessation of the stream of study as it departs; since a portion of the stream of cognition situated [in the student] is being relinquished, the primary meaning of "giving" (dadāti) is indeed present here, characterized by the removal of one's own ownership and the establishment of another's ownership.

Others, however, say that [the term] is not used in its primary sense because the relationship between the giver and the recipient is not perceived; for instance, in the expression "he gives a gift to Kāṇvī," although the relationship of progenitor and offspring is not excluded, the relationship of owner and owned has ceased, and thus the meaning of the verb *dadāti* (gives) is indeed primary, as in: "The teacher Khaṇḍika gave him a slap."
In such cases as "he gives," although in reality there is no ownership of the slap or similar object, the donor nonetheless possesses the intention of ownership based on its utility; even though,
due to its contrary nature, the slap has no utility at that moment, nevertheless—

Indeed, there is utility for others through the excellence of the result; for when one is capable of enduring a slap, one attains the fruit because of fitness for the study of the scriptures. The dative case is used in the sense of "for the sake of that," according to the rule: *mṛjiḥ asmāy upadiṣṭo viśeṣeṇa* (Pāṇini 1.3.57).
The meaning is that the root *mṛj*, being listed in the *gaṇa* without distinction, also possesses the sense of the word "mārjaka" (a cleaner).

Thus, the first [type of] recipient (*sampradāna*) has been explained. Now, in order to explain the subsequent one, he says: "Even when it functions as a cause (*hetu*), or is designated as the object (*karman*), or remains as a residual factor (*śeṣa*), that *kāraka* is termed 'recipient' (*sampradāna*) by the treatise in the case of roots meaning 'to please' (*rucy-artha*) and others. (130)
(125) Just as it was previously stated that an action is preceded by a change of designation, so too this recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is preceded by something else,
according to the grammatical rule: "In the case of verbs meaning 'to please,' the one who is being pleased [is the recipient]" (Pāṇini 1.4.33).

This is explained by the following passage: "For instance, in the sentence *devadattāya rocate modakaḥ* ('The sweetmeat is pleasing to Devadatta'), the meaning of the root *ruc* is a desire whose agent is another.
Thus, Devadatta employs the sweetmeat—which has become the object of that desire—and, out of greed, acts in accordance with it."

When the designation *hetu* (cause) would apply to Devadatta as the instigator (*prayojaka*), the designation *sampradāna* (recipient) is stated [to supersede it]. Thus, when the designation *hetu* is sublated, there is an absence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*);
consequently, since a second action inherent in the cause is not perceived, the sweetmeat (*modaka*) [is understood] in relation to its own action expressed by the verbal root.
The agent does not become the object of the action. "Is pleasing" means that it attains the state of being the object of desire.
This is because even the designation of "agent," though formally applicable through the designation of "cause," is set aside in the case of Devadatta;
for the agent lacks the status of being the most desired by the action. This remains so even when the definition is intended to characterize independence (*svātantrya*).

In the case of the verbal root *hā* (to lose) when the agent is expressed by the suffix, the designation "object" (*karman*) does not apply to the sweetmeat (*modaka*) for the purpose of justifying the *l*-suffix in the sense of an object. For the status of being an object based on that [action] would only occur where independence (*svātantrya*) is perceived with respect to an action denoted by the word itself, as is the case with the verb *hīyate* in the sense of "losing."

In the case of "the caravan [arrives] at the sound," the designation of the traveler as the *karman* (object) is based on that [sound]. But here, in the case of the action of eating sweets (*modaka*) expressed by the word, Devadatta’s independence is not perceived from the verb "he likes" (*rocate*);
however, when independent of the operation of the word, his actual independence [is evident].

Since [the rule] would have as its scope only the mere *kāraka*, the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) would be purposeless. However, when the meaning of "the sweetmeat is pleasing to Devadatta" is "the sweetmeat pleases Devadatta," and thus the qualifier "being pleased" (*prīyamāṇa*) applies, then [Devadatta] receives the designation of "object" (*karman*).

The designation *sampradāna* (recipient) is initiated when [the verb] has attained [this status]. For when a verbal root functions with a different meaning, it becomes transitive (*sakarmaka*). Thus, in the expression "he praises Devadatta" (*devadattāya ślāghate*), Devadatta is being praised through the excellence of his qualities; because he acts in a manner consistent with possessing those qualities, the status of an instigator (*prayojaka*) is superimposed upon him.

One who has attained the notion of being a cause, or one who is intended to be made known by the proclamation of qualities— being that which is to be made known— is designated as the object (*karman*), according to Pāṇini 1.4.34: *ślāghahuṅ*.
By these and other such statements, the technical designation *sampradāna* (recipient) is explained. In the same way, this should be stated as appropriate for the roots beginning with *hnauti*.
