For the roots beginning with *hnauti* are transitive (*sakarmaka*) in this context, because their verbal expression has the making known of something as a subordinate element to its own primary meaning. And thus, the term "the one being made to know" (*jñīpsyamāna*) is employed as a qualifier of the designated entity (*saṃjñin*).
In the expression "he owes a hundred to Devadatta," the debtor establishes the hundred while remaining within its own nature; here,
the creditor Devadatta is the cause for the act of owing by way of the act of giving, since he gives the hundred and yet [the debt remains].

In that context, since the action of "giving" (*dadāti*) is heard [in the rule], while in this case where no such action is heard— concerning the remaining *kārakas* (factors of action)— the genitive case would otherwise apply; however, by the rule "The creditor in the case of *dhārayati*" (Pāṇini 1.4.35), [the creditor is designated as the agent].

Thus ends the designation of the recipient (*sampradāna*). For it is stated that the triad beginning with the cause (*hetu*) is designated as such according to their applicability, but not individually. Regarding the example "he desires flowers" (*puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhayati*), it was stated that there would be the undesirable consequence of the designation of object (*karman*) for the flowers, because they are the most desired (*īpsitatama*). However, in the case of [verbs] such as *druhyati* (to bear malice),...

There would be the undesirable consequence [of these roots] being designated as *sakarmaka* (having an object). Since *droha* (malice) is a form of injury (*apakāra*), those roots whose meaning is that [injury] are *sakarmaka*.

The same applies to those whose meaning is *īrṣyā* (envy) and *asūyā* (cavil). However, in the case of "he consults/devatā for Devadatta" (*devadattāya rādhyati*) or "he gazes at Devadatta" (*īkṣate*), because he employs the astrologer Devadatta to deliberate upon fate (*daiva*), the designation of *hetu* (cause/agent) [applies].
When [the action] has been attained, there is the status of recipient (*sampradāna*) according to Pāṇini 1.4.39, *arādhīkṣyoḥ*.
This is seen in examples such as "He promises or agrees to give a cow to Devadatta."
But in the case of "Devadatta employs [the cowherd] by requesting him to promise the cow," since the technical designation *hetu* (cause/motive) would apply, [it is superseded] by Pāṇini 1.4.40:
*pratyāṅbhyāṃ śruvaḥ*.

Thus [is established] the status of being a recipient (*sampradāna*). For Devadatta, being the agent of the preceding verbal action characterized by begging, becomes the instigator (*prayojaka*) with respect to the subsequent act of assent (*pratiśrava*), which consists of acceptance. This is also the case in expressions such as *hotre 'nugṛṇāti* ("he responds to the Hotṛ") and *pratigṛṇāti* ("he chants in response"), where [the meaning is] "he [instigates] the Hotṛ by means of praising."
In the case where the status of the *hotṛ* as the object (*karman*) would otherwise apply due to the rule "he encourages" (*protsāhayati*),

the status of the recipient (*sampradāna*) is established by the rule "and after *anu*, *pra*, *guṇa*" (Pāṇini 1.4.41). In the example "recite for one hired for a hundred," the status of the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) applies.

In the case of *parikrayaṇa* (hiring for a fixed period), the status of being a recipient (*sampradāna*) is stated as an option. In that context, because the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the rule *rucy-arthādiṣu* includes [the term *parikrayaṇa*], it is easily understood; therefore, the undesirable application of the technical term "instrument" (*karaṇa-saṃjñā*) has not been mentioned. Furthermore, when there is no intention to express a specific distinction, this [recipient status] applies everywhere.
When it is argued that [the cow] is a *śeṣa* (subsidiary element) based merely on its being the cause (*nimitta*) of the action, the status of being a *sampradāna* (recipient) should be invoked.

For, due to the specific enumeration of roots such as *duh* (to milk), there is no status of being an "unspoken object" (*akathita-karman*) here. But was this not already stated previously by the very rule concerning the *sampradāna*?

Regarding the statement, "He whom one intends by means of an action" (Pāṇini 1.4.32), how is it that here in this treatise [the word] is qualified by the term "by means of the scripture" (śāstreṇa)? It is said in reply: because the term *sampradāna* is etymological (*anvartha*), the worldly meaning of "recipient" was stated previously; however, here—

Regarding objects such as those denoted by roots meaning "to please" (*rucy-artha*), because the actual [transfer of] that object is absent, the status of being a recipient (*sampradānatva*) is stated for the purpose of establishing merely the grammatical refinement (*śabda-saṃskāra*) of the word; thus, the recipient is explained as being twofold, according to the distinction between technical (*śāstrīya*) and worldly (*laukika*). || 130 ||

In this context, since there is no object in the domain of intransitive roots— as in "he swallows with faith," "he girds himself for battle," and "she lies down for her husband"— the status of the recipient (*sampradāna*) for that which is intended [by the agent] is not established.

"The term 'action' (kriyā) must also be included," as stated in the Vārttika; [this would mean that] that which is intended by means of an action should here receive the designation of recipient (sampradāna). This was refuted in the Bhāṣya.

Action (*kriyā*) is also an artificial object (*kṛtrima-karma*), because it is that which is brought about by another action. And in examples such as *śrāddhāya nigarhate* ("he reproaches for the sake of the funeral rite"), it is explained by what action the [reproaching] action is being brought about—namely, by the action of showing and so forth;
for in that case, it is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) without distinction from the action of showing and so forth.
In order to establish how the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākārakabhāva) is tenable when based on non-difference, he says:

"And when difference is intended to be expressed, because each subsequent factor becomes the object (*karman*) with respect to each preceding action, the term 'action' was not [explicitly] included [in the definition of *karman*]. (131)
(126) Since it is attained through the determination of [actions] such as seeing and desiring, even an action (*kriyā*) is an artificial object (*karma*).

In that regard, for one who acts with prior deliberation, seeing and the other [mental factors] are necessarily perceived as being present during the engagement [in action]; thus, when there is a desire to express the distinction from the primary action, [they are designated as objects].

With respect to each preceding action, it is not contradictory for each subsequent factor— which serves the purpose of the principal action— to function as its object (*karman*), because it is being brought about by that preceding action; thus, even when an action itself functions as an object, the status of the recipient (*sampradāna*) for that which is connected with it is established by the very rule (*sūtra*).
The inclusion of the term "action" (*kriyā*) has been rejected; this [term] "the object of the act of giving" (*dadāti-karman*) is not accepted.

Therefore, in this context, only the primary action is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*). However, since acts such as "showing" (*saṃdarśana*) and so forth—which are obtained through contextual implication—are distinct from that [primary action], the relationship between action and its factors (*kāraka*) is established. For example:
The independence of the caravan (*sārtha*), which is understood from the expression "he is separated from the caravan," is the cause for its status as the object (*karman*).

Alternatively, because it serves that purpose, even though the [caravan]— which has attained non-difference from the primary action— is denoted by verbal roots, there is nevertheless no total disregard for its distinctness.
Thus, the status of being an object (*karmatā*) is established through the cognition of difference, which is inferred from the effect known as non-difference. || 131 ||

If this were so, then even in cases such as "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), that which is intended by the object of the action would receive the designation *sampradāna* (recipient). However, since the designation *karman* (object) for the rice and so forth has its own scope of application regarding the objects of the action, [the author] says:

But when unity is intended to be expressed regarding a collection of actions, then the object (karman), by virtue of its connection with the action, is figuratively designated by its own name [as "action"]. (132)
(127) When the collection of actions such as "showing" and so forth— which have not lost their mutual status as subordinate factors (*aṅga*),

but are combined as being of equal rank— is accepted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) as non-distinct because they share a single result, then [the objection regarding] that which is based on distinction...

Since the relationship of action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*) is not perceived, the object such as boiled rice (*odana*), which is connected to an action that has not yet attained the status of an object (*karmabhāva*), is designated by the very term "object" (*karman*)— a designation based precisely on the fact that it is the most desired (*īpsitatama*) by the action; it is not [designated otherwise].

The meaning is: by means of the technical designation *sampradāna*. Because they are expressed as being in conjunction (*samuccaya*) and because there is no relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*), in this view the action does not possess the nature of an object (*karman*). || 132 ||
Anticipating the objection that "in that case, if one intends to express a distinction [between the agent and the recipient], there would be the status of a *sampradāna* (recipient) here," he says:
"The intention to express either distinction or non-distinction is established by its own nature (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, no deviation is observed regarding the status of being the object of a verb meaning 'to go'. (133)

(128) Since worldly usage is well-established, when explaining [words] with reference to that usage, the intention to express either difference or non-difference is determined by the conceptualization of means according to the usage itself. And thus,
the rules prescribing the second and fourth cases for the object of a verb meaning "to go" are also established on the basis of this twofold intention.

There is no purpose in undertaking that [objection], because there is neither deviation nor over-extension, since elsewhere there is a restriction based on the intention to express non-difference. || 133 ||
He confirms this very point with scripture:
"If both designations were applicable everywhere solely by way of conceptual construction, then the rejection of yoga through its formal undertaking would be inconsistent. (134)

(129) If one does not rely on a restriction regarding the intention to express either difference or non-difference, then because the designations of *karman* and *sampradāna* would apply everywhere, the author of the Bhāṣya would not have rejected the rule beginning with *gatyarthakarmaṇi* as being merely restrictive (*niyamārtha*). For if it were rejected, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). When...

If, however, the restriction of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā-niyama*) flashes in the mind of the author of the Bhāṣya, then, considering there to be no difference between undertaking [the analysis] and rejecting it, it is appropriate that he should reject it.
Thus, regarding the domain of verbal roots meaning "to go," there are two possible intentions; as in the example *śrāddhāya nigalhati* ("he swallows for the sake of the funeral rite"), and so forth.
But in cases such as *pacaty odanam* ("he cooks rice"), there is indeed an intention to express non-difference (*abheda-vivakṣā*).

In the counter-examples for the rule *ceṣṭāyām anadhvani*, there too there is only an intention to express non-difference, namely: *manasā pāṭaliputram gacchati* ("he goes to Pāṭaliputra mentally") and *adhvānam gacchati* ("he goes along the road"). Furthermore, regarding the commencement of the Sūtra, [the example] *striyam*...

Regarding the over-extension [of the rule] in cases such as *gacchatyajām nayati* ("he leads the goat"), it has been stated: "But [the accusative] is not established here because of the statement concerning that which has not been reached" (*Pāṇini* 2.3.12). When the object is not yet reached—that is, when it is not connected with the action of going—the second and fourth [case endings] are used.
It should be stated [in the rule]: "But when *ajā* and *strī* are reached as the objects (*karman*)," so that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
And thus, regarding the formulation of this specific sūtra, it is said: "And for *adhvan*, there is no exception" (*ja.od.gh.* 2.3.12).
The prohibition "in *adhvan*" need not be stated; for here, *adhvan* is indeed an object that has been reached.
It is intended to be prohibited. And its exclusion is established simply by the statement that it has not yet been reached (*asamprāpta*). For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya:
"A prohibition of what has already been established must be stated" (*āsthitapratiṣedho vaktavyaḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.84).
Thus, the path established here should be understood as the object of negation. || 134 ||

(130) By the rule *adhvanyarthagrahaṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.12), there is a prohibition [of the suffix *kta*] even after synonyms for "road," as in *panthānaṃ gacchati* ("he goes along the road") and so forth. A "road" (*adhvan*) is that which has been traversed or occupied by the action of going. An example is: *pravṛtagamanaḥ* ("one who has set out on a journey").
One is said to be "established on the path. In this context, this act of going is twofold:
with respect to that portion of the traversed path which is yet to be passed over, it is the action in the form of relinquishment, characterized by leaving behind;
whereas with respect to the portion to be reached and attained, it is the action in the form of conjunction, characterized by arrival.

Action is twofold due to the distinction between its constituent parts characterized by relinquishing (*tyāga*) and taking up (*upādāna*). Thus, a path traversed by an action consisting of an uninterrupted flow in the form of relinquishing and taking up falls within the scope of the technical designation "object" (*karman*), which is prescribed merely by virtue of being the objective domain of action, but not [as such] by the action itself.
Because there is no distinction in the action, it is connected with that which has become the object (*karman*); thus, the designation of "recipient" (*sampradāna*) does not apply.
Only for [a destination] such as a village—which is not reached by that means and whose nature is a non-path—is there a connection with that [action].
However, in the case of a path that is not fixed, only two case-endings occur. How so?

And the path becomes non-abiding [in its nature]. When one reaches the path by way of a wrong path, as in "one goes on the path" (*pathe gacchati*), or "one goes to the path" (*panthānaṃ gacchati*), then in such a case, a distinction must be stated at the beginning of the sūtra.
However, if it is rejected, the desired result is established simply through the restriction of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣāniyama*). || 135 ||
Thus ends the section on the recipient (*sampradāna*) in the *Sādhanasamuddeśa* of the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja.

(131) Now, having determined the meaning of the fourth case within the sequence of the rules for the formation of case-endings, the author states the following, as the occasion has arrived, to investigate the fifth case-meaning, *apādāna* (the point of departure).
The ablative (apādāna) is said to be threefold: that whose object is explicitly stated, that whose object is implied, and that which requires an action [to be supplied]. || 136 ||
When "departure" (apāya) is the property to be established,
that which is constant, uniform, and characterized by an action not entered by departure— even when another [entity] is entered by departure—
is the *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure), because it depends upon a specific limit (*avadhi*).

The locus of the *apādāna* (ablative) is that which is the agent of separation (*apāya*)—whether characterized by agitation, indifference, or both—and which is either explicitly mentioned by its own word or implied as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāvena*) in another action. That which is thus specified constitutes a single *apādāna*. For example: "He comes from the village" (*grāmād āgacchati*), "He descends from the mountain" (*parvatād avarohati*), and so forth. [In these cases], it is implied as a subordinate factor in another action.

Or, when the object characterized by departure (*apāya*) is subordinate (*pradhāna-bhāva*), there is the taking of another object as the basis (*upātta-viṣaya-pādāna*). For example: "He flashes from the cloud," "He cooks from the granary," and "He recites from the Brāhmaṇa. For in these cases, [the action] has the act of exiting as its constituent part (*niḥsaraṇāṅga*).

The root *vidyaut* occurs in the sense of "lightning" (*vidyotana*), or in the sense of "emerging" (*niḥsaraṇa*) as a subordinate member of the compound "lightning of men" (*nṛvidyotanāṅga*). Thus, the "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*) moment is presented as the primary factor (*guṇapradhānabhāvena*) for the lightning;
[the meaning is] that light emerges from a cloud and then flashes, or that it flashes while emerging from a cloud.
The meaning is "he goes out. In expressions such as "having taken [grain] from the granary, he cooks," the root *pac* (to cook) refers to the cooking which is a subordinate part of the act of taking.
In "having received [the text] from the Brāhmaṇa, he recites," the root *śaṃs* (to recite) occurs with reference to the recitation which is a subordinate part of the act of receiving.
As stated in the section on the fifth case (*pañcamī*): "An addition should be made for the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* priest."

[The suffix *cha* is applied] with the elision (*aluk*) [of the case-ending]. In this regard, the author of the Vārttika intends this to be in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the sense of the accusative (*dvitīyārthe*). As he says:
"And in the sense of 'other' (*anyārthe ca*). (Pāṇini 6.3.2).

Thus: he who recites the *brāhmaṇas*, which are specific types of texts, is called a *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*. In this context, regarding the formation of the compound, it should be stated that the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of the accusative (*dvitīyārthe*).
However, the author of the *Bhāṣya* says that he recites after having taken [them] from the *brāhmaṇa*, meaning he recites as part of the act of bringing them forth (*āharaṇāṅge*).
By stating that "the root *śaṃs* occurs in the sense of praising," he considers this mention of the [root] to have as its scope only what is explicitly mentioned (*upātta*).
However, the *apādāna* (ablative) is that which requires an action (*apekṣitakriya*), where, because a verbal expression for the action is not found at all,
an unexpressed action is inferred among the related substances as the cause of specific technical designations (*saṃjñāviśeṣa*).

It serves as the cause for the manifestation of various degrees of capacity; for example, "The people of Mathurā are more prosperous than those of Pāṭaliputra. For here, by the force of the suffix expressing excellence (*prakarṣa*), an action of removal characterized by the loss of a state of division is inferred, and that [action] is required in this context.

[This refers to] the verbal action (*kriyā*). However, in cases where [the action] is implied, the departure (*apāya*) is already encompassed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself, because verbal roots possess multiple meanings.
This is seen in examples such as *valāhako vidyotate* ("the cloud flashes"), *caitraḥ pacati* ("Caitra cooks"), and *dāśatayīḥ śaṃsati* ("he recites the ten Mandalas of the Rigveda");
although these express merely the act of flashing and so forth, in other contexts they include components such as "emerging" (*niḥsaraṇa*).

Because there is no contradiction with the sense of "covering," and because the power of the ablative case-ending (*pañcamī-śruti*) implies a departure (*apāya*), that departure is logically possible only if the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is subordinate to the act of exiting; it is not otherwise.
Thus, its status as having that [exiting] as its purpose is determined. || 136 ||
What, then, is this "departure" (apāya)? Is it merely a movement? No; he says:

Just as movement itself, though having a single nature, appears divided due to the difference in its conjoined objects—as in the case of whirling—so too does departure, though inherent in a fixed limit, appear [divided] when [the object] is not fixed. (137)

(132) By association through concomitance (*sāhacarya*), even disjunction (*vibhāga*) is accepted as a limiting factor (*avadhi*). Therefore, just as the effect consisting of conjunction and disjunction delimited by a specific direction is designated as "going" (*gamana*) itself—such that "revolving" (*bhramaṇa*) is so called—and just as by the mention of "going," revolving, receding (*recana*), vibrating (*spandana*), and so forth are included; [so too is the case here].

The followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) maintain that [separation] is not a distinct category (*jātyantara*). Thus, one must understand that "separation" (*apāya*)—which has as its limit (*avadhi*) something fixed (*dhruva*), immovable (*acala*), and not involved in the action (*anāviṣṭāpāya*)—is in fact a specific kind of motion (*gativiśeṣa*). It belongs to that which is joined with what is unfixed (*adhruva*) and movable (*cala*); it is accomplished by means of an instrument (*sādhana*) that is either active (*saṃrabdha*) or indifferent (*udāsīna*); and its fruit is characterized by the disjunction (*vibhāga*) residing in both causal factors (*kāraka*). Even though this action inheres in the mover (*gantṛ*), it receives the name "separation" because it depends upon a limit; therefore, the intention is that the status of being a causal factor (*kārakatva*) is established for the fixed object insofar as it serves as the cause for the accomplishment of the action.

Furthermore, that *apāya* (separation), which exists as the objective domain (*viṣayabhāvena*) for the designation *apādāna*, is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), whether explicitly stated or inferred; since *apāya* is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) with respect to that which is fixed (*dhruva*) and bears the designation *apādāna*, the fixed factor (*kāraka*) possesses the status of being the cause (*nimittatva*) therein. Thus has *apāya* been explained. For in common worldly usage, "fixed" (*dhruva*) is well-known to mean stable and immovable. Consequently, this was raised as an objection in the *Vārttika*: "The designation *apādāna* is not applicable to things joined with motion (*gatiyukteṣu*), because they lack fixity (*adhrutvāt*)" (on Pāṇini 1.4.25).
[This applies in cases such as: "He fell from a running horse," or "He lagged behind a departing caravan," and so forth.

The meaning is that since there is an absence of fixity (*dhruvatva*), stability (*sthititva*), and immobility (*acalatva*) in those things designated as *apādāna* when they possess motion, the technical designation does not apply. Regarding this, the following resolution is stated:
"Or rather, it is not so, because fixity is not intended to be expressed" (Pāṇini 1.4.25).
Thus [ends the section]. || 137 ||
To explain this, he says:
"The state of being a substance is not permanence; rather, it is understood from the sūtra that permanence refers to the domain of non-departure (apāya). (138)

(133) "Fixed" (*dhruva*), "unchanging" (*kūṭastha*), and "inactive" (*niṣkriya*)—these are not to be understood in the Sūtra as the inherent nature of a substance (*dravyasvabhāva*). Rather, the word "fixed" here refers to that which is unshakable by dissatisfaction. For instance, when something is fixed in relation to a means of removal (*apāya*), the meaning is that it is untouched by that removal. And having established it thus:

In the expression "he fell from a running horse," although the act of falling lacks the horse as its agent, the horse nevertheless possesses the status of the fixed point (*dhruva*) therein; for separation (*apāya*) is accomplished by means of an agent who is either active or indifferent. In that case, the horse is indifferent, while the one who has fallen is active. [Similarly in] "he comes to the village by way of the path."

In the case of the expression *parvatam*, however, because the instrument (*karaṇa*), namely the mountain (*parvata*), does not coexist with its removal (*apāya*)—which is the object (*karman*)—the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) does not apply. This is because, although the mountain possesses the status of being fixed (*dhruva*), it is superseded by the designations of "instrument" and so forth due to their higher priority. Thus, the Vārttika states:
The subsequent [kārakas] are the ablative (apādāna). He pierces with a bow; he eats from a bronze vessel; he milks the cow;
he bends the bow.
"By [the rule] *ja-od-ghuṭ-svare* (Pāṇini 6.1.159)," it is said.

Thus, because the object of departure (*apāya*) is resorted to, and because the horse is not permeated by that departure, its instability—which is actually directed toward that object—did indeed exist, yet it was not intended to be expressed; such is the meaning of the Vārttika. || 138 ||
For instance:

"In the case of Devadatta, there is permanence in his running, but in the case of the horse, there is permanence in its falling; that which is permeated by passing away is declared to be impermanent. (139)

(134) Just as Devadatta possesses stability because he is not permeated by that running which is inherent in the horse and characterized by speed, so too the horse possesses stability because it is not permeated by the falling— the action of falling— which is inherent in Devadatta.

This example is included by way of the relationship between the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*). Although there is no entry into the state of being an *apādāna* (ablative) as a cause, permanence (*dhrauvya*) is established in both cases by way of negation (*vyatireka-mukhena*). And although Devadatta’s permanence exists in the act of running away on horseback, nevertheless, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *apādāna* [is not applied].
Because it will be stated that "there is no going without a limit,
nor is there any departure [so] understood," Devadatta is not presented as the limit (*avadhi*); for if he were so presented, [the fault would follow].
"But it is indeed the case that one says, 'the horse runs away from Devadatta' [when Devadatta himself is moving].
In that case, however, where both are in motion, how can the distinction between the stationary (*dhruva*) and the moving (*adhruva*) be determined?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
Although both rams are unstable when the disjunction is produced by the actions of both, the two actions are nevertheless intended to be distinguished there.

(135) In the case of "the hawk flies away from the post," since the disjunction produced by the action of only one [of the two] lacks a clear connection with the act of going away (*apāya*), the post is determined to possess fixedness (*dhruvatā*). Similarly, in the case of "one ram flies away from the other ram," although the disjunction is produced by the actions of both, even though both [rams] are...

Because the entry into destruction occurs through the destruction of the ram, and because the entry into the destruction of the other occurs through the destruction of the other, the two actions characterized as destruction are indeed distinct due to the difference in their agents. (140)

Consequently, the status of being a limit (avadhitva) for each of the two rams is distinct, depending respectively upon the action of the other ram; and their status as agents (kartṛtva) is also distinct, depending upon their own respective actions. (141)
(136) This is a case of mutual action because there is no entry of one into the other;

while in the action of the other, the second remains stable, both possess agency in their own respective actions. However, when the state of being a relative limit (*avadhi*) between them is not intended to be expressed, but rather they are referred to by a single word—
Even when the action belongs to two [entities], it is intended to be expressed [as belonging to one]. || 141 ||

Regarding this, he says: "If, however, without distinction, a single action intended to be accomplished by two agents is meant to be expressed, then the two [rams] are the agents at the time of their departure, provided that another limit exists. (142)

(137) In the verbal form *meṣāv apasarpatas* ("the two rams move away"), the action is conveyed as a single entity accomplished by two agents; thus, both rams possess agency through their involvement in the action.

However, because one of them serves as the point of departure (*avadhi*) for the act of going away (*apāya*), it does not possess the status of an *apādāna* (ablative). And having established this, [it follows that] the agency in the act of going away—

When it is said, "one of the two rams moves away from the mountain," [it is understood as] "the two rams move away from each other," or "the two rams move away from one another. In such a designation,
the status of being a point of reference (*avadhitva*) for both rams is relative to the action of the other ram, and relative to their own respective actions.

It has been stated that [the suffix] denotes agency (*kartṛtva*). For here, even though the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is a single unit, an inference regarding a difference in action based on a difference in agent is perceived. || 142 ||
If another limit exists, then [the two] are the causes of the sheep's departure and not otherwise; he says this in order to establish it through agreement with the text of the Bhāṣya:
"But it is understood that there is no departure without a limit."
"The leaf of the tree falls"—thus it is illustrated in the Bhāṣya. || 143 ||

(138) In the *Kāraka-sūtra*, it was enjoined that the designation of the designatum (*saṃjñin*) must be stated; it should be said that "the *kāraka* is that which effects [an action]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of even that which is not a cause of action being called a *kāraka*, as in the example: "And the ablative (*apādāna*): 'The leaf of the tree falls'" (Jainendra-vyākaraṇa on Pāṇini 1.4.23).

Thus it is stated in the Vārttika. Since the Bhāṣya is accompanied by the Vārttika, he refers to it as "the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, this is not an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that the departure (*apāya*) has a limit; rather, it is for the purpose of refuting that [objection] with the words: "Or rather, no, because the departure is not intended to be expressed" (*na vāpāyasyāvivakṣitatvāt*, Jaiminīya Nyāyamālāvistara 1.4.23).
Thus, by the phrase "as has been stated," the body of the Bhāṣya is indicated here. And this is the meaning:

since the intended sense of the sentence is the falling of a leaf belonging to a tree, there is no intention here to represent the tree as a limit (*avadhi*). Consequently, this does not constitute a case of "separation" (*apāya*).
Because the state of "separation" (*apāya*) is not intended here in the form of a requirement for a limit (*avadhi*), the tree does not possess the status of an ablative (*apādāna*).

However, if separation were intended here, then because the tree serves as the limit, the expression "the leaf falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt parṇaṃ patati*) would be valid; yet in that case, it would not be known to what the leaf belongs.

It has been stated [in the Mahābhāṣya] as "of the *kaṅka* or the *kura*. Therefore, since the tree is intended to be specified as a qualifier of the leaf (*parṇa*), this usage indeed occurs even when the leaf, though not leaving the tree, touches the ground while on the branch; thus, the intention to express "separation" (*apāya*) has been declared. And from this, it is inferred:
A movement with a limit (*sāvadhika-gati*) is not pure *apāya* (separation);
otherwise, if there were no intention to express a limit (*avadhi*), the status of being an ablative (*apādānatva*) would indeed apply here because *apāya* is possible.
This is the indicator (*jñāpaka*). And thus, since the limit is implied by the very fact of separation, it is merely an attribute of that [separation].
The inclusion of the word "dhruva" (constant) is explained as being for the purpose of indicating that the term applies to both sentient beings and [non-sentient] things,
and to demonstrate that ruin can be brought about by both those who are actively engaged and those who are indifferent.

The pride [of thinking one has understood] has departed. This must now be stated: Kātyāyana has declared a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) based on the rule "the subsequent [kārakas] supersede the ablative" (*apādānam uttarāṇi*). Thus, because the ablative is superseded by the aforementioned kārakas, one says:
*valāhakād vidyotate*, *valāhake vidyotate*, or *valāhako vidyotate*.
Having raised the objection that the coexistence of designations shown in the Bhāṣya is contradictory, he says the following in order to justify the Bhāṣya:
"Difference and non-difference, separateness and persistence— these are mutually opposed."
All phenomena do not intend to be expressed simultaneously, like clouds in the sky.

(139) A cloud is a conglomeration of smoke, light, water, and wind; therein, there is the flashing of the constituent element, light. And when that light is intended to be expressed as distinct from that cloud which is of the nature of a composite whole, then, under such an intention of distinction, it exists precisely as a separate entity.

Or it is intended [to be expressed] there by way of its location. When it is intended to be expressed as a separate entity, then the cloud (*valāhaka*) is the limit (*avadhi*) of the departure (*apāya*) characterized by separation; thus, this is an *apādāna* where the object is explicitly mentioned.

It has been explained that "it flashes from the cloud" means it flashes as light in the form of lightning, having become separate and emerged from the cloud; thus, the verbal root *vidyotate* refers to the act of emerging as a factor of departure. However, since there can be no subsistence of light without a support...

When a cloud (valāhaka) is intended to be expressed as a substratum because it serves as the cause of its location, it acquires the designation of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), as in "it lightens in the cloud" (*valāhake vidyotate*); the meaning is that it shines while remaining within the cloud. This is because the fire of lightning (*vidyut*) has the cloud as its fuel.

Even though a cloud is filled with water, it is appropriate that it serves as a receptacle; yet, because it is indistinguishable from the earth due to its connection with water and its being obscured by smoke, there is no difference between the cloud and fire insofar as they lack the capacity to act as illuminators—
this is said when one intends to emphasize their non-difference.

The manifestation of two powers has been shown in the case of a cloud (*valāhaka*): their separate existence and their persistence [as distinct entities] occur only when they occupy different locations. However, because the substance of the cloud is transparent, even in that state, water and the like do not act as an obstruction to the light of fire; thus, they appear as non-different.

When the entity called a "cloud" (*valāhaka*) is intended to be expressed as a whole capable of flashing due to its constituent parts of light, then here it is the power of the agent (*kartṛ-śakti*) alone that manifests, as in the expression: "the cloud flashes" (*valāhako vidyotate*).
For designations based on the parts indeed follow upon the whole. For example:
In the expression "the grove has put forth new shoots" (*kisalayitam upavanam*), when the term *upavana* (grove) denotes a collection of trees,
that collection is fit to be designated in such a way provided its constituent parts have produced new shoots.
Thus, due to a difference in intended meaning (*vivakṣābheda*), the word *valāhaka* (cloud), which possesses distinct capacities in turn, is cited as an example in the Bhāṣya.

But this is not the case when there is an intention to express the power of the *yup* [prefix]; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the statement regarding the prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*). || 144 ||
Regarding the example given for contradiction, he states that in that case there is a simultaneous intention to express both [the agent and the instrument]:

"In the expression *dhanuṣā vidhyati* (he pierces with a bow), since there is no intention to express the departure [of the arrow], there is no status as the instrument; therefore, those two [agent and instrument] are expressed together. (145)

(140) It has been illustrated that in the expression *dhanuṣā vidhyati* ("he pierces with a bow"), the designation of the instrument (*karaṇa-saṃjñā*) prevails over the designation of the point of departure (*apādāna-saṃjñā*) due to its higher status. In that case, there is necessarily a simultaneous application of the two designations;
thus, both the state of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) and the state of being the point of departure (*apāya*) reside together in a single substance.

For, in the act of piercing, the status of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamatva*) does not belong to the bow unless there is the intention [to express] its removal from the path of obstruction;
for one does not pierce with a bow as one does with a staff,
but rather the bow, by assuming the role of an auxiliary to the arrow as it moves forward, becomes the instrumental cause of the piercing.

When there is a simultaneous intention to express both [functions], even though the two powers have different objects, they coexist in a single substance by virtue of standing in a relationship of cause and effect; thus, while serving as the cause for two distinct technical designations based on their respective causes, they arise simultaneously from a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Because it is impossible for two case-endings (vibhakti) that denote its respective functions to arise simultaneously, when a conflict arises due to the application of two designations (*saṃjñā*) under a single governing rule (*adhikāra*), the case-ending conditioned by the designation "instrument" (*karaṇa*) prevails because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Indeed, there is no conflict here between the two capacities (*śakti*), as they have different domains: for the "ablative" (*apādāna*) applies to the arrow's departure, while the "object" (*karman*) applies to the piercing.

But the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the bow, and since even the power (*śakti*) of the axe is merely a substance (*dravya*) that falls within the scope of technical designations (*saṃjñā*), there is an application [of the designation] to one thing independently of that [power]. For instance, in the formulation of case-endings (*vibhakti*), it is the very nature of being a substance (*dravyatva*) that is qualified by specific designations such as "ablative" (*apādāna*) or "instrument" (*karaṇa*).

Furthermore, since there is no contradiction even when multiple notions arise regarding a single object, the contradiction here should be explained by way of the differentiation of the functions of those notions.
This example is cited merely as an illustration; thus, it applies elsewhere as well.

In the example of contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*), the lack of intention to express simultaneity (*yugapad-avivakṣā*) should be applied. For instance, in the case of "he eats from a bronze vessel" (*kaṃsapātryāṃ bhuṅkte*), the bronze vessel is the substratum for the act of eating—which consists of consuming food—and so forth; however, that status as its substratum is not possible [if the two actions were intended to be simultaneous].

As long as there is no status of being an ablative (*apādāna*), it is because food is taken out from a bronze vessel (*kaṃsapātrī*) and then eaten that the vessel functions as an ablative. For one who consumes food with a leaf-cup (*parṇapuṭa*), there is no cognition of it as a locus (*ādhāra*) such that one would say of an elephant or similar creature, "he eats therein. And if [it were] a bronze vessel...

If there were no limit to the taking of food, then eating itself could never be accomplished; thus, because there can be no status as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) without the intention to exclude [the source], when both [statuses] are intended simultaneously, there arises the contingency of two technical designations (*saṃjñā*).

In this case, by the rule "the subsequent [designation] prevails over the preceding" (*apādānam uttarāṇi*), the subsequent designation of locus supersedes the prior designation of ablative (*apādāna*).

It is indeed stated: in the expression "he milks the cow" (*gāṃ dogdhi*), where *duh* signifies the act of milking, the separation (*apāya*) is inseparable [from the milking]. For the act of milking does not take place unless the milk has departed from the cow;

thus, the cow's capacity for being an object (*karma-śakti*) is inseparable from its status as the source (*apādāna*). Because it is predominant (*paratvāt*), it brings about the grammatical operation [of the accusative case].

Thus, in the expression "he shoots with a bow," since there is no intention to express the bow as the point of departure (*apāya*), the bow lacks independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to the act of piercing; therefore, when both [the bow and the agent] are present, the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) alone prevails over the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) by the rule "the subsequent [designation] supersedes the preceding. || 145 ||

Thus, having accepted two distinct powers (*śakti*) here in this irregular case, when they coexist in a single substance due to their necessary connection (*nāntarīyakatva*), and when a conflict arises between the two operations known as "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) and "nominal suffix" (*ākhyā*) upon the attainment of two designations, the established rule was stated based on their relative priority (*paratva*). Now, however, [the author] proceeds by relying on the non-difference of the powers.
He states the occurrence of two designations with respect to a non-distinct object:
"That single power, being one, exists in a dual form;
therein, the secondary [designation] is sublated by the primary. (146)
(141) Even when directed toward different actions, the substance possesses only a single power; for by that [single power], the substance accomplishes two actions.
Thus, in that case, with respect to the two actions, it receives two designations—*apādāna* and *karaṇa*—in a single instance.

When two designations are simultaneously applicable, the subsequent designation does not sublate the preceding one— the former being subordinate due to conflict— because of the governing rule that only one designation may apply at a time. In the case of an arrow's departure, the status of the bow as the limit (*avadhi*) is already included within its very power as the most efficient instrument (*sādhakatama*).
Or rather, because of its non-connection with that [other effect], it is held that there is only one single power;
for there is no basis for postulating two distinct powers of form for two effects that are mutually independent. Indeed, as for the act of piercing...
Since the action of the arrow's departure is subordinate here, it does not imply a separate power within the self.

Rather, there is only a single power which, by having two actions—one subordinate and one primary—as its objects, appears as if it were of different forms. In that case, let the substance itself be the instrument that accomplishes the two actions; why [posit a separate power]?

[The opponent argues: "By means of the conceptualization of powers (śakti). [The author replies: This is not tenable. Because this [entity] has an undifferentiated intrinsic nature (abhinnasvabhāva), it is impossible for it to be the object of various distinct activities. Power, however, is capacity (sāmarthya), and it can indeed have multiple effects.
As it has been said:
"The distinction among powers is not such as the status of the possessors of power.
If this were so, then in the case of the expression "Let the cooked rice be eaten," there too let there be only a single power.
This is not tenable, because [the powers] do not attain a separate nature from the means (upāya) that is included within them.
It is established that this is because there is no implication of the various powers produced by its own causes. || 146 ||
Previously, however, two powers were described with reference solely to two actions, without relying on the relationship of subordinate and principal; that is this *apādāna*,
defined by the rule "that which is fixed in separation is the *apādāna*" (Pāṇini 1.4.24).
By this very [rule], everything characterized as such is the domain of the ablative case (*apādāna-pañcamī*). However, there is another:

"The rule concerning selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), separation (*vibhakta*), and that which concerns fear (*bhī*), protection (*trā*), and so forth—where the departure (*apāya*) is not perceived—that is for the sake of the understanding of the unlearned. (147)

(142) Regarding the rule *pañcamī vibhakte* (Pāṇini 2.3.42), the prescription characterized by the fifth case (*pañcamī*) which is stated when a distinction (*nirdhāraṇa*) qualified by a case ending is understood, requires the notion of separation (*apāya*).

Because there is a requirement for that which is inferred to be the point of departure (*apāya*), it is established by the technical designation of *apādāna* itself. For its illustrative example is: "The people of Mathurā are more wealthy than those of Pāṭaliputra. In this case, since the act of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) pertains to a domain already differentiated, [the term] is used for the purpose of conveying a state of absolute differentiation.

The mention of "distinct" (*vibhakta*) means that only those things presented as separate entities constitute the scope of this [rule], and not such cases as "among cows, the black one has the most excellent milk," because [the black cow] is not distinct from "cowness.
In that case, even when absolute distinction is intended to be expressed, it is first apprehended by the intellect as being identical.

Equivalence must necessarily be required. For instance, by means of the common quality of wealth, a unity of cognition is brought about; then, due to the distinction of superior wealth, a separation occurs.
Thus, there exists a disjunction preceded by a conjunction of cognitions, which is termed "departure" (apāya); therefore, the status of the *apādāna* (ablative) is established here.
The fifth [case ending]. For this *apādāna* requires an implied action (*apekṣitakriya*). This has been stated in the Bhāṣya:

"Only one who has attained equality with them employs [the word] in this way" (G.eṇa.od.gh. 1.4.24). Since the suffix *-tamap* is mentioned in the section on *kāraka*s, excellence (*atiśaya*) is not intended to be expressed here.

Even here, in the case of a figurative (gauṇa) departure consisting of a mental [conception], the status of being the point of departure (apādānatā) is contradictory. For indeed, the entire linguistic usage regarding grammatical factors (*kāraka*) is based solely upon states of the intellect (*buddhi*). As it was stated previously: "When the Pañcālas are mentally conceived as one with the Kurus..."
Furthermore, when the speaker analyzes [the matter], its undesirable consequence (apāya) is understood.

Thus, since [the rule] is already established by this general principle alone, the commencement of the sūtra is for the purpose of restricting the intended meaning (vivakṣāniyama) with respect to one who does not understand the Buddhist exception; the meaning is that here only the intention to express an "apāya" (separation/departure) must be applied. Likewise, there is the rule:
"The cause of fear [is the ablative] in the case of roots meaning fear" (Pāṇini 1.4.25).

And the rule beginning with "parājer asoḍhaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.4.26), which defines the technical term *apādāna* (ablative), has as its scope that [agent] by whom the action characterized as separation (*apāya*) is undertaken in a subordinate manner; such is the one [referred to].

The illustration of the distinctions among the types of *apādāna*—namely, that which pertains to the vicinity (*upātta*), the object (*viṣaya*), and the source (*apādāna*)—is, as before, solely for the purpose of awakening the unawakened. To explain: when it is said, "fear from wolves" (*vṛkebhyaḥ bhayam*) or "he fears the thief" (*corād bibheti*), a person who acts with foresight perceives through his intellect: "If wolves [should seize] me..."

Thinking, "An undesirable event will certainly occur," one first perceives the wolves through the intellect and then, by means of another cognition, effects a separation from them; thus, because the root *bhī* (to fear) functions in this cessation preceded by fear, there is indeed an "apāya" (separation). And so it is said: "He protects from thieves."

Thus, regarding the expression "preventing harm," there is the possibility of misfortune: having mentally determined that association with thieves constitutes harm, one might remove a kinsman from that situation thinking, "He is a friend. Or, in the case of "he fails because of study," it refers to one who is exhausted by the practice of study and fears the exertion of attending upon a teacher.

Having attained the study, one then desists; thus, there is indeed "departure" (apaya). Furthermore, the verb *parājayati* here functions in the sense of desisting out of weariness, meaning that being weary of study, one desists from it.
Even before engaging in practice, weariness was examined by his intellect;
he constantly observed his teachers with great hardship and austerity.

Thus, in the case of "he wards off the cow from the barley," one prevents the transgression caused by the destruction of the barley that would occur when the cows reach the barley; therefore, this is indeed a primary *apāya* (separation). Similarly, in the expressions "he wards off the blind man from the well" and "he wards off the boy from the fire," [the separation is understood] through the intellect (*buddhyā*).

Thinking that falling into a well or fire is an undesirable cause, one turns back from them out of compassion; thus, this is a departure preceded by a mental connection [to the object]. In the case of "he disappears from the teacher," the suffering associated with being sent away or rebuked upon reaching the vicinity of the teacher is apprehended by the intellect.

"Apāya" (separation) means that having ascertained [the object], one departs from it. In the expressions "he studies from the teacher" (*upādhyāyād adhīte*) and "he causes [the student] to acquire [it]," there is separation from the teacher because he takes up the text from him. For the words uttered from the mouth of the teacher proceed by way of a continuous stream (*santāna*).
Because they enter after the disciple, it is understood that there is a departure from those who stand in the position of the preceptor (*upādhyāya*). This is stated in the Bhāṣya:
"Because of continuity" (Pāṇini 1.4.29).
However, in the case of non-utility, as in "he hears the actor," the departure (*apāya*) is not intended to be expressed; for indeed—
One does not take up the book from the actor;

rather, the true nature of the matter here is simply that one hears what pertains to the actor. As for the worldly understanding that "an arrow is produced from horn," there is indeed a process of passing away [from the source], insofar as it emerges from that. And so it is stated in the treatise:

It has been stated that "the worldly category of entities is analyzed"; this expresses disregard for the systems imagined by the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*). For some of these outsiders maintain a distinction between cause and effect based on the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*).

Since it is said that "the Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat," the Gaṅgā spreads forth from there in the form of a stream; thus, this is indeed a primary departure (*apāya*). And by resorting to a figurative departure, the Vārttika states:
"An addition [to the rule] should be made for the senses of 'disgust' (*jugupsā*), 'cessation' (*virāma*), and 'negligence' (*pramāda*). (Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.4.24).
This has been refuted. For instance, one who possesses right faith (*āstika*) feels disgust for unrighteousness (*adharma*) and desists from it;

having understood that unrighteousness entails suffering in the hereafter, he withdraws from it preceded by a sense of revulsion—thus, there is indeed "passing away" (*apāya*). On the other hand, the nihilist (*nāstika*) [experiences] the fruit of affliction even in this very life.
"Having understood the Dharma, one then turns away from it through negligence"; thus, it is said that "one becomes negligent.
In all such cases, since the designation of the *apādāna* (ablative) is already established by the preceding rule, the subsequent injunction is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*).
For grammar proceeds by means of both definitions and elaborations; as it has been stated, "from that very [source] come the injunctions."
Thus, [the rule] beginning with "ityādi" is established. || 147 ||
Thus ends the section on the Ablative (*apādāna*) in the *Sādhanasamuddeśa* of the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja.

(143) Now, having bypassed the meaning of the genitive case— which follows the sequence of the rules for case-inflection and is characterized as the "remainder" (*śeṣa*)— he examines the locative case, the meaning of the seventh [case], which follows the sequence of the specific *kārakas*.
[The locus] sustains the action indirectly, being separated from the agent and the object.
The locus (adhikaraṇa) is traditionally taught in the treatise as that which assists in the accomplishment of an action. || 148 ||

In common worldly usage, [the term *adhikaraṇa*] is expressed with reference to a specific substratum (*adhikaraṇaviśeṣa*) as having substance, quality, or action as its object. However, in this treatise, because it deals with the section on *kārakas*, when an action is implied, the designation *adhikaraṇa* applies specifically to that action itself by virtue of a particular assistance characterized by "containing" (*dhāraṇa*). In that context, the action resides in the agent (*kartṛ*) or in the object (*karman*).

Regarding the statement "they both remain," because they serve as the substratum for the action (*kriyādhāraṇa*), the designation of locus (*adhikaraṇa*) would apply to them by virtue of the explicit rule (*vacana*). Alternatively, the designation of agent (*kartṛ*) would apply when the action resides in the object (*karmasthakriyā*), or the designation of object (*karman*) would apply when the action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyā*); thus, in that case, it should be applied according to the circumstances.

Anticipating the objection that, in the absence of the designations "agent" (*kartṛ*) and "object" (*karman*), the designation "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) would necessarily apply [to everything], it is stated: "that which is intervened by the agent and the object," and so forth. In such cases as "he sits on a mat" (*kaṭe āste*) or "he cooks in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ pacati*), the locus is that which assists the action inherent in the agent or the object, because it supports them.
Indirectly. For if there were no substratum (*ādhāra*), the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) would not receive the assistance required for the action;

thus, by assisting those two, the substratum also assists the action situated within them. Furthermore, in the section concerning the factors of action (*kāraka-adhikāra*), there is no application of degrees of intensity (*taratama-yoga*). In this regard:
Since the designation of *adhikaraṇa* (locus) has scope in the case of that which supports an action indirectly (*paramparayā*),
whereas the designations of *kartṛ* (agent) and *karman* (object) apply by virtue of being more proximate (*paratvāt*) to those that support the action directly,
the status of the *kārakas* as being causes of action is accepted by you exactly as it is, even when there is an intervention (*vyavadhānena*).

The status of being an instrument of action (*kriyāpakārakatva*) is not contradictory. Even though it has been stated that [the locus] is "separated" (*vyavahitā*), the mention of "not immediate" (*asākṣāt*) is for the purpose of reinforcing the separation of the locus from the support of the action, even in the determination of word-meanings according to worldly convention. For instance, from the word...

The worldly meaning that is being understood is said to be caused by linguistic refinement (*saṃskāra*). In cases such as "he sleeps on the ground" (*pṛthivyāṃ śete*) or "it is cooked in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ pacyate*), from the verbal form (*ākhyāta-śabda*) one understands the agent or the object as qualified by the action, not the action alone in its abstracted form.
In the world, the assistance rendered by a locus to an action is understood precisely because it supports the substratum of that action, not directly.
Now, he states that this general definition of the locus (adhikaraṇa) applies even to its various divisions, such as the contiguous (aupaśleṣika) and others:
"And there is no difference in the contiguity [of the locus] in cases such as sesame seeds, space, and a mat."
But the auxiliaries of those things that are conjoined or inherent differ [in their manner of assistance]. || 149 ||

(144) *Upaśleṣa* is the connection of the locus (*ādhāra*) with the located (*ādheya*), by virtue of which that [locus] is a locus. This [connection] is non-different across all three types of loci. Otherwise, however, the connection would be one way in the case of a locus through conjunction (*saṃyogin*) and another way in the case of a locus through inherence (*samavāyin*); thus, it is designated as distinct due to the difference in the related entities (*saṃbandhin*). Likewise...
In the case of "Devadatta sits on the mat," the contact of Devadatta with the mat, which is a conjoined object, is not seen to pervade all its parts;
rather, it pervades only a few parts. Because there is no distinction [in this regard from other types of proximity], it is called *aupāśleṣika* (proximal).

This locus is stated by way of a general designation. However, in the expression "oil in sesame seeds," because of the worldly convention regarding the connection between the sesame seeds and the oil-essence—which is inherent and pervades all parts of the seeds—this locus is pervasive. But in the case of "birds in the sky," [the relation] of space...

Because there is an absence of real constituent parts, this locus is based on a conceptualized region due to a relationship; furthermore, "not existing elsewhere" is the meaning of the subject here. Thus, in the expression "fish in water," it is with respect to the location of the substratum.

This is an *adhi-karaṇa* (locus) by way of proximity (*upaśleṣika*). In the expression "the disciple dwells with the teacher" (*gurau vasati*), the teacher is the *vaiṣayika-adhikaraṇa* (locus by way of being the object of experience), because the disciple's mode of life is dependent upon the teacher. Here too, the "proximity" is conceptual (*bauddha*). Similarly, in the expression "he arms himself for battle" (*yuddhe saṃnahyati*), there is a conceptual proximity between the act of arming and the battle, as the arming is directed toward the battle.

In the case of activity consisting of binding armor and so forth, battle is the object (*viṣaya*). In the expression "cows on the Gaṅgā," the word *gaṅgā* refers to the region by way of proximity; thus, this is a metaphorical locus (*aupacārikam adhikaraṇam*).

As for such cases as "happiness in the absence of an enemy," the status of the non-existence as a causal factor (*kārakatvam*) is purely conceptual (*bauddham*), as has already been explained previously.
It has been determined. || 149 ||

What, then, are these benefits? He says: "Non-destruction, independence when there is an obstruction of gravity, delimitation by a specific direction, and so forth—these are the causes of differentiation. (150)

(145) The non-destruction of the oil is the benefit conferred by the sesame seed; for if the sesame seed were destroyed, the oil would be dispersed and perish. In the expression "he sleeps on a couch," the agent who is independent in obstructing the gravity of the sleeper is the locus (*ādhāra*); otherwise, falling would occur due to gravity. In the sky...

In cases such as "the birds [are] on the tree," the very utility of the substratum (*ādhāra*) consists in this: that by means of the suffix *kha* (denoting location), the connection of the birds and so forth with the lower direction is excluded.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one includes reaching a specific location by means of a substratum such as a cart, and likewise by means of a teacher.

The excellence of the disciples' refinement, their physical well-being through postures such as the *paryaṅka*, and other such benefits are thus established. Furthermore, it is taught that the sun rises in the east and sets in the west;
Agastya is in the south and Dhruva is in the north.
This section serves solely to establish the connection with specific directions. 150.
Since the existence of all material things is dependent on something else, and even the material substratum itself requires another locus, he asks: what is the ultimate, primary locus?
He says:
For some, due to the conceptualization of spatial distinctions, space itself is considered the primary supporting power (ādhāra-śakti) for all things that possess conjunction. (151)

(146) First, it is well known that the planets, stars, celestial mansions, and so forth, have space as their locus. Even for those things, such as chariots and the like, of which a portion of the earth is the locus,
since that portion of the earth itself rests upon space, space alone is their locus by way of a traditional succession (*pāramparyeṇa*).

By the term "all," he says: for things that possess parts (*samavāyin*), their own constituent parts are the substratum; even there, ultimately, atoms are [the substrata]. And for those [atoms], space alone is the substratum that causes the differentiation of location.
Thus, the primary power of being a substratum for entities resides in space. Nor is it [a matter of] having a single location in this way.

Saṃkara [states] that space attains the status of being a location by means of its conceptualization as distinct parts within the limited spatial regions occupied by itself, since it is said: "due to the conceptualization of a distinction of locations.
This refers to the differentiation of space—which is conventionally treated as the locus of conjoined objects—by those very objects themselves.

The meaning is that space is the substratum for all things without confusion, due to its conceptualization by those who associate [it with objects] while not being [itself] pervasive. The phrase "of some" refers to the view of those proponents of transmigration (saṃsāravādins) who indeed accept space. In this regard, the following...

It may be asked: what is this so-called "space" (ākāśa) that is not perceived by direct observation? If it is argued that the substance [of space] is inferred from its quality, sound, we reply that this is irrelevant because the very fact of sound being a quality of space is unestablished. Sound is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of a tangible substance (*sparśavat*).

Or rather, this presentation of reasons—such as "because it does not exist as long as the substance exists" and "because it is perceived elsewhere than its substratum"—applies to form and the other [sensory qualities] as well. // 151 //

Even if a substratum exists, since transformation is observed due to other causes, and since the substantiality of space (*ākāśa*) is unestablished— and because its being the substratum of sound is a matter of dispute—
the quality of "existing as long as the substance lasts" is unestablished in sound with respect to that portion of space delimited by the ear-cavity.
Thus, since it is perceived elsewhere than its substratum, [the opponent's] reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, the possession of multiple momentary specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) perceivable by the same sense organ is a principle established by one's own tenets (*svakṛtānta*) for those things that possess touch.
Anticipating this objection, he states a mark (*liṅga*) well-known in the world for the existence of the soul (*ātman*):
Since there is no existence of entities "here" or "there," designation is not possible;
they declare that [designation] to be based upon space.

(147) Here, it is the power of support (*ādhāra-śakti*) itself that, by the principle of "otherwise being inexplicable" (*anyathānupapatti*), leads one to infer the existence of space (*ākāśa*). For instance, for those for whom verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition, the meaning of a word is the referent of that word. And this word exists: "This constellation stands here. That which is indicated by the term "here" must be some kind of entity.

Because it is distinct from earth and the other elements, it relies upon the designation "space" (*ākāśa*). Nor is this a non-entity (*avastu*), for a non-entity—characterized by the absence of all causal capacity—does not possess such a designation. Indeed, in verbal discourse, both designation and the investigation that precedes it are based upon real entities.

Because only that which has been defined possesses the nature of a real entity (*vastu*). For this very reason, in cases such as "pleasure in the absence of the enemy," there exists a basis for the worldly convention of designating space as the locus of the absence being defined; thus, space becomes the substratum of absence. Of all categories of entities...

However, when investigating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), everything that has the nature of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is non-existent, because only the non-dual is real; thus, the intention is that the application of definitions—which relies upon worldly objects that are charming only so long as they are not investigated—is itself contradictory. || 152 ||
Regarding that which was stated—that space (*ākāśa*) is the substratum of all entities—that refers to entities whose nature is already established (*siddhasvabhāva*);
however, he states that time (*kāla*) is the substratum with respect to entities whose nature is yet to be established (*sādhyasvabhāva*):
"From time actions are differentiated; from space all material forms [are differentiated]."
And this distinction is precisely such that it is based upon non-distinction. || 153 ||

(148) "By means of prohibition and permission, the universe is divided by him"— according to this principle to be stated later, time (*kāla*), assisting entities through the differentiation of birth, persistence, and cessation, establishes their distinction by becoming the substratum for their activities. Space (*ākāśa*)...

By assuming the state of a substratum without confusion, through a differentiation produced by its conjunction with the categories of substance, dimension, and non-pervasive entities, it distinguishes the individual manifestations of objects according to their fixed locations. Furthermore, this universe—which consists of the transformations of form and action and is characterized by an abundance of the appearance of difference—is obtained in worldly transaction as being, in its primordial state, undivided; it is in relation to this that the non-differentiation caused by what are called time and space is established.

The meaning is that the non-difference called "time and space" (*kālākāśa*) is the basis and cause of this manifestation of form and action. For even the differentiation of form caused by the power of direction (*dik-śakti*) reaches its final determination through the spatial divisions of the substratum, which is space, consisting as it does of "eastern" and "western" locations. Furthermore, the difference between time and space is caused by the Supreme Brahman, with whom they are absolutely non-different due to their being powers (*śakti*); for it has been established in the First Book (*prathama-kāṇḍa*) that those two powers are distinguished only separately [from Him].
[As stated in Pāṇini’s rule: *upānvadhyāṅvasaḥ* (P. 1.4.48).

Thus, it has been stated that for the root *vas* preceded by prefixes such as *upa*, the locus is designated as the object (*karma*). Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika says: "There is a prohibition [of the designation of the locus as object] for *vas* when it does not mean 'eating'. (Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.4.48)

Thus: "He fasts in the village. Just as the root *sthā* denotes a state characterized by the cessation of motion, so the author of the Vārttika considers that *upa-vas* denotes a dwelling characterized by the cessation of eating.

And thus, just as in the case of *upavasati* (he fasts) and *tiṣṭhati* (he stands), the designation of "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*)—which would otherwise apply because there is a connection with the village—is set aside. Furthermore, this Vārttika makes known the restriction of speaker's intention (*vivakṣāniyama*).

The meaning is that here the village and so forth are not intended to be expressed as the "most desired" (*īpsitatama*), but rather by way of being a substratum (*ādhārabhāva*). [Thus it is stated] in the Bhāṣya.
However, this Vārttika has been rejected:
"In this case, the village is not the locus of the root *vas* preceded by the prefix *upa*. Of what, then? Of [the root *vas*] without a prefix.
[The meaning is: 'While staying in the village, he fasts for three nights. (Pāṇini 1.4.48)

In this regard, the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya is as follows: here, the meaning of *upavāsa* (fasting) is the cessation of eating delimited by a specific time. Among these, the specific time is the internal factor (*antaraṅga*), while the action itself remains its original nature. However, for one who does not eat, there is a state of remaining that is without a locus (*niradhikaraṇa*).

Since [the action] does not occur [without a locus], a fixed substratum is required; and since that [substratum] is not connected with the root *vas* preceded by the prefix *upa*, the designation "object" (*karma*) is indeed not applicable. 153.

For even if, as in the case of time, space is also required to be restricted— as in examples such as "he fasts at a sacred site" (*tīrthe upavasati*)— and thus there would indeed be a connection with a location for the verb *upavasati*, leading one to suspect that the designation "object" (*karman*) would apply; having raised this objection, he speaks in order to justify the Bhāṣya.
Although the act of fasting depends upon a specific location, the application of the term relies solely upon time. (154)

(149) Even though there is a connection with a specific location when the cessation of eating and so forth is intended by relying on a particular place such as a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), nevertheless, that connection with a location is not one that arises from the inherent expressive power (*śabdasāmarthya*) of the word *upavasati*. It is merely the cessation of eating.

The purpose [of the suffix] is fasting (*upavāsa*). Since that [fasting] cannot occur at an indefinite time, a specific time (*kāla-viśeṣa*) is implicitly included within the word *antakaṅga*. The operation of denotation (*abhidhāna-vyāpāra*) is the very function of the word; its property (*dharma*), its inherent nature (*svabhāva*), is what is called "the power of the word" (*śabda-śakti*).

...up to this point: although a location such as a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) is intended [as the locus] because it is impossible for the giving to Devadatta to be without a basis, it is not included within the meaning of the word, because there is no connection with the location through the cessation of eating. In that regard, however, that which is a subordinate factor (*aṅga*)—

The connection with the place [is established] by that very [act of staying]. Thus, through the intermediary of the act of staying (*vasati-kriyā*), which serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*), the place is understood to function as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the fast (*upavāsa*). However, its connection with time is direct, because the cessation of eating is restricted to a specific time.
Because it possesses the nature of food through the mediation of time, its location is restricted to that [specific] part;
thus, by means of that [food], there is a locus in this place. For this very reason, the Bhāṣya states:
"In the village, he fasts for three nights" (Pāṇini 1.4.48).

Thus, the connection of the village with the *vāsa* (staying) that is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the fast is shown, but not directly with the fast itself. And since that act of staying is here implied by virtue of being an auxiliary to the [fast], it is intended [as the object] by means of that [staying].

This is the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasaṃbandha*). For the meaning of "fasting" (*upavāsa*) is the cessation of eating for a fixed period, which has dwelling as its subordinate element (*aṅga*). Therefore, when it is said, "he fasts in the village," the location possesses the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇatā*) with respect to the act of dwelling, which is a subordinate element [of the fasting]. || 154 ||
And since the status of time as an object (*karman*) is understood even when it is not explicitly employed— due to its dependence on the cessation of the primary act of eating— it is said:
"Therefore, even when the verb 'to dwell' (*vasati*) is not employed, the location (*deśa*) is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)."
Furthermore, it is traditionally taught that for one who has not performed the preliminary rites, the fast begins three nights prior.

(150) The word "in the commentary" (*bhāṣye*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Because the village and so forth are unfit to be connected with the expressed action of fasting (*upavāsa*), they are the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the action of dwelling (*vasati*), which is obtained through implication even though it is not explicitly employed. For a factor of accomplishment (*sādhana*) [is the locus] even when the action is not heard, provided it is appropriate.

It implies an action; for example, in the command "Enter the village," the object is the act of eating. And here, because there is no basis for perceiving a specific [action], it is understood in its general form as that which has an invariable connection. And for one who has the village as the locus, it is said: "He dwells in the village."

With respect to the act of dwelling (*vāsa*), a location such as a village or a region is established as the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). However, in the case of the act of fasting (*upavasati*) which is being heard [in the verbal root], time alone is the internal substratum; thus, although not explicitly employed, this [time] is implied by virtue of its suitability.

Just as by the very act of entering, one reaches the house, so too here, once the designation "object" (*karman*) has achieved its purpose with respect to the direct substratum (*ādhāra*) where [the action] resides, it does not further penetrate the substratum— characterized as a location such as a village— that arrives through the secondary action of "staying" (*vasati*) which is a constituent part of the [primary] action; for the effect is understood to reside in the primary element rather than the secondary.

Furthermore, in the section concerning *kārakas*, because of the inclusion of the suffix *-tamap*, the excellence of the *kāraka* capacities themselves is not being emphasized; rather, it is not a case of disregarding the internal (*antaraṅga*) and external (*bahiraṅga*) relationship caused by the connection with the action, for otherwise—

Because of its independence in its own operation, the object (*karman*) should receive the designation of agent (*kartṛ*). Since the designation of object is seen to apply to that which is most desired through actions such as "seeing" and so forth, the designation of object is already fulfilled even in the case of location, as in "he dwells near the village" (*grāmam upavasati*), which means "he stays in the vicinity. And therefore—

It is established that when *upavasa* has the sense of abstaining from food, time is its direct substratum (*ādhāra*) and is designated as the object (*karman*); however, even if a location is intended, it is a substratum only indirectly through its being a constituent part of the act of fasting, not directly.
As for the objection that *upavasa*, being of the nature of an abstention, cannot be connected with a substratum—[this is addressed as follows:]...

He explains that in this case, there would be no connection with time as a substratum (*ādhāra*). Yet, even for the verb *tiṣṭhati*, which expresses the cessation of motion, there is a connection with a substratum;
for instance, in the expression "he stays in the village" (*grāme āste*), the cessation characterized by the suspension of all activity is connected to the village.

There is no contradiction in its being an action (*kriyā*) even while it precludes other actions; for an action is indeed a specific activity of the causal factors (*kāraka*) that is inferred from its result, and here that [activity]—consisting in the cessation of eating at restricted times—is clearly evident. Nor is it merely a particular volition (*saṃkalpa*).

Mental activity is cessation (*nivṛtti*). Since there is no distinction between the primary action and [subsidiary acts] such as looking at [the enemy], it was stated that the desire for distinction occurs only in cases such as "he arms himself for battle.
Likewise, in this case, the agent's activity preceded by a resolution [is characterized] by a fixed temporal interval.
The meaning of the verbal root *upa-vas* consists of such things as eating; although it is of the nature of an action, even when there is a connection with a locus (*adhikaraṇa*),
