it does not connect directly with that locus characterized by "hating" (or "dwelling"), because such a connection is impossible except through the medium of the subordinate action of "staying" (*vasati*).

It is thus established that the rule for the designation *karman* applies precisely to those relations with a substratum (*ādhāra*) designated as time (*kāla*) which are invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*).
Thus ends the section on the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) in the *Sādhanasamuddeśa* of the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa*, composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja.
(151) Now, the sixth case-meaning (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*), the seventh type of *kāraka* distinction, is being examined.
And that is the relation characterized as "remainder" (*śeṣa*). How is it a type of *kāraka* distinction, and how...
In order to establish this status as a *śeṣa* (subsidiary), he says:
"The relation, which is distinct from the *kārakas*, is preceded by action and *kāraka*;
it is denoted whether the action is explicitly mentioned or not. (156)

The *śeṣa* is that relation which is other than the six specific types of relations characterized as *karman* (object) and so forth; this is based on the word *śeṣa* meaning "that which is other than what has been employed.
[As stated: "The non-intentional expression (*avivakṣā*) of the *kārakas* is *śeṣa*" (Pāṇini 2.3.50).

Thus the commentary has been explained. By the phrase "preceded by action and its factors" (*kriyākārakapūrvakaḥ*), he explains the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action) for the *śeṣa* (the remaining relation). For instance, in cases such as "the king's man," "the tree's branch," "the animal's foot," or "the father's son," where no action is explicitly heard, [the relationship is established].
In relations such as those of owner and owned, part and whole, or produced and producer, where the action— such as giving, abiding, or being produced— is manifested through the connection,
the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action) existing in the prior state persists even in the subsequent state; thus, it indeed constitutes a "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

The *kāraka* (participant in an action). For when a king gives [something] to a man, because of that, the relation of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*)—namely, "the king's man"—is established. In that case, the relationship between the action and the *kāraka* is the cause, whereas the residual relationship (*śeṣasaṃbandha*) is the result. Indeed, the relationship between the action and the *kāraka*, once it has occurred, resides in its own substratum.

Having established the fruit through its remaining relationship (*śeṣasaṃbandha*), [the treatise] concludes. In that regard, previously the king and his servant existed in the form of agent (*kartṛ*) and recipient (*saṃpradāna*). However, at the time of the remaining relationship, since their specific forms as agent and so forth are no longer perceived, it is the generality (*sāmānya*) that constitutes that remainder.

The status of being a *kāraka* (participant in action) remains established, because there is an absence of any designation based on the distinctions between means such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth.

"The remainder" (*śeṣa*) is that which is other than the *kārakas*, occurring when the *kārakas* are not intended to be expressed. And in the phrase "preceded by a *kāraka*," the distinctions of means such as the instrument and so forth are those which reside in the same substrate as the state of being a *kāraka*.

They are designated by the term "kāraka" (factor), but not as the general category of "kāraka" itself. For substances, which possess an established nature and are like iron rods, there is no mutual connection [inherently]; rather, that connection is produced solely by action (*kriyā*). Indeed, action, like a ladder, brings substances into contact with one another. Thus...
And the Bhāṣya says:
"Distinctions among the meanings of nominal stems arise through action, such as 'object,' 'instrument,' and so forth."
In that regard, since no other specific quality is observed apart from the forms of the *karman* (object) and so forth, the relation termed "residual" (*śeṣa*)—
which exists in the form of the *karman* and so forth— is established within its own substratum, which has experienced those specific qualities such as being an object.
By attaching the word, it reveals its own nature as not intending to express distinctions such as the object (*karman*) and so forth.

Consequently, in the case of "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣayoḥ*), the relationship exists in a general form between the states of being the giver and the recipient (*dātṛtva-sampradānatve*) which, at the stage of the result, do not exceed their own essential natures.

[It] deserves to be designated [as such]. And thus, this seventh case (saptamī), whose specific form is not explicitly indicated, is reckoned as a source of the factor of action (kāraka-yoni), due to the difference in the comprehension of the word's meaning.
For the comprehension is indeed different in the case of "the king gives to the man. Indeed, from this [statement], there is no necessary [restriction].

The gift is understood to be caused by the relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*), since the gift can also occur through other causes such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth. On the other hand, in the case of "the king's man," [the relationship] is understood from the cognition of the relationship of owner and owned.
Therefore, since difference is established due to this difference in cognition, just as in the case of specific distinctions such as the object (*karman*) and so forth...
Even by this [suffix] called *śeṣa*, the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is expressed as being differentiated;
thus, this relation has for its object an unexpressed action, because actions such as giving— which are caused by relations such as that of owner and owned— are not heard [in the expression].

Furthermore, since the acts of giving and so forth are inferred through the otherwise inexplicable nature of the relationship that constitutes the effect, they are indeed present; thus, by means of them, the coherence [of the Vedic texts] is established.

Moreover, the fact that the relationship between the two related parties as well as the fruit is caused by action is certainly based upon their status as *kārakas* (factors of action), just as it is in the case of an object (*karman*).

Everything is logically consistent. Even in cases such as "He comes from near the village" (*grāmasya samīpād āgacchati*) or "The leaf falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati*), there is indeed a precedence of action and factor (*kriyākāraka*) in the relationship of proximity and that which is proximate (*samīpa-samīpibhāva*), and so forth. For the village is the locus (*āśraya*) of the proximity, and likewise, the tree is the locus of the leaf.

Thus it is said. This same principle applies everywhere. However, with respect to actions such as coming and so forth, the village and other such entities are said to be non-factors (*akāraka*). But the relation that has an expressed action as its object is indeed a specific factor (*kāraka-bheda*); it is a general nature of relation whose specific distinctions, such as "object" (*karman*) and so forth, are not intended to be expressed.

This is merely a relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasaṃbandha*); it is not preceded by [the application of] those [technical designations]. For example, in expressions such as *naṭasya śṛṇoti* ("he hears from the actor"), the technical designations such as "instrument" (*karaṇa*) do not apply here because their respective conditions are absent. Furthermore, because [the actor] is included in the specific enumeration of roots beginning with *duh* (e.g., Pāṇini 1.4.51), he does not possess the status of an "unspoken object" (*akathitakarma*). Thus, this [actor] is distinct from the [standard] *kārakas*.

The *śeṣa* (remainder) is indeed a *kāraka* itself; thus, it has been stated that the mention of "application" (*upayoga*) is purposeful. Likewise, in examples such as *mātuḥ smarati* ("he remembers his mother"), *na māṣāṇām aśnīyāt* ("one should not eat beans"), and *sarpiṣo jānīte* ("he takes notice of the ghee"), it is stated that the *śeṣa* is simply the distinction between the *karman* and other *kārakas*, where that specific form is not intended to be expressed. And in this case, regarding the *śeṣa*:
The genitive case has been explained. Since a relationship resides in two things, it was raised as an objection that the genitive would consequently apply to both related entities:
"If it is argued that 'the genitive is used for the remainder' (Pāṇini 2.3.50), there is a prohibition regarding the substantive."

Thus, the meaning is that since the sixth case (genitive) would also result from the word *puruṣa* in the expression *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*, a prohibition must be applied; and because the relation has already emerged [as expressed], the first case does not apply to the substantive (*viśeṣya*), so it too must be prescribed— so it has been stated.
Regarding that, [the rule] "tatra prathamāvidhiḥ" (Pāṇini 2.3.46) applies.
Here, for the sake of resolving both cases, it is stated:
"it has been explained by the preceding [rule]" (G.eṇa. od dyaṇe aḍodhe dyadhro dhaddhdyattas).

Thus it was stated. In the *Prātipadikārtha-sūtra*, when the objection was raised: "An addition [to the rule] is required regarding co-referentiality with 'cloth' (*paṭa*), because of its being additional" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 2.3.46).

Or rather, it has been stated [in the Mahābhāṣya] that "it is not so, because it is the meaning of a sentence" (*na vā vākyārthatvāt*, Pāṇini 2.3.46). That very point has been restated here for the purpose of extended application (*atideśa*). By means of the analysis of the constituent parts of this word *rājñaḥ* ("of the king"), the relatedness of the person is understood.

The meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), which is the relationship (*saṃbandha*), does not serve as the cause for the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) based solely on the word-meanings (*padārtha*), because it is external (*bahiraṅga*). Thus, the meaning is that the absence of the genitive case and the presence of the nominative case are established here, just as in examples such as *vīraḥ puruṣaḥ* (the brave man) or *nīlam utpalam* (the blue lotus). If this is so—

By this same logic, even from the word *rājan* (king), the genitive case would not occur—as it does not from words such as *vīra* (hero)—and the nominative would instead apply. This is not so, because the "excess" residing in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) alone constitutes the meaning of the sentence; for that [qualificand] is indeed the primary element.

First, that very [substance], without abandoning its own nature, attains the state of being assisted (*upakāryatā*) with respect to the quality (*guṇa*) which is required; thus, its very predominance (*ādhikya*) is said to be the meaning of the sentence. However, for the quality, which proceeds for the sake of assisting the principal (*pradhāna*), it is impossible for it to be both established in itself and to be an assistant; therefore, from the very outset—
A different form arises, capable of serving the primary purpose, in relation to the commonality of its constituent parts.
As it is stated in the Bhāṣya:
"This kind of thing is indeed the very form of the meaning... (Pāṇini 6.1.79).

Thus, it is logical that the sixth case (genitive) should be used for a quality (*guṇa*) as a residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). However, a coreferential qualifier (*samānādhikaraṇa-viśeṣaṇa*), such as "blue" (*nīla*), attains as it were a state of identity with the principal term (*pradhāna*), such as "lotus" (*utpala*);
since it does not maintain a sense of distinction (*vyatireka*) [from the principal], the sixth case does not occur there. || 146 ||
This establishes the true nature of the entity:
"Although it resides in both, because its purpose is for another, it is distinguished among the qualities;
being expressed therein, it is also experienced in the primary [subject]. (157)

(152) A single relation resides in two [relata]. In that case, it is logical that there be only one genitive. If there were two genitives, two relations would be understood. And that single genitive occurs only with respect to the subordinate element (*guṇa*), not the principal element (*pradhāna*). This is because that relation subsists in both relata.

Since these two form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) through the relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*), and since it is appropriate for subordinate elements to conform to the principal by undergoing a modification of their form, the genitive case expressing the relation of connection (*saṃbandhakāryā ṣaṣṭhī*) properly results from the subordinate element alone. For indeed, in the case of subordinate elements, there is a predominance of distinction (*vyatireka*).

The connection is demonstrated: the primary [element], however, experiences the connection while remaining entirely unmoved from its own nature. For its primacy exists only if it does not undergo a transformation of form in accordance with the subordinate elements; and this is because it serves as the substratum for those subordinate elements.

When the relation is expressed by the genitive case, even the form residing in the principal [substantive] is experienced, touched, and indeed denoted; this is what is meant. It is stated that the predominance residing in the principal constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), because it is perceived through its connection with the subordinate element (*guṇa*). This applies to that which possesses mutual expectancy.

Because a collection of words constitutes a sentence; for when "of the king" (*rājñaḥ*) is understood as denoting lordship, it indicates a distinct relation characterized by ownership (*svatva*) in the person as well, since that [lordship] would otherwise be untenable. And thus, [the meaning] is more intimate than the person.

It remains the first [case-ending] because the external relation is already understood through the very necessity of connecting it with another word, and thus no additional element enters into the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). However, when there exists a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*),...

When it is said that a person is called "king" because of his exercise of power (*kāmacāra*), then the genitive case is used from the person himself on account of that quality; thus, the grammatical rule is not violated. || 157 ||

It has been stated that a relation is preceded by an action and its factors (kriyākāraka). In that regard, the relation between the action and its factors is the cause of this [relation]; and since that [cause] is inferred from the relation which is its effect, it cannot be inferred in its specific detail, but rather—
Since inference has such a nature by its very definition, from where does this determination of a specific [object] arise?
To this he says:
"The restriction of the causal basis for the relationship is not grasped through the word."
But by means of *karmapravacanīyas*, it is restricted to a specific [meaning]. || 158 ||

(153) In expressions such as "the son of the father" or "the foot of the animal," it is precisely through the determination of the specific nature of the related entities that the relation is perceived as being conditioned by restricted actions such as the act of generating or the act of standing.

In expressions such as "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*), although the restriction [of the relationship] cannot be determined as the sole cause because the master-servant relation can also arise through begging, bartering, seizure, and so forth, nevertheless,
an action is indeed inferred because any one of these— such as giving and the rest— is invariably concomitant with it.

Because it arises from the very nature of the relationship, this is not a domain of the *karmapravacanīya*s. In some cases, however, a specific cause is not determined by the power of the word; rather, there is a determination of the cause in its general sense.
Such is the scope of the *karmapravacanīya*s.
The meaning of the relationship is delimited by the restriction of the cause (*nimitta*) through those [words] beginning with *anu*. For instance,
in the expression "it rained after Śākalya’s *saṃhitā*," the causal relationship between the *saṃhitā* and the rain is produced by the act of hearing.
Thus it is announced. Likewise, because concomitance is observed in such cases as "having heard this elsewhere through action" (*tathā kriyayāsyānyatrānuniśamya*),

and because it is accepted that among the *karmapravacanīyas* (prepositional particles) the term "proktavantaḥ" (*those who have spoken*) indicates an action that has already passed, [the same applies] now.

It does not illuminate that which consists of action (*kriyāmaya*), because no verbal root (*kriyāpada*) is heard; and in the absence of a word that expresses what is to be illuminated, there can be no illumination directed toward it. Furthermore, since the relation [of the suffix] with its own form is conveyed by the case-ending itself, it is not a denoter of that either. However, as for the implication of a verbal root, this [suffix] does not [perform that function].

Because there is an absence of a case-ending denoting an agent (*kāraka*), it has been established that *karmapravacanīyas* indicate a specific type of relationship. As it was said in the subsequent section:
"This [term] is neither an indicator of an action nor an expresser of a relationship."
Nor does it imply a verbal action, but rather differentiates the relationship itself.
Thus, even in the case of "The Pañcālas are under Brahmadatta," the relationship of owner and owned is made known by the term *adhi* through its being based on actions such as protection;
likewise in "Abhimanyu is a match for Arjuna."

The relationship between Arjuna and Abhimanyu, consisting of the imitation of the actions performed by one who defeats another and so forth, is revealed by means of the *prati* [prefix]. In other cases as well, this should be understood accordingly. Thus, this is the power of the *karmapravacanīya*s when the relationship concerns an unstated action (*aśrutakriyā*). However, when the action is stated (*śrutakriyā*), the action itself, as it is being heard, is invariably determined to be the cause [of the relationship]. || 158 ||

In this regard, however, the following is considered: since the genitive case is already established by the rule *śeṣe*, what is the purpose of its re-vidhāna (re-statement) by the rule *adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi*? Furthermore, there is an impossibility of the qualifier [in the phrase] *karmaṇi śeṣe* being in grammatical apposition [with the word *śeṣe*]; for if the intention were to express the status of being an object (*karmatva*), [the genitive would not apply].

The "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is so called because it is defined as the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) of the case-factors (*kāraka*s). Anticipating the objection that if one intends to express the remainder as the resulting fruit, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) would be obscured, he says:
"And when [the action] is designated by its means (*sādhana*s), even though the action is explicitly heard..."
The genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) has been prescribed at every step for the purpose of precluding compound formation. || 159 ||

(154) The factors of action (*sādhana*), such as the object (*karman*) and so forth, are employed elsewhere for the purpose of designating the "residual" (*śeṣa*), but not for their own sake. The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs when there is a residual relation. In what sense is it residual? It is because the residual is qualified by means of the states of being an object, an instrument, and so on, which have already occurred [in a previous grammatical operation].

The meaning established is that the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is that which inheres in the same object as the action and so forth, and which constitutes the result; thus, the application of the qualifier is justified. Although the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is already established by general rules, it is prescribed here with a restricted scope by the rule beginning with *adhi-i-artha* (Pāṇini 2.3.52), so that through this specific prescription, a compound may be formed, as for example: [The text continues: *punarvidhānena samāso yathā...* (By this re-prescription, a compound is formed, as follows...)

"‘It would be excluded’—for a restatement (*punaḥ-śruti*) serves the purpose of restriction (*niyamārthā*). Thus, the meaning of the sentence is that ‘only the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs. In a restrictive rule, the exclusion of others is primary, and the other [element] is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogī*) to be excluded. And here, that [other] is the absence of the genitive; and since that [absence] occurs in a compound (*samāsa*), it follows by implication (*sāmarthyāt*)."

This remains a prohibition of compounding (*samāsa*). Thus it has been said: "The genitive case prescribed by specific rules (*pratipadavidhānā*) is not compounded. By this *vārttika*, the operation of the rule itself is merely restated; no new matter is introduced. But where does this prohibition of compounding apply? Wherever the application of compounding would otherwise occur. And where does that application occur?
"In the case of the secondary wives, it is prescribed that [the inheritance] belongs to the mother. || 159 ||
For it is said here:
"In the case of a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), a genitive denoting the object (*karma*) is not prohibited;
however, a compound with that genitive, when it is characterized as 'the remainder' (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*), is not desired. (160)

(155) It has been stated that the genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is compounded when connected with a *kṛt* suffix. Accordingly, in accordance with the rule "the genitive of the agent and the object [is compounded] with a *kṛt* suffix" (Pāṇini 2.3.65), there is indeed compounding in such cases as *dharmānusmaraṇam*.

In the passage beginning with "recollection of the object" (*arthānusmaraṇam*), this is not a restrictive rule for the genitive case based on *Pāṇini* 2.3.65, "the [genitive] of the agent and the object when a *kṛt*-suffix follows. Because of the repeated mention of "object" (*karman*) in that sūtra, the mention of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is excluded;
therefore, this is an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhāna*). Consequently, it means that the genitive alone [is used].

By means of the restriction regarding the sixth case (genitive), he indicates the prohibition of compound formation; for instance, in examples such as *mātuḥ smṛtam* ("remembered from the mother"), when used with a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), [the rule] "na lokāvyaya... (Pāṇini 2.3.69) applies.
By these and other such statements, the genitive case prescribed by the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti" (Pāṇini 2.3.65) is prohibited;
for, by the rule "adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 2.3.52),
the genitive is already established in general when the object is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (śeṣatva).

Because of the restatement [of the rule], it is understood that [the prohibition] is for the purpose of excluding compound formation. But is it not the case that [the sūtra] "ktasya ca vartamāne" (Pāṇini 2.3.67) and the supplementary rule "napuṃsake bhāve upasaṃkhyānam" (vārttika on Pāṇini 2.3.67) [already establish this]?
Thus, by this [rule], the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is applied here. This is not so;

for since the rule "it is established through the understanding of the remainder" (*śeṣavijñānāt siddham*, *Jaiminīya-nyāyamālāvistara* 2.3.67) has been rejected, this is simply the "remainder-genitive" (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), because of its being restated.
This indicates the absence of compounding. Even so, the usage *mātuḥ smṛtam* (the mother is remembered) would be untenable;

because the root *smṛ* is transitive, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) would necessarily apply to the object, and due to its coreferentiality with "mother," the form would have to be *mātā smṛtā*.
However, when there is a requirement for another related term, the usage *mātuḥ smṛtāyāḥ* (of the mother who was remembered) is logical.
This is true; [it is stated in the rule]:
"In the case of [verbs] having objects and so forth, they should be treated as if they were intransitive."

Thus it has been stated. And so, in this case, because the action is expressed by a word ending in the *kta* suffix through its treatment as if it were intransitive (*akarmakavadbhāva*), when there is a desire to express the remaining relation (*śeṣavivakṣā*), the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is prescribed again; consequently, it is established that this results in the prohibition of compounding (*samāsapratiṣedha*). Thus...

In rules such as *jño 'vidarthasya karaṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.51), one should cite examples of the prohibition of compounding when the rule is prescribed by specific wording (*pratipadavidhāna*), such as *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("the knowledge of ghee") and *madhuno jñānam* ("the knowledge of honey"). Now, one might object: once the compound has been formed here, only a general relationship (*saṃbandhamātra*) [is expressed].

"It is understood, but since there is no capacity to express the meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*)—namely, that 'the relation is not preceded by an instrument'—there will be no compound here; so what is the use of this effort?
This is not so. Even in the analytical sentence, there is no verbal determination of a specific relation, because of similarity [to the compound].

For instance, the genitive case used with the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*) is of this very same nature. In that regard, when the meaning of the root *jñā* is understood as "to know" (or "to find out") through the context or other factors—as in expressions such as *tattvajñānam* ("knowledge of reality") or *varṇajñānam* ("knowledge of letters")—the compound with the genitive of the object is formed. And thus, it is the same even in the case of *sarpiṣo jānāmi*.

It is established that even if the genitive case of the instrument (*karaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*) were to occur when there is an understanding that the *prakaraṇa* (context) and so forth do not have the meaning of an object (*karman*), the compound would still be possible;
therefore, that [objection] is to be refuted by relying on a restatement of the rule here as well, through the continued application of the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*).
This concerns the prescription of the case endings.

Even though there is syntactic unity with the rules for *svādi* suffixes, since the individual constituent sentences have ceased their own respective operations, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in [the rule] being one prescribed for each specific word (*pratipadavidhāna*). || 160 ||

It has been stated that a relation residing in two [terms] is distinguished when applied to qualities (*guṇa*). Furthermore, because the status of quality and primary subject is contradictory in a single instance, it is said in the Bhāṣya:
"In that case, this [expression] would not now occur: *rājñaḥ puruṣasya* (the king's man)" (Pāṇini 2.3.51).
In that regard, the resolution has been stated:
"It occurs in dependence upon an external object" (Pāṇini 2.3.51).
He now explains this Bhāṣya.
When that which is designated by one [word] undergoes a distinction (vyatireka) in another [context], it acquires two properties in that different domain. (161)

(156) In expressions such as "the king's man's blanket," there arises a relation— namely, a connection characterized by *vyatireka* (distinction), *ādhikya* (superiority), or predominance— of the primary element, the "man" who is designated (*vyapadiṣṭa*) by the qualifier "king" and thus indicated as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), with respect to another primary correlate (*pratiyogin*), such as the "blanket. This is that [relation].
It attains two distinct properties, characterized by the relationship of subordinate and principal;

thus he says that there is no contradiction in the connection between two related entities occurring at different times, as indicated by the use of the past tense in the word "vyapadiṣṭasya" (of that which has been designated). || 161 ||
And therefore:
Having attained primacy through its own quality, it becomes subordinate to the principal [element];
thus, in a construction with *saha*, its status as the principal is not lost. (162)

(157) Therefore, for this reason of the difference in objects, the predominance of the person with respect to the king as a relative does not cease; for in that case, predominance had already been obtained by him with respect to his own subordinate quality characterized as "kingly. However, in the case of another predominant object such as a blanket (*kambala*), [the situation is different].

The meaning is that since "the remainder" (śeṣa) attains the status of a subordinate factor (guṇatva), when it is connected with its own [other] items such as a blanket (kambala) and so forth, one does not perceive the predominance (prādhānya) previously understood [in relation to the primary], because the objects differ; for the relationship of subordinate and predominant is not contradictory in a single instance. This refers to the rule "in connection with 'saha'."
In this context, he provides an illustration where there is no difference in the state of security and well-being (*yogakṣema*):

by the rule "when used with [the word] *saha*, the third case ending is prescribed for the subordinate element" (Pāṇini 2.3.19), the third case is enjoined after the subordinate term in the example "he has come together with his son" (*putreṇa sahāgataḥ*). In that regard:

Just as in the case of "the son of Devadatta," where the son, being qualified by that [paternity], is primary with respect to him, yet becomes secondary with respect to the act of coming—because of the capacity of the sense of "together" (saha) and the resulting connection to the act of coming which is inferred—the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) applies by virtue of its being secondary. Similarly, although a man is primary in relation to the king, he is secondary in relation to his own qualifier; thus, in the expression "the king's man's wealth" (*rājñaḥ puruṣasya dhanam*), the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is established. This is proven. || 162 ||
Thus ends the section on the remaining topics (*śeṣādhikāra*) within the *Sādhanasamuddeśa* of the *Prakīrṇakaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja.

(158) Thus far, the meaning of the case-ending as the agent (*kāraka*) has been examined. As for the nominative (*prathamā*), however, it is governed by the rule: "The nominative is used when [the *kāraka*] has already been expressed" (*abhihite prathamā*, Pāṇini 2.3.46).

Thus it has been prescribed by some: when a *kāraka* such as the object (*karman*) is already expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and so forth, the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used. For example, in sequence: *odanaḥ pacyate* (the rice is being cooked), *māṃsapacano vahniḥ* (a fire that cooks meat), *godhno 'tithiḥ* (a guest who kills a cow), *praskandanaḥ stambhaḥ* (a pillar that causes one to stumble), *niśā nīśāṇā* (a night that wears away), and *pacati devadattaḥ* (Devadatta cooks).

The designation of the *kārakas* beginning with the object (*karman*) and ending with the agent (*kartṛ*) has been illustrated by means of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and so forth. The designation of the object is expressed by the *kṛt*-suffix in "the mat is made" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ*); the designation of the relationship is expressed by the *taddhita*-suffix in "descendant of Upagu" (*aupagavaḥ*); and [it is expressed] by the compound in "one who has brindled cows" (*citraguḥ*). In the case of "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), [the relationship is expressed] by the mutual dependence of the two [words].
Or, when the sentence is concluded by the mere relation itself, if the relation residing in both [relata] is expressed by a genitive case affix attached to either one of the two words,
then the nominative case (*prathamā*) follows precisely from the definition provided for another [type of relation]. However, regarding this definition, it has been objected:

It has been stated: "The verb *as* (to be), followed by the forms *bhavanti* and so on, exists even when not explicitly employed in the first person. [This is because] a word-meaning cannot function in linguistic usage without the connection to an action (*kriyā*).
Since the action of existence (*astikriyā*), which possesses a relationship that is never deviant from its general form, is present everywhere,
this nominative case is used for the agent when it is expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) in the sentence "the tree exists" (*vṛkṣo 'sti*).
As it is stated in the Bhāṣya:

"The referent of a word does not deviate from what exists. This means that since the employment of words has as its locus a determined object, and since both determination and [the use of] words depend upon existence (*sat*), every meaning expressed by a word is permeated by figurative existence (*upacārasat*).
And so it was stated previously:
"This metaphorical [function] is the cause of application for all words; for no real entity (padārtha) indeed transcends this."

Thus, even the connection with [verbs] such as "is not," "is bound," or "is led" occurs only for that which exists; this is the general rule everywhere regarding existence. And so, the word remains established in this very state, even amidst both contradictory and non-contradictory attributes.

It has already been stated that [the suffix] *samanveti*, and it was settled in that very context. Nevertheless, it was objected: "In the case of both the expressed and the unexpressed [agent], there is an absence of the nominative case" (*abhihitānabhihite prathamābhāvaḥ*). [As an example: "The grace remains" (*prasāda āste*).

In such cases as these, the locative capacity (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*) with respect to the action of sitting (*āsikriyā*) has not been expressed (*anabhihitā*), whereas it has been expressed (*abhihitā*) and rendered (*kṛtā*) with respect to the action of being (*sattākriyā*). Consequently, the nominative case (*prathamā*)—which is characterized by being expressed—would result. This is likewise the case in examples such as "the trees have borne fruit" (*phalitā vanaspatayaḥ*) and "the cuckoos [sing] with melodious notes" (*tārasvarāḥ parabhṛtāḥ*).

In the case of a relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), since there is no departure from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), nothing would be expressed by anything else; consequently, the nominative case (*prathamā*)—which is defined as being used for that which is [already] expressed—would not occur. This applies to words such as *uccaiḥ* ("high") and *nīcaiḥ* ("low").

Furthermore, since an indeclinable (avyaya), which primarily expresses the locative case-power (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*), cannot be connected [with another word] through the ellipsis of a word meaning "existence" (*asti*), it is not denoted by anything; how then could the nominative case apply?
Thus [it is argued against the rule]: "The nominative is used when coreferential with a finite verb" (*tiṅ-samānādhikaraṇe prathamā*, Pāṇini 2.3.46).

This [objection] is also refuted by this very same example: the definition is not a non-definition. Furthermore, another fault has been stated here: "There would be an absence of the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* because of the absence of a cause, since those two are exceptions (*apavāda*)."

Regarding the rule *ja-od-gha-dh-ām-gha-t-ṭī-t-ṅā-nā-si-ghu-bhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.34): here, according to the view that analyzes the derivation step-by-step (*vibhājyānvākhyāna-pakṣa*), when the state *devadatta pac l* has been reached,
as long as the suffix *tiṅ* has not yet arisen, there is an absence of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a *tiṅ*-ending word.

The first case ending (*prathamā*) would not be obtained. Consequently, since all suffixes beginning with *sva* (the nominative) are established as being prescribed without distinction after the word "Devadatta," the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes— which are prescribed as exceptions (*apavāda*) in place of the present tense marker (*laṭ*) when there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*) and so forth— would apply, and not the verbal endings (*tiṅ*).

However, the scope for the *liṅ* (optative) and other suffixes would remain; and since that same scope would also belong to the nominative (*prathamā*), a usage such as "pacati devadattaḥ" (Devadatta cooks), which is coreferential with the present tense (*laṭ*), would not result in a nominative ending. Thus, when this alternative definition has been rejected:
The definition of the Master [Pāṇini] himself, beginning with *prātipadikārthaliṅgaparimāṇa...* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.46), has been established as the correct one. In this regard, it is considered:
since the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a feminine suffix (*ṅī*) or a long vowel (*āp*) is understood to be the base for the case-endings (*svādi*), [the following is examined].

Since it is already understood that the meaning belongs to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself, the mention of the nominal stem as a qualifier is not required for the meaning; thus, it remains unconnected with the word "meaning" (*artha*). This is done in order to prescribe the nominative case even for that which is meaningless, as in the examples "he comes from over" (*adhyāgacchati*) and "he comes from around" (*paryāgacchati*).

The designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) is prescribed for particles (*nipāta*). If this is so, then the nominative case will occur by virtue of the power of that designation; for there is no possibility here of any other nominal stem function than the prescription of a case-ending. Furthermore:
Regarding the rule *adhiparī anarthakau* (Pāṇini 1.4.93):

because the prescription of the technical term *karmapravacanīya* serves to set aside the technical term *gati*, it is inferred from this indicative mark (*liṅga*) that these [prepositions] possess meaning.
Otherwise, in the absence of the indication of a specific action (*kriyāviśeṣa*), the designation *gati* would not even be applicable.

Regarding the rule for the introduction of case-endings (*svādi*), even under the view that there is a separate sentence (*bhinnavākyatā*), the case-endings produced without distinction are already established.
Here, even under the view of a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*), since the restriction on suffixes depends upon the base (*prakṛti*), the restriction [applies] accordingly.

If [the rule] were "the second case ending occurs only after the object (*karman*) and not after the instrument (*karaṇa*"), there would be no exclusion of the meaningless [words]. Alternatively, a restriction of meaning (*arthaniyama*) must be adopted, such as: "the second case ending occurs only after the object," and so forth. And having done so, the case endings beginning with *su* (nominative) are found after indeclinables (*avyaya*), which lack number.

The words *uccais* and *nīcais* have not been cited here either; furthermore, there is an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule regarding the elision (*luk*) of case endings after indeclinables (*avyaya*). Since there is no purpose for deviating from the sequence, the first [word] arrived at by the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is the one intended here. Therefore, the mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) serves solely as a qualifier of the meaning.

Although it is obtained through the force of implication (*sāmarthya*), the rule prescribes the nominative (*prathamā*) for the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone, and not from an indeclinable (*avyaya*) itself. In that regard, some say that the meaning qualified by the general category of the nominal stem is "existence" (*satā*); for that [existence] is first [established] as having an invariable connection with all meanings.

It is established that the meaning [of the base] is the sense of the mere nominal stem (*prātipadika*) independent of its connection with case-endings and the like. For the determination of the technical meaning of words is indeed based on the application of imagined positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). And in that regard, when the pure nominal stem occurs in forms such as *vṛkṣam* (accusative) or *vṛkṣeṇa* (instrumental), [it is understood to denote the object and so forth].
Even when there is a following of the case-meanings (*vibhaktyartha*), because there is only a following of "existence" (*satā*), the determination of that meaning [is as follows]:

since existence is not possible without a substratum (*anadhikaraṇa*), its referent must necessarily have substance (*dravya*) as its substratum; for the word is independent [of other factors] up to that point. This applies even in the case of gender (*liṅga*) and so forth.
Because it depends on conditions and because of the inclusion of the suffix *mātra*, this meaning is established as something to be abandoned;

consequently, there is no contradiction with the position that there are five [categories]. Furthermore, even by one who has stated that "the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is the accomplished state," that too is due to the difference between noun-words (*nāmapada*) and verb-words (*ākhyātapada*).

It has been stated that [the word] denotes an object whose nature is already established (*siddha-svabhāva*), but its "establishedness" (*siddhatā*) is not intended as something to be produced by a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). For if it were so, one might raise the objection that because it is understood through the employment of another word, it would not constitute the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone. And this applies to the word when it refers to a mere property (*dharma-mātra*).

Some clearly state that because there is no resting [in its own nature], the *nimita*—the meaning of the nominal stem—is brought to the state of being the self-nature (*ātmarūpatā*) by means of the *nimitta*. The *nimitta* consists of genus, quality, and action;
the *nimitī* is their substratum, whose form is indeed concealed due to its complete identity with them. For this very reason:

It is said that [the object] is as if brought to the state of being the self-nature by means of the cause (nimitta); however, what is intended here is not an actual transformation into another nature in reality. Rather, there is merely a superimposition (ācchuraṇa) of that [nature], because of such a determination (adhyavasāya). Furthermore, there is no operation involving a cessation [of the process], for [the cognition] is precisely that which is colored by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

Because the substance is cognized from the word itself; for it is not the case that the pure substance, which is to be expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), is first understood and only later the specific gender and so forth are perceived as emerging. For if that were so, the meaning of the nominal stem would be differentiated [from the substance] even when conveyed by a single word, just as it is by the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) and the like.

And you [should not argue] that because the meaning qualified by gender is indeed denoted by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and since even that which is colored by gender constitutes the meaning of the nominal stem, the use of the word "only" (*mātra*) serves to exclude anything additional; for otherwise, [the term *strī*] would apply to "girl," "tree," and "pot."

An example for the mention of "gender" (*liṅga*) has been given. For just as the nominative case does not occur when the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) exceeds [the mere thing] because of the mention of "only" (*mātra*) and because of the evidence (*liṅga*) consisting in the rule for the nominative in the vocative, so too it would not occur when gender exceeds [the meaning of the nominal stem]; therefore, the mention of "gender" is made.

The mention of "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is intended so that the usage of words denoting the delimiters of measures, such as *prastha* and the like, may be grammatically correct through non-difference from that which possesses the measure—just as one says: "A *prastha* is the measure of these grains; the *prastha* of rice," or "a *khārī*, an *āḍhaka*. This occurs when there is a metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) of non-difference [between the measure and the measured], despite the fact that they are distinct entities.

The relationship between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge is not perceived; or else, some other relationship such as immediate succession might be perceived. Therefore, when the referent of the nominal stem exceeds its measure, the nominative case is prescribed for the sake of expressing the specific function (*abhidheya-artha*) through the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of the relationship between the means and the object of knowledge.

But if this first rule were not prescribed, then by means of the division of the *yoga* [of the sūtra] "that is its measure" (Pāṇini 5.1.57), the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) would apply, and in the alternative case, a full sentence construction would occur. Now, however—

By the force of the statement, all three also come into being. This he will say: "When a specific relationship between the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and so forth is accepted, then the invalidity of [terms like] *prastha* and the rest would follow in the absence of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)."
"Whether it be a derivative (taddhita) [form] or a sentence, it may optionally occur according to the distinction of connection;
furthermore, in that case, when there is a measure or something exceeding it, the nominative case is prescribed.
Since the word "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is used here in its sense of being the cause of an action, it includes "height" (*unmāna*) and so forth as well.

Regarding the inclusion [of words like *śukla*]: because the possessive suffix (*matup*) has been elided in the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the first case ending is established by the very fact that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, provided there is no intention to express a distinction [between the quality and the qualified]. Similarly, this applies to words such as *viṃśati* when they denote the possessor of the quality. By the word "number" (*vacana*), "count" (*saṅkhyā*) is meant according to the convention of the ancient teachers.
Therefore, even when a number has already been expressed, the nominative case is prescribed by this [rule]. For example:

*ekaḥ*, *dvau*, *bahavaḥ*. However, the accusative and other cases are established after these [words] according to their respective roles as objects (*karman*) and so forth, because these [case endings] do not convey singularity and the rest as qualified by the object and other factors.

The word *mātra* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*); thus, the nominative case does not occur when [the referent] is qualified by the object (*karman*) and so forth. Alternatively, in that case, the accusative and other cases serve as sublaters (*bādhaka*). Or rather, because the nominative is prescribed for what is qualified by the vocative (*saṃbodhana*), it follows as a logical indicator (*liṅga*) that its absence is established when there is something in addition to the object and so forth; for [the nominative] does not occur where there is such an addition.

The rule for the first case ending (*prathamā*) in the sense of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*), and in address (*saṃbodhana*) is established by this very [sūtra]; thus, the mention of the word *mātrā* is rejected. That which is measured (*mīyate*) by it is a measure (*mātrā*), namely, number (*saṃkhyā*). Its indication is made here by means of a collective compound (*samāhāradvandva*). In that regard:

When the term *saṃkhyā* (number) is already mentioned [in the rule], the purpose of including the word *mātra*—namely, so that [the suffix] may apply to *eka* and so on—is already established by the inclusion of the word *vacana* (gender/number). Thus, it is said:
"Either one [of these two words] could have been omitted" (G.eṇa od gh. 2.3.46).

Thus it is stated in the Bhāṣya. However, some maintain that the inclusion of the word *mātra* is for the sake of completeness (*sākalyārtha*), intended to include measures such as *unmāna* (height), by dispelling the suspicion that the word *parimāṇa* is a conventional term (*rūḍhi*) restricted to specific types of measurement.
This is so provided that the word *mātra* is established as having the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇārtha*).
It has been stated: "An addition [to the rule] is required for coreferentiality with a word, because of its being something additional" (Jainendra-vyākaraṇa on Pāṇini 2.3.46).
And: "Or rather, it is not so, because it is the meaning of a sentence" (Jainendra-vyākaraṇa on Pāṇini 2.3.46).
Thus, a solution has been stated here:

the meaning is that the rule for the nominative case applies to the nominal stem-meaning (*prātipadikārtha*) alone—without regard for the connection with other word-meanings—in instances such as *vīraḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the hero is a man"). Therefore, it is exactly according to the traditional formulation (*yathānyāsam*).
The use of the nominative case is appropriate; it is also prescribed for the vocative. Regarding that, he explains the nature of the vocative:
"They know the vocative to be the mere act of bringing an established entity to face [the speaker]."
For the essence of an object, having attained presence, is employed in actions. || 163 ||

The form of address (*saṃbodhana*) is that which consists merely in the act of directing attention toward an object whose form is already complete, for the purpose of employing it in an action; this is a form additional to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
By the inclusion of the word "merely" (*mātra*), [the author] excludes the status of the address as being a grammatical factor (*sādhana*) such as the object (*karman*) and so forth. That very...
For it is the agent who is enjoined to go and so forth; that very person is the one brought face-to-face, who is the object of the vocative.

And for one who has been brought face-to-face, the vocative—while not being a direct *kāraka*—experiences its status as an indirect helper to the action by means of the time of the injunction and the accomplishment of the action through a causal sequence. || 163 ||

Even in the case of action (*kriyā*), there is no status as the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthatā*) for the vocative, just as there is none for the relationship between qualifier and qualified; rather, it is merely a word-meaning (*padārthatva*), like the instrumental factors such as the object (*karman*).
Thus he says: "The tradition from the elders is that the vocative is not the sentence-meaning."

(160) Scripture (*āgama*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that brings about certainty. Even though the meaning of a word (*padārtha*)—such as a vocative—is understood independently of other words, it constitutes a "vocative" (*saṃbodhana*) precisely because it requires an action (*kriyā*). For instance, it is not possible for objects such as the direct object (*karman*) to function as means (*sādhana*) unless they are connected with an action. Thus, [the vocative] is also a factor required by the action.
Action is not to be relied upon [as the primary meaning], and therefore it does not constitute the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*); the same applies to the vocative as well.
Furthermore, even a single word whose action is implied—such as "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) and so forth—is a sentence;
thus, the vocative is indeed the sentence-meaning. Now, he concludes the present topic.
The meanings of the case-endings are extracted from the sentence-meaning by way of a general indication. (164)

A brief statement is an enumeration (*uddeśa*). For that reason, the meanings of the case-endings— namely, the *kārakas* such as the object (*karman*) and so forth— are derived from the ultimate, indivisible sentence-meaning, which consists of an action qualified by various *kārakas* and attributes.

They are extracted through the analytical cognition of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Just as words are extracted from an indivisible sentence, so too are word-meanings extracted from the sentence-meaning.
Furthermore, the meaning of a case-ending is indeed a word-meaning; for even there, upon analysis, it is extracted from the word-meaning.

"The extraction of the meaning of the case-endings (*vibhaktyarthāpoddhāra*) is to be explained; however, since the sentence-meaning alone possesses the established definition while the word-meaning is non-existent, he says 'from the sentence-meaning' (*vākyārthāt*). Others, however, say: "From the sentence-meaning as characterized by the 'subject' (*uddeśena*), which is a constituent part of the sentence-meaning."
Thus, the clear meaning is this very one: they are distinguished from the word-meanings themselves, which constitute a single part of the sentence-meaning. || 164 ||
Now, [the author] states the scriptural authority for the fact that the meaning of a case-ending is distinct from the meaning of the nominal stem:

"Since it is stated that an *avyayībhāva* compound occurs when there is the sense of a case-ending, let it be understood that the meaning of a case-ending is something other than substance (*dravya*); that [meaning] is expressed by means of an indeclinable. (165)

(161) Regarding the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti-* (Pāṇini 2.1.6), it has been stated that an indeclinable (*avyaya*) expressing the sense of a case ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is compounded with a compatible subsequent member (*samarthenottarapadena*), as in the example *adhistri*. In that context, if the sense of a case ending were to consist solely of a substance (*dravya*), [the following would apply].
In that case, since it has already been expressed by the word "strī" itself, the indeclinable [suffix] is simply not fit for usage.

Since it is not being used, how could there be a compound? Therefore, because of the rule prescribing the *avyayībhāva* compound for the sense of a case-ending, it is understood that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone [expresses] the object and other grammatical relations.
It does not denote the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). For instance, when denoting an indeclinable word that serves as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), it forms a compound with a subsequent word.
As it has been said: "For even in the absence of exclusion (*vyatireka*), exclusion is observed when there is concomitance (*anvaya*)."

By these and other such means, this matter was previously established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); now, it is further reinforced by the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*). But surely, under the view that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of five factors, since the qualified, partless substance is already expressed by the nominal stem, [how can there be a need for a case ending?]

Just as case endings (*vibhakti*) are employed to indicate specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*), so too should an indeclinable (*avyaya*) be fit for usage; since there is no restrictive rule regarding indicators (*dyotaka*), how can this [absence of] gender (*liṅga*) be justified? This is true; however, this gender is presented according to the "triad" (*trika*) position. For it is said: "An indeclinable..."
In the phrase "vibhakti...," the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is indicated. However, according to the view that [the word] consists of five parts (*pañcakapakṣa*),

since the particularity (*viśeṣa*) which constitutes the essence of the substance is manifested by the case-endings, the meaning would be apprehended by the *pada* alone, because that [word] denotes the aggregate, and not by the case-ending alone.

Even in the view that there are five categories (pañcakapakṣa), since a specific [quality] consisting of a fixed power is not perceived from the nominal stem alone, it is the domain of the case-endings themselves. And thus,
the meaning of the case-ending is a substance with a fixed power, distinct from the substance denoted by the nominal stem which possesses an unfixed power.

Thus it is rightly said. And this being the case, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) operate, as appropriate, in both ways—either in the denotation (*abhidhāna*) or the indication (*dyotana*) of that which has not been previously established. || 165 ||

Now, one might object: since the status of a substance as a means (*sādhana*) is understood from such indicative marks (*liṅga*) as "when there are two [actions] having the same agent" (*samānakartṛkayoḥ*) and "when the animal is the agent" (*paśau kartari*), how can the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) be something other than the substance?
Anticipating this objection, the author states the following in order to establish that it is the capacity (*śakti*) which is the means.
But whatever substance exists in a certain way, it must remain exactly so;
even when there is a difference in activity, its essential nature as a substance is not lost. (166)

If a substance were always immovable, possessing a single nature that never departs across all its states, then the distinction between grammatical means (*sādhana*) in expressions such as "tree by tree" would be groundless. Furthermore, the claim that a difference in the substance arises based on a variety of actions— such as "see the tree" or "the tree has borne fruit"— is also false.
Even though there is a diversity of activities, substance certainly does not deviate from its own nature;
for it is impossible for a thing to become something else merely through a difference in its relations. (166)
And if this were the case, then that substance which is the instrument would not be the object;
furthermore, there would be a transformation of its entire substantial nature. (167)

(163) A substance that has been established as an instrument (*karaṇa*) is not manifested as an object (*karman*). This is also an illustration for other *kārakas*. Furthermore, that which is understood as an object should not be cognized as a residual relation (*śeṣa*).
And because the substance, as the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), is unitary, [one says] "he sits in the palace" (*prāsāde āste*) or "he lies on the seat" (*āsane śete*).

Because the locative case would not apply to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) due to its being denoted by a *lyuṭ* suffix, [the following argument is made]: however, if the capacity (*śakti*) is the means (*sādhana*), then because that capacity differs according to the difference in actions, when the capacity as locus is already denoted with respect to the action of "sitting" (*sadikriyā*), yet remains undenoted with respect to the action of "sitting" (*āsikriyā*), the locative case is established by resorting to the principle of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), which states that the locative applies where it has not been denoted elsewhere. And thus says the Vārttika:
"For there is a prescription [of the passive voice] when [the agent] is not expressed" (Pāṇini 1.4.51).

Now, if in connection with another action the instrument undergoes a transformation into the nature of the object, then the entire substance would undergo the state of becoming another entity, and not merely the instrumental aspect of it. For...

Because [the power] is distinct from the substance (*dravya*). However, when the power (*śakti*) functions as the means (*sādhana*), even though it differs according to the difference in the action, the substance which is its substratum persists as a common element; therefore, it is logical that it can assume the form of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth through the process of relinquishing one power and assuming another.

Since an inefficient substance (*dravya*) is not a factor (*aṅga*) in the accomplishment of an action, it is only efficiency (*sāmarthya*)—which has that [substance] as its substrate—that is rightly considered the means (*sādhana*). Nor, on this account, is it logical to postulate that the substance itself possesses the status of a means simply because it is the substrate of the means; for even though Devadatta is a means for the act of cooking, [he is not the means itself].

Since that [power] is also conceived as belonging to the pedestal which serves as its support, it is the powers alone that constitute the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and not the substance possessing power (*śaktimat*).
This is according to the rule: "When two actions have the same agent" (Pāṇini 3.4.21).

Thus, the identity between the two capacities of the agent is based on the superimposition of the unity of the substance that serves as the substratum for those capacities. In the expressions "the agent in the form of the animal" (*paśau kartari*) and "the agents in the form of the elephant and the spy" (*hastisūcakayoḥ kartroḥ*),
[it is understood as] "the agent which is the substance in the form of the animal" and "the two agents which are the substances in the form of the elephant and the spy."

This must be explained. Alternatively, since the animal itself is the agent by virtue of the agent's power, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). [This is supported by the rule] "The second case ending is used for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.2).
In such cases as well, because numbers are connected with powers (*śakti*), it is the substance (*dravya*) which serves as their substratum that is being indicated.
Therefore, the meaning is that case-endings (*vibhakti*) express number as it inheres in the same object as the action.
Since a power cannot exist without a substratum, it is the substance itself, as permeated by power, that constitutes the instrument (*sādhana*).

That which is denoted by the suffix *lakāra* is indeed specific in nature; it performs an action, and while not explicitly expressed by its own form, it is manifested by another word through a restricted nature.
Thus, the use of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as "Devadatta cooks" is logically established, and everything is well-ordered.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Section on the Means of Accomplishment (*sādhanasamuddeśa*), in the *Prakīrṇakaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja.

The Blessed One said this: “Ānanda, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? “Here, Ānanda, one person dwells having conquered the unconquered by others; he does not become one who conquers those already conquered by others. This is the first kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, Ānanda, another person dwells having conquered those already conquered by others; he does not become one who conquers the unconquered by others. This is the second kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, Ānanda, another person dwells having conquered both those already conquered by others and the unconquered by others. This is the third kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, Ānanda, another person dwells neither having conquered those already conquered by others nor the unconquered by others; yet he is one who does not become one who conquers those already conquered by others, nor does he become one who conquers the unconquered by others. This is the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. “These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
